concept.technique_name: constraint substitution on a letter-number code

examples.problem_statement: In some code, letters a, b, c, d and e represent numbers 2, 4, 5, 6 and 10. We don't know which letter represents which number. Consider the following relationships: (i) a + c = e (ii) b - d = d (iii) e + a = b. Which statement below is true? (a) b = 4, d = 2 (b) a = 4, e = 6 (c) b = 6, e = 2 (d) a = 4, c = 6

solution.operation: b - d = d \Rightarrow b = 2d, with b, d \in \{2, 4, 5, 6, 10\}
solution.description: Read relationship (ii) as saying b is twice d, then look for the only pair inside the given number set where one value is double the other: 10 and 5.

solution.operation: a + c = e over the leftover values \{2, 4, 6\}: 2 + 4 = 6
solution.description: With 10 and 5 used up, only 2, 4 and 6 remain for a, c and e, and relationship (i) fixes the sum: 2 + 4 = 6, so e must be 6 while a and c share 2 and 4 in some order.
Use relationship (iii) to break the tie left over from the previous step: 6 plus a must reach b = 10, which forces a = 4 and leaves c = 2.

solution.operation: compare a = 4, e = 6 against the four options
solution.description: Check the assignment just derived against each choice; only the option stating a = 4 and e = 6 matches it.

key_reminders: b - d = d is the same as b = 2d, so scan the value set for a double.
Each letter takes a distinct value from the list, so every value fixed removes it from the remaining choices.
Use the third relationship to settle any pair still ambiguous after the first two.
common_mistakes: Reading b - d = d as b = d and discarding relationship (ii) as useless.
Stopping at \{a, c\} = \{2, 4\} and guessing the order instead of applying e + a = b.

concept.technique_name: strengthen the argument by supplying the missing link

examples.problem_statement: In the 18th and 19th centuries, it was believed in many coastal American cities that the waterfront was an undesirable location for residential buildings. As a result, much of the waterfront in these cities was never developed aesthetically and instead was left to industry and commerce. Today, however, waterfront properties are generally seen as prestigious, as evidenced by the large sums paid for homes along the beach front. A developer who wishes to make a large profit would be wise to buy urban waterfront lots and erect residential buildings on them. Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the claim made about urban waterfront properties? (A) People today have more money, relatively speaking, to spend on real estate than they did in previous centuries. (B) Homeowners will be willing to spend large sums on residential properties in traditionally industrial or commercial districts. (C) Many urban waterfront lots are available for purchase. (D) Many coastal American cities are encouraging developers to rehabilitate the waterfront through tax incentives. (E) Properties in interior residential districts in coastal American cities are significantly more expensive than those along the waterfront.

solution.operation: isolate the conclusion and the evidence offered for it
solution.result: Conclusion: a developer would be wise to buy urban waterfront lots and build residences there. Evidence: people pay large sums for beach front homes.
solution.description: Separate the claim being argued from the support given for it, since a strengthener must reinforce the link between exactly these two, and note that the task is to strengthen.

solution.operation: test (A): buyers have more money today than in past centuries
solution.description: Greater general buying power says nothing about whether the urban waterfront in particular will earn the developer money, so it leaves the argument no stronger.

solution.operation: test (B): homeowners will pay large sums in traditionally industrial or commercial districts
solution.description: The passage already told you urban waterfronts were left to industry and commerce, so a willingness to pay well in exactly those districts supplies the missing buyer for the developer's new homes.

solution.operation: test (C): many urban waterfront lots are available for purchase
solution.description: Being able to buy the lots is not being able to sell what is built on them, so availability alone does not support the profit claim.

solution.operation: test (D): coastal cities offer tax incentives for waterfront rehabilitation
solution.description: Tax breaks cut the developer's cost but still give no reason to think anyone will buy the developed properties.

solution.operation: test (E): interior properties cost significantly more than waterfront ones
solution.description: Cheaper land to acquire does not by itself establish that a profit can be made after building, and it may even hint that waterfront homes fetch less.

key_reminders: A strengthener must connect this argument's own evidence to its own conclusion, not merely be agreeable.
The profit claim needs buyers for the finished homes, so cost-side facts do not close the gap.
Details already stated in the passage (here, that urban waterfronts were industrial) are what make the right choice relevant.
common_mistakes: Picking (D) or (E) because they make the project cheaper, while the conclusion turns on whether the homes will sell.
Treating (C) as support because it makes the plan feasible rather than profitable.

concept.technique_name: counting favourable odd-day outcomes

examples.problem_statement: (i) What is the chance that a leap year selected randomly will have 53 Sundays? (ii) What is the chance, if the year selected is not a leap year?

solution.result: 52 Sundays are guaranteed; a 53rd depends only on the 2 leftover days
solution.description: Split the leap year's days into whole weeks plus a remainder, because the whole weeks already contribute exactly 52 Sundays and only the leftover days can add another.

solution.operation: enumerate the 7 possible consecutive-day pairs for the 2 leftover days
solution.description: The two spare days are consecutive and can start on any weekday, giving seven equally likely pairs to serve as the sample space.

solution.operation: count the pairs containing a Sunday: \{Sun-Mon, Sat-Sun\}
solution.description: Pick out the pairs that include a Sunday from the seven listed and divide that count by the total to get the leap-year chance.

solution.operation: non-leap year = 52 weeks + 1 day; favourable outcome \{Sunday\}
solution.description: Repeat the same split for a 365-day year, where only one spare day remains, so just one of the seven weekday outcomes gives a 53rd Sunday.

key_reminders: 366 = 52 weeks + 2 days and 365 = 52 weeks + 1 day; the whole weeks always supply 52 Sundays.
The leftover days of a leap year are consecutive, so the sample space is 7 day-pairs, not 7 single days.
common_mistakes: Counting Sun-Mon and Sat-Sun as one outcome and answering 1/7 for the leap year.
Treating the two extra days as independent picks and using 7 x 7 outcomes.

concept.technique_name: LCM with a constant deficit remainder

examples.problem_statement: What is the least multiple of 7, which when divided by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, leaves the remainders 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 respectively?

solution.result: the numbers divisible by all five divisors are 60k
solution.description: Take the LCM of the divisors so that a single expression 60k captures every number leaving remainder 0 with all of them.
Notice each required remainder falls short of its divisor by the same 1, so the number sits one below a common multiple rather than one above it.
Rewrite 60k - 1 by pulling out the largest multiple of 7 available, leaving only the small term 4k - 1 to be tested for divisibility by 7.
Try k = 1, 2, ... until 4k - 1 is a multiple of 7; k = 2 is the smallest that works, which also keeps the answer least.
Substitute the k just found back into 60k - 1 to produce the required number.

key_reminders: When each remainder is a fixed amount less than its divisor, the number is LCM x k minus that amount.
LCM(2, 3, 4, 5, 6) = 60, not the product of the divisors.
Splitting 60k - 1 as 7(8k) + (4k - 1) turns the 7-divisibility test into a check on a small term.
common_mistakes: Adding the remainders instead of spotting the constant deficit of 1 and writing 60k + 1.
Taking k = 1 and answering 59 without enforcing the multiple-of-7 condition.

concept.technique_name: sum of all pairwise groups

examples.problem_statement: There are four numbers w, x, y, z. If the sum of all possible distinct groups, each having two numbers from amongst w, x, y, z is 1440, then what is the average of these four numbers?

solution.description: List every distinct group of two numbers that can be formed from w, x, y, z; there are six such groups.

solution.result: each of w, x, y, z appears 3 times in the total
solution.description: Write the given total as the sum of those six groups written out term by term, and notice each letter occurs three times across the list.
Factor the repeated count of 3 out of the expanded sum and divide 1440 by 3 to get the plain sum of the four numbers.
Divide that sum of the four numbers by 4 to get their average.

key_reminders: Each of the four numbers appears in exactly 3 of the 6 distinct pairs, so the pairwise total equals 3 times the plain sum.
Average = (sum of the numbers) / (count of the numbers).
common_mistakes: Dividing 1440 by 4 straight away and reporting 360, forgetting that the pairwise total counts every number three times.
Counting ordered pairs (12 of them) instead of the 6 distinct two-number groups, which halves the multiplier.

concept.technique_name: conditional rule contrapositive

examples.problem_statement:
Six doctors—Haddad, Johnson, Kwong, Lester, Murray, and Nelson—are assigned to the following three training rotations: orthopedics, pediatrics, surgery. Each doctor is assigned to exactly one rotation, and each rotation is assigned exactly two doctors. No other doctors are assigned. The following conditions must be met: Kwong is not assigned to the same rotation as Lester. Murray is not assigned to surgery. If Lester is assigned to orthopedics, then Haddad is assigned to surgery. Johnson is assigned to surgery.

It can be determined to which rotation each of the six doctors is assigned if which one of the following statements is true?
(A) Both Murray and Kwong are assigned to orthopedics.
(B) Both Kwong and Nelson are assigned to pediatrics.
(C) Both Haddad and Johnson are assigned to surgery.
(D) Both Johnson and Lester are assigned to surgery.
(E) Both Haddad and Nelson are assigned to pediatrics.

solution.result: the conditional rule is the rule most likely to break the question open
solution.description: Instead of testing answers by trial and error, single out the major conditional rule and hunt for the answer choices that engage it directly.

Check (C): it places H in surgery, which is the back end of the conditional and cannot be read backwards, and its other placement, J in surgery, is already known — so it wastes one of the two placements the answer gives you.

solution.operation: \text{test (E): } H \to P,\; N \to P \;\Rightarrow\; H \nrightarrow S \;\Rightarrow\; L \nrightarrow O
solution.description: Move to (E): putting H in pediatrics triggers the contrapositive of the conditional, because H not being in surgery forces L out of orthopedics.

solution.operation: P = \{H, N\},\; M \nrightarrow S \;\Rightarrow\; M \to O
solution.description: With pediatrics already filled by H and N, and M forbidden from surgery, the only rotation left for M is orthopedics.

solution.operation: L \nrightarrow O,\; L \nrightarrow P \;\Rightarrow\; L \to S
solution.result: L joins surgery and the diagram is complete
solution.description: Since L cannot be in orthopedics and pediatrics is full, L must go to surgery — at which point every doctor's rotation is fixed, which is exactly what the question asks for.

key_reminders: A conditional rule runs one way only — satisfying its result does not let you conclude its trigger.
The contrapositive of 'if L is in orthopedics then H is in surgery' is 'if H is not in surgery then L is not in orthopedics'.
Each of the three rotations takes exactly two doctors, so filling one rotation removes it as an option for everyone else.
common_mistakes: Reading the conditional backwards in (C) and concluding that H in surgery forces L into orthopedics.
Picking an answer that spends one of its two placements on J in surgery, a placement the rules already fixed.

concept.technique_name: order of operations (PEMDAS)

examples.problem_statement: Which of the parentheses in the following expressions could be removed without changing the value of the expression and are therefore unnecessary? (a) -(5^2) - (12 - 7)   (b) (x + y) - (w + z) - (a \times b)

solution.operation: -(5^2): exponent before negation and before subtraction
solution.description: Check the parentheses around the squared term: exponentiation already outranks both the negation and the subtraction, so grouping it changes nothing and the parentheses can be dropped.
Evaluate the second expression as it is printed: the parentheses force 7 to be subtracted from 12 first, giving 5, which is then subtracted from 25 to yield 20.
Now delete those parentheses and work strictly left to right; the value drops to 6, so the value did change and the parentheses around 12 - 7 are necessary.

solution.operation: (x + y) - \ldots : addition and subtraction run left to right
solution.result: the parentheses around x + y are unnecessary
solution.description: Look at the leading group in (b): addition and subtraction are performed left to right by default, so x + y is already computed before the neighboring subtraction and the parentheses add nothing.

solution.result: the parentheses around a \times b are unnecessary
solution.description: Look at the trailing group: multiplication is the first operation performed anyway, so surrounding a \times b with parentheses does not change the order and they can be removed.

solution.result: the parentheses around w + z are necessary
solution.description: Test the middle group: with the parentheses you subtract both w and z, but without them you would subtract w and add z, so this pair must stay.

key_reminders: Exponents are evaluated before negation and before addition or subtraction.
Multiplication outranks addition and subtraction, so parentheses around a product next to a sum are redundant.
A minus sign in front of a parenthesized sum distributes to every term inside it.
common_mistakes: Dropping the parentheses in 25 - (12 - 7) and computing left to right to get 6 instead of 20.
Removing the parentheses in -(w + z) and then adding z instead of subtracting it.

concept.technique_name: symmetric cancellation of a consecutive-integer sum about zero

examples.problem_statement: What is the sum of all the integers from -457 to 459, inclusive?

solution.operation: recognize that adding 917 terms one by one is not feasible; test a smaller analogue, the sum from -2 to 4
solution.description: Since summing this many numbers directly is impossible under test conditions, look for the trick by shrinking the range to a case small enough to add by hand.
In the small case, pair each negative with its positive twin: each pair sums to zero, and the 0 in the middle contributes nothing, so the symmetric block vanishes.
Add only the leftover terms past the symmetric block; their total is the whole sum, confirming that the sum equals the unpaired tail.
Carry the pattern to the real range: every integer from -457 up to 457 pairs off with its opposite and cancels, leaving only the terms above 457.
Add the two surviving integers at the top of the range to get the sum of the entire list.

key_reminders: Any integer and its opposite sum to zero, so a range symmetric about 0 contributes nothing.
After cancelling the symmetric block, only the unpaired tail of the range remains to be added.
Testing the idea on a tiny analogous range confirms the pattern before applying it to large numbers.
common_mistakes: Cancelling only up to 456 or up to 458 and adding the wrong leftover terms (457 + 458 + 459 or just 459).
Treating the range as symmetric and answering 0 because the endpoints -457 and 459 look nearly balanced.

concept.technique_name: resolve-the-conflict argument evaluation with answer-choice elimination

examples.problem_statement:
The passage outlines a conflict between two standard theories - one of planet formation, the other of companion stars - and observations of one large body, and later two others, orbiting close to the star Upsilon Andromedae. Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the status of the orbiting body without casting doubt on the two standard theories mentioned?
(A) The smaller a planet orbiting a star is, and the farther away it is from the star, the less likely it is to be discovered.
(B) If a planet's orbit is disturbed, the planet can be drawn by gravity toward the star it is orbiting.
(C) The largest of the bodies orbiting Upsilon Andromedae is the farthest away from the star, and the smallest is the nearest.
(D) It is likely that there are many stars, in addition to Upsilon Andromedae and the Sun, that are orbited by more than one smaller body.
(E) In most cases of companion stars, the smaller companion is much fainter than the larger star.

solution.operation: state the conflict: two standard theories (planet formation, companion stars) versus the observation of large bodies orbiting close to the star
solution.result: a conflict between theory and observation
solution.description: Pin down what is actually at odds before reading the choices: the observed large bodies sit close to Upsilon Andromedae, which neither standard theory allows.

solution.operation: restate the task: find the choice that explains the observation while leaving both theories intact
solution.result: a two-part test each choice must pass
solution.description: Fix the criterion for a correct answer, because a choice that explains the observation by contradicting one of the theories fails the question's second requirement.

solution.operation: test (B): a planet may form far from a star and later be drawn closer
solution.result: (B) passes both parts of the test
solution.description: Apply the criterion to (B): if orbits can be disturbed inward, the close-in large bodies can be planets formed far out, so the observation is explained and the planet-formation theory survives; the companion-star theory is untouched as well.

solution.operation: test (A): difficulty of discovering a small, distant planet
solution.description: Reject (A) because it speaks to why small far-off planets go undetected, not to the status of a large body found near a star.

solution.operation: test (C): relative sizes and distances of the three bodies
solution.description: Reject (C) because whatever their relative size and position, all three bodies are still too close to the star for the standard theories, so the conflict remains.

solution.operation: test (D): many stars have more than one orbiting body
solution.description: Reject (D) because how common multi-body systems are says nothing about the status of the large bodies in question.

solution.operation: test (E): companion stars are usually much fainter
solution.description: Reject (E) as irrelevant: relative brightness of companion stars does not clarify what the large close-in bodies are.

examples.answer: Choice B: If a planet’s orbit is disturbed, the planet can be drawn by gravity toward the star it is orbiting.

key_reminders: The correct choice must both explain the observation and leave both stated theories standing.
A choice about detection difficulty or general prevalence does not bear on the status of a specific observed body.
Explaining an anomaly by a later change in circumstances (an orbit shifting inward) reconciles data with a formation theory instead of contradicting it.
common_mistakes: Picking (C) by treating the ordering of the three bodies as a resolution, when all three remain too close under both theories.
Picking (A) or (E) because they mention planets and companion stars, matching the passage's vocabulary rather than its conflict.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal blank filling

examples.problem_statement:
(i) _________ the law had little impact, but it was (ii) _________ by subsequent legislation providing funding and enforcement.
Blank (i): Justifiably / Unbelievably / Initially
Blank (ii): rendered moot / given teeth / kept at bay

solution.operation: Locate the time-contrast clue for blank (i): the later clause says "subsequent" legislation.
solution.description: Read the second half of the sentence for the word that constrains blank (i); "subsequent" is the clue that sets up a contrast in time.

solution.operation: Choose the blank (i) word meaning "at first".
solution.description: Since the blank must contrast with "subsequent", pick the option that means "at first" rather than the evaluative words.

solution.operation: Set the requirement for blank (ii): it must contrast with "little impact" and match a law now gaining funding and enforcement.
solution.result: Blank (ii) needs a phrase meaning the law became forceful.
solution.description: Read the constraints on the second blank: it opposes the earlier weakness and agrees with the new funding and enforcement.

solution.operation: Test the blank (ii) options against that requirement.
solution.description: Only "given teeth" carries the (metaphorical) meaning of being made forceful, so it is the sole option satisfying the requirement built in the previous step.

key_reminders: A blank that contrasts with "subsequent" must express "at first".
The second blank must reverse "little impact" to match funding and enforcement.
Metaphorical idioms count as literal meaning matches in Text Completions.
common_mistakes: Choosing an evaluative adverb such as "Justifiably" or "Unbelievably" for blank (i) when the clue "subsequent" demands a time word.
Reading "rendered moot" or "kept at bay" as strengthening when both mean the law stayed powerless.

concept.technique_name: evidence-dependency blank filling

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for the blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill the blank in the way that best completes the text.
When she first came to France from Bulgaria, she was hardly the ______ student she later made herself out to be, since she had access to considerable family wealth.
A naive  B precocious  C impecunious  D ambitious  E assiduous

solution.operation: Identify the evidence clause: "she had access to considerable family wealth".
solution.result: Family wealth is the proof offered against her later self-portrayal.
solution.description: Find the fact the sentence gives as proof; everything else in the sentence must be judged against it.

solution.operation: State what the blank describes: the later, false depiction of herself.
solution.result: The blank word must be incompatible with wealth.
solution.description: Because the wealth is cited to show the depiction was false, the word filling the blank has to be something wealth rules out.

solution.operation: Match the choices against "incompatible with wealth".
solution.description: Scan the options for the one whose meaning wealth directly contradicts; "impecunious" means penniless, so wealth disproves it.

solution.operation: Eliminate naive, precocious (advanced for her age), ambitious, and assiduous (diligent).
solution.result: None depends on wealth, so all four fail the test.
solution.description: Check each remaining option: family finances have no bearing on whether she was naive, precocious, ambitious, or diligent, so none can be disproved by the evidence clause.

key_reminders: The blank must name a trait the cited evidence (family wealth) can actually disprove.
"Hardly ... she later made herself out to be" marks the depiction as false.
A correct choice must be logically dependent on the evidence, not merely negative in tone.
common_mistakes: Picking "naive" or "precocious" because they suit a young foreign student, though wealth says nothing about either.
Treating "assiduous" or "ambitious" as opposites of wealth when diligence and drive are independent of money.

concept.technique_name: percent change applied to area
concept.sub_category: Quantitative Comparison with percent increase and decrease

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. A, B, and C are three rectangles. The length and width of rectangle A are 10 percent greater and 10 percent less, respectively, than the length and width of rectangle C. The length and width of rectangle B are 20 percent greater and 20 percent less, respectively, than the length and width of rectangle C. Quantity A: the area of rectangle A. Quantity B: the area of rectangle B. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: Let \ell = \text{length of } C,\ w = \text{width of } C
solution.result: Both rectangles A and B are now expressible through C's dimensions.
solution.description: Name the length and width of rectangle C with variables, since the given information relates A and B to C.
Translate "10 percent greater" into a multiplier of 1.1 on the length and "10 percent less" into a multiplier of 0.9 on the width.
Translate the 20 percent increase and 20 percent decrease for rectangle B into multipliers of 1.2 and 0.8.
Multiply rectangle A's length expression by its width expression to get its area in terms of \ell and w.
Multiply rectangle B's length expression by its width expression to get its area in the same terms.

solution.result: Quantity A is greater than Quantity B.
solution.description: Compare the two area expressions, which share the factor \ell w, so the larger decimal coefficient decides the comparison.

examples.answer: Choice A: Quantity A is greater.

key_reminders: A p percent increase multiplies by 1 + p/100; a p percent decrease multiplies by 1 - p/100.
Raising and lowering the two dimensions by the same percent does not leave the area unchanged.
Expressing both quantities through the same variables lets the shared factor \ell w cancel out of the comparison.
common_mistakes: Assuming +10% and -10% cancel (and likewise +20% and -20%), which would wrongly give Choice C.
Choosing D because \ell and w are unknown, missing that the common factor \ell w cancels.
Reasoning that B's larger 20 percent swings make its area larger, when 0.96 < 0.99.

concept.technique_name: synonym-pair elimination in sentence equivalence

examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.
Though feminist in its implications, Yvonne Rainer's 1974 film ______ the filmmaker's active involvement in feminist politics.
A antedated  B cloaked  C portrayed  D preceded  E renewed  F represented

solution.operation: Read the constraint set by "Though feminist in its implications".
solution.result: The film has feminist implications, but they are limited compared with her other activities.
solution.description: Use the concessive opener to fix what the blank must express: feminist content that is nonetheless limited relative to her later activism.

solution.operation: Group the six choices into pairs alike in meaning.
solution.description: Since the completed sentences must be alike in meaning, sort the options for pairs that are near synonyms.

solution.operation: Test the pair portrayed / represented against the sentence's logic.
solution.result: Rejected: it makes the film depict her activism, contradicting the limitation.
solution.description: Check whether this synonym pair fits the context; saying the film portrayed her political involvement does not fit the concession that its feminism is limited.

solution.operation: Test the pair antedated / preceded against the sentence's logic.
solution.result: Accepted: the 1974 film came before she became active in feminist politics.
solution.description: Check the remaining pair; it makes sense of the concession, because the film exhibits feminist themes in a limited way precisely by coming before her activism.

examples.answer: Choice A: antedated AND Choice D: preceded

key_reminders: The two chosen words must produce sentences alike in meaning, so look for a synonym pair.
A synonym pair only qualifies if it also fits the sentence's logic; meaning-alike alone is not enough.
"Though" signals that the film's feminism is limited relative to her later political involvement.
common_mistakes: Selecting portrayed and represented because they pair neatly, without testing the pair against the concessive "Though".
Pairing "cloaked" with "renewed", though the two are not alike in meaning and no synonym partner exists for either.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence pair matching

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Although cosmic objects have struck Earth since the planet's very formation, humanity has only recently become aware of these events: two centuries ago the idea that objects orbiting the Sun could collide with Earth was widely ______ . Choices: A ridiculed, B doubted, C disseminated, D promulgated, E marginalized, F disbelieved.

solution.operation: Read the colon as introducing an example of the clause before it
solution.result: The blank must illustrate humanity's former lack of awareness of cosmic collisions
solution.description: Use the colon's function: it signals that what follows explains or demonstrates the preceding statement, so the completed clause has to demonstrate that people were formerly unaware of these events.

solution.operation: Test 'disseminated' and 'promulgated' against that lack of awareness
solution.description: Because people were not aware that such events existed, the idea of their possibility could not have been spread or proclaimed, so neither of these two words fits the meaning of the sentence.

solution.operation: Test 'ridiculed' and 'marginalized' for sense, then for pairing
solution.result: Both make sense in the blank but do not produce sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Check the remaining candidates against the second requirement of the task: each of these works when inserted, but they do not yield two completed sentences with the same meaning, so neither can be part of the answer pair.

solution.result: Two completed sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Select the remaining two words, which both fit the sentence's demonstration of former unawareness and are close enough in meaning to produce equivalent completed sentences.

examples.answer: Choice B: doubted; AND Choice F: disbelieved

key_reminders: A colon introduces material that explains or demonstrates the clause preceding it.
Sentence Equivalence requires two words that both fit the sentence AND produce completed sentences alike in meaning.
A word that merely makes sense in the blank is not enough if it has no equivalent partner among the choices.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'ridiculed' and 'marginalized' because each reads plausibly, ignoring that they do not form an equivalent-meaning pair.
Picking 'disseminated' or 'promulgated' by associating them loosely with 'idea' rather than checking them against the sentence's point about lack of awareness.

concept.technique_name: describe the argument (four-step Critical Reasoning process)

examples.problem_statement: Answer the question using the 4-step Critical Reasoning process. Sania: The newest workers in the workforce are the most effective digital marketing employees because they are more likely to use social networking websites and tools themselves. Carlos: But effective digital marketing also requires very technical expertise, such as search engine optimization, that is best learned on the job via prolonged exposure and instruction. Carlos responds to Sania by (A) demonstrating that Sania's conclusion is based upon evidence that is not relevant to the given situation (B) questioning the accuracy of the evidence presented by Sania in support of her conclusion (C) reinforcing Sania's argument by contributing an additional piece of evidence in support of her conclusion (D) pointing out differences in the qualifications desired by different employers seeking digital marketing employees (E) providing an additional piece of evidence that undermines a portion of Sania's claim

solution.operation: Identify the question from the stem 'Carlos responds to Sania by'
solution.description: Classify the question first: the two-person structure and the focus on how Carlos responds mark this as a Describe the Argument question rather than a Describe the Role question.

solution.operation: Map Sania's argument: new employees use social networking → most effective digital marketers
solution.result: Sania's conclusion is that the newest workers are the most effective, supported by their greater use of social networking tools
solution.description: Deconstruct the first speaker: note that Sania claims the workers who use these online tools are the most effective at digital marketing, and that those people are the newest workers.

solution.operation: Map Carlos's response: effective digital marketing also needs technical expertise best learned on the job over prolonged exposure
solution.result: A new consideration that works against 'newest workers are most effective'
solution.description: Deconstruct the second speaker: Carlos does not dispute Sania's evidence; he raises a further skill requirement that takes a long time on the job to acquire, which cuts against her claim about the newest workers.

solution.operation: State the goal: articulate how Carlos responds
solution.result: The right answer must say Carlos adds new evidence that weakens Sania's claim, not that he attacks her evidence
solution.description: Set the standard the correct choice has to meet before reading the options, so that the elimination work has a fixed target.

solution.operation: Eliminate (A) and (B), both of which attack Sania's evidence
solution.description: Rule out the two choices that describe Carlos as challenging the relevance or the accuracy of Sania's evidence; he says nothing negative about her evidence, he introduces new evidence instead.

solution.operation: Eliminate (C), which says the new evidence supports Sania
solution.description: Rule out the choice that gets the direction backwards: Carlos does contribute an additional piece of evidence, but that evidence hurts rather than reinforces Sania's conclusion.

solution.operation: Eliminate (D), which requires a contrast among employers
solution.description: Rule out the choice that adds content not in the exchange: Carlos raises a different way to assess effectiveness, but he never mentions employers or differences among them.

solution.operation: Confirm (E): additional evidence undermining part of Sania's claim
solution.description: Select the remaining choice, which describes exactly what Carlos does, adding new information that damages the 'newest workers' portion of Sania's claim.

key_reminders: Describe the Argument answers characterize the structure of a speaker's move, not the truth of the content.
Attacking an assumption by adding new evidence is different from disputing the opponent's evidence itself.
Work from wrong to right: eliminate four choices against a goal stated before reading them.
common_mistakes: Reading Carlos as questioning Sania's evidence (A or B) when he never disputes that new workers use social networking tools.
Seeing 'additional piece of evidence' in (C) and selecting it without checking that Carlos's addition works against Sania.
Stretching Carlos's technical-expertise point in (D) into a claim about different employers' qualifications, which the exchange never mentions.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via a governing sentence cue

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. In her startlingly original writing, she went further than any other twentieth-century author in English (perhaps in any language) in (i) ______ literary language and form, (ii) ______ stylistic conventions, and (iii) ______ a rich and diverse structure of meaning. Blank (i): A reinventing, B canonizing, C stabilizing. Blank (ii): D undoing, E overpraising, F misunderstanding. Blank (iii): G replicating, H borrowing, I introducing.

solution.operation: Extract the governing cue 'startlingly original' and note the three parallel ways it is achieved
solution.result: Every blank must carry a sense of innovation rather than convention
solution.description: Fix the constraint that controls all three columns: the writing is described as startlingly original and the sentence lists three ways the author achieved that originality, so each blank needs an innovation word.

solution.operation: Apply the innovation constraint to Blank (i) against 'canonizing' and 'stabilizing'
solution.description: Choose the Blank (i) word that indicates a break with traditional forms or language; neither of the other two options in that column signals such a break.

solution.operation: Apply the innovation constraint to Blank (ii), which describes the writer's relationship with convention
solution.description: Choose the Blank (ii) word that expresses originality in how the writer treats stylistic conventions; it is the only option in that column that reflects originality.

solution.operation: Rule out 'replicating' and 'borrowing' in Blank (iii) as derivative
solution.description: Test the Blank (iii) options against the novelty requirement: both of these suggest a derivative approach to writing, which contradicts the sentence's claim of originality.
Take the remaining Blank (iii) option, which implies that the writer's rich and diverse structure of meaning is new, matching the novelty the sentence requires.

examples.answer: Choice A: reinventing; Choice D: undoing; Choice I: introducing

key_reminders: A single descriptive cue such as 'startlingly original' can govern every blank in a multi-blank text completion.
In parallel lists, each blank must carry the same evaluative direction as the governing cue.
Eliminate options that imply derivative or conventional work when the text asserts innovation.
common_mistakes: Reading 'canonizing' as a compliment about literary greatness and letting it into Blank (i), though it points to tradition rather than a break with it.
Choosing 'borrowing' or 'replicating' for Blank (iii) because 'a rich and diverse structure of meaning' sounds like assembled material, missing that both imply derivative writing.

concept.technique_name: Paravartya/Nikhilam iterative division with cross-product adjustment

examples.problem_statement: Using the Division Algorithm (Nikhilam/Paravartya) method, division by 20 is performed iteratively with adjustments for cross products. Given: divisor = 20; step 2 gross dividend = 222, net dividend = 202; step 3 gross dividend = 221, net dividend = 180; step 4 gross dividend = 204, net dividend = 153. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Lay out the division with divisor 20 and the dividend digits in the Paravartya arrangement
solution.result: Working layout ready, with columns for gross dividend, cross product, and net dividend
solution.description: Set up the initial division: write the divisor 20 and the dividend in the method's layout so each column can carry a gross dividend, a cross-product correction, and a net dividend.
Run the first division column: divide 182 by 20 to get quotient digit 8 with remainder 22, form the gross dividend 222, then subtract the cross product of 13 and 48 to obtain the net dividend 202.
Carry the net dividend forward and repeat: divide 202 by 20 for quotient digit 9 and remainder 22, form the gross dividend 221, and subtract the cross product 41 to get the net dividend 180.
Repeat the cycle on 180: divide by 20 for quotient digit 8 and remainder 20, form the gross dividend 204, and subtract the cross product 51 to get the net dividend 153.
Finish the last column: divide 153 by 20 to get quotient digit 7 and remainder 13, then read the quotient digits collected across the columns in order together with that final remainder.

key_reminders: Each column's remainder is prefixed to the next dividend digit to form the next gross dividend.
The net dividend is the gross dividend minus the cross product of the accumulated figures, and only the net dividend is carried into the next division.
The final answer reads the quotient digits in column order, with the last column's remainder as the remainder.
common_mistakes: Dividing the gross dividend instead of the net dividend, e.g. taking 221 \div 20 at step 3 rather than the corrected 180.
Forgetting the cross-product subtraction entirely and carrying 222, 221, 204 forward unchanged.
Recording the intermediate remainders 22, 22, 20 as the answer's remainder instead of the last one, 13.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion solved from the most constrained blank outward

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Managers who think that strong environmental performance will (i) ______ their company's financial performance often (ii) ______ claims that systems designed to help them manage environmental concerns are valuable tools. By contrast, managers who perceive environmental performance to be (iii) ______ to financial success may view an environmental management system as extraneous. In either situation, and whatever their perceptions, it is a manager's commitment to achieving environmental improvement rather than the mere presence of a system that determines environmental performance. Blank (i): A eclipse, B bolster, C degrade. Blank (ii): D uncritically accept, E appropriately acknowledge, F hotly dispute. Blank (iii): G complementary, H intrinsic, I peripheral.

solution.operation: Start at Blank (iii), anchored by 'extraneous' in the same sentence
solution.description: Attack the most constrained blank first: the second group of managers view the systems as extraneous, so they must regard environmental performance as peripheral to financial performance.
Confirm the Blank (iii) choice by testing the alternatives; neither is consistent with the idea that environmental management systems are extraneous.

solution.operation: Use the 'By contrast' relation to fill Blank (i)
solution.description: With Blank (iii) settled, read the two sets of managers as holding contrasting views, which makes the positive relation the right one for Blank (i).
Narrow Blank (ii) by direction: managers who think environmental performance helps financial performance clearly would not dispute the claim that such systems are valuable tools.

solution.operation: Weigh 'uncritically accept' against 'appropriately acknowledge' using the final sentence
solution.result: The author does not regard the systems as particularly valuable
solution.description: Resolve the harder Blank (ii) split by reading the last sentence, where the author warns that the mere presence of a system is not enough and is not even necessary.
Since the author does not treat these systems as particularly valuable, calling the managers' acceptance appropriate is ruled out and the remaining option is the correct one.

examples.answer: Choice B: bolster; Choice D: uncritically accept; Choice I: peripheral

key_reminders: Fill the blank with the strongest local anchor first, then use it to constrain the remaining blanks.
'By contrast' sets the two described groups in opposition, fixing the direction of the earlier blank.
The author's own stance, often stated in the closing sentence, can decide between two otherwise plausible options.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'appropriately acknowledge' for Blank (ii) because it reads neutrally, without checking it against the final sentence's dismissal of the systems' value.
Filling Blank (i) with 'eclipse' or 'degrade' and thereby losing the contrast that 'By contrast' requires between the two groups of managers.
Reading Blank (iii) as 'complementary' from the general topic instead of from 'extraneous' in the same sentence.

concept.technique_name: divisibility test by division

examples.problem_statement: Which of the following are factors of 18? Indicate all such factors. (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 6 (D) 12 (E) 18 (F) 36

solution.operation: \text{choice } n \text{ is a factor of } 18 \iff 18 \div n \in \mathbb{Z}
solution.result: test rule: divide 18 by the choice and check for an integer
solution.description: Set up the test the book uses: take 18 and divide it by each answer choice; an integer result means that choice is a factor.

solution.result: 9, an integer, so 2 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (A) by dividing 18 by 2; the quotient is a whole number, so 2 qualifies.

solution.result: 6, an integer, so 3 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (B) by dividing 18 by 3; the quotient is a whole number, so 3 qualifies.

solution.result: 3, an integer, so 6 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (C) by dividing 18 by 6; the quotient is a whole number, so 6 qualifies.

solution.result: 1.5, not an integer, so 12 is not a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (D) by dividing 18 by 12; the quotient is not a whole number, so 12 is rejected.

solution.result: 1, an integer, so 18 is a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (E) by dividing 18 by itself; the quotient 1 is a whole number, so 18 qualifies.

solution.result: 0.5, not an integer, so 36 is not a factor
solution.description: Apply the test to choice (F) by dividing 18 by 36; the quotient is less than 1 and not a whole number, so 36 is rejected.

solution.result: the choices that passed the division test
solution.description: Collect every choice whose division produced an integer; on an all-that-apply question each surviving choice must be selected.

key_reminders: n is a factor of 18 only when 18 \div n leaves no remainder.
A number is always a factor of itself, so 18 must be tested and kept.
Indicate-all questions require every passing choice to be selected, not just one.
common_mistakes: Treating 12 as a factor because 12 shares the digits and factors of 18's neighbours, when 18 \div 12 = 1.5 is not an integer.
Testing divisibility in the wrong direction, checking 36 \div 18 instead of 18 \div 36, and wrongly accepting 36 (a multiple, not a factor).

concept.technique_name: ratio with unknown multiplier

examples.problem_statement: The ratio of cheese to sauce for a single pizza is 1 cup to 1/2 cup. If Bob used 15 cups of sauce to make a number of pizzas, how many cups of cheese did he use on those pizzas?

solution.description: Work with the part-to-part ratio and attach an unknown multiplier x, so the actual amounts are 1x of cheese and one-half x of sauce.
Set the sauce expression equal to the actual sauce Bob used, 15 cups, which pins down the multiplier.
Solve for x by undoing the one-half, multiplying 15 by 2.
Read the cheese amount off the ratio: since cheese is 1x, the multiplier x is itself the number of cups of cheese.

key_reminders: A part-to-part ratio becomes actual amounts only after an unknown multiplier x is attached to each part.
The multiplier is found from the one quantity whose actual value is given.
When a part carries coefficient 1, that part's actual value equals the multiplier itself.
common_mistakes: Reversing the ratio and taking half of 15 to get 7.5 cups, which the book flags explicitly as the trap here.
Solving \tfrac{1}{2}x = 15 by dividing by 2 instead of multiplying by 2.

concept.technique_name: set overlap via Venn diagram

examples.problem_statement: In a graduating class of 236 students, 142 took algebra and 121 took chemistry. What is the greatest possible number of students that could have taken both algebra and chemistry?

solution.result: a Venn diagram of the given counts
solution.description: Translate the words into a figure, drawing one circle for algebra and one for chemistry, since the 142 and 121 given do not yet separate the overlap.

solution.result: redrawn diagram with the overlap split out
solution.description: Redraw the Venn diagram with the students who took both labelled x, so each circle's exclusive region is its total minus x.
Require both exclusive regions to be non-negative, since a region of the diagram cannot hold a negative number of students.
Combine the two bounds; the tighter one, coming from the smaller circle, is what actually limits x.

solution.result: x = 121 is attainable, so it is the greatest value
solution.description: Confirm nothing in the problem excludes x from reaching its bound, so the largest possible overlap is that bound itself.

key_reminders: Totals given for each group already include the overlap, so split the overlap out before reasoning.
Every region of a Venn diagram must hold a count of zero or more.
The overlap of two groups can never exceed the size of the smaller group.
common_mistakes: Using the class size 236 as a constraint on x, when the binding limit comes from the smaller subject total 121.
Applying 142 + 121 - 236 = 27 (the least possible overlap) as the answer to a greatest-possible question.

concept.technique_name: Nikhilam Sutra multiplication (base method)

examples.problem_statement: Using the Nikhilam Sutra multiplication technique, compute 122 \times 98 with base 100. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.description: Pick the working base: both 122 and 98 lie close to 100, so 100 is the base the Nikhilam method will deviate from.
Subtract the base from each number to get its deviation; 122 is 22 above the base and 98 is 2 below it.
Write the multiplication with each number tagged by its deviation, which is the layout the cross and vertical operations act on.
Do the cross operation: add one number to the other number's deviation. Either diagonal gives the same left-hand part, 120.
Multiply the two deviations vertically to get the right-hand part, which comes out negative here because the deviations have opposite signs.
Apply the Nikhilam rule for a negative right part: subtract it from the base to make it positive, and reduce the left part by 1 to compensate.
Combine the corrected left part and right part side by side to read off the product.

key_reminders: Deviation = number - base; above the base is positive, below is negative.
The left part comes from the cross operation and the right part from multiplying the deviations.
A negative right part is subtracted from the base and the left part drops by 1.
common_mistakes: Leaving the right part as -44 and writing 120-44 instead of applying the base-complement correction 119 | 56.
Forgetting to decrement the left part from 120 to 119 after borrowing from the base.

concept.technique_name: repeated replacement / successive fraction removal

examples.problem_statement:
A vessel is full of milk. 1/4 of the milk is taken out and the vessel is filled with water. If the process is repeated 4 times and 100 liters of milk is finally left in the vessel, what is the capacity of the vessel?
(a) 25600/243 liters
(b) 2461/81 liters
(c) 25600/81 liters
(d) 30 liters

solution.result: unknown Q, equal to the vessel's capacity
solution.description: Name the quantity of milk present at the start as Q; since the vessel begins full of milk, Q is also the capacity being asked for.
Each operation removes one quarter of the milk, so multiply by 3/4 to get the milk remaining after a single round.
Chain the factor 3/4 once for each of the four repetitions and set the result equal to the 100 litres of milk finally left.
Solve the equation for Q to obtain the vessel's capacity, matching option (c).

key_reminders: Removing 1/4 of the mixture leaves 3/4 of the milk that was present.
Repeating the operation t times multiplies the milk by (3/4) raised to the power t.
The vessel starts full of milk, so the initial milk quantity equals the capacity.
common_mistakes: Using the factor 1/4 (the part taken out) instead of 3/4 (the part left) in the chain.
Applying the factor three times instead of four and landing on the 25600/243 style answer.

concept.technique_name: substitution into a defined-symbol function

examples.problem_statement:
If \sim x = |14x|, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such answers.
I. \sim 2 = \sim(-2)
II. \sim 3 + \sim 4 = \sim 7
III. The minimum possible value of \sim x is zero

solution.description: Read the made-up symbol as a rule: wherever \sim appears in front of a value, replace it with the absolute value of 14 times that value. Each statement then has to be tested against this rule.
Substitute 2 and -2 into the definition; both sides collapse to 28 through the absolute value, so the first statement must be true.
Substitute 3, 4 and 7 into the definition and evaluate each side; the left side sums to 98 and matches the right, so the second statement must be true.
Note that \sim x is an absolute value, so whatever x is, the output can never drop below zero.

solution.result: minimum of \sim x is 0, statement III is TRUE
solution.description: Show the floor of zero is actually reached by taking x = 0, which makes the value 0 and confirms the third statement.

key_reminders: A made-up symbol is just a substitution rule: replace \sim x by |14x| everywhere.
An absolute value is never negative, so its minimum is 0 whenever 0 is attainable.
For a 'must be true' question, each statement is tested separately.
common_mistakes: Assuming \sim 3 + \sim 4 = \sim 7 fails because absolute values usually do not add, without actually evaluating 42 + 56 = 98.
Treating \sim(-2) as negative and rejecting statement I.

concept.technique_name: CI to SI conversion via per-rupee interest ratio

examples.problem_statement: Given the CI, to find the SI: if the CI on a certain sum for 2 yrs at 3% be Rs 101.50, what would be the SI?

solution.description: Work out the compound interest earned by a single rupee over 2 years at 3%: grow it by the factor (103/100) twice and subtract the original rupee.
Work out the simple interest on the same single rupee: rate times time over 100, giving 6/100.
Divide the per-rupee simple interest by the per-rupee compound interest; the principal cancels, leaving a ratio that holds for the actual sum too.
Apply that ratio to the given compound interest of Rs 101.50 to get the corresponding simple interest.

solution.result: direct formula for converting CI to SI
solution.description: Record the book's direct formula, which packages the same ratio so the conversion can be done in one shot next time.

key_reminders: Per-rupee interest lets you form the SI : CI ratio without ever knowing the principal.
CI on 1 rupee = (1 + r/100)^t - 1; SI on 1 rupee = rt/100.
Direct formula: SI = rt / (100[(1 + r/100)^t - 1]) times CI.
common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio and computing (203/200) x 101.5, which makes the SI larger than the CI.
Squaring 103/100 carelessly and losing the 609/10000 numerator.

concept.technique_name: solving the compound interest growth equation for the rate

examples.problem_statement: To find the rate: at what rate per cent compound interest does a sum of money become nine-fold in 2 years?

solution.result: growth equation in x and r
solution.description: Let the sum be Rs x and the rate r%. After 2 years of compounding the amount is x(1 + r/100)^2, and the problem says that equals nine times the sum.
Divide both sides by x so the unknown principal cancels, leaving an equation purely in the rate.
Take the square root of both sides; 9 becomes 3, which isolates r/100 as 2.
Multiply through by 100 to convert r/100 back into the rate per cent.
Check with the book's direct formula for a sum becoming m times in t years, substituting m = 9 and t = 2 to reach the same rate in one line.

key_reminders: Amount after t years of CI is P(1 + r/100)^t, so the principal always cancels in a 'becomes m times' problem.
Direct formula: r = 100[m^(1/t) - 1] when a sum becomes m times in t years.
Take only the positive root, since 1 + r/100 must be positive.
common_mistakes: Reading 'nine-fold' as nine times the interest rather than nine times the sum, and setting the amount to 9 instead of 9x.
Halving 9 instead of taking its square root, giving a rate near 350% or 4.5 style errors.

concept.technique_name: number picking for quantitative comparison

examples.problem_statement: For the integers a, b, and c, the sum of a and b is 75% of c. Quantity A: (3/4)(a + b). Quantity B: (4/3)(c). Compare the two quantities.

solution.result: a constraint linking a, b and c that any test values must satisfy
solution.description: Write the given condition as an equation: the sum of a and b equals 75% of c. Every set of numbers you try later has to obey this.

solution.result: a valid positive test case, in which Quantity B is greater
solution.description: Pick positive integers that satisfy the constraint. The book notes these are valid because 1 + 2 is 75% of 4, and with all variables positive Quantity B comes out greater.

solution.result: an equally valid negative test case, in which Quantity A is greater
solution.description: Pick negative integers that also satisfy the constraint. Nothing in the problem rules out negatives, and with negative variables the comparison flips so that Quantity A is greater.

solution.result: opposite outcomes from two legal cases, so no fixed relationship holds
solution.description: Set the two results side by side. Because one legal set of values makes B greater and another makes A greater, the relationship is not determined by the given information.

key_reminders: The variables are only said to be integers, so negative values and zero must be tested, not just positives.
Any test values you pick must still satisfy the stated condition a + b = 75% of c.
In quantitative comparison, two admissible cases with opposite outcomes force the 'cannot be determined' answer.
common_mistakes: Testing only positive numbers such as a = 1, b = 2, c = 4 and concluding Quantity B is greater.
Reading 'integers' as 'positive integers' and never trying a = -1, b = -2, c = -4.

concept.technique_name: digit-count ranges in a given base

examples.problem_statement: What is the difference between the highest and the least 4-digit natural numbers that have exactly 4 digits when expressed in Base 6 and Base 7.

solution.description: Write the range of numbers that have 4 digits in the decimal system: from 10 cubed up to one less than 10 to the fourth.
Apply the same rule in Base 7: a 4-digit Base 7 number runs from 7 cubed up to one less than 7 to the fourth.
Do it once more in Base 6: a 4-digit Base 6 number runs from 6 cubed up to one less than 6 to the fourth.
Overlap the three ranges to keep only the numbers common to all of them. The largest lower bound is 1000 and the smallest upper bound is 1295.
Subtract the least common value from the highest common value to get the required difference.

key_reminders: A number has exactly 4 digits in base b when it lies from b^3 up to b^4 - 1.
'Common to all bases' means intersecting the ranges: take the largest lower bound and the smallest upper bound.
common_mistakes: Using 6^4 and 7^4 as the upper limits instead of 6^4 - 1 = 1295 and 7^4 - 1 = 2400.
Forgetting the decimal 4-digit condition and starting the overlap at 343 instead of 1000.

concept.technique_name: sum-from-average substitution

examples.problem_statement: If the average of x and y is 50, and the average of y and z is 80, what is the value of z - x ?

solution.description: Use the rule that the sum of two numbers is twice their average on the pair x and y, then isolate x.
Apply the same rule to the pair y and z, then isolate z so both unknowns are written in terms of y.
Substitute these two expressions into the quantity being asked for, z minus x.
Expand the subtraction and simplify. The y terms cancel, leaving a plain numerical difference.

solution.operation: \text{Smart Numbers: } x = 50,\ y = 50 \Rightarrow z = 160 - 50 = 110,\ z - x = 110 - 50
solution.description: Check the result the book's alternative way: choose x = 50 and y = 50 so their average is 50, force y + z = 160 to get z = 110, and take the difference.

key_reminders: The sum of two numbers is twice their average.
Writing both x and z in terms of y lets y cancel, so no individual value is ever needed.
Smart Numbers work here only if the chosen values satisfy both average conditions.
common_mistakes: Dropping the parentheses in (160 - y) - (100 - y) so the y terms do not cancel.
Trying to solve for x, y and z individually when the system has infinitely many solutions and only z - x is fixed.

concept.technique_name: pattern cancellation then column summation

examples.problem_statement: What is the sum of the numbers in the grid below?

solution.result: the leading positive and negative terms of row 1 cancel to 0
solution.description: Look across the first row and pair each negative term with its positive twin; each pair sums to zero, so those columns add nothing.
Add only the terms of row 1 that survived the cancellation, which sit in the two far-right columns.

solution.operation: \text{grid sum} = \text{sum of the two far-right columns}
solution.result: the problem reduces to summing six row-pairs
solution.description: Apply the same cancellation to every other row, since each row repeats the pattern; only the two far-right columns ever contribute.
Compute the far-right-column total for each row in turn, from the first row down to the final row.
Add the six surviving row totals together to get the sum of the whole grid.

key_reminders: A term and its negative cancel to zero, so those columns can be dropped before adding anything.
When every row repeats the same cancellation pattern, the grid sum collapses to the sum of the surviving columns.
common_mistakes: Adding all of the grid's entries one by one instead of noticing the cancelling pairs in each row.
Cancelling the pairs but then forgetting to carry the same reduction through the remaining rows.

concept.technique_name: circle area formula comparison

examples.problem_statement: Quantity A: The combined area of four circles, each with radius 1. Quantity B: The area of a circle with radius 2. Compare the two quantities.

solution.description: Start with Quantity A and find the area of just one of its circles by putting radius 1 into the circle-area formula.
Multiply that single-circle area by four, since Quantity A asks for the combined area of four identical circles.
Turn to Quantity B and use its radius of 2 in the same area formula.

solution.result: the two quantities are always equal
solution.description: Set the two computed quantities side by side and see that they match exactly, which selects the 'equal' answer choice.

key_reminders: The area of a circle is \pi r^2, so radius enters squared, not linearly.
For a combined area, compute one shape's area first and then multiply by the count.
common_mistakes: Assuming doubling the radius from 1 to 2 doubles the area, which would make Quantity B only 2\pi instead of 4\pi.
Comparing radii or circumferences (four circles of radius 1 versus one of radius 2) rather than the areas actually asked for.

concept.technique_name: function-of-a-sentence analysis with choice elimination
concept.sub_category: Reading Comprehension - function of a sentence

examples.problem_statement: For each of Questions 1 to 9, select one answer choice unless otherwise instructed. Which of the following best describes the function of the second sentence (“A Dream … essayists”) in the context of the passage as a whole?

solution.operation: Read the second sentence against the passage's overall description and name what it does there.
solution.result: the sentence describes what is appealing about the collection in the context of the author's childhood tastes
solution.description: Fix the sentence's job in the passage before touching the choices, since the question asks for function rather than content.

solution.operation: Test Choice A: does the sentence give examples, and does the collection show awareness of the tenuous nature of representations of reality?
solution.description: Reject A because the sentence provides no examples and the collection is never credited with that awareness.

solution.operation: Test Choice C: does the passage discuss adult enjoyment being more sophisticated than childhood enjoyment?
solution.description: Reject C because the passage contains no discussion or even suggestion of a more sophisticated adult basis for enjoyment, however plausible that idea sounds on its own.

solution.operation: Test Choice D: does the sentence present inadequacies of the collection?
solution.description: Reject D because this sentence describes the collection's virtues; the aspects the author finds inadequate are not addressed until later in the passage.

solution.operation: Test Choice E: does the passage treat the collection's variety as a hindrance to contextualization?
solution.description: Reject E because the passage says the variety is what makes the collection a rich read, with no suggestion that it hinders contextualization.

solution.operation: Match the function identified in step 1 to the surviving choice.
solution.description: Confirm B, which states that the sentence elaborates on how the collection fulfills the author's childhood criteria for a pleasurable book.

examples.answer: Choice B: To elaborate on how A Dream fulfills the author’s childhood criteria for a pleasurable book

key_reminders: A function question asks what a sentence does in the passage, not merely what it says.
A wrong choice can be true of the world and still be unsupported by the passage.
Locate where in the passage a claim appears; material introduced later cannot be the function of this sentence.
common_mistakes: Choosing C because the sophistication contrast feels reasonable, even though the passage never raises it.
Choosing D by importing the author's later criticisms into a sentence that is describing virtues.
Choosing E by reading the collection's variety as a flaw when the passage calls it a source of richness.

concept.technique_name: contrast and echo signal words in text completion

examples.problem_statement: Though some judges have found in the Third Amendment to the US Constitution a (i) _________ for a right to privacy, it was drafted primarily to appease opponents of the Constitution, and was particularly a (ii) _________ to those antifederalists who sought to prevent the new state from maintaining a standing army. Since Article 1, section 8 of the Constitution explicitly grants to Congress the power to raise and maintain an army, the Third Amendment was largely (iii) _________ before it was written.

solution.operation: Register the opening signal word "though" and set the first clause in opposition to the second clause
solution.result: The clause holding blank (i) must oppose the statement that the Amendment was actually meant to appease opponents
solution.description: Read the sentence's pivot word first: "though" forces the judges' privacy reading to stand against the Amendment's real appeasement purpose, which is what fixes the direction of blank (i).

solution.operation: Select the blank (i) word that names something judges could find in the Amendment as support for a privacy right
solution.description: Apply the opposition you just established: the word must make the judges' reading a genuine grounding for privacy, and "basis" is the best choice among the options.

solution.operation: Echo the word "appease" from the same sentence into blank (ii)
solution.result: sop, which can mean "something given to pacify"
solution.description: The second blank is not a contrast but a restatement, so copy the sentence's own word "appease" and pick the option closest in meaning to it.

solution.operation: Use the fact that Article 1, section 8 already granted Congress army powers to fix blank (iii)
solution.description: Since the cited Article makes the Third Amendment a matter of only abstract concern, the blank needs a word meaning "of no practical importance," and "moot" delivers exactly that.

key_reminders: "Though" at the head of a sentence signals that the clause containing the blank opposes what follows.
A blank can echo a nearby word rather than contrast with it -- look for the word the sentence hands you (here, "appease").
A supporting fact cited later in the passage can define a blank's meaning outright.
common_mistakes: Treating blank (ii) as another contrast and reversing it, when the sentence asks it to echo "appease."
Filling blank (i) with a negative word such as "detriment" or "counterargument" by attaching the contrast to the wrong half of the "though" construction.

concept.technique_name: contrast clue sentence completion

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for the blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling the blank in the way that best completes the text. The children's ______ natures were in sharp contrast to the even-tempered dispositions of their parents.

solution.operation: Read "in sharp contrast to" as instructing that the children's natures oppose the parents' natures
solution.result: The blank must mean the opposite of "even-tempered"
solution.description: Identify the sentence's contrast marker and use it to set the required meaning of the blank against the described parents.

solution.operation: Match "the opposite of even-tempered" to a choice meaning quickly changing
solution.description: Test the choices against the meaning you derived; "mercurial," meaning quickly changing, fits that requirement exactly.

solution.operation: Check blithe (happy), phlegmatic (unemotional), apathetic (uncaring), and cunning for any sense of changing from one state to another
solution.result: None of them suggests a tendency to change, so none contrasts with "even-tempered" as well
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining temperament words by confirming they describe a temperament without describing instability, which is the specific quality the contrast demands.

key_reminders: "In sharp contrast to" requires the blank to mean the opposite of the trait it is contrasted with.
"Even-tempered" opposes not any temperament, but specifically a changeable one.
common_mistakes: Choosing any word that merely names a temperament (blithe, phlegmatic, apathetic) instead of one that specifically means changeable.

concept.technique_name: testing cases against a median definition
concept.sub_category: median of a data set / quantitative comparison

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B, using the additional information given. In a set of 24 positive integers, 12 of the integers are less than 50. The rest are greater than 50. Quantity A: the median of the 24 integers. Quantity B: 50.

solution.operation: State the median rule for a set of n integers with n even: order them least to greatest and average the two middle integers
solution.description: Begin from the definition of the median for an even-sized set, since that is what determines Quantity A.

solution.operation: Apply the given split of the 24 integers to identify what is known about the two middle values
solution.result: 12 integers are below 50 and 12 above 50, so a_{12} < 50 < a_{13}, but neither value itself is known
solution.description: Translate the condition on the set into a statement about the two middle positions, which is the only place the median comes from.

solution.result: \frac{49 + 51}{2} = 50, so Quantity A equals Quantity B
solution.description: Test a first admissible case to see one possible relationship between the median and 50.

solution.result: \frac{49 + 53}{2} = 51, so Quantity A exceeds Quantity B
solution.description: Test a second admissible case that still respects the split, producing a different relationship from the first case.

solution.operation: Compare the two cases, which give different relationships under the same given information
solution.description: Conclude from the conflicting cases that no single relationship follows from the information given, which selects the "cannot be determined" choice.

examples.answer: Choice D: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

key_reminders: For an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values after ordering.
Knowing only how many values fall on each side of a number does not pin down the middle values themselves.
Two admissible cases giving different relationships is sufficient to answer "cannot be determined."
common_mistakes: Assuming the 12-below / 12-above split forces the median to equal 50.
Stopping after the single case 49 and 51 and answering "the two quantities are equal."

concept.technique_name: sign rules for products and odd exponents

examples.problem_statement: If B^3 A < 0 and A > 0, which of the following must be negative? (A) AB (B) B^2 A (C) B^4

solution.operation: Recognize that the inequality has 0 on one side, so the question is testing rules of positives and negatives
solution.result: Treat B^3 A < 0 as a statement about signs rather than magnitudes
solution.description: Notice the zero on one side of the inequality, which is the cue to reason about signs instead of trying to solve for values.

solution.operation: Given A > 0 and B^3 A < 0, deduce the sign of B^3
solution.description: Since a positive factor cannot make a product negative on its own, the other factor must carry the negative sign.

solution.operation: Apply the rule that a number raised to an odd exponent retains the sign of its base
solution.description: Move from the sign of B^3 back to the sign of B itself, which is valid because the exponent 3 is odd.

solution.operation: Multiply the positive A by the negative B
solution.description: Combine the two established signs: a positive times a negative is negative, so AB must be negative.

key_reminders: A product is negative only if exactly one of its factors is negative.
A number raised to an odd exponent keeps the sign of its base.
An inequality compared with 0 is a sign question, not a magnitude question.
common_mistakes: Concluding B^2 A or B^4 is negative, when an even exponent makes B^2 and B^4 nonnegative regardless of B's sign.
Failing to carry the sign of B^3 back to B because the odd-exponent rule was overlooked.

concept.technique_name: range of a data list
concept.sub_category: Range and spread of a numeric list

examples.problem_statement: List K consists of the numbers −10, −5, 0, 5, and 10. Which of the following lists of numbers have the same range as the numbers in list K ? Indicate all such lists. (A) −15, −1, 0, 1, 15  (B) −7, −4, −2, 1, 13  (C) 0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 10  (D) 2, 3, 5, 15, 19, 22  (E) 4, 5, 6, 24

solution.result: definition to apply to every list
solution.description: Recall the definition the whole question turns on: a list's range is the difference between its greatest and its least number.
Apply that definition to list K, whose greatest number is 10 and least number is -10, to get the target range every answer choice must match.

solution.result: only the two end numbers of each choice matter
solution.description: Notice that in every choice the numbers are already listed from least to greatest, so you only need to read the first and last number of a list rather than scan all of it.
Take the end numbers of Choice A, greatest 15 and least -15, subtract, and compare the result with 20; it does not match.
Do the same subtraction for Choice B, greatest 13 and least -7, and find a range equal to the target 20.
Subtract Choice C's least number 0 from its greatest number 10; the range is half the target, so this list is rejected.
Subtract Choice D's least number 2 from its greatest number 22 and find the range equals the target 20.
Subtract Choice E's least number 4 from its greatest number 24 and find the range again equals the target 20.

solution.result: the three lists whose range is 20
solution.description: Collect every choice whose computed range came out to 20 and select all of them, since the question asks you to indicate all such lists.

examples.answer: Choice B: − 7, − 4, − 2, 1, 13 AND Choice D: 2, 3, 5, 15, 19, 22 AND Choice E: 4, 5, 6, 24

key_reminders: Range is greatest minus least, so it depends only on the two extreme values, never on the count of numbers in between.
Subtracting a negative least value adds its magnitude: 13 - (-7) = 13 + 7.
When a list is already written in increasing order, its extremes are the first and last entries.
common_mistakes: Reading list K's range as 10 by using the largest value alone instead of subtracting the least value -10.
Sign-slipping on Choices A and B, where the least number is negative, and computing 15 - 15 = 0 or 13 - 7 = 6.
Stopping after finding one matching list, when this multi-select question has three correct choices.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by shared-meaning pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Through its state associations, the American Medical Association controlled who could become a physician and dominated ______ professions like nursing and occupational therapy. (A) commensurate (B) proportionate (C) kindred (D) affiliated (E) imperative (F) voluntary

solution.operation: blank \to \text{describes nursing and occupational therapy relative to physicians}
solution.result: the blank needs a word for the relation between those professions and physicians
solution.description: Read what the blank is doing in the sentence: it must describe professions such as nursing and occupational therapy as they relate to physicians.

solution.result: a word signalling a close relationship is required
solution.description: Use the sentence's own examples as the clue: these professions are also in the health-care field, so the blank calls for a word suggesting that close relationship.

solution.result: a pair that both fit and are alike in meaning
solution.description: Test the choices against that requirement and find that kindred and affiliated both suggest the close relationship and produce two completed sentences similar in meaning.
Rule out commensurate and proportionate because they suggest a comparative measurement between the professions, something the rest of the sentence gives no support for.

solution.result: both rejected, and neither has a partner
solution.description: Rule out imperative and voluntary because neither would typically describe a profession, and neither has a close-in-meaning partner among the remaining choices to pair with.

examples.answer: Choice C: kindred; AND Choice D: affiliated

key_reminders: The two correct choices must both fit the sentence and produce completed sentences alike in meaning.
A choice with no meaning-partner among the other options cannot be part of the answer pair.
Only a relationship the sentence itself supports counts; do not import an idea the text never states.
