common_mistakes: Pairing commensurate with proportionate because they are synonyms, ignoring that the sentence never sets up a comparison of measure.
Choosing a single best word and stopping, when this format requires exactly two.

concept.technique_name: 4-step Evaluate the Argument process

examples.problem_statement: Ethanol, a fuel derived from corn, can be used alone to power vehicles or along with gasoline to reduce the amount of gasoline consumed. Compared with conventional gasoline, pure ethanol produces significantly less pollution per gallon used. In order to combat pollution, many individuals advocate the increased usage of ethanol as a fuel source for vehicles in conjunction with or in place of gasoline. In evaluating the recommendation to increase the use of ethanol, it would be most important to research which of the following? (A) Whether the majority of existing vehicles are capable of using ethanol for fuel, either alone or in conjunction with gasoline (B) Whether the process of growing corn to produce ethanol results in significant amounts of pollution (C) Whether completely replacing gasoline with ethanol results in less pollution than using ethanol in conjunction with gasoline (D) Whether ethanol is more expensive to produce than conventional gasoline (E) Whether there are some vehicles in which using ethanol fuel would not result in a significant reduction in pollution compared to conventional gasoline

solution.description: Identify the question type from the stem: it asks what would be most important to research in evaluating a recommendation, which marks it as an Evaluate question.

solution.operation: \text{eth OR eth}+\text{gas can power veh};\ \text{PURE eth pollution} < \text{gas}
solution.result: two premises, the second only about pure ethanol
solution.description: Deconstruct the premises and map them: ethanol alone or with gasoline can power vehicles, and pure ethanol pollutes less per gallon than gasoline, noting that the second fact covers only pure ethanol.

solution.result: the conclusion, stated in terms of pollution
solution.description: Mark the conclusion: to combat pollution we should increase ethanol use, alone or with gasoline. It is specifically about reducing pollution.

solution.operation: \text{right answer: strengthens if answered one way, weakens if answered the other}
solution.result: the goal for testing each choice
solution.description: State the goal for an Evaluate question: the correct choice must be able to both strengthen and weaken the argument, showing the ethanol plan might cut pollution or might not, and it must actually mention pollution.

Test choice A: if most vehicles can use ethanol the plan proceeds, but if they cannot, switching as many as possible would still reduce pollution. It says switching might be difficult, not that it would fail to reduce pollution.

Test choice B: if growing corn produces a lot of pollution the switch would not actually cut pollution, while if ethanol can be produced cleanly the switch cuts pollution a lot. It swings the argument either way, which is what an Evaluate answer must do.
Test choice C: it splits apart the two options the conclusion combines, and knowing which of them pollutes less still says nothing about whether either beats pure gasoline.
Test choice D: production cost may be a drawback of ethanol generally, but the conclusion is about pollution, not cost, so cost cannot evaluate this argument.
Test choice E: it speaks only of some vehicles, and without knowing how many, it tells you neither that the overall switch would work nor that it would not.

key_reminders: An Evaluate answer must be able to cut both ways: answered one way it strengthens the plan, answered the other it weakens it.
The right answer has to bear on the conclusion's own terms, which here is pollution, not cost or feasibility.
Work from wrong to right, eliminating four choices rather than hunting for the one that sounds best.
common_mistakes: Picking (D) because cost feels like a real objection to ethanol, though the conclusion is about pollution only.
Picking (A) by treating a practical obstacle to adoption as evidence that pollution would not fall.
Picking (E) without noticing that 'some vehicles' gives no quantity, so it cannot swing the argument either way.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion by charge matching

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. At their best, (i) ______ book reviews are written in defense of value and in the tacit hope that the author, having had his or her (ii) ______ pointed out, might secretly agree that the book could be improved. Blank (i): (A) abstruse (B) adverse (C) hortatory. Blank (ii): (D) strengths (E) transgressions (F) assumptions.

solution.operation: \text{clue: author might agree the book could be improved}
solution.description: Use the second half of the sentence as the clue for Blank (ii): whatever is pointed out makes the author concede the book could be improved, so it must be something negative whose presence calls for improvement.
Scan the Blank (ii) column against that requirement; transgressions is the only choice negative in meaning, so it fills the second blank.

solution.result: Blank (i) must also be negative in meaning
solution.description: Carry that result back to the first blank: reviews that point out an author's transgressions are negative in nature, so Blank (i) needs a negative word too.
Check the Blank (i) column for a negative word; adverse is the only choice that meets the condition, so it fills the first blank.

examples.answer: Choice B: adverse; AND Choice E: transgressions

key_reminders: Fill the blank whose clue is most explicit first, then use that filled word as the clue for the remaining blank.
Matching the charge of the word, positive or negative, is often enough to isolate the single valid choice in a column.
Each blank draws only from its own column of choices.
common_mistakes: Starting at Blank (i), where all three words are unfamiliar in tone, instead of at Blank (ii), where the clue is explicit.
Choosing 'strengths' for Blank (ii) by reading 'in defense of value' as praise, which contradicts the book needing improvement.
Confusing 'adverse' with 'averse' and rejecting it as describing a person rather than the reviews.

concept.technique_name: context clue and contrast analysis

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. It is (i) ______ that so many portrait paintings hang in art museums, since the subject matter seems to dictate a status closer to pictures in the family photograph album than to high art. But perhaps it is the artistic skill with which the portraits are painted that (ii) ______ their presence in art museums. Blank (i): A surprising, B understandable, C irrelevant. Blank (ii): D challenges, E justifies, F changes.

solution.operation: Read the clause after "since" in sentence 1: portrait subject matter belongs closer to the family photo album than to high art.
solution.result: Sentence 1 signals that portrait subject matter does not fit the idea of high art.
solution.description: Use the "since" clause as the context clue for the first sentence: it tells you how the writer characterizes the subject matter of portraits.

solution.operation: Translate that mismatch into the sense Blank (i) must carry: the presence of portraits in art museums is odd or unfitting.
solution.result: Blank (i) needs a word meaning odd/unfitting.
solution.description: Convert the clue into a required meaning for the blank before looking at the answer choices, so the choice is tested against a prediction.

solution.operation: Match the Blank (i) choices to "odd or unfitting": surprising, understandable, irrelevant.
solution.description: Compare each first-column choice with the predicted meaning and keep the only one that expresses oddness.

solution.operation: Read sentence 2, which contrasts with sentence 1 and offers a point in favor of portraits: their artistic skill.
solution.result: Sentence 2 supplies a reason why portraits should be in art museums.
solution.description: Track the contrast marked by "But": the second sentence argues for museum placement rather than against it.

solution.operation: Match the Blank (ii) choices to "gives a reason for their presence": challenges, justifies, changes.
solution.description: Pick the second-column word that makes artistic skill support the portraits' presence, which is what the sentence's logic requires.

examples.answer: Choice A: surprising; Choice E: justifies

key_reminders: The clause after "since" states the reason the writer has in mind and controls the first blank.
"But" marks a reversal: the second sentence argues for what the first sentence made look odd.
Predict the meaning each blank needs before scanning its column of choices.
common_mistakes: Choosing "understandable" for Blank (i), which contradicts the "since" clause instead of following it.
Choosing "challenges" for Blank (ii), which reverses the pro-portrait direction set up by "But" and "artistic skill".

concept.technique_name: checking with assumed values

examples.problem_statement: If x+\frac{1}{yz},\; y+\frac{1}{zx},\; z+\frac{1}{xy} are in A.P., then x, y, z are in:

solution.result: A concrete triple that is itself in A.P. (common difference 1).
solution.description: Instead of manipulating the general expressions, assume x, y, z are in A.P. and pick easy values to test the claim.
Substitute the assumed values into the first given expression to get its numerical value.
Substitute the same values into the second expression to get its numerical value.
Substitute the same values into the third expression to get its numerical value.
Compare the two consecutive differences of the three computed values to see whether they form an A.P.

solution.operation: Read the verified implication back: x, y, z in A.P. produced the three expressions in A.P.
solution.result: The condition given in the question is met exactly when x, y, z are in A.P.
solution.description: Conclude from the checked case which progression x, y, z belong to.

key_reminders: Three terms are in A.P. when the difference between consecutive terms is the same.
For a multiple-choice style relation question, assuming convenient values that satisfy one option can confirm it.
common_mistakes: Mis-reading x+1/yz as (x+1)/(yz) instead of x plus the reciprocal of yz, which changes every computed value.

concept.technique_name: odd/even parity rules with value testing

examples.problem_statement: If pq is odd, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) [statement stating a quantity is odd] (B) p + q is even. (C) p - q is odd.

solution.operation: pq \text{ odd} \Rightarrow p \text{ odd and } q \text{ odd}
solution.result: Both p and q must be odd.
solution.description: Apply the parity rule for products: an even factor would force an even product, so a product that is odd forces both factors odd.

solution.operation: Substitute a pair of odd values for p and q into each answer statement.
solution.result: Each statement is evaluated on a case allowed by the constraint.
solution.description: Test the statements with concrete odd values rather than reasoning abstractly, since only odd values are permitted by step 1.

solution.operation: Eliminate every statement that the odd values make false.
solution.result: Only one statement survives the test.
solution.description: Discard any option that fails on a legitimate case, because a "must be true" statement cannot fail on any allowed case.

solution.result: p + q is even is the one that remains.
solution.description: Report the only statement not eliminated as the sole correct answer.

key_reminders: A product is odd only when every factor is odd.
"Must be true" means true in every allowed case, so a single counterexample eliminates a statement.
common_mistakes: Treating pq as a two-digit number or as p times q ambiguously, instead of the product whose odd value forces both p and q odd.

concept.technique_name: weighted average reasoning
concept.sub_category: averages, median and range of combined samples

examples.problem_statement: The earthworms in Sample A have an average length of 2.4 inches, and the earthworms in Sample B have an average length of 3.8 inches. The average length of the earthworms in both samples combined is 3.0 inches. Which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. I. There are more earthworms in Sample A than in Sample B. II. The median length of the earthworms is 3.2 inches. III. The range of lengths of the earthworms is 1.4.

solution.operation: Compare the combined average 3.0 with the two sample averages 2.4 and 3.8.
solution.result: 3.0 is closer to Sample A's 2.4 than to Sample B's 3.8.
solution.description: Locate the overall average between the two sample averages and see which one it sits nearer to.

solution.operation: Read that closeness as a weighting: the combined average is pulled toward the larger sample.
solution.result: Sample A contains more earthworms than Sample B, so statement I must be true.
solution.description: Apply weighted-average reasoning: the sample that pulls the overall average toward its own average is the one with more members.

solution.operation: Ask whether the median can be pinned down from averages alone; note the lengths in Sample A could all equal 2.4 or be spread widely around it.
solution.result: The median is not determined by the given information, so statement II need not be true.
solution.description: Check statement II by observing that many different individual-value distributions produce the same averages, and they do not share one median.

solution.operation: Ask the same of the range; Sample B's lengths could likewise be identical or vary widely while keeping their average.
solution.result: The range is not determined either, so statement III need not be true.
solution.description: Check statement III the same way: without the individual values, the spread of the data set can vary a great deal.

solution.operation: Collect the statements that survived: I only.
solution.result: Only statement I must be true.
solution.description: Report the statements that are forced by the given averages and drop the two that depend on unknown individual values.

key_reminders: A combined average lies nearer the average of the larger group.
Averages alone fix neither the median nor the range; those need the individual values.
common_mistakes: Taking 3.2 as the median because it looks like a plausible middle value between 2.4 and 3.8.
Computing 3.8 - 2.4 = 1.4 and calling it the range, when 1.4 is only the gap between the two sample averages, not between the longest and shortest worms.

concept.technique_name: digit-grouping column addition for multiplication by 1111

examples.problem_statement: Using the Multiplication Techniques technique: A Vedic Mathematics technique for multiplying 2172 by 1111 using a digit-grouping and column addition method. Given: multiplicand = 2172; multiplier = 1111; product = 2413092; group size = 4; intermediate steps = 7; intermediate sequence = 2, 3, 10, 12, 10, 9, 2. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Write 2172 with leading zeros as 0 0 2 1 7 2 and set the multiplier 1111 to mean 'sum four consecutive digits'
solution.result: a digit strip ready for overlapping groups of four
solution.description: Because every digit of 1111 is a 1, each column of the product is just the sum of four consecutive digits of the multiplicand; pad with zeros so every window has four entries.
Take the rightmost window of four digits and add them; this gives the units column of the raw sequence.
Shift the window one digit to the left and add the four digits it now covers to get the next column.
Shift left again and add; this column exceeds 9, which will need a carry later.
Shift left again and add the four digits now inside the window, giving the next raw column value.
Shift left past the leading digit of the multiplicand and add the four digits covered, using zeros where digits have run out.
Shift left once more and add; only two real digits remain inside the window.
Shift left a final time; only the leading digit 2 is still inside the window, so the last raw column is 2.

solution.operation: Write the seven column values in order from left to right
solution.description: Collect the seven window sums into the intermediate sequence before any carrying is done.

solution.operation: Carry from the right: 10 \to 0 carry 1, so 12 becomes 13
solution.description: Start the carry-over pass at the right end: reduce the first two-digit column to its units digit and push the carry into the column on its left.

solution.operation: 13 \to 3 carry 1, so the 10 on its left becomes 11
solution.description: Continue leftwards with the same rule on the column just increased by the previous carry.

solution.operation: 11 \to 1 carry 1, so the 3 on its left becomes 4
solution.description: Apply the carry rule to the last two-digit column; every column is now a single digit.

solution.operation: Read the adjusted sequence as one number
solution.description: String the single-digit columns together from left to right to read off the product.

key_reminders: Multiplying by 1111 means each column of the product is the sum of four consecutive digits of the multiplicand.
Pad the multiplicand with leading and trailing zeros so every sliding window holds exactly four digits.
Carry-over is done only after all seven column sums are written, working from right to left.
common_mistakes: Stopping the carry pass after one column: here the carry cascades, turning 12 into 13, then 10 into 11, then 3 into 4.
Reading the raw sequence 2 | 3 | 10 | 12 | 10 | 9 | 2 as the answer because it already has seven entries, without reducing the two-digit columns.

concept.technique_name: speed from distance and time, then distance covered in the winner's time

examples.problem_statement:
Vinay runs 100 metres in 20 seconds and Ajay runs the same distance in 25 seconds. By what distance will Vinay beat Ajay in a hundred metre race?
(a) 10 m  (b) 20 m  (c) 25 m  (d) 12 m

solution.description: Divide the race distance by Vinay's time to convert his performance into a speed.
Do the same division for Ajay so both runners are expressed in metres per second.
Fix the clock reading at the moment the race ends: it ends when the faster runner, Vinay, crosses the line.

solution.result: Ajay has covered 80 m at that moment
solution.description: Multiply Ajay's speed by the 20 seconds available to find how far he has run when Vinay finishes.
Subtract Ajay's covered distance from the full 100 m; the remaining gap is the beating distance.

key_reminders: Speed = distance / time, applied separately to each runner.
A 'beats by distance' answer is measured at the instant the winner finishes, not at the loser's finish.
Distance covered in that instant = loser's speed multiplied by the winner's time.
common_mistakes: Converting the 5-second time gap into distance with the wrong runner's speed (5 \times 5 = 25) and picking option (c).
Using Ajay's 25 seconds instead of Vinay's 20 seconds as the time window, which makes Ajay finish and the gap vanish.

concept.technique_name: successive percentage change formula

examples.problem_statement: If the salary of a worker is first decreased by 20% and then increased by 10%. What is the percentage effect on his salary?

solution.result: the single-shot formula for one increase combined with one decrease
solution.description: Recall the Quicker Maths formula that collapses a successive increase and decrease into one net percentage.
Read the two percentage changes out of the problem and label which one is the increase and which the decrease.
Put the labelled values into the formula, keeping the product term over 100.
Evaluate the expression: the product term is 2, and the arithmetic gives a net figure of -12 per cent.
Read the sign of the result: negative means the net effect is a fall, so the salary ends 12 per cent lower.

key_reminders: Net effect of one increase and one decrease = increase - decrease - (increase x decrease)/100.
A negative net percentage means an overall decrease; a positive one means an overall increase.
The order of the increase and the decrease does not change the net effect.
common_mistakes: Dropping the correction term and reporting 10 - 20 = -10, i.e. a 10% decrease instead of 12%.
Entering the values by order of occurrence rather than by role, so the decrease of 20 is placed in the increase slot and the sign of the answer flips.

concept.technique_name: ratio proportion

examples.problem_statement: If the heights of two cones are in the ratio 1 : 4 and their diameters are in the ratio 4 : 5, what is the ratio of their volumes ?

solution.result: Volume depends on r^2 and h
solution.description: Write down the cone volume formula the book starts from, so you can see which measurements the volume is sensitive to: the radius squared and the height.

solution.result: Ratio of volumes = (ratio of diameters)^2 \times (ratio of heights)
solution.description: Turn the formula into a ratio statement: the constant \frac{1}{3}\pi cancels, so substitute the given diameter ratio 4 : 5 in place of the radius ratio (diameters scale exactly like radii) and the height ratio 1 : 4.
Square the diameter ratio on its own first, because the radius enters the volume formula squared.
Multiply that squared diameter ratio by the height ratio to finish, and read the resulting fraction back as a ratio.

key_reminders: Cone volume is V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h, so volume scales with the square of the radius and the first power of the height.
Ratio of volumes = (ratio of radii or diameters)^2 \times (ratio of heights).
Diameters may be used in place of radii in the ratio, since d = 2r and the factor 2 cancels.
common_mistakes: Squaring the height ratio 1 : 4 instead of the diameter ratio 4 : 5.
Halving 4 : 5 to get radii before squaring, an unnecessary step that invites arithmetic slips.
Multiplying 16 : 25 by 4 rather than by \frac{1}{4}, which reverses the height ratio.

concept.technique_name: unit rate conversion and estimation

examples.problem_statement: In a certain barter system, one sack of rice can be traded for two and a half chickens or a third of a medallion. Quantity A: The value of a chicken in sacks of rice. Quantity B: The value of a medallion in sacks of rice.

solution.description: Invert the medallion rate: if one sack buys only a third of a medallion, buying the whole medallion takes three sacks, so Quantity B has the exact value 3.

solution.result: One chicken is worth less than one sack
solution.description: Read the chicken rate the same way: a single sack fetches 2.5 chickens, so each chicken must be worth less than a whole sack of rice.
Bound Quantity A rather than computing it exactly, as the book does: the value of one chicken in sacks of rice is less than 1, which is all the comparison needs.
Compare the bound with the exact value: anything below 1 is below 3, so Quantity B wins without any further calculation.

key_reminders: A rate stated as "one X trades for n Y" inverts to "one Y is worth \frac{1}{n} of an X".
In quantitative comparison, a bound on one quantity is enough when it cannot overlap the other quantity's value.
common_mistakes: Reading "a third of a medallion" as three medallions per sack, which would make Quantity B equal to \frac{1}{3}.
Taking a chicken to be worth 2.5 sacks instead of \frac{1}{2.5} of a sack by failing to invert the rate.
Spending time computing the exact value 0.4 for Quantity A when a bound below 1 already settles it.

concept.technique_name: odd days method
concept.sub_category: Calendar - finding the day of the week

examples.problem_statement: Mahatma Gandhi was born on 2 Oct 1869. The day of the week was: 1) Friday 2) Thursday 3) Saturday 4) Monday 5) None of these

solution.description: Break the elapsed time into blocks and take the first block: a complete span of 1600 years contributes 0 odd days, so it can be dropped from the count.
Take the next block of 200 years: each century of the pair carries 5 odd days, giving 10, which reduces to 3 odd days after removing complete weeks.
Handle the leftover 68 years by splitting them into 17 leap years worth 2 odd days each and 51 ordinary years worth 1 each; the total 85 reduces to 1 odd day.
Count the days elapsed within 1869 itself, from 1 January through 2 October, by adding the month lengths and the 2 days of October; 275 reduces to 2 odd days.
Add the odd days from all four blocks and map the total onto the week: 6 odd days lands on Saturday.

key_reminders: An ordinary year carries 1 odd day and a leap year 2 odd days; 400 years carry 0.
Counting by centuries, 100 years carry 5 odd days, so 200 years carry 10, reducing to 3.
Odd days are the remainder after removing whole weeks, so any total is reduced modulo 7 before reading off the day.
common_mistakes: Including 1869 itself in the 68-year block instead of counting its days separately up to 2 October.
Adding 29 for February 1869, which is not a leap year, when totalling the 275 days.
Forgetting to reduce 10 odd days for the 200-year block down to 3, or 85 down to 1.

concept.technique_name: percent change

examples.problem_statement: If a student successfully lobbied a professor to change her score on a certain exam to 1,600, then her new score was what percent greater than her original score of 1,250 ?

solution.description: Fix the original score as the base of the comparison, since the question asks how much greater the new score is than the original.
Subtract the original score from the new score to get the amount of change.
Apply the percent change equation by dividing the change by the original, using the calculator for this last line of math.
Convert the decimal into a percent to state how much the score increased.

key_reminders: Percent change = (change) / (original), never divided by the new value.
The original value is the one the comparison is made against — here 1,250, not 1,600.
common_mistakes: Dividing the 350 change by the new score 1,600 (giving about 22%) instead of by the original 1,250.
Reporting the ratio 1600/1250 = 1.28 as 128% greater rather than 28% greater.

concept.technique_name: conditional grouping (contrapositive chaining)

examples.problem_statement: One or more of six violinists—Greene, Holiday, Liu, Mann, Underwood, and Wilson—will be selected to perform at the year-end concert. No other violinists will be selected. The following conditions apply: If Holiday is selected, then Mann is not selected. If Liu is selected, then both Mann and Wilson are selected. If Underwood is not selected, then Holiday is selected. Wilson is not selected unless Greene is selected. Which of the following CANNOT be a complete and accurate list of the violinists who are selected for the concert? (A) Greene, Liu, Mann, Underwood, Wilson (B) Greene, Mann, Underwood (C) Greene, Mann, Wilson (D) Greene, Underwood (E) Holiday

solution.operation: Choose an approach: test each list against the diagram rather than running a rule-by-rule Orientation sweep
solution.result: Answers are evaluated one at a time against the conditional diagram
solution.description: Recognize that because four of the five lists are workable scenarios, most rules eliminate no answer choices, so the standard Orientation approach of applying each rule across all answers will not pay off here.

solution.operation: Check (A): G, L, M, U, W against the implications of each selected violinist
solution.result: No violinist on the list is forced out by another, and nobody required is missing — (A) is possible
solution.description: Review the implications of selecting G, L, M, U, and W together; this is exactly the list that results when L is selected, as seen in the earlier work on question #2.
Run the implications of placing G, M, and U into the selected group; nothing conflicts, so it appears (B) could be true and it is set aside in the hope of finding a cleaner answer further down.

solution.operation: Check (C): G, M, W — apply M \rightarrow U
solution.result: Underwood is required but absent, so (C) is an incomplete list
solution.description: Apply the rule that if Mann is selected then Underwood must also be selected; since (C) selects Mann without Underwood, this list cannot be a complete and accurate one.
Once a list is shown to violate a required implication, the remaining answers need not be tested, since exactly one answer can be impossible.

key_reminders: A 'complete and accurate list' must already contain everyone the selected members force into the group.
If Mann is selected, Underwood must be selected as well.
On a CANNOT-be-a-list question, evaluate answers against the diagram instead of sweeping rule by rule.
common_mistakes: Treating (C) as acceptable because no listed violinist is directly forbidden, while overlooking that Underwood is missing.
Rejecting (A) for containing five of the six violinists, even though selecting Liu forces exactly that group.

concept.technique_name: translate to two equations and solve by substitution

examples.problem_statement: The length of a rectangle is two more than twice the width, and the area of the rectangle is 40. What is the rectangle’s perimeter?

solution.result: First equation relating length and width
solution.description: Translate 'the length is two more than twice the width' directly into an equation in the two variables.
Translate the given area using area = length \times width.
Since the first equation is already solved for L, substitute 2W + 2 in for L in the area equation and distribute.
Because both a W^2 term and a W term are present, move all terms to one side so the quadratic is set to zero.
Simplify before factoring by dividing the entire equation by 2.
Factor the simplified quadratic and set each factor equal to zero to get the two candidate widths.
Discard the negative root because a width cannot be negative, then use LW = 40 to recover the length from the surviving width.
Substitute the length and width into the perimeter formula to answer the question that was actually asked.

key_reminders: Two unknowns need two equations; solve one for a variable and substitute into the other.
When both a squared term and a linear term appear, set the equation to zero before factoring.
Simplify a quadratic by its common factor before attempting to factor it.
A physical dimension such as width cannot be negative, so negative roots are discarded.
common_mistakes: Guessing the sides 4 and 10 by trying values — nothing in the problem guarantees the dimensions are integers.
Keeping W = -5 as a second valid width and reporting two perimeters.
Attempting to factor 2W^2 + 2W - 40 without first dividing through by 2.
Stopping at W = 4 or at the area rather than computing the requested perimeter.

concept.technique_name: perfect square trinomial factoring

examples.problem_statement: Write x^2 + 22xy + 121y^2 = 0 in factored form.

solution.result: The trinomial is a candidate for the perfect square pattern
solution.description: Notice that the first and third terms are both perfect squares, which is the signal to try the square-of-a-binomial form.
Take the square roots of those two terms to get the pieces that would sit inside the binomial.

solution.result: The expansion matches the original expression
solution.description: Expand the candidate factored form and check it against the original trinomial, confirming the middle term comes out as 22xy.
Since the math is a match, rewrite the given equation in the verified factored form.

key_reminders: When the first and third terms of a trinomial are perfect squares, test the square-of-a-binomial form.
A candidate factorization is only confirmed once its expansion reproduces the middle term.
common_mistakes: Taking the square root of 121y^2 as 121y instead of 11y.
Accepting the perfect square form without checking that 2(x)(11y) reproduces the 22xy middle term.

concept.technique_name: percent of a total then ratio approximation

examples.problem_statement: Questions are based on the accompanying data for College X. [From the graphs: College X has 200 adjunct faculty and 250 non-adjunct faculty; 2 percent of the adjunct faculty and 12 percent of the non-adjunct faculty are in the engineering field.] There are 275 students in the field of engineering at College X. Approximately what is the ratio of the number of students in engineering to the number of faculty in engineering? Select a single answer choice: (A) 8 to 1 (B) 10 to 1 (C) 12 to 1 (D) 14 to 1 (E) 20 to 1

solution.description: Read off the graph the two percentages that apply to engineering: 2 percent of the adjunct faculty and 12 percent of the non-adjunct faculty.
Apply the adjunct percentage to the 200 adjunct faculty to get the number of adjunct faculty in engineering.
Apply the non-adjunct percentage to the 250 non-adjunct faculty to get the number of non-adjunct faculty in engineering.
Add the two faculty counts to get the total number of faculty in engineering.
Form the ratio asked for, students in engineering to faculty in engineering.
Estimate by rounding both terms to numbers that divide evenly, then reduce the ratio to lowest terms.

key_reminders: A percent shown on a graph must be applied to that group's own total, not to a combined total.
Counts for two separate groups are added before the ratio is formed.
When the question says 'approximately', round both ratio terms to a pair that divides evenly.
common_mistakes: Adding the percentages (2\% + 12\%) and applying the sum to one total instead of computing 2\% of 200 and 12\% of 250 separately.
Applying 2 percent to the 250 non-adjunct group and 12 percent to the 200 adjunct group, swapping the two faculty categories.
Dividing 275 by only one of the faculty counts (4 or 30) instead of by the total 34.

concept.technique_name: clue-and-contrast blank filling

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Frederick the Great of Prussia was known for his (i) _________ under fire during his military victories; however, when confronting issues of domestic policy, this equilibrium sometimes failed him. He was often (ii) _________ with his ministers, who never knew when they might be subjected to one of his tirades. Blank (i): intrepidity / cruelty / sangfroid. Blank (ii): fascist / mercurial / vainglorious.

solution.description: Locate the clue: the sentence calls the quality in blank (i) 'this equilibrium', so the word the second clause reuses is the anchor for both blanks.
Because 'this equilibrium' refers back to blank (i), the first blank must have the same meaning as equilibrium, not the opposite one the sentence's structure tempts you toward.
Apply the pivot: 'however' plus 'this equilibrium sometimes failed him' flips the direction, so the second blank must be opposite in meaning to equilibrium.
Choose from each column the word that matches the direction just fixed: composure for blank (i) and volatility for blank (ii).

key_reminders: A demonstrative phrase such as 'this equilibrium' points back at the earlier blank and defines it.
'However' reverses direction for the clause that follows it, not for the clause it refers back to.
In a two-blank text completion the two blanks can point in opposite directions from the same clue word.
common_mistakes: Treating 'however' as reversing blank (i) as well, and so making the first blank the opposite of equilibrium.
Picking a blank (i) word that fits 'under fire' by association (intrepidity, bravery) rather than one that matches the clue word equilibrium.

concept.technique_name: mean of combined equal-sized lists versus median
concept.sub_category: average and median of a combined frequency distribution

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. Frequency Distribution for List X: number 1, 2, 3, 5 with frequency 10, 20, 18, 12. Frequency Distribution for List Y: number 6, 7, 8, 9 with frequency 24, 17, 10, 9. List X and list Y each contain 60 numbers. The average (arithmetic mean) of the numbers in list X is 2.7, and the average of the numbers in list Y is 7.1. List Z contains 120 numbers: the 60 numbers in list X and the 60 numbers in list Y. Quantity A: the average of the 120 numbers in list Z. Quantity B: the median of the 120 numbers in list Z. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Note that lists X and Y contribute the same count of numbers to list Z, which is what lets the two given averages be combined directly.
Because the two lists are the same size, average the two individual averages to get the average of the 120 numbers in list Z.

solution.operation: 120 \text{ numbers} \Rightarrow \text{median} = \text{average of the two middle numbers}
solution.description: Since list Z holds an even count of numbers, its median is the average of the two middle values once the numbers are placed in increasing order.

Check the two distributions: every one of the 60 numbers in list X is at most 5 and every one of the 60 numbers in list Y is at least 6, so the 60th and 61st values in order are the largest of X and the smallest of Y.
Average those two middle numbers to obtain the median of list Z.
Compare the median against the average and pick the larger quantity.

examples.answer: Choice B: Quantity B is greater.

key_reminders: The average of two combined lists equals the average of their averages only when the lists contain the same count of numbers.
For an even count of values the median is the average of the two middle values in increasing order.
When every value of one list is below every value of another, the split point of the ordered combined list falls between them.
common_mistakes: Averaging 2.7 and 7.1 with unequal weights, or summing them without dividing by 2.
Taking the median of list Z to be a single middle value rather than the average of the 60th and 61st numbers.
Reading the median off the frequency table of one list alone (for example calling it 5 or 6) instead of averaging the two middle numbers 5 and 6.

concept.technique_name: percent of a total from combined graphs

examples.problem_statement: Approximately how many more miscellaneous public transit vehicles than public transit trolley buses were there in 2000? (Use the top graph for the total number of public transit vehicles by year and the bottom graph for the percent breakdown by vehicle type.)

solution.operation: Combine the top graph (totals by year) with the bottom graph (percent breakdown by vehicle type)
solution.result: Both the total number of vehicles and the two relevant percentages are needed
solution.description: Recognize that neither graph alone gives a count of miscellaneous vehicles or trolley buses, so read the total from the top graph and the shares from the bottom graph.

solution.operation: Read the 2000 bar on the top graph
solution.description: Take the approximate 2000 total off the top graph; the question says 'approximately', so a rounded read of 120,000 is intended.

solution.operation: Read the miscellaneous and trolley bus shares off the bottom graph
solution.description: Pull the two percentages that apply to the 120,000 vehicles: 4% are miscellaneous and 1.5% are trolley buses.
Rather than computing both counts and subtracting, subtract the percentages first, since both apply to the same 120,000 total.
Apply the 2.5 percentage-point difference to the total to get the difference in vehicle counts directly.

key_reminders: Percent-breakdown graphs give shares, not counts -- multiply by the total from the companion graph.
When two percents are taken of the same base, subtract the percents first and multiply once.
'Approximately' licenses reading the bar as a round number such as 120,000.
common_mistakes: Answering with the percentage difference (2.5) or a mis-scaled version of it instead of converting to a vehicle count.
Reading 1.5% as 1% or 2%, which shifts the difference away from 3,000.
Computing 4% and 1.5% of the total separately and subtracting with a rounding slip in each.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by contrast clue and synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

Her ______ should not be confused with miserliness; as long as I have known her, she has always been willing to assist those who are in need.

A stinginess  B diffidence  C frugality  D illiberality  E intolerance  F thrift

solution.operation: Read the second clause: she has always been willing to assist those in need
solution.result: The person is generous, not miserly
solution.description: Take the evidence clause as the controlling clue -- her readiness to help establishes generosity.

solution.operation: Read 'should not be confused with miserliness' as a constraint on the blank
solution.result: The blank must be consistent with generosity yet mistakable for miserliness
solution.description: The sentence explicitly separates the blank from miserliness, so the word must be a trait an uninformed observer could wrongly read as miserly.
Reject these two because they are synonyms of miserliness itself and therefore inconsistent with her demonstrated generosity.

solution.operation: Test 'diffidence' (B) and 'intolerance' (E) for a same-meaning partner
solution.description: Even where a choice like 'diffidence' could produce a sensible sentence, drop it because no other choice pairs with it to yield two sentences alike in meaning.

solution.result: Both fit the constraint and mean the same thing
solution.description: Keep this pair: careful economy is compatible with generosity, can be misread as miserliness, and the two words yield sentences alike in meaning.

examples.answer: Choice C: frugality; AND Choice F: thrift

key_reminders: Sentence equivalence requires both a sentence that makes sense and a pair alike in meaning.
A 'should not be confused with X' construction means the blank is near X but not X.
A choice with no same-meaning partner cannot be part of the answer, however sensible it reads.
common_mistakes: Picking 'stinginess' and 'illiberality' as the synonym pair while ignoring that the sentence denies miserliness.
Choosing 'diffidence' because it produces a readable sentence, despite it having no partner.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by example-clue charge matching

examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

In a strong indication of the way the entire party is ______ the candidate with moderate credentials, the outspokenly conservative former mayor of a major city has promised to raise a substantial amount of money for the candidate's campaign.

A rallying behind  B incensed over  C undecided about  D mortified over  E embarrassed about  F coalescing around

solution.operation: Identify the mayor's fundraising promise as the example that illustrates the blank
solution.result: The blank describes the party's attitude or action toward the candidate
solution.description: Treat the second clause as an instance of what the blank names, since the sentence calls it 'a strong indication of the way' the party behaves.

solution.operation: Assign a charge to the clue: raising funds is a way of supporting a candidate
solution.description: Convert the example into a required charge -- fundraising is support, so only a positive attitude word can fill the blank.

solution.operation: Screen B, C, D, E against the required positive charge
solution.description: Drop 'incensed over', 'mortified over' and 'embarrassed about' as negative, and 'undecided about' as indifferent -- none would be exemplified by a promise of fund-raising.

solution.operation: Check the remaining pair 'rallying behind' (A) and 'coalescing around' (F)
solution.result: Both positive and similar in meaning
solution.description: Keep both: they alone indicate a positive attitude toward the candidate and they produce completed sentences alike in meaning.

examples.answer: Choice A: rallying behind; AND Choice F: coalescing around

key_reminders: An illustrating example fixes the charge of the blank before any vocabulary nuance matters.
The two correct choices must both fit the sentence and be similar to each other in meaning.
common_mistakes: Reading 'outspokenly conservative' versus 'moderate credentials' as tension and choosing a negative word, when the mayor's action is supportive.
Pairing negative choices such as 'mortified over' and 'embarrassed about' purely because they are synonyms.

concept.technique_name: strengthen a causal claim via analogous-control comparison

examples.problem_statement:
Machu Picchu
In 2001, the Peruvian government began requiring tourists to buy permits to hike the Inca Trail to the ancient city of Machu Picchu. Only 500 people per day are given permission to hike the Inca Trail, whereas before 2001 daily visitors numbered in the thousands. The Peruvian government claims that this permit program has successfully prevented deterioration of archaeological treasures along the Inca Trail. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument above?

solution.operation: Identify the question from the words 'if true' and 'most strengthens the argument'
solution.description: Classify the question stem first, so you know the right answer must make the argument more likely to hold rather than test it or explain it.

solution.operation: Map the premises: 2001 permits required; now 500 hikers/day where thousands came before
solution.result: 2001 Peru gov: permits required; now 500/day, previously thousands/day
solution.description: Record the two factual sentences as background -- they only establish that the visitor count dropped sharply after the program began.

solution.operation: Isolate the conclusion: the permit program has prevented deterioration of treasures along the trail
solution.description: Separate the government's claim from the facts; it is a cause-and-effect assertion, not another observation.

solution.operation: State the goal for a cause-and-effect conclusion
solution.result: The right answer should show the permit program probably did reduce the damage
solution.description: Set the target before reading choices: strengthen the causal link between the permit program and the absence of deterioration.

solution.operation: Evaluate (A): similar Incan ruins with no visitor limit disintegrated at a significantly greater rate
solution.description: This supplies a comparison case without the limit that did deteriorate, making it more likely the visitor limit is what protected the Inca Trail.

solution.operation: Evaluate (B): nearby villages lost income from fewer tourist purchases
solution.description: Bad news for the villages says nothing about deterioration along the trail, so it does not touch the specific claim.

solution.operation: Evaluate (C): permit revenue funds guards at sites without permit programs
solution.description: This shows other sites are better protected by guards, not whether the program is protecting the Inca Trail itself.

solution.operation: Evaluate (D): guides' take-home pay rose 50 to 100 percent since 2001
solution.description: Guide pay tells us nothing about damage to the trail, which is the only outcome the conclusion is about.

solution.operation: Evaluate (E): limited enforcement means most hikers currently go without a permit
solution.description: This suggests actual traffic far exceeds 500 per day, so it weakens rather than strengthens the claim that the program is working.

key_reminders: Strengthening a causal claim means making the stated cause a likelier explanation of the observed effect.
A comparison group lacking the cause, which shows the effect absent, supports the causal link.
Watch for Reverse Logic choices that weaken; every problem in this set has at least one.
common_mistakes: Choosing (E) because it discusses permits and enforcement, when it undercuts the program's effectiveness.
Choosing (C) because it sounds like a benefit of the program, though it concerns sites other than the Inca Trail.
Treating economic effects in (B) or (D) as relevant when the conclusion is only about archaeological deterioration.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion by easiest-blank-first with contrast signal

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

In the nineteenth century the (i) ______ advanced mechanical printing techniques made it possible for newspaper owners to print newspapers cheaply and in mass quantities, but unlike many other mechanized industries, where machines (ii) ______ workers, the new printing machines required trained compositors to run them, thereby (iii) ______ the demand for skilled printing labor.

Blank (i): A wide application of, B extensive resistance to, C great expense of
Blank (ii): D marginalized, E intrigued, F isolated
Blank (iii): G ignoring, H anticipating, I increasing

solution.operation: Set the requirement for Blank (i) from 'print newspapers cheaply and in mass quantities'
solution.result: The blank needs something about advanced techniques that caused cheap mass printing
solution.description: Anchor Blank (i) to the stated outcome: whatever fills it must explain how the techniques produced cheap, high-volume newspapers.

solution.operation: Test C 'great expense of' and B 'extensive resistance to' against that outcome
solution.result: Both eliminated; A 'wide application of' remains
solution.description: Reject 'great expense of' because it contradicts cheapness, and 'extensive resistance to' because resistance would produce no notable change in the industry.

solution.operation: Set the requirement for Blank (iii): the effect of machines needing trained compositors on the skilled labor market
solution.result: Jobs would have been created that did not previously exist
solution.description: Read Blank (iii) as the consequence clause -- because the machines require trained workers, the effect on skilled labor demand follows directly.

solution.operation: Test G 'ignoring' and H 'anticipating' against that effect
solution.description: Drop 'ignoring' since nothing indicates the demand was disregarded, and 'anticipating' since no future demand is mentioned.

solution.operation: Set the requirement for Blank (ii) from the contrast 'unlike many other mechanized industries'
solution.result: Other industries' machines did not require trained workers but simply replaced human labor
solution.description: Use the contrast signal: Blank (ii) must characterize an effect on workers opposite to the printing trade's need for trained operators.

solution.operation: Test E 'intrigued' and F 'isolated' against the passage's content
solution.description: Reject 'intrigued' and 'isolated' because the passage says nothing about workers' interest in the machines or their working conditions, whereas replacement of labor is marginalization.

examples.answer: Choice A: wide application of; Choice D: marginalized; Choice I: increasing

key_reminders: Fill the blank whose clue is most explicit first, then use the settled sense to constrain the others.
'unlike' sets up a contrast: the other industries must behave oppositely to the printing case.
A choice must be supported by something the passage actually states, not merely be plausible.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'great expense of' for Blank (i) by associating advanced machinery with cost, against the sentence's 'cheaply'.
Choosing 'isolated' for Blank (ii) on a vague sense of machines harming workers, though working conditions are never mentioned.
Choosing 'anticipating' for Blank (iii) when the passage describes demand actually created, not foreseen.

concept.technique_name: multiplication using working base

examples.problem_statement: Using the Multiplication using Working Base Method technique: multiply 251 \times 252 with a theoretical base of 1000 and a working base of 250. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.description: Fix the two bases the method runs on: the theoretical base 1000 and the working base 250, and note that 250 is 1000 divided by 4, so 4 is the division factor used later.
Subtract the working base from each multiplicand to get its deviation; both numbers sit above 250, so both deviations are positive.

solution.result: each number paired with its deviation
solution.description: Write the two numbers side by side with their deviations attached, which sets up the diagonal and vertical operations of the working base layout.
Do the diagonal addition: add either number to the other's deviation. Both diagonals give 253, which is the left-hand side of the raw answer.
Multiply the two deviations vertically; their product 2 becomes the right-hand side of the raw answer, giving the intermediate 253 | 2.
Because the working base is the theoretical base divided by 4, divide the LHS by that same factor 4; the division leaves a whole part 63 and a fractional part.
Convert the leftover fraction from the previous division back into units of the theoretical base by taking that fraction of 1000.
Add the converted fractional amount to the right-hand side, so the deviation product absorbs the remainder carried down from the LHS division.
Pad the right-hand side with leading zeros until it has as many digits as the theoretical base has zeros; 252 already fills the three places, so no zeros are added.
Join the LHS quotient 63 to the three-digit RHS 252 to read off the finished product.

examples.answer: 251 × 252 = 63252 using working base method with theoretical base 1000, working base 250, deviations +1 and +2, resulting in intermediate 253|2, then 63¼ quotient with fractional conversion 250 added to RHS to get 63252

key_reminders: Deviations are measured from the working base (250), not from the theoretical base.
When working base = theoretical base / n, the LHS must be divided by that same n.
A fractional remainder from the LHS division converts to that fraction of the theoretical base and is added to the RHS.
The RHS carries as many digits as the theoretical base has zeros.
common_mistakes: Writing the answer as 253252 by skipping the division of the LHS by 4.
Dropping the 1/4 remainder instead of converting it to 250 and adding it to the RHS of 2.
Padding the RHS to fewer than three digits, giving 6352 instead of 63252.

concept.technique_name: sentence-logic clue matching in text completion

examples.problem_statement: What readers most commonly remember about John Stuart Mill's classic exploration of the liberty of thought and discussion concerns the danger of (i) ______ : in the absence of challenge, one's opinions, even when they are correct, grow weak and flabby. Yet Mill had another reason for encouraging the liberty of thought and discussion: the danger of partiality and incompleteness. Since one's opinions, even under the best circumstances, tend to (ii) ______ , and because opinions opposed to one's own rarely turn out to be completely (iii) ______ , it is crucial to supplement one's opinions with alternative points of view. Blank (i): A tendentiousness, B complacency, C fractiousness. Blank (ii): D embrace only a portion of the truth, E change over time, F focus on matters close at hand. Blank (iii): G erroneous, H antithetical, I immutable.

solution.operation: Survey the passage and note that the first sentence is self-contained while the later sentences shift topic
solution.result: Blank (i) can be settled from sentence one alone
solution.description: Read the whole passage first to see how it divides: the opening sentence stands on its own, so the first blank is answerable before reading on, while the topic changes afterwards.

solution.operation: Read the colon after blank (i) as a signal that the following clause defines the blank
solution.result: The definition is 'in the absence of challenge, opinions grow weak and flabby'
solution.description: Use the punctuation clue: the colon announces that what follows names the very danger the blank labels, so the clause after it supplies the definition to match.

solution.operation: Match 'weak and flabby for want of challenge' against tendentiousness, complacency, fractiousness
solution.description: Test each first-blank option against that definition; unchallenged opinions make one complacent rather than tendentious or fractious, so complacency is the fit.

solution.operation: Read the next two sentences for the second danger Mill describes
solution.result: The theme is 'the danger of partiality and incompleteness'
solution.description: Scan forward to identify the controlling idea for the remaining blanks, which the passage states outright as partiality and incompleteness.

solution.operation: Fit blank (ii) to partiality: each person's opinion tends to embrace only a portion of the truth
solution.result: embrace only a portion of the truth (Choice D)
solution.description: Choose the second-blank option that expresses partiality itself, since that is the danger the sentence is explaining.

solution.operation: Fit blank (iii): opposing views are partially right, hence never completely erroneous
solution.description: Complete the parallel reasoning for the third blank, where saying opposing views are rarely completely wrong is what makes them worth consulting.

solution.operation: Reject E, F, H, I as dealing with change, immediacy, and antithesis
solution.result: Only B, D, G relate to partiality and incompleteness
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining options by showing that none of them touches the partiality-and-incompleteness theme that governs the second and third blanks.

examples.answer: Choice B: complacency; Choice D: embrace only a portion of the truth; Choice G: erroneous

key_reminders: A colon signals that the words after it define or explain the blank before it.
A self-contained opening sentence can be completed without reading the rest of the passage.
Later blanks are governed by the passage's explicitly stated theme, here 'partiality and incompleteness'.
common_mistakes: Choosing tendentiousness or fractiousness for blank (i), which describe combativeness rather than the flabbiness the colon defines.
Picking 'change over time' or 'focus on matters close at hand' for blank (ii), which address change and immediacy instead of partiality.
Picking 'antithetical' or 'immutable' for blank (iii) instead of the wrongness that 'rarely completely' negates.

concept.technique_name: relative ordering constraint chain

examples.problem_statement: In the relative ordering diagram for this game, what is the earliest position that T could occupy?

solution.operation: Read off the elements the diagram places before T: X, S, and W
solution.result: X, S and W must all come before T
solution.description: Trace the ordering constraints back from T to collect every element that the diagram forces to precede it.

solution.operation: Three elements occupy the positions ahead of T, so T is pushed to position 3 + 1
solution.description: Count the forced predecessors and place T immediately after them, since three slots must be filled before T can appear.

key_reminders: Every element that a chain places before T must occupy an earlier slot than T.
The earliest slot for an element is one more than the count of elements forced to precede it.
common_mistakes: Answering 3RD by counting the predecessors X, S and W as the position number instead of the slots ahead of T.

concept.technique_name: area by decomposition into rectangles

examples.problem_statement: What is the area of the region shown above? (The figure is an L-shaped region: a full rectangle of length 15 and width 8 sits on top of a further strip of length 9 and width 12 - 8, so the overall bounding rectangle measures 15 by 12 with a 6 by 4 corner removed.)

solution.operation: split the region into rectangle R and rectangle S
solution.result: area of region = area of R + area of S
solution.description: Cut the L-shaped region along the internal edge so it becomes two non-overlapping rectangles; the total area is then just the sum of the two rectangle areas.
Multiply the length 15 by the width 8 to get the area of rectangle R.
Find the width of rectangle S by subtracting the width already used by rectangle R from the overall width 12.
Multiply rectangle S's length 9 by the width 4 just found to get its area.
Add the two rectangle areas to get the area of the whole region.
Check with the book's second approach: take the full 15 by 12 rectangle and subtract the missing 6 by 4 corner rectangle; the same 156 confirms the decomposition.

key_reminders: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
A composite region can be split into non-overlapping rectangles whose areas add.
The same region can be handled by completing it to a full rectangle and subtracting the removed piece.
common_mistakes: Using the full overall width 12 for rectangle S instead of the leftover 12 - 8 = 4.
Using the full length 15 for the removed corner rectangle instead of 15 - 9 = 6.
Multiplying 15 by 12 and reporting 180 as the answer, forgetting the missing corner.

concept.technique_name: compound interest with half-yearly compounding

examples.problem_statement: In what time will Rs 6250 amount to Rs 6632.55 at 4 p.c. compound interest payable half-yearly?

solution.description: Write the compound interest equation using the half-yearly rate: the annual 4 percent is halved to 2 percent per period, and t counts half-yearly periods.
Divide both sides by the principal and clear the decimals so the left side is a plain fraction of whole numbers.
Reduce the fraction and recognise it as an exact cube of 51/50; matching the exponents on both sides gives the number of half-yearly periods.
Convert back from half-yearly periods to years by halving t, since compounding half-yearly replaced r by r/2 and t by 2t.

key_reminders: For half-yearly compounding, use rate r/2 per period and count 2t periods.
A = P(1 + r/100)^t with r and t taken per compounding period.
Reduce the amount-to-principal ratio to a fraction and match it against powers of the growth factor to read off the exponent.
common_mistakes: Using 4 percent per period instead of halving it to 2 percent for half-yearly compounding.
Reporting t = 3 as 3 years instead of dividing by 2 to get 3/2 years.
Failing to recognise 132651/125000 as (51/50)^3 and abandoning the exact match.

concept.technique_name: difference series / perfect squares recognition

examples.problem_statement: Preliminary screening: look at the series and give the next term. 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, ?

solution.description: Subtract each term from the next to expose the difference pattern; the gaps are consecutive odd numbers.
Continue the odd-number pattern to get the difference that leads to the missing term.
Add that next difference to the last given term to produce the answer.
Confirm with the book's second approach: the terms are consecutive perfect squares, so the eighth term is 8 squared.

key_reminders: First-difference chains often reveal the rule at a glance.
Consecutive odd differences are the signature of a perfect-square series.
Preliminary screening: try recognising the pattern by sight before any calculation.
common_mistakes: Adding the last observed difference 13 again instead of advancing it to 15, giving 62.
Reading the series as 7^2 next and answering 49 twice, losing track of the term index.

concept.technique_name: solving a linear function equation for its input

examples.problem_statement: f(x) = 2x - 3 and f(m) = -11. Quantity A: the value of m. Quantity B: half the value of f(m). Compare the two quantities.

solution.description: Plug m into the rule f(x) = 2x - 3 and set the output equal to the given value -11, turning the function statement into a linear equation.
Add 3 to both sides to clear the constant term and leave the m-term alone on the left.
Divide both sides by 2 to isolate m, which is the value Quantity A asks for.
Quantity B is defined as half of f(m), and the problem states f(m) = -11, so halve -11 to get Quantity B.
Compare the two values on the number line: -4 lies to the right of -5.5, so Quantity A is greater.

key_reminders: f(m) = -11 means substituting m into the rule produces -11, so 2m - 3 = -11.
Quantity B uses the output f(m) = -11, not the input m.
For negative numbers, the one closer to zero is the greater one.
common_mistakes: Halving m (-4) instead of f(m) (-11) when building Quantity B.
Treating -5.5 as greater than -4 because 5.5 exceeds 4 in absolute value.

concept.technique_name: units digit of a factorial sum and of its powers

solution.result: every term from 5! onward contributes 0 to the units digit
solution.description: Note that each factorial from 5! upward contains the factors 2 and 5, so it ends in 0; all those terms can be dropped when only the units digit is wanted.
Add and subtract only the surviving terms 1!, 2!, 3! and 4! with their given signs to get the units digit of N.
Since N ends in 1, raising it to any power leaves the units digit unchanged, so N^N also ends in 1.

key_reminders: Any factorial 5! or higher ends in 0, so it never affects a units digit.
A number ending in 1 keeps units digit 1 under every positive power.
common_mistakes: Attempting to evaluate the full alternating factorial sum instead of truncating at 4!.
Dropping the alternating signs and computing 1 + 2 + 6 + 4 for the leading terms.

concept.technique_name: approximation by rounding to tens
concept.sub_category: approximate values in addition and subtraction

solution.description: The answer choices are spread far apart, so round each value to the nearest ten; the first value is rounded up and the second rounded down so the two errors offset.
Work in units of ten: add the two rounded known values as tens, giving 409 tens.
Subtract that total from the right-hand side expressed in tens to find the missing value in tens.
Multiply back by 10 to return the missing value to ordinary units, matching choice 1.

key_reminders: Approximate only as coarsely as the spread of the answer choices allows.
Round one addend up and another down so the rounding errors cancel.
Small changes in the last rounded value do not shift the answer when the choices are far apart.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the tens-scale result 134 back by 10.
Rounding both known addends in the same direction so the errors accumulate instead of cancelling.

concept.technique_name: point-on-line test by substitution
concept.sub_category: coordinate plane: verifying a point lies on a line

examples.problem_statement: True or False? The point (9, 21) is on the line y = 2x + 1.

solution.description: Set up the test the book prescribes: if the point really lies on the line, substituting its coordinates into the equation must produce a true statement, so plug x = 9 and y = 21 into y = 2x + 1.
Evaluate the right-hand side of the substituted equation to see what the line actually yields at x = 9.
Compare the point's y-value with the value the line produces. The outcome of the substitution is false, so the point (9, 21) does not fall on this line.

key_reminders: A point lies on a line only if substituting its coordinates makes the line's equation a true statement.
Substitute both coordinates, not just one: x goes in for x and y for y.
A false outcome after substitution is itself the answer; no further algebra is needed.
common_mistakes: Reading 21 as 'close enough' to 2(9) + 1 = 19 and calling it True; a point is either exactly on the line or not.
Substituting 9 for y and 21 for x, which reverses the ordered pair.

concept.technique_name: slot method (fundamental counting principle)
concept.sub_category: combinatorics: counting integers under digit constraints

examples.problem_statement: How many integers between 2,000 and 6,999 are even and have a digit that is a prime number in the tens place?

solution.description: Treat this as a combinatorics problem: every number in the range is a four-digit number, so draw four slots and count the possibilities allowed in each one.
Fill the thousands slot first. Because the number lies between 2,000 and 6,999, it must begin with 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6, giving 5 possibilities.
Fill the tens slot next. The tens digit must be prime, and there are only four prime single-digit numbers, so there are 4 options.
Fill the units slot. Saying a four-digit number is even is simply saying it ends in an even digit, so the final digit has 5 possibilities.
Fill the hundreds slot last. No restriction was placed on it, so all 10 digits from 0 to 9 are allowed.
Multiply the counts of the four independent slots together to get the total number of qualifying integers.

key_reminders: With independent digit slots, multiply the number of options per slot rather than adding them.
The single-digit primes are 2, 3, 5, and 7 only.
A multi-digit integer is even exactly when its units digit is even.
A slot with no stated restriction still contributes a factor of 10, not 1.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the unrestricted hundreds slot and reporting 5 x 4 x 5 = 100.
Counting 1 as prime and using 5 options in the tens place.
Reading 'between 2,000 and 6,999' as excluding the endpoints and dropping the leading digits 2 or 6.

concept.technique_name: pick numbers to test a quantitative comparison
concept.sub_category: quantitative comparison: number properties of negatives

examples.problem_statement: x < 0. Quantity A: x^3. Quantity B: x. Choose (A) if Quantity A is greater, (B) if Quantity B is greater, (C) if the two quantities are equal, or (D) if the relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: x < 0 \Rightarrow x \text{ may be a negative fraction or a negative integer}
solution.result: \text{more than one kind of value is allowed}
solution.description: Read what the given information actually pins down. It defines x as negative but does not say whether x is a fraction or an integer, which is the signal to pick more than one number.
Pick the first permitted number, x = -1, and evaluate both quantities with it.
Compare the two results from this case. They are equal, so neither quantity is always greater and both of those answer choices are ruled out.
Pick a second permitted number, x = -2, and evaluate both quantities again to test whether the first case's outcome always holds.
Compare the results of the second case. They are not equal, so the quantities are not always equal and that choice is ruled out too.
Collect the eliminations: two permitted values of x gave different relationships, so the relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

key_reminders: When a quantitative comparison constrains only the sign of a variable, test both a fraction and an integer of that sign.
Two picked values that give different relationships are enough to force the 'cannot be determined' choice.
A single case that makes the quantities equal eliminates 'A is greater' and 'B is greater' at once.
common_mistakes: Testing only x = -2, seeing x^3 < x, and choosing (B).
Assuming x must be an integer and never trying a value like -1 or a negative fraction.
Mishandling the sign of the cube and treating (-2)^3 as 8 rather than -8.

concept.technique_name: clue-word and pivot analysis for multi-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: The more deeply one delves into the relevant literature, the more apparent it becomes that psychoanalysis is a practice (i) ___________. Even tenets that some might deem (ii) __________ to the general philosophy, such as the notion that the human psyche is primarily governed by conflicting desires and is formed in large part by early childhood experiences, are by no means accepted as gospel, even by some of its most (iii) ___________. Blank (i): teeming with ridicule / devoid of substance / rife with contention. Blank (ii): critical / immaterial / anathema. Blank (iii): esteemed beneficiaries / quarrelsome factions / seasoned practitioners.

solution.operation: Extract the revealing clue words: gospel, tenet, even
solution.result: gospel = "accepted fact" or "agreed-upon truth"; tenet = "accepted principle"; even = a pivot signalling contrast
solution.description: Before touching any blank, pin down the words that carry the sentence's logic. Note that gospel here takes its secondary sense of agreed-upon truth rather than its religious sense, that tenet also means an accepted principle, and that even flags a relationship of surprise.

solution.operation: Apply the pivot even to blank (ii): the tenets deemed ___ are by no means accepted as gospel, and that should be surprising
solution.description: Start with the second blank because even tells you to be surprised that these tenets are not accepted truth. Surprise only arises if the tenets are crucial to the general philosophy, so the blank must mean central or critical.

solution.operation: Apply the second even to blank (iii): even the most ___ do not accept the central tenets
solution.description: Again the even marks something contrary to expectation, so fill the blank with the group you would most expect to subscribe to the field's central tenets: the people most experienced in it, the seasoned practitioners.

solution.operation: Carry the second sentence's disagreement back into blank (i): psychoanalysis is a practice ___
solution.description: With blanks (ii) and (iii) settled, the second sentence establishes that even the most experienced practitioners disagree about the fundamental tenets. Describe the field accordingly as subject to great debate.

examples.answer: Rife with contention, critical, seasoned practitioners

key_reminders: In this context gospel means accepted fact or agreed-upon truth, not the religious sense.
A tenet is an accepted principle of a field.
The word even is a pivot signalling a relationship contrary to expectation; use it to set the direction of the blank.
common_mistakes: Filling blank (i) first, when the even pivot makes blank (ii) the only blank with a determinate clue.
Reading gospel in its religious sense and losing the accepted-truth logic that drives blank (ii).
Choosing quarrelsome factions for blank (iii): the sentence needs the group you would expect to agree, not one already defined by disagreement.

concept.technique_name: factoring out a common power, then prime factorization

examples.problem_statement: If x = 4^{20} + 4^{21} + 4^{22}, what is the greatest prime factor of x?

solution.description: All three terms contain 4^{20}, so pull that common power out of the sum, leaving each term divided by 4^{20} inside the parentheses.
Evaluate the small powers inside the parentheses and add them, which collapses the bracket to the single number 21.

solution.operation: Take the prime factors of each part of 4^{20}(21)
solution.result: prime factors are 2 from 4^{20}, and 3 and 7 from 21
solution.description: Read off the primes of the factored form: the 4^{20} term contributes only 2, and the 21 term contributes 3 and 7.
Pick the largest of the three prime factors found.

key_reminders: A sum of powers with the same base can be factored by pulling out the lowest power.
The prime factors of a product are the union of the prime factors of its factors.
4^{20} contributes only the prime 2, since 4 = 2^{2}.
common_mistakes: Trying to evaluate 4^{20} + 4^{21} + 4^{22} numerically instead of factoring out the common power.
Stopping at 21 and reporting 21 as the answer without splitting it into 3 and 7.

concept.technique_name: key-phrase matching for sentence equivalence

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Some scientists argue that carbon compounds play such a central role in life on Earth because of the possibility of ______ resulting from the carbon atom's ability to form an unending series of different molecules. Choices: A diversity, B deviation, C variety, D reproduction, E stability, F invigoration.

solution.operation: Locate the phrase that governs the blank: "the ability to form an unending series of different molecules"
solution.result: the blank must name what an unending series of different molecules makes possible
solution.description: Find the part of the sentence that tells you how to fill the blank; here the trailing phrase about unending and different molecules is the key indicator.

solution.result: diversity and variety both fit logically
solution.description: Check which words follow from many different molecules. Diversity and variety clearly do, and each produces a sentence that means the same as the other.

solution.operation: Check whether any other pairing of the six choices yields two sentences alike in meaning
solution.result: no other pair produces sentences as similar in meaning
solution.description: Sentence equivalence requires a matched pair, so confirm that the remaining choices cannot be paired into two equivalent sentences before committing.

examples.answer: Choice A: diversity AND Choice C: variety

key_reminders: The correct pair must both fit the sentence and produce two sentences alike in meaning.
Fill the blank from the sentence's own key phrase rather than from general plausibility.
common_mistakes: Selecting a single word that fits well without checking that a second choice makes a sentence alike in meaning.
Picking deviation on the strength of "different" alone, which does not match the sense of an unending series of molecules.

concept.technique_name: synonym-pair matching with contrast signal

examples.problem_statement: Select the TWO answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Deacon attempts what seems impossible: a book rich in scientific insights, in a demanding discipline, that nevertheless is accessible to ______ . (A) skeptics (B) experts (C) nonspecialists (D) zealots (E) authorities (F) laypersons

solution.operation: Mark the signal word "nevertheless" that sits immediately before the blank
solution.result: The blank must name an audience whose access to the book contrasts with its scientific richness and demanding discipline
solution.description: Locate the pivot word and read off what logical relationship it imposes: "nevertheless" announces that the accessibility clashes with the book's difficulty, so the audience named in the blank has to be one you would not expect to reach.

solution.operation: Sort the six choices into synonym pairs: experts / authorities, and nonspecialists / laypersons
solution.result: Two candidate pairs survive; skeptics and zealots are left with no partner
solution.description: Because the question demands two choices that yield alike meanings, pair the options up first. Only two genuine pairings exist, which narrows the work to testing those two pairs.
