solution.operation: Test the pairing experts / authorities against the required contrast
solution.result: No contrast is produced — a book rich in scientific insights being accessible to experts is unsurprising
solution.description: Substitute the first pair and check it against the demand set up in step 1. Since specialists would naturally follow a demanding scientific book, this pair fails to deliver the clash "nevertheless" promises.

solution.operation: Test the pairing nonspecialists / laypersons against the required contrast
solution.result: The contrast holds — writing a dense scientific book accessible to those outside the field is the feat the sentence calls impossible
solution.description: Substitute the second pair and re-check the same demand. Accessibility to readers not in the discipline is exactly the unexpected outcome, so this pair supplies the necessary contrast.

solution.result: Both are ruled out on two counts: neither has a synonym among the remaining choices, and neither builds the required contrast
solution.description: Clear away the unpaired options explicitly so the answer rests on the surviving pair alone; note that they fail the equivalence requirement and the logic requirement at once.

examples.answer: Choice C: nonspecialists AND Choice F: laypersons

key_reminders: A contrast word such as "nevertheless" tells you the blank must oppose, not echo, the surrounding description.
Sentence Equivalence requires two choices that produce sentences alike in meaning, so a choice with no synonym partner cannot be correct.
Both requirements must hold at once: the pair must be synonymous AND must satisfy the sentence's logic.
common_mistakes: Picking experts/authorities because they fit the "scientific insights" vocabulary, ignoring that "nevertheless" demands the opposite audience.
Choosing a single well-fitting word such as skeptics without checking whether a synonym partner exists among the other five choices.

concept.technique_name: boldface role analysis (fact/opinion secondary method plus conclusion mapping)

examples.problem_statement: Answer using the 4-step Critical Reasoning process. Many people praise High Renaissance painting for creating very realistic images from observation, but [BOLDFACE 1] scholars have documented that some High Renaissance painters used pinhole cameras to project the likeness of their subjects onto the canvas and painted from there. Thus, people who credit High Renaissance painters with superior artistic skills are misguided. [BOLDFACE 2] Painting from a projected image requires only an insignificant amount of additional skill beyond that needed to copy a picture outright. In the argument given, the two boldfaced portions play which of the following roles? (A) The first is a finding that has been used to support a conclusion that the argument rejects; the second is a claim that supports that conclusion. (B) The first is a finding that has been used to support a conclusion that the argument rejects; the second is that conclusion. (C) The first is a claim put forth to support a conclusion that the argument rejects; the second is a consideration that is introduced to counter the force of that evidence. (D) The first is evidence that forms the basis for the position that the argument seeks to establish; the second is a claim presented to solidify that position. (E) The first is evidence that forms the basis for the position that the argument seeks to establish; the second is that position.

solution.operation: Identify the question type from the stem wording "the two boldfaced portions play which of the following roles"
solution.result: This is a Describe the Role question
solution.description: Read the question stem before the argument. The word "boldfaced" together with the boldface font signals a Role question, which tells you to track how each boldface functions relative to the author's conclusion.

solution.operation: Map the opening: "Many people praise High Renaissance painting for creating very realistic images from observation"
solution.result: Background note — many people like High Renaissance pictures because they look realistic
solution.description: Write down the first piece plainly. The "many people" opener signals a contrast is coming, so record the popular view as the position the author will push against.

solution.operation: Map the first boldface: scholars documented that some painters projected images onto the canvas and painted from there
solution.result: A documented fact: some painters projected and traced rather than painting purely from observation
solution.description: Capture the first boldface as its own unit and note its character. It reports what scholars documented, so it is a fact, and it cuts against the praise recorded in step 2.

solution.operation: Map the "Thus" sentence: people who credit High Renaissance painters with superior artistic skills are misguided
solution.description: The connector "thus" marks the author's own position. Note also that the previous sentence covered only some painters while this one condemns the credit given generally, which is the argument's weak joint.

solution.operation: Map the second boldface: painting from a projected image requires only an insignificant amount of additional skill beyond copying a picture outright
solution.result: An opinion that supports the conclusion, not the conclusion itself
solution.description: Classify the last sentence. Since the conclusion was already stated in step 4, this sentence functions as support for it, and its evaluative wording ("insignificant") marks it as an opinion rather than a fact.

solution.operation: State the goal: first boldface = fact FOR the author's conclusion; second boldface = opinion FOR the author's conclusion
solution.result: Both boldfaces are premises supporting the author's position
solution.description: Before touching the choices, fix what the right answer must say. Both statements point the same direction, and the fact/opinion split gives a secondary filter for eliminating choices.

solution.result: (C) calls the first boldface a claim rather than a fact; (B) and (E) both label the second boldface as the conclusion itself
solution.description: Apply the two labels from step 6 to each choice. A "claim" is an opinion, so (C) mislabels the first boldface, and (B) and (E) mislabel the supporting opinion as the conclusion it supports.

solution.operation: Compare the survivors (A) and (D) on the phrase "a conclusion that the argument rejects"
solution.result: (A) is eliminated because the argument endorses, not rejects, the conclusion both boldfaces support; (D) stands
solution.description: The fact/opinion filter cannot separate the last two, so return to the main technique: both boldfaces support the author's own conclusion, so the answer describing that conclusion as rejected must go.

key_reminders: Find and label the author's conclusion before evaluating any answer choice.
A statement that supports the conclusion is not the conclusion, no matter how strongly worded it is.
"Finding" and "evidence" can describe a fact; "claim" describes an opinion — use the fact/opinion split as a secondary filter when the main analysis leaves two choices standing.
common_mistakes: Selecting (A) because its fact/opinion labels fit, without noticing that it says the argument rejects the conclusion the boldfaces support.
Treating the second boldface as the conclusion because it is the final sentence, when the conclusion is the earlier "Thus" sentence.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion solved out of order from the most constrained blank

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The serious study of popular culture by intellectuals is regularly credited with having rendered obsolete a once-dominant view that popular culture is inherently inferior to high art. Yet this alteration of attitudes may be somewhat (i) ______ . Although it is now academically respectable to analyze popular culture, the fact that many intellectuals feel compelled to rationalize their own (ii) ______ action movies or mass-market fiction reveals, perhaps unwittingly, their continued (iii) ______ the old hierarchy of high and low culture. Blank (i): A counterproductive, B underappreciated, C overstated. Blank (ii): D penchant for, E distaste for, F indifference to. Blank (iii): G aversion to, H investment in, I misunderstanding of.

solution.operation: Frame the passage: the author scrutinizes the claim that academic study of popular culture has raised its once lowly status
solution.result: The author's stance is skeptical of the reported change in how popular culture and high art are valued
solution.description: Read the whole text for its argumentative posture before filling anything in. Fixing that the author doubts the reported change gives the direction every blank must respect.

solution.operation: Attack Blank (iii) first, using the word "continued" that precedes it
solution.result: "investment in" — the only choice expressing an unchanged attachment to a hierarchy the first sentence calls once-dominant
solution.description: Start with the blank carrying the strongest local clue. "Continued" requires something that persists from before, and since the hierarchy was previously dominant, a continued investment in it is what carries over.

solution.operation: Eliminate "aversion to" (G) and "misunderstanding of" (I) for Blank (iii)
solution.result: Both are unsupported — the passage never says intellectuals long held an aversion to or misunderstanding of the hierarchy
solution.description: Check the two rejected options against the same word "continued." Each would require a prior long-held aversion or misunderstanding that the text never establishes, so neither can be what continues.

solution.operation: Use the "Although" opening of the last sentence to fix Blank (ii)
solution.result: "penchant for" — needing to justify a liking for action movies or mass-market fiction reveals allegiance to the hierarchy
solution.description: The concessive "although" sets the respectability of analyzing popular culture against something that nonetheless betrays continued allegiance. Only a liking that intellectuals feel compelled to explain away shows that allegiance; a distaste for or indifference to such works would need no rationalizing.

solution.operation: Return to Blank (i) now that the argument of the final sentence is settled
solution.result: "overstated" — since the hierarchy is not in fact obsolete, the reported shift in attitudes is exaggerated
solution.description: Fill the first blank last, from the conclusion the rest of the passage supports. "Underappreciated" says the opposite, and "counterproductive" judges the hierarchy's value while the passage is concerned only with whether it still exists.

examples.answer: Choice C: overstated; Choice D: penchant for; Choice H: investment in

key_reminders: Fill the blank with the strongest textual clue first, not necessarily blank (i); the answers may then cascade.
"Continued" requires something that persists from a state the passage has already established.
A concessive "although" demands that the two halves of the sentence pull against each other.
common_mistakes: Choosing "distaste for" at Blank (ii) on the assumption that intellectuals look down on action movies, when the sentence says they rationalize their own behavior — which only makes sense if they like such works.
Choosing "underappreciated" at Blank (i), which reverses the author's skepticism about the reported change.

concept.technique_name: cube root extraction by the Beejank method with even-number reduction

examples.problem_statement: Using the Cube Root Extraction (Beejank Method) technique: a two-step process for finding cube roots of even numbers. Given: original number = 7738893352; unit digit R = 9; left digit L = 9; R^3 = 729; 3R^2 = 3 \times 9^2 = 243; middle digit M = 8; cube root of the odd number = 989. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.description: For an even perfect cube, divide by 8 repeatedly until an odd number remains; this removes the ambiguity that even numbers introduce in the digit tables, and each division by 8 will be undone at the end.

solution.result: Three groups, read right to left
solution.description: Group the odd number in sets of three digits starting from the right. The leftmost group drives the leading digit of the root and the rightmost group drives the unit digit.

solution.operation: Read the unit digit R from Table 1 using the last digit of 967361669
solution.description: The final digit of a cube determines the final digit of its cube root uniquely, so look it up in Table 1 to obtain the unit digit of the root directly.
Compare the leftmost group against the cubes in Table 2 and take the largest cube not exceeding it; that cube's base is the leftmost digit of the root.

solution.operation: 967 - R^3 = 967 - 729 = 238, then bring down the next group
solution.result: A new dividend formed from 238 and the digits brought down
solution.description: Subtract the cube of the unit digit from the first group and append the following group, producing the working dividend from which the middle digit is extracted.

solution.operation: 3R^2 = 3 \times 9^2 = 243, then choose M so that the unit digit of 243M matches the required unit digit of the intermediate result
solution.description: Compute the multiplier 3R^2 and test digits for M, selecting the one whose product ends in the digit the intermediate result demands; this pins down the middle digit of the root.
Assemble the three digits in place order — leftmost, middle, unit — to form the cube root of the odd number produced in step 1.
Undo the division of step 1: dividing the original number by 8 divided its cube root by 2, so multiply the odd number's cube root by 2 to recover the cube root of the original number.

examples.answer: The cube root of 7738893352 is 1978, obtained by first dividing by 8 to get 967361669, then applying the Beejank method to find its cube root as 989, and finally multiplying by 2.

key_reminders: Dividing a perfect cube by 8 divides its cube root by 2, so every division by 8 must be repaid by a multiplication by 2 at the end.
The last digit of a perfect cube determines the last digit of its cube root uniquely (Table 1).
The leftmost digit of the root is the base of the largest cube not exceeding the leftmost three-digit group.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the final \times 2 and reporting 989 as the cube root of 7738893352.
Grouping the digits from the left instead of from the right, which misidentifies the leading group as 773 rather than 967 after the reduction.

concept.technique_name: paradox-driven pairing of two blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Certain music lovers yearn for (i) ______ , but when it is achieved, there is something missing; perhaps they feel uncomfortable in a world where nothing discernible is (ii) ______ . Blank (i): A novelty, B beauty, C flawlessness. Blank (ii): D wrong, E visionary, F changed.

solution.operation: Read the sentence structure: they yearn for something, "but when it is achieved, there is something missing"
solution.result: The sentence describes a contradiction or paradox
solution.description: Identify the shape of the sentence before testing any word. Getting what you want and then finding a cause for dissatisfaction is a paradox, and both blanks must work together to produce it.

solution.operation: Link the two blanks: achieving (i) must be what makes nothing discernible be (ii)
solution.result: The pair must be related so that the arrival of (i) removes (ii) from the world
solution.description: The second clause explains the dissatisfaction of the first, so the blanks cannot be chosen independently; the word in (ii) has to be the thing that the word in (i) abolishes.

solution.operation: Test the available combinations against that requirement
solution.description: Run through the choices looking for the one pairing where achieving the first eliminates the second; flawlessness is precisely a state in which nothing is wrong, and no other combination has that relationship.

solution.result: The music lovers long for flawlessness but are unsatisfied in a world where nothing is wrong
solution.description: Confirm the choice by substituting both words and rereading; the dissatisfaction now follows sensibly from the achievement, which is the paradox identified in step 1.

examples.answer: Choice C: flawlessness; Choice D: wrong

key_reminders: When a sentence says a wish is granted yet something is missing, the two blanks must be chosen as a linked pair, not one at a time.
The second blank should name exactly what achieving the first blank removes.
common_mistakes: Choosing "novelty" at Blank (i) and "changed" at Blank (ii), which describes a consistent situation rather than the paradox the sentence sets up.

concept.technique_name: extreme-value substitution on bounded ranges

examples.problem_statement: If 3 ≤ x ≤ 5 and 4 ≤ y ≤ 7. Find the greatest value of xy and the least value of x/y.

solution.description: Read the endpoints off each given range, since every extreme value of an expression in x and y will come from these boundary values.
The book's rule for the product: both x and y should be highest for xy to be maximum, so take each variable at its upper endpoint.
Multiply the two chosen maxima to get the greatest value of the product xy.
The book's rule for the quotient: x should be minimum and y should be maximum for x/y to be minimum, so pair the smallest numerator with the largest denominator.

key_reminders: A product of two positive quantities is largest when both factors are at their maximum.
A quotient is smallest when the numerator is at its minimum and the denominator at its maximum.
Extremes of such expressions occur at the endpoints of the given ranges, not inside them.
common_mistakes: Using y at its minimum (4) for the least value of x/y, giving 3/4 instead of 3/7.
Mixing the two rules and pairing x_max with y_max for the quotient as well as the product.

concept.technique_name: testing cases to eliminate must-be-true statements

examples.problem_statement: If |x| > |y|, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) xy is positive (B) x + y > 0 (C) x^2 > y^2

solution.description: Choose a first test case and double-check it against the stem's condition, so nothing you conclude rests on values that break the given fact.
Evaluate all three statements on this first case; every one of them holds, so none can be eliminated yet.
Pick a second case that still satisfies the stem but flips the sign of x, since the absolute value signs mean x and y may be positive or negative.
Evaluate the first two statements on the sign-flipped case; the product is negative and the sum is negative, so eliminate both (A) and (B).
Check the remaining statement on the same case; it still holds, and since only one choice is left you can stop testing there.

key_reminders: A "must be true" statement is disproved by a single valid counterexample.
|x| > |y| constrains only magnitudes, so both variables may still be positive or negative.
Stop testing cases once exactly one choice survives; there is always at least one correct answer.
common_mistakes: Testing only the all-positive case x = 5, y = 3, where all three statements happen to be true.
Reading |x| > |y| as x > y and concluding x + y > 0.

concept.technique_name: area of a border as a difference of rectangles

examples.problem_statement: The figure above represents a rectangular garden with a walkway around it. The garden is 18 feet long and 12 feet wide. The walkway is uniformly 3 feet wide, and its edges meet at right angles. What is the area of the walkway?

solution.description: Find the area of the smaller rectangle, which is the garden itself, from its given length and width in square feet.
Get the length of the larger rectangle by adding twice the walkway width to the garden's length, since the walkway runs along both ends.
Get the width of the larger rectangle the same way, adding twice the walkway width to the garden's width.
Multiply those outer dimensions to find the area of the garden and walkway combined, in square feet.
Subtract the garden's area from the combined area, because the walkway is exactly the region between the two rectangles.
Confirm with the book's second approach, cutting the walkway into four 3-by-3 corner squares plus two 18-by-3 and two 12-by-3 strips.

key_reminders: A uniform border's area equals the outer rectangle's area minus the inner rectangle's area.
A border of width w adds 2w to each outer dimension, not w.
The four corner squares must be counted once when decomposing a border into pieces.
common_mistakes: Adding the walkway width only once, using 21 by 15 instead of 24 by 18.
Decomposing the walkway into four strips and double-counting or omitting the four corner squares.
Reporting the garden's area, which is also 216, without performing the subtraction that justifies it.

concept.technique_name: sentence-logic vocabulary elimination

examples.problem_statement: The substitute French teacher accidentally walked into the wrong classroom, creating _________ situation when she began speaking French to 15 mystified physics students.

solution.operation: Read the situation the blank describes: a teacher speaking French to 15 mystified physics students in the wrong room
solution.result: the situation is an absurd, comical mix-up
solution.description: Extract from the sentence itself what kind of situation is being created, so the blank has a meaning to match: everyone is confused by French in a physics class, which is funny.

solution.operation: Match 'risible', which means laughable, against that comical mix-up
solution.result: risible fits and is the only choice that makes sense
solution.description: Test the candidate word by substituting its definition: calling the mix-up a laughable situation matches the confusion described, and no other option carries that meaning.

solution.operation: Check 'arch', which can mean mischievous, playful, roguish, against the word 'accidentally' in the sentence
solution.description: Rule out the one tempting alternative: arch implies deliberate playfulness, but the sentence says the teacher walked in accidentally, so that sense cannot apply.

key_reminders: Risible means laughable.
Arch means mischievous, playful, roguish.
A word only fits if it is consistent with every clue in the sentence, including adverbs like 'accidentally'.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'arch' for its playful sense while ignoring that the mix-up was accidental, not intentional.

concept.technique_name: inverse proportion wage sharing

examples.problem_statement: A can do a work in 6 days and B can do the same work in 5 days. The contract for the work is Rs 220. How much shall B get if both of them work together?

solution.operation: A's one day's work = \frac{1}{6}, B's one day's work = \frac{1}{5}
solution.description: Convert each person's total days into the fraction of the job done in a single day, since wages follow the work actually done.
Form the ratio of the two daily-work fractions and clear the denominators; this is the same as sharing in inverse proportion to the days taken, 6 and 5.
Add the ratio terms so the Rs 220 contract can be split into that many equal parts.
Give B the 6 parts of the ratio that belong to him: divide the contract by the 11 parts and multiply by B's 6.

key_reminders: Wages are distributed in proportion to the work done, hence in inverse proportion to the time each person takes.
The ratio 1/6 : 1/5 inverts to 5 : 6, so the faster worker takes the larger share.
common_mistakes: Splitting Rs 220 in the ratio 6 : 5 (the days) instead of 5 : 6, which hands B only Rs 100.

concept.technique_name: ratio from bar chart values

examples.problem_statement: The bar chart presents the total number of Boys and Girls in five different departments in a college. What is the respective ratio of number of girls from Philosophy department to the number of girls from Psychology department?

solution.operation: Read the girls bar for the Philosophy department: 140
solution.description: Pick off the girls value for Philosophy from the chart, ignoring the boys bar since the question asks only about girls.

solution.operation: Read the girls bar for the Psychology department: 240
solution.description: Pick off the girls value for the second named department, again taking only the girls bar.
Write the two girls counts as a ratio in the order asked and reduce by their common factor of 20, which matches option (b).

key_reminders: Read only the bar for the category asked about (girls), not the department total.
Keep the ratio in the order named in the question: Philosophy first, Psychology second.
common_mistakes: Reversing the order to 240 : 140 and picking 12 : 7, which is not among the options.
Reducing 140 : 240 only partially (for example to 14 : 24) and failing to reach 7 : 12.

concept.technique_name: percentage complement and weighted mixture

examples.problem_statement: Mixture A weighs 18 grams and is 50% aluminum. Mixture B weighs 32 grams and is 37.5% aluminum. The two mixtures are combined. Quantity A: the percent of the resultant combination that is not aluminum. Quantity B: 58%. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Take the complement of Mixture A's aluminum percentage, because the question asks for the part that is NOT aluminum.
Multiply Mixture A's 18 gram weight by its non-aluminum fraction 0.5 to get the grams of A that are not aluminum.
Take the complement of Mixture B's aluminum percentage and rewrite it as the fraction 5/8 to make the next multiplication clean.
Multiply Mixture B's 32 gram weight by its non-aluminum fraction 5/8 to get the grams of B that are not aluminum.

solution.result: 29 grams non-aluminum out of 50 total grams
solution.description: Add the two non-aluminum amounts, and separately add the two mixture weights, to get the part and the whole of the combination.

solution.result: Quantity A = 58\%, equal to Quantity B
solution.description: Convert the part-over-whole ratio to a percent by scaling the denominator to 100, then compare it with Quantity B.

key_reminders: If a mixture is p% one component, it is (100 - p)% everything else.
Combine mixtures by summing the component amounts and summing the total weights separately; percentages themselves do not add.
A fraction over 50 becomes a percent by doubling numerator and denominator to reach /100.
common_mistakes: Averaging 50% and 37.5% (or their complements) directly instead of weighting by the 18 g and 32 g masses.
Answering with the aluminum percentage (42%) instead of the NOT-aluminum percentage the question asks for.

concept.technique_name: cyclicity of unit digits

examples.problem_statement: The unit digit in 1^7 \times 2^7 \times 3^7 \times \dots \times 9^7 \times 11^7 \times 12^7 \dots 19^7 \times 21^7 \dots 99^7 is

solution.operation: Apply the cyclicity principle to the units digits of the factors
solution.result: Only units digits matter for the units digit of a product
solution.description: Recognise that the units digit of the whole product depends solely on the units digits of the factors, so the cyclicity principle applies.

solution.operation: Units digits of 1^7, 2^7, \dots, 9^7 repeat once for every block of ten numbers
solution.result: The pattern of 1^7 \times 2^7 \times \dots \times 9^7 repeats ten times
solution.description: Note that each range of ten numbers contributes the same set of units digits, so the same block repeats ten times across the expression.

solution.operation: Reduce the problem to the units digit of 1^7 \times 2^7 \times \dots \times 9^7
solution.result: One block of nine factors to evaluate
solution.description: Because the block repeats, check the units digit of a single block of 1^7 through 9^7 instead of the whole expression.

solution.operation: 1^7 \text{ ends in } 1,\; 2^7 \text{ ends in } 8,\; 3^7 \text{ ends in } 7,\; 4^7 \text{ ends in } 4,\; 5^7 \text{ ends in } 5
solution.description: List the units digit of each seventh power in the block, using the cyclicity of each base.
Multiply those units digits together; the block ends in 0, and since the same block repeats for the entire expression, the units digit of the whole product is 0.

key_reminders: The units digit of a product depends only on the units digits of its factors (cyclicity principle).
A repeating block of factors contributes the same units-digit pattern in every range of ten.
common_mistakes: Trying to evaluate the seventh powers themselves instead of tracking only units digits.
Overlooking that the block from 1 to 9 repeats identically for 11-19, 21-29, and so on, and attempting to treat each decade separately.

concept.technique_name: squaring a binomial identity

examples.problem_statement: When x + \frac{1}{x} = 3, find the value of x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2}. Options: 1) 3  2) 6  3) 9  4) 27  5) None of these

solution.description: Square both sides of the given equation so that the squared terms you need appear.
Expand the squared binomial; the cross term 2 \cdot x \cdot (1/x) simplifies to the constant 2.
Subtract the constant cross term from both sides to isolate the requested expression.

key_reminders: For a = x and b = 1/x the cross term 2ab collapses to the constant 2.
common_mistakes: Reporting 9, the square of 3, as the answer without subtracting the cross term.
Squaring termwise as x^2 + 1/x^2 = 9 and forgetting the 2ab middle term entirely.

concept.technique_name: successive percent change

examples.problem_statement: If y is decreased by 20% and then increased by 60%, what is the new number, expressed in terms of y ?

solution.description: No concrete value is specified, so assign y the smart number 100, which makes percent arithmetic direct.
Apply the first change: decreasing the assigned value by 20% means multiplying it by 1 - 0.20.
Apply the second change to the result of the first: increasing 80 by 60% means multiplying by 1 + 0.60.
Compare the final value with the starting value of 100 to read off the overall percentage change of the two successive steps.
Translate the overall 28% increase back into terms of y, since the original value 100 stood in for y; substituting y = 100 confirms the value 128.

key_reminders: When no concrete value is given, pick 100 for the unknown so percents convert to plain numbers.
Successive percents must be applied one after the other, each to the previous result, not added together.
An increase of p% is a multiplication by 1 + p/100; a decrease of p% is a multiplication by 1 - p/100.
common_mistakes: Adding the changes as -20\% + 60\% = +40\% and answering 1.4y instead of chaining the multipliers.
Applying the 60% increase to the original 100 rather than to the reduced value 80.

concept.technique_name: weighted average by repeated counting

examples.problem_statement: In Clarice's class, each test weights her overall grade average three times as much as each quiz does. If Clarice scored 88 and 94 on two quizzes, respectively, and she scored 90 on the only test, what is her current overall grade average?

solution.result: the test score 90 is counted three times
solution.description: Account for the triple weighting by treating the single test as if it were three identical quizzes scoring 90 each.
Count the total number of quiz-equivalents: the 2 real quizzes plus the 3 that stand in for the test, giving the denominator of the average.
Add all five quiz-equivalent scores, listing the test score three times to carry its weight.
Divide the weighted sum by the 5 quiz-equivalents to get the overall grade average.

key_reminders: A weighted average is the sum of all values divided by the total weight, not by the number of distinct assessments.
An item weighted three times as much can simply be listed three times in both the sum and the count.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 3 (the number of actual scores) instead of 5, the total quiz-equivalents.
Taking the plain average of 88, 94, and 90 and reporting 90.67, ignoring the test's triple weight.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence via causal-clue reasoning

examples.problem_statement: For questions 1 to 8, select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks. There may be a threshold below which blood pressure reductions become ______, given that a long-running study showed no decreased heart risk for drops in blood pressure below a certain point.

solution.operation: identify the role of the clause beginning "given that"
solution.result: it supplies the reason for the conclusion stated in the first part of the sentence
solution.description: Read the sentence structurally: the second clause is evidence, so the blank must be consistent with what that evidence supports.

solution.operation: extract the study finding: "no decreased heart risk for drops in blood pressure below a certain point"
solution.result: below that point, further reductions bring no benefit
solution.description: State plainly what the cited study reports, since this is the fact the blank has to be justified by.

solution.operation: infer the property of reductions below the threshold
solution.description: Convert the study finding into the characterization the sentence needs for reductions past the threshold.

solution.operation: match "provide no benefit" to the answer choices
solution.description: Select the choice whose meaning matches the no-benefit characterization derived in the previous step.

key_reminders: A clause introduced by "given that" supplies the reason for the conclusion, so the blank must agree with that evidence.
Predict the meaning the blank needs from the sentence's own logic before looking at the choices.
common_mistakes: Choosing "indiscernible", which describes the reductions themselves as undetectable, whereas the study reports that the reductions occur but yield no heart-risk benefit.
Choosing "significant" or "worthwhile", which reverse the no-decreased-risk evidence.

concept.technique_name: clue-driven blank matching in a three-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: According to supporters of progressive taxation, the payment of higher tax rates by those with higher incomes, those who (i) _________ such taxation systems tend to fall into two camps: the (ii) _________, who feel it unjust that the “most industrious” among us are “penalized” for their success, and the (iii) _________, who argue that higher taxes on the rich will harm us all by dampening the entrepreneurial spirit that drives the economy. Blank (i): rail against / vote for / depredate. Blank (ii): autodidacts / moralists / recidivists. Blank (iii): libertines / utilitarians / myrmidons.

solution.operation: Read the definition of progressive taxation given in the sentence, then read how the two camps are described: they “feel it unjust” that the “most industrious” are “penalized”
solution.result: The people named in blank (i) are definitely against progressive taxation
solution.description: Take the sentence's own description of the two camps as the clue that fixes the stance of the group in blank (i) before looking at any answer choice.

solution.operation: Test the blank (i) choices against the meaning “be against”: rail against, vote for, depredate
solution.description: Pick the blank (i) word that expresses opposition; the sentence's clue about feeling penalized rules out an approving word.

solution.operation: Match blank (ii) to the clue word “unjust”, and check the rejects: autodidacts are people who teach themselves, recidivists are people who return to committing crimes
solution.description: Use the justice language in the clause attached to blank (ii) to select the group defined by a moral objection, discarding the two words whose definitions have nothing to do with the sentence.

solution.operation: For blank (iii), find a second opposed group that differs from the moralists because it makes a practical argument — higher taxes harm us all by dampening the entrepreneurial spirit
solution.description: Select the blank (iii) word for people who judge by practical consequences rather than by justice, which is what distinguishes this camp from the one in blank (ii).

key_reminders: The clause attached to each blank supplies the clue for that blank; read it before the choices.
The second and third camps must both oppose progressive taxation yet differ in kind — moral objection versus practical objection.
A choice whose dictionary definition is irrelevant to the sentence is wrong no matter how hard the word is.
common_mistakes: Choosing “vote for” in blank (i) by reading the sentence as describing supporters of progressive taxation rather than the camps that object to it.
Picking “autodidacts” or “recidivists” for blank (ii) on the strength of difficulty alone, when neither definition connects to the word “unjust”.
Filling blank (iii) with another moral-sounding word instead of one that captures a practical, consequence-based argument.

concept.technique_name: contrast-clue sentence equivalence by elimination

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for the blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill the blank in the way that best completes the text. Even as the economy struggled, the secretary stood by his ______ long-term outlook, saying that technology was allowing businesses to make deep-rooted improvements in their productivity, the best indicator of an economy’s ability to grow. (A) arcane (B) sanguine (C) equivocal (D) ambivalent (E) irresolute

solution.operation: Set the current struggles of the economy against the secretary's predictions for its long-term prospects, as the word “Even” signals
solution.result: The blank must describe an outlook that runs counter to the present struggle
solution.description: Read the concessive opening as a contrast so the blank is anchored to the secretary's long-term view rather than to the economy's current state.

solution.operation: Read what the secretary says: technology is allowing deep-rooted productivity improvements, the best indicator of an economy's ability to grow
solution.result: The secretary believes technology will lead to economic growth, so his outlook is optimistic
solution.description: Use the second half of the sentence, which states the secretary's reasoning, to name the outlook precisely: optimistic.

solution.result: Choices C, D, E are out
solution.description: Discard the three words that imply wavering or openness to alternate interpretations, since nothing in the sentence indicates the secretary's view has wavered.
Drop the remaining wrong choice because the sentence explains the rationale for the outlook straightforwardly, so the outlook is not an obscure one.

solution.operation: Match the surviving choice to “optimistic”: sanguine
solution.description: Confirm that the one word left carries the meaning the clue demanded, which makes it the answer.

key_reminders: “Even as” marks a contrast: the blank opposes the struggling economy, not matches it.
The stated rationale in the second half of the sentence defines the blank; predict the meaning before reading the choices.
Sanguine can mean optimistic.
common_mistakes: Treating the struggling economy as the clue and choosing a doubt word such as equivocal, ambivalent, or irresolute.
Choosing arcane because the sentence sounds technical, even though its explanation of the outlook is plainly given.

concept.technique_name: drawing radii to form right triangles and applying the Pythagorean theorem
concept.sub_category: circles and right triangles in quantitative comparison

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. O is the center of the circle above, and x is the length of a line segment drawn from O to a point inside the circle (the figure supplies a right triangle with legs of length 3 and 4). Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 5. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: State the comparison: x is the length of a line segment from the center of the circle to a point inside the circle, to be compared with 5
solution.description: Fix what x actually measures in the figure before doing any computation, since it is a segment from the center to an interior point.

solution.operation: Draw two radii in the figure, each one completing a right triangle
solution.result: Two right triangles, one of them with both legs known
solution.description: Add the easiest segments to work with in a circle — the radii — so that the figure yields right triangles you can compute with.

solution.operation: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to the triangle whose legs have lengths 3 and 4 and whose hypotenuse is the radius r: r^2 = 3^2 + 4^2
solution.description: Use the triangle in which both leg lengths are known to set up an equation for the radius.

solution.operation: Take the positive square root: r = \sqrt{25}
solution.description: Solve for the radius, keeping only the positive root because a length cannot be negative.

solution.operation: Compare the segment of length x with the radius, since x is clearly shorter than the radius in the figure
solution.description: Read the size relation off the figure now that the radius has a number attached, which settles the comparison.

solution.operation: Alternatively, observe that the two right triangles are congruent, so x equals the leg of length 4
solution.description: Confirm the same conclusion by the congruence route, which pins x to an exact value instead of only bounding it.

examples.answer: Choice B: Quantity B is greater.

key_reminders: In a circle, the radius and the diameter are the easiest segments to work with; drawing radii often creates usable right triangles.
Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs.
Any segment from the center to a point strictly inside the circle is shorter than the radius.
common_mistakes: Comparing x with the leg lengths 3 and 4 instead of first computing that the radius is 5.
Assuming the relationship cannot be determined because x is not labeled with a number, when the 3-4 triangle determines the radius.
Concluding the quantities are equal by mistaking x for the radius rather than for a shorter interior segment.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The problem of avoiding duplicate names—such as for Internet domain names or for e-mail accounts—is particularly ______ when the name has to fit into a format that allows only a finite number of possibilities. Choices: A meager, B acute, C agreeable, D severe, E beneficial, F productive.

solution.operation: Read what the sentence says the blank must describe: the challenge of ensuring unique names under stated limitations
solution.result: The blank characterizes a problem, not a benefit
solution.description: Locate the noun the blank modifies — the problem of avoiding duplicate names — so you know the blank has to say something about a difficulty.

solution.operation: Use the 'when the name has to fit into a format that allows only a finite number of possibilities' clause as the directional clue
solution.result: The limitation adds to the difficulty, so the blank must reflect the arduousness of the task
solution.description: Read the closing clause: it names a restriction that makes duplicate-avoidance harder, which fixes the required meaning of the blank as 'intensely difficult'.

solution.operation: Test each choice against the required meaning 'arduous / intensified difficulty'
solution.result: acute and severe both indicate the added difficulty of the problem; meager, agreeable, beneficial and productive do not describe that difficulty
solution.description: Screen the six options one by one, keeping only those that characterize the problem as harder under the described circumstances and discarding the four that do not describe difficulty at all.

solution.operation: Check that the two surviving words produce completed sentences alike in meaning
solution.result: acute and severe form a matched pair yielding sentences with similar meanings
solution.description: Apply the Sentence Equivalence requirement to the survivors: substitute each into the sentence and confirm the two completed sentences say the same thing, which they do.

examples.answer: Choice B: acute; AND Choice D: severe

key_reminders: Sentence Equivalence needs two choices that both fit AND yield sentences alike in meaning.
The blank's direction is set by the clue clause — here, a limitation that increases difficulty.
A word that fits grammatically but has no synonym among the options cannot be part of the answer.
common_mistakes: Choosing a positively-valenced option such as agreeable, beneficial or productive when the clue clause describes an aggravating restriction.
Picking meager on the idea that a 'finite number of possibilities' is small, when the blank modifies the problem rather than the supply of names.

concept.technique_name: boldface role analysis (4-step Critical Reasoning process)

examples.problem_statement: Answer using the 4-step Critical Reasoning process. Innovative Design: Products with innovative and appealing designs relative to competing products can often command substantially higher prices in the marketplace. Because design innovations are quickly copied by other manufacturers, many consumer technology companies charge as much as possible for their new designs to extract as much value as possible from them. But large profits generated by the innovative designs give competitors stronger incentives to copy the designs. Therefore, the best strategy to maximize overall profit from an innovative new design is to charge less than the greatest possible price. In the argument above, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles? (A) The first is an assumption that supports a described course of action; the second provides a consideration to support a preferred course of action. (B) The first is a consideration that helps explain the appeal of a certain strategy; the second presents an alternative strategy endorsed by the argument. (C) The first is a phenomenon that makes a specific strategy unlikely to be successful; the second is that strategy. (D) The first is a consideration that demonstrates why a particular approach is flawed; the second describes a way to amend that approach. (E) The first is a factor used to rationalize a particular strategy; the second is a factor against that strategy.

solution.operation: Identify the question type from the wording 'the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles'
solution.result: This is a Role question — find the function of each bold statement
solution.description: Step 1 of the process: read the question stem first and classify it; the word boldface plus 'roles' marks it as a Describe the Role question.

solution.operation: Map sentence 1: innovative designs command substantially higher prices
solution.result: Between a fact and a claim — probably a premise; noted as 'Innov designs → higher price'
solution.description: Begin Step 2, deconstructing the argument: label the opening statement, which reads as background support rather than as anything the author is arguing for.

solution.operation: Map sentence 2: because innovations are quickly copied, many companies charge as much as possible
solution.result: Claim-based material whose first half supports its second half; not yet confirmed as the conclusion
solution.description: Label the second sentence, noticing the internal because-structure that makes the first half support the charge-maximum strategy stated in the second half.

solution.operation: Map sentence 3, opening with 'But': large profits give competitors stronger incentives to copy
solution.result: Contrast — a drawback of making very large profits
solution.description: Register the BUT as a pivot: the author is introducing a downside to the charge-the-maximum approach just described.

solution.operation: Map sentence 4, opening with 'Therefore': the best strategy is to charge less than the greatest possible price
solution.result: This is the conclusion; the second boldface = C (conclusion)
solution.description: Identify the conclusion from the Therefore signal and assign the second boldface its role — it is the strategy the argument itself endorses.

solution.operation: Assign the first boldface its role given that conclusion
solution.result: A premise supporting the rival strategy (charge the greatest possible price) that the argument disagrees with; labelled X
solution.description: Back-fill the first boldface's role: since the author argues against charging the maximum, the opening statement functions as support for the strategy the author opposes.

solution.operation: State the goal: find an answer giving X then C, in that order
solution.result: Want: premise supporting the alternate strategy, then the argument's own conclusion
solution.description: Step 3 of the process: fix the target before reading the choices, so each option is judged against a pre-set standard rather than reconsidered from scratch.

solution.operation: Test (A): first as an assumption supporting a described course of action; second as a consideration supporting a preferred course of action
solution.result: Eliminate — 'assumption' is tolerable, but the second is the actual conclusion, not another supporting consideration
solution.description: Step 4 begins, working from wrong to right: reject (A) because it demotes the conclusion to the status of a premise.

solution.operation: Test (B): first as a consideration explaining the appeal of a certain strategy; second as an alternative strategy endorsed by the argument
solution.result: Keep — the first does support the greatest-possible-price strategy, and the second is the strategy the argument supports
solution.description: Check (B) against the X-then-C target: the awkwardly worded first half still describes a premise backing the rival strategy, and the second half names the author's endorsed strategy.

solution.operation: Test (C): first as a phenomenon making a specific strategy unlikely to succeed
solution.result: Eliminate — the first boldface supports the first strategy rather than weakening any strategy
solution.description: Reject (C) because it casts the first boldface as an objection, whereas it actually provides support.

solution.operation: Test (D) and (E): (D) first demonstrates why an approach is flawed; (E) second is a factor against that strategy
solution.result: Eliminate both — (D) misreads the first boldface as illustrating a flaw; (E) misreads the second boldface as opposing the strategy when it is the author's own strategy
solution.description: Clear the last two choices on their decisive halves: (D) fails on its first half, so the second half need not be read, and (E) fails because the second boldface is the endorsed strategy, not an argument against one.

key_reminders: Find the conclusion first — Therefore marks it — then define each boldface relative to it.
A boldface that supports a strategy the author rejects is still a premise, just a premise for the opposing side.
Eliminate a choice as soon as one half misdescribes its boldface; the other half need not be read.
common_mistakes: Treating the second boldface (the Therefore sentence) as supporting evidence rather than as the argument's conclusion, which is what makes (A) tempting.
Assuming the first boldface opposes the author's strategy because the author ultimately disagrees with charging the maximum — the trap in (C) and (D).

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via clue words

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The lizards snapped up insects that are so (i) ______ that other potential predators avoid them. Among the lizards’ prey were some beetles that they initially (ii) ______ because the insects were spraying their hot, irritant defense chemical at the time. Yet even these produced no apparent ill effects, since the lizards, having eaten, proceeded on their way (iii) ______ enough. Blank (i): A rare, B nutritious, C noxious. Blank (ii): D sought, E rejected, F resembled. Blank (iii): G erratically, H laboriously, I nonchalantly.

solution.operation: Read what Blank (i) must describe: insects that other potential predators avoid
solution.result: The blank needs a word meaning harmful — 'noxious'
solution.description: Set the requirement for the first blank from the clause that follows it: predators avoid these insects, so the adjective must give a reason for avoidance.

solution.operation: Test the other Blank (i) options, rare and nutritious, against that requirement
solution.result: Eliminated — there is no reason to suspect predators would avoid rare or nutritious prey
solution.description: Reject the two rivals in column (i) because neither property would cause a predator to stay away.

solution.operation: Read Blank (ii) as the lizards' initial response to beetles they eventually ate, explained by the following 'because' clause about irritant spraying
solution.result: The response must be caused by the spraying — 'rejected' fits, since animals routinely avoid unpleasant stimuli
solution.description: Use the because-clause as the causal clue for the second blank: whatever the lizards did at first has to be a reaction to being sprayed with an irritant.

solution.operation: Test the other Blank (ii) options, sought and resembled
solution.result: Eliminated — lizards are unlikely to seek out prey with such defensive behavior, and nothing in the passage suggests the lizards share that behavior
solution.description: Discard the two rivals in column (ii): one contradicts the causal clue, the other imports a similarity the passage never mentions.

solution.operation: Read Blank (iii) through the 'since' clause, which supplies the evidence that eating the beetles did not harm the lizards
solution.result: The blank must describe post-meal movement suggesting the lizards were unharmed
solution.description: Identify what the third blank has to prove: since introduces the evidence for the claim of no ill effects, so the manner word must signal that the lizards were fine.

solution.result: Erratic or laborious locomotion would indicate the opposite, so 'nonchalantly' is correct
solution.description: Compare the three manner adverbs: two would be signs of distress and therefore contradict the sentence's claim, leaving the one that conveys unconcerned normality.

examples.answer: Choice C: noxious; Choice E: rejected; Choice I: nonchalantly

key_reminders: Each blank is fixed by an explicit connector: 'so...that' for (i), 'because' for (ii), 'since' for (iii).
The 'since' clause supplies evidence for the preceding claim, so blank (iii) must be consistent with no ill effects.
Fill the blank with the strongest clue first; the columns are independent, so a wrong choice in one does not force another.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'sought' for blank (ii) by reading 'snapped up' as eagerness, ignoring that the because-clause explains a deterrent.
Choosing 'erratically' or 'laboriously' for blank (iii) because the beetles sprayed an irritant, which reverses the sentence's stated finding of no ill effects.

concept.technique_name: fourth power by tabular column method with multipliers 3, 5, 3

examples.problem_statement: Using the Fourth Power Computation technique of Vedic Mathematics (tabular approach with specific coefficients): base number = 11, a = 1, b = 1, ratio b/a = 1, multipliers = 3, 5, 3. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Identify the number to be raised to the fourth power: (11)^4
solution.description: Write down what is being computed so the tabular layout is set up for a fourth power rather than a square or cube.

solution.operation: Set a = 1 and b = 1, the digits of 11
solution.description: Split the base number into its two parts a and b, which are the values the whole table will be built from.
Form the ratio of the second part to the first; it is the factor used to step from one column to the next.

solution.operation: Write the fourth power of a in the first column: 1^4
solution.description: Seed the table with a^4 in the leftmost column, which anchors the row of five entries.

solution.operation: Fill the remaining four columns by repeatedly multiplying by the ratio: 1 \times 1 in each column
solution.description: Propagate across the table by multiplying each entry by the ratio 1, giving the base row before the coefficients are applied.

solution.operation: Multiply the second column digit by 3: 1 \times 3
solution.description: Apply the first of the fixed multipliers 3, 5, 3 to the second column, producing the extra amount to be added there.

solution.operation: Multiply the third column digit by 5: 1 \times 5
solution.description: Apply the middle multiplier 5 to the third column, the largest coefficient in the pattern.

solution.operation: Multiply the fourth column digit by 3: 1 \times 3
solution.description: Apply the last multiplier 3 to the fourth column, mirroring what was done to the second column.
Sum the base row entry and the multiplier-derived entry within each column independently, keeping the five columns separate.

solution.operation: Read the result off the columns: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1
solution.description: Concatenate the column totals in order to read the final answer, since no column total exceeds 9 and therefore no carrying is required.

examples.answer: The fourth power of 11 is 14641, calculated using Vedic Mathematics tabular method with multipliers 3, 5, and 3 applied to columns.

key_reminders: The fourth-power table has five columns, seeded with a^4 and extended by the ratio b/a.
The fixed multipliers for the inner columns are 3, 5, 3 in that order.
Column totals are read off left to right as digits.
common_mistakes: Applying a multiplier to the first or fifth column; only the three inner columns take the 3, 5, 3 coefficients.
Ordering the multipliers as 3, 3, 5 rather than the symmetric 3, 5, 3, which would give 1, 4, 4, 6, 1 instead of 14641.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion via contrast clues

examples.problem_statement: Indicate the best answer for each blank. There is nothing quite like this movie, and indeed I am not altogether sure there is much more to it than its lovely (i) ______ . At a moment when so many films strive to be as (ii) ______ as possible, it is gratifying to find one that is so subtle and puzzling. Blank (i): A peculiarity, B pellucidity, C conventionality. Blank (ii): D indirect, E assertive, F enigmatic.

solution.operation: Collect the two descriptions the sentences give of the movie: 'nothing quite like it' and 'subtle and puzzling'
solution.result: Two clues that any choice must satisfy simultaneously
solution.description: Gather the explicit characterizations of the film before touching the columns, since both blanks are judged against these same clues.

solution.operation: Test Blank (i) options against 'nothing quite like it'
solution.result: 'Peculiarity' is a solid fit; 'conventionality' clearly does not work
solution.description: Match the first column to the uniqueness clue: a word meaning oddness fits, while a word meaning ordinariness directly contradicts it.

solution.operation: Test the remaining Blank (i) option, pellucidity, against 'subtle and puzzling'
solution.result: Eliminated — it could fit the first sentence in isolation but not the later claim that the movie is subtle and puzzling
solution.description: Check the surviving rival against the second clue rather than the first alone: clarity cannot describe a film the writer calls puzzling.

solution.operation: Read Blank (ii) as needing a contrast with 'subtle and puzzling'
solution.result: Only 'assertive' clearly provides that contrast, so it fills blank (ii)
solution.description: Use the contrast set up by 'it is gratifying to find one that is so subtle and puzzling' to require an opposite quality in the second blank, and pick the only option that supplies it.

examples.answer: Choice A: peculiarity; Choice E: assertive

key_reminders: A choice must fit every clue in the passage, not just the clause nearest the blank.
'At a moment when so many films strive to be...' sets up a contrast with the film being praised, so blank (ii) is the opposite of subtle and puzzling.
common_mistakes: Selecting 'pellucidity' for blank (i) because it reads as praise ('lovely'), overlooking that the movie is described as puzzling.
Selecting 'indirect' or 'enigmatic' for blank (ii), which restate 'subtle and puzzling' instead of contrasting with it.

concept.technique_name: HCF-LCM consistency check

examples.problem_statement: The HCF of two natural numbers a, b is 10 & LCM of these numbers is 45. If a = 15 then b = ?

solution.result: The pair of values that must satisfy the HCF-LCM relationship
solution.description: Write down the two quantities the question supplies about the pair a, b before attempting to solve for b.

solution.result: The LCM of two numbers is always a multiple of their HCF
solution.description: Apply the standing rule the book invokes: the HCF divides both numbers, so it must also divide their LCM.

solution.result: 45 is not a multiple of 10, so the rule is violated
solution.description: Test the given LCM against the given HCF; the quotient is not an integer, so the stated HCF and LCM cannot belong to the same pair of numbers.

solution.result: No such natural number b exists
solution.description: Conclude that because the data are internally impossible, no value of b can be produced from them.

key_reminders: The LCM of two numbers is always a multiple of their HCF.
Check the internal consistency of given HCF/LCM data before solving for the unknown.
common_mistakes: Reflexively using a \times b = \gcd \times \operatorname{lcm} to compute b = (10 \times 45)/15 = 30 without first noticing that 45 is not a multiple of 10.
Overlooking that the stated HCF of 10 cannot divide a = 15 either.

concept.technique_name: divisibility of consecutive integers
concept.sub_category: Divisibility and properties of consecutive integers

examples.problem_statement: What must be true about 3 consecutive positive integers? Indicate all such statements. (A) The product is a multiple of 3. (B) The sum is a multiple of 3. (C) The product is a multiple of 4. (D) The product is a multiple of 6.

solution.result: The product is divisible by 3 and by 2, hence by 6
solution.description: Among any three consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even, so the product carries both factors; this settles statements (A) and (D) as must-be-true.

solution.result: 24 is divisible by 4 but 6 is not
solution.description: Test statement (C) by running two concrete triples of consecutive integers rather than assuming the factor of 4 is always present.

solution.result: The triple 1, 2, 3 is a counterexample, so (C) need not be true
solution.description: Confirm the second triple fails divisibility by 4, which eliminates statement (C) since a single counterexample defeats a must-be-true claim.

solution.result: The sum of three consecutive integers equals 3n + 3
solution.description: Turn to statement (B), which concerns the sum, and add the three integers in standard consecutive-integer notation.

solution.result: The sum is always a multiple of 3, so (B) must be true
solution.description: Note that both 3n and 3 are multiples of 3, so their sum is a multiple of 3 for every integer n.

examples.answer: (A) the product is a multiple of 3; (B) the sum is a multiple of 3; (D)

key_reminders: Among any three consecutive integers, exactly one is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even, so the product is always a multiple of 6.
A sum of two multiples of 3 is itself a multiple of 3.
One counterexample is enough to defeat a 'must be true' statement.
common_mistakes: Assuming the product of three consecutive integers is always a multiple of 4 because the case (2)(3)(4) = 24 happens to work, while (1)(2)(3) = 6 does not.
Applying the product reasoning to statement (B), which asks about the sum rather than the product.

concept.technique_name: fraction of a fraction via smart numbers

examples.problem_statement: A pot of soup is divided equally into two bowls. If Manuel eats 1/4 of one of the bowls of soup and 2/5 of the other bowl of soup, how much of the soup did Manuel eat?

solution.description: Pick a convenient total with many factors, since the amount will be divided several times, then split it equally between the two bowls.

solution.result: 15 ounces eaten from the first bowl
solution.description: Take the stated one-quarter share of the first bowl.

solution.result: 24 ounces eaten from the second bowl
solution.description: Take the stated two-fifths share of the other bowl.

solution.result: 39 ounces eaten out of the 120-ounce pot
solution.description: Add the two amounts to get the total quantity Manuel ate.
Express the amount eaten as a fraction of the whole pot and reduce by dividing numerator and denominator by 3.

key_reminders: Each bowl is one half of the whole pot, so a fraction of one bowl is that fraction of one half of the total.
When picking a number for an unspecified total, choose one divisible by every denominator in play (here 2, 4, and 5).
The final answer must be expressed relative to the whole pot, not to a single bowl.
common_mistakes: Adding 1/4 and 2/5 directly to get 13/20, which measures the shares against a single bowl instead of the whole pot.
Leaving the answer as 39/120 when the reduced form 13/40 is expected (though equivalent fractions are accepted here).

concept.technique_name: Pythagorean theorem to find a rectangle side, then area
concept.sub_category: Solid geometry — cross-sections of a rectangular solid

examples.problem_statement: In the rectangular solid above, TU = 3, UV = 4, and VR = 2. What is the area of the shaded rectangular region, which has VR as one side and the diagonal VT of the front face as the other?

solution.result: One side of the shaded rectangle is 2
solution.description: Set up the area formula for the shaded rectangle and identify VR, given as 2, as one of its sides.

solution.operation: VT = \text{hypotenuse of right triangle } VUT, \quad UV = 4, \; TU = 3
solution.result: The missing width VT is the hypotenuse of a 3-4 right triangle on the front face
solution.description: Locate the other side of the shaded rectangle: VT lies on the front face of the solid, where it is the hypotenuse of right triangle VUT whose legs are the two given edges.
Apply the Pythagorean theorem to the legs 3 and 4 to obtain the width of the shaded rectangle.
Multiply the width just found by the length VR to get the area of the shaded rectangular region.

key_reminders: The area of a rectangle is the product of its two adjacent side lengths.
A diagonal drawn across a face of a rectangular solid is the hypotenuse of a right triangle formed by two edges of that face.
Edges of a rectangular solid meet at right angles, which licenses the Pythagorean theorem on triangle VUT.
common_mistakes: Multiplying two given edge lengths such as 3 and 2 or 4 and 2 directly, instead of first finding the diagonal VT.
Treating VT as 3 + 4 = 7 rather than as the hypotenuse \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5.

concept.technique_name: linear pair of interior and exterior angle with exterior-angle sum

examples.problem_statement: Difference between interior and exterior angle of a polygon is 100^\circ. Then the number of sides in the polygon is: (a) 8 (b) 9 (c) 10 (d) 11

solution.result: sum equation relating the two angles
solution.description: Name the interior angle x and the exterior angle y, and write that they add to a straight angle, as the book does.
Translate the given difference between interior and exterior angle into the second equation.
Solve the pair of equations for x, the interior angle.
Solve the same pair for y, the exterior angle.
Divide the full 360 degrees of exterior angles by one exterior angle to get the number of sides.

key_reminders: An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle form a linear pair summing to 180^\circ.
The exterior angles of any polygon total 360^\circ, so for a regular polygon n = 360^\circ / (\text{one exterior angle}).
Two linear equations in x and y (sum and difference) pin both angles down uniquely.
common_mistakes: Dividing 360 by the interior angle 140 instead of the exterior angle 40.
Reading the 100^\circ difference as one of the angles themselves rather than as x - y.

concept.technique_name: average speed as total distance over total time

examples.problem_statement: Jack traveled the first 75% of an 80-mile trip at 45 miles per hour and the remainder at 30 miles per hour. What was Jack's average speed for the entire 80-mile trip, in miles per hour? (A) 37.5 (B) 38.25 (C) 40 (D) 41.25 (E) 42.5

solution.description: Take 75% of the 80-mile trip to get the distance covered at the faster rate.
Subtract the first-part distance from the total to get the remaining distance.
Apply D = RT to the first leg, dividing 60 miles by 45 miles per hour for its time.
Apply D = RT to the second leg, dividing 20 miles by 30 miles per hour for its time.
Add the two leg times to get the total time for the trip.
Divide the total distance by the total time to get the average speed.

key_reminders: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, not the average of the two rates.
Use D = RT separately on each leg because the rates differ.
The two leg times must be in the same unit before adding.
common_mistakes: Averaging 45 and 30 to get 37.5, which is choice (A).
Weighting the rates by distance share (0.75 \times 45 + 0.25 \times 30 = 41.25), which is choice (D), instead of by time.

concept.technique_name: base multiplication with deficiencies from base 1000

examples.problem_statement: Using base 1000 (the right-hand portion of the answer should therefore be of three digits), compute 978 \times 983 = ?

solution.result: deficiency of -22 for the first number
solution.description: Write the first number against base 1000 and record how far short of the base it falls.

solution.result: deficiency of -17 for the second number
solution.description: Do the same for the second number, recording its shortfall from 1000 beside it.
Cross-subtract: take one number minus the other number's deficiency to get the left-hand portion of the answer.
Multiply the two deficiencies to get the right-hand portion, padded to the three digits that base 1000 demands.
Join the left-hand and right-hand portions to read off the product.

key_reminders: With base 1000 the right-hand portion must carry exactly three digits.
The left-hand portion is one number minus the other number's deficiency (both cross-subtractions give the same value).
Both numbers are below the base, so the product of the two deficiencies is positive.
common_mistakes: Writing the right-hand part as 374 without checking it fills three digits, which breaks the moment the deficiency product is smaller (e.g. two digits).
Cross-subtracting with the wrong pairing, e.g. 978 - 22 or 983 - 17, instead of subtracting the other number's deficiency.

concept.technique_name: sign analysis of products

examples.problem_statement: x, y, and z are integers, xyz \ge 0, yz < 0, and y < 0. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: z. Choose whether Quantity A is greater, Quantity B is greater, the two quantities are equal, or the relationship cannot be determined.

solution.description: Combine the two given facts about y and z: a negative product with a negative first factor forces the second factor to be positive, so z is positive.
Treat yz as a single negative factor; for x times a negative quantity to be non-negative, x itself must be negative or zero.
Substitute the bounds just derived into the two quantities: Quantity A is at most 0 while Quantity B is strictly positive.
Compare the bounds; since the largest A can be is 0 and B is always above 0, Quantity B is greater in every case.

key_reminders: A product of two numbers is negative only when the two factors have opposite signs.
If a product of three integers is non-negative and two of them multiply to a negative, the third must be negative or zero.
In quantitative comparison, a conclusion holds only if it holds for every value allowed by the constraints.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that x = 0 is allowed by xyz \ge 0, and then wrongly treating x as strictly negative.
Reading yz < 0 with y < 0 as forcing z negative instead of positive.

concept.technique_name: ratio proportion
concept.sub_category: table-based data interpretation with percentages and ratios

examples.problem_statement: Study the table of the number of boys of standard XI participating in different games (class XI D column: Chess 4, Badminton 12, Table Tennis 8, Hockey 4, Football 12, Total No. of Boys 40). Every student of each class of standard XI participates in exactly one game, and in each class the number of girls participating in each game is 25% of the number of boys participating in that game. All the boys of class XI D passed the annual examination but a few girls failed. If all the boys and girls who passed and entered XII D are in the ratio of boys to girls as 5:1, what would be the number of girls who failed in class XI D?

solution.description: Read the total number of boys in class XI D straight from the last row of the table's XI D column.
Apply the note that girls number 25% of the boys to get the total number of girls in class XI D.
Carry the boys forward unchanged, because the question states every boy of XI D passed and moved into XII D.
Use the 5:1 boys-to-girls ratio in XII D to convert the 40 boys into the matching number of girls who passed.
Subtract the girls who passed from the girls originally in XI D to find how many girls failed.

key_reminders: Girls in any class or game equal 25% of the corresponding number of boys.
A boys-to-girls ratio of 5:1 means the number of girls is the number of boys divided by 5.
Students who failed are the difference between the original class strength and those who entered the next class.
common_mistakes: Using a games-row figure from the XI D column (such as 12) instead of the class total of 40.
Multiplying 40 by 5 instead of dividing when applying the 5:1 ratio.

concept.technique_name: conditional ordering deduction
concept.sub_category: ordering games with conditional entry rules

examples.problem_statement: The six messages on an answering machine were each left by one of Fleure, Greta, Hildy, Liam, Pasquale, or Theodore, consistent with the following: At most one person left more than one message. No person left more than three messages. If the first message is Hildy's, the last is Pasquale's. If Greta left any message, Fleure and Pasquale did also. If Fleure left any message, Pasquale and Theodore did also, all of Pasquale's preceding any of Theodore's. If Pasquale left any message, Hildy and Liam did also, all of Hildy's preceding any of Liam's. The first and last messages on the answering machine could be the first and second messages left by which one of the following? (A) Fleure (B) Hildy (C) Liam (D) Pasquale (E) Theodore

solution.operation: Apply the rule 'if the first message is Hildy's, the last is Pasquale's' to answer choice (B).
solution.description: Rule out Hildy immediately: if Hildy is first, the last message must be Pasquale's, so Hildy cannot own both the first and the last message.

solution.operation: Read the stem: the named person leaves the first and last messages as their first and second messages.
solution.result: That person leaves exactly two messages, and four other people leave one each to reach six.
solution.description: Interpret the question stem rather than testing choices: since at most one person leaves more than one message and this person's second message is the last one, that person leaves exactly two, so four more distinct people are needed for the remaining four messages.

solution.operation: Fill the four remaining slots from the always-required P, T, H, L plus one more person.
solution.result: The fifth person must be Fleure.
solution.description: Determine who joins the doubler: P, T, H and L are always in, and choosing Greta would drag Fleure in as well, giving six people with no room for anyone to leave two messages, so Fleure is the fifth.

solution.operation: With F and P in, trigger 'all Pasquale's precede any Theodore's' and 'all Hildy's precede any Liam's'.
solution.result: P - T (all) and H - L (all) are active.
solution.description: Activate the ordering consequences of Fleure and Pasquale being present, which lock Pasquale entirely before Theodore and Hildy entirely before Liam.

solution.operation: Test P, T, H, L against those ordering blocks for holding both the first and last message.
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining ordered players: Pasquale could be first but a Theodore must follow every Pasquale so Pasquale cannot also be last, and Theodore cannot be first for the mirror reason, with Liam similarly blocked, leaving Fleure.

key_reminders: At most one person leaves more than one message, so the person holding the first and last message leaves exactly two.
Fleure's presence forces Pasquale and Theodore in with all Pasquale's messages before any of Theodore's.
Pasquale's presence forces Hildy and Liam in with all Hildy's messages before any of Liam's.
common_mistakes: Testing each answer choice by building full orderings instead of first deducing that exactly five people leave messages.
Overlooking that adding Greta forces Fleure in too, which would need six people and leave no one able to double up.

concept.technique_name: unit conversion then rate-time-distance formula

examples.problem_statement: A cat travels at a speed of 60 inches/second. How long will it take this cat, in seconds, to travel 300 feet? (12 inches = 1 foot)

solution.description: The question asks about a distance in feet, so first convert the given rate out of inches per second by multiplying it by the conversion factor 1 foot per 12 inches.
Everything is now expressed in feet and seconds, so substitute the converted rate and the given distance into the rate-time-distance formula.
Solve the equation from the previous step for the unknown time by dividing the distance by the rate.

key_reminders: Convert every quantity into a single consistent unit system before applying a rate formula.
The rate-time-distance relationship is r \times t = d.
12 inches = 1 foot, so dividing an inches-per-second rate by 12 gives feet per second.
common_mistakes: Converting the distance 300 feet into inches but leaving the rate in inches per second and then reporting the answer in the wrong unit.
