Multiplying by 12 instead of dividing by 12 when turning 60 inches per second into feet per second.

concept.technique_name: Pythagorean theorem then area-matching to find a missing side

examples.problem_statement: Triangle ABC and Rectangle JKLM have equal areas. In Triangle ABC the leg BC measures 12 and the hypotenuse AC measures 15, with the right angle at B; Rectangle JKLM has one side measuring 6. What is the perimeter of Rectangle JKLM?

solution.description: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to the right triangle, squaring the known leg 12 and the known hypotenuse 15 to set up an equation in the unknown side AB.
Isolate (AB)^2 and take the square root to get the missing leg; this is a 9-12-15 triangle, a 3-4-5 triangle with every measurement tripled.
Now that both legs are known, use the triangle area formula with 12 as the base and 9 as the height.
The rectangle has the same area, 54, and one side is 6, so divide to solve for the other side of the rectangle.
With both rectangle side lengths known, apply the rectangle perimeter formula, doubling the sum of the two sides.

key_reminders: In a right triangle, leg^2 + leg^2 = hypotenuse^2.
The area of a triangle is \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}; for a right triangle the two legs serve as base and height.
Equal areas let you transfer a computed area from one figure to another and solve for a missing dimension.
common_mistakes: Treating 12 and 15 as the two legs and computing a hypotenuse instead of recognizing 15 as the hypotenuse, which gives a wrong AB.
Stopping at JM = 9 and reporting the side length rather than the requested perimeter.
Reporting 6 + 9 = 15 as the perimeter by forgetting to double the sum of the sides.

concept.technique_name: picking numbers to test a quantitative comparison, including the value zero

examples.problem_statement:
x is a non-negative even integer.
Quantity A: x
Quantity B: 1
(A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: 0 is an allowed value of x
solution.description: Read the phrasing carefully: the problem says non-negative rather than positive, which is the test-writer's sneaky signal that 0 is permitted alongside the positive even integers.

solution.result: Quantity B is greater; eliminate (A) and (C)
solution.description: Test the boundary value 0 first, since ZONEF reminds you to try 0 whenever it is allowed, and compare the two quantities for that value.
Test a positive even integer such as 2, which reverses the comparison and rules out the remaining single-relationship choice.
Because different permitted values of x produce different relationships, no single comparison holds, so the relationship cannot be determined.

key_reminders: Non-negative means positive values and 0; only positive excludes 0.
In quantitative comparison, if two allowed values of the variable give opposite comparisons, the answer is (D).
ZONEF prompts you to test Zero, One, Negatives, Extremes, and Fractions when the constraints allow them.
common_mistakes: Reading non-negative as positive, testing only x = 2, 4, 6, and choosing (A).
Stopping after the x = 0 case and choosing (B) without testing a positive even value.

concept.technique_name: context clue and pivot-word analysis

examples.problem_statement: Ernest Hemingway, the novelist and proponent of traditional masculine virtues that were already considered (i) _________ by his more progressive peers, eventually lost currency with the general public; although his earlier literary works remained popular, his continuing adherence to that code drove him to disdain society, which, in turn, (ii) _________ him. Blank (i) choices: effeminate, anachronistic, sardonic. Blank (ii) choices: shunned, eulogized, murdered.

solution.operation: Locate the clue governing blank (i): the judgment of his "more progressive peers" on virtues described as "traditional"
solution.result: Blank (i) must state how forward-looking people regard something traditional
solution.description: Read the blank against the words the sentence supplies about who is judging and what is being judged, so the blank is filled from the sentence's own evidence rather than from a guess.

solution.operation: Unpack "progressive" as wanting to move forward, away from traditions
solution.result: The needed word must brand the virtues as belonging to an earlier time
solution.description: Convert the clue word into the meaning it forces on the blank; progressive peers would fault traditional virtues for being out of their era.

solution.operation: Match that requirement to "anachronistic," meaning "in the wrong time period"
solution.description: Select the choice whose definition is exactly the out-of-its-time meaning the clue demands.

solution.operation: Read the pivot "in turn" joining his disdain for society to society's response
solution.result: Blank (ii) must reciprocate the disdain, that is, get him back for it
solution.description: Use the transition phrase to fix the direction of the second blank: it mirrors, rather than reverses, the action just described.

solution.operation: Pick the blank (ii) choice that matches disdain returned
solution.description: Choose the word that carries the same disdainful charge back toward Hemingway, completing the reciprocal pair.

key_reminders: "Progressive" signals a move away from tradition, so it dates whatever is traditional.
"In turn" marks reciprocation: the second blank repeats the direction of the first action, not its opposite.
common_mistakes: Choosing "effeminate" by reacting to "masculine virtues" instead of to the progressive-versus-traditional time clue.
Choosing "eulogized" for blank (ii), which reverses the direction that "in turn" after "disdain" requires.

concept.technique_name: set union by inclusion-exclusion

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. Set A consists of 40 integers, and set B consists of 150 integers. The number of integers that are in both set A and set B is 20. Quantity A: The total number of integers that are in set A or set B, or both. Quantity B: 170. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: The three given counts are recorded
solution.description: Write down what the problem supplies before comparing anything, since the comparison is built entirely from these three counts.

solution.operation: Draw a Venn diagram of two overlapping circles labeled 40 and 150 with 20 in the overlap
solution.result: A picture in which the 20 shared integers sit inside both the 40 and the 150
solution.description: Translate the words into a figure; the diagram makes visible that the shared integers have been counted inside each circle's total.

solution.operation: Redraw with three separate regions: A only = 40 - 20, both = 20, B only = 150 - 20
solution.result: 20 in A only, 20 in both, 130 in B only
solution.description: Split the diagram so each integer is counted exactly once, which is what a total of A or B or both requires.
Add the three disjoint regions to get the total number of integers that are in set A or set B or both.
Check the same total the second way the book gives: listing both sets counts the shared integers twice, so subtract the overlap once.

solution.operation: Compare Quantity A = 170 with Quantity B = 170
solution.description: Set the computed union count against the given 170 and read off the comparison the question asks for.

examples.answer: Choice C: The two quantities are equal.

key_reminders: The count of a union is n(A) + n(B) - n(A \text{ and } B); the overlap is subtracted once because it was counted twice.
In a two-circle Venn diagram the given circle totals already include the overlap, so subtract it out before adding regions.
common_mistakes: Adding 40 + 150 to get 190 and calling Quantity A greater, forgetting that the 20 shared integers were counted twice.
Reading the circle labels 40 and 150 as the counts of A only and B only, which makes the regions 40, 20, and 150.

concept.technique_name: part-to-whole comparison by ratio estimation from a bar chart

examples.problem_statement: Using the column chart of monthly fruit and vegetable sales, which month had the greatest percentage of vegetable sales relative to total sales? (A) Jan (B) Mar (C) Jun (D) Oct (E) Nov

solution.operation: Recast "greatest percentage of vegetable sales relative to total sales" as "greatest ratio of vegetable sales to fruit sales"
solution.result: The task becomes a ratio comparison, not a percent computation
solution.description: Because total sales are only fruit plus vegetables, whichever month has vegetables largest against fruit also has them largest against the total.

solution.operation: Restrict attention to the five months named in the answer choices
solution.result: Only Jan, Mar, Jun, Oct, and Nov need to be examined
solution.description: Glance at the choices first so the chart is scanned for five columns instead of twelve.

solution.operation: Check Jan and Mar: vegetable bar above fruit bar
solution.result: In both months vegetables are more than half of total sales
solution.description: Compare the two bars within each month to see which side of one-half the vegetable share falls on.

solution.operation: Check Jun: fruit bar above vegetable bar
solution.result: Vegetables are less than half of total sales, so eliminate (C)
solution.description: A month where vegetables trail fruit cannot beat a month where they lead, so June is discarded.

solution.operation: Check Oct and Nov: fruit and vegetable bars about equal
solution.result: Vegetable share is about half, so eliminate (D) and (E)
solution.description: Near-equal bars give roughly a one-half share, which loses to Jan and Mar; only Jan and Mar remain.

solution.operation: Read the values: Jan vegetables \approx 2200, fruit \approx 1700; Mar vegetables \approx 2400, fruit \approx 2000
solution.result: January differential \approx 500 on a smaller total; March differential \approx 400 on a larger total
solution.description: The two survivors are close, so take approximate amounts off the chart and form the gap and the total for each month.

solution.operation: Compare a larger vegetable-over-fruit gap on a smaller total against a smaller gap on a larger total
solution.result: January's vegetable sales are the greater share of that month's total
solution.description: A bigger surplus spread over a smaller total is necessarily a bigger fraction of it, which settles January over March conceptually.

solution.operation: Confirm with the calculator by dividing each month's vegetable sales by that month's total
solution.result: January's percentage is slightly greater than March's
solution.description: Run the arithmetic check the book offers as the alternative to the conceptual comparison, confirming January.

key_reminders: With only two categories in a column, vegetables exceeding fruit is the same as vegetables exceeding half the total.
Scan the answer choices before the chart so only the listed months are read.
A larger surplus over a smaller total gives the larger share.
common_mistakes: Picking March because its vegetable bar is the tallest in absolute terms, when the question asks for a share of that month's total.
Treating Oct and Nov's roughly equal bars as a tie for the top instead of recognizing a share of about one-half.

concept.technique_name: charge and direction matching across answer choices

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Some of the company's supporters charged that the negative report had been motivated by a broader political assault on the company that was designed to help market rivals who would like to see the company ______ . (A) reined in (B) bolstered (C) indemnified (D) propped up (E) manacled (F) lionized

solution.operation: Identify whose wish the blank expresses: the company's "market rivals"
solution.result: The blank states what competitors want to happen to the company
solution.description: Anchor the blank to the party named right before it, since the sentence makes their preference the thing being described.

solution.operation: Fix the direction rivals would want
solution.result: Market rivals would clearly like to see the company experience some negative outcome
solution.description: Reason from who the rivals are to the charge of the missing word, so the choices can be sorted before any of them are weighed individually.

solution.operation: Sort the choices by charge: bolstered, indemnified, propped up, and lionized all describe positive results for the company
solution.result: Choices B, C, D, and F are eliminated
solution.description: Discard every option that would benefit the company, because none of them matches the negative direction the sentence requires.

solution.operation: Keep the choices that describe a negative outcome: reined in and manacled
solution.result: Only these two describe such an outcome
solution.description: The remaining pair both mean restrained or held back, which is the negative sense the rivals would welcome.

solution.operation: Confirm the surviving pair produces two sentences alike in meaning
solution.result: Reined in (Choice A) and manacled (Choice E)
solution.description: Sentence equivalence needs a matched pair, and these two restraint words satisfy that requirement together.

examples.answer: Choice A: reined in AND Choice E: manacled

key_reminders: Sorting the six choices by positive or negative charge usually removes most of them at once.
The blank must express what the named party, here the market rivals, would want.
The two selected words must yield sentences alike in meaning, so they come as a synonym pair.
common_mistakes: Pairing bolstered with propped up because they are synonyms of each other, ignoring that they give the company a positive outcome.
Choosing indemnified for its legal ring in a sentence about a negative report, though it protects rather than harms the company.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by contrast signal and synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. In film studies—a visually oriented discipline that is ______ backlit close-ups, eyeline matches, and voyeuristic gazes—scholars have often been tone-deaf to the sounds of music. Choices: (A) fixated on, (B) obsessed with, (C) unconcerned with, (D) amused by, (E) bothered by, (F) indifferent to.

solution.operation: Read the sentence as a contrast between the discipline's treatment of the visual and its treatment of the aural ("tone-deaf to the sounds of music").
solution.result: The visual is attended to; the aural is relatively ignored in favor of it.
solution.description: Establish the sentence's internal opposition first: the second half says scholars ignore sound, so the first half must say what they do attend to. This fixes the direction the blank has to point.

solution.operation: Require the blank to designate attention to the visual elements listed (backlit close-ups, eyeline matches, voyeuristic gazes).
solution.result: The blank must express strong attention, not lack of it.
solution.description: Convert the contrast into a concrete requirement on the missing word, so each option can be tested against a single criterion rather than judged by feel.

solution.operation: Eliminate "unconcerned with" (C) and "indifferent to" (F) because they do not designate attention.
solution.description: Drop the choices that fail the attention criterion outright — they describe the discipline's stance toward music, not toward the visual.

solution.operation: Test "amused by" (D): compare its degree of attention and its affect against "fixated on" and "obsessed with," and look for a second choice that would give it the same meaning.
solution.result: "Amused by" conveys a lesser degree of attention and a more positive affect, and has no partner word among the choices.
solution.description: Because the answer must be a pair producing sentences alike in meaning, a word with no equivalent partner is eliminated even before its fit is judged; "amused by" also understates the attention required in step 2.

solution.operation: Pair the two remaining attention words, "fixated on" (A) and "obsessed with" (B).
solution.result: Choice A and Choice B both satisfy the blank and produce sentences alike in meaning.
solution.description: Confirm the surviving two are synonymous in this context, which is what a Sentence Equivalence answer requires — both fit and both yield the same completed sentence.

examples.answer: Choice A: fixated on AND Choice B: obsessed with

key_reminders: A Sentence Equivalence answer is a pair: a word that fits alone but has no synonymous partner among the choices cannot be correct.
A contrast cue elsewhere in the sentence (here, "tone-deaf to the sounds of music") fixes the direction the blank must take.
Match degree and affect, not just topic — a milder or more positive word can fit loosely and still be wrong.
common_mistakes: Picking "unconcerned with" or "indifferent to" by carrying over the sentence's "tone-deaf" idea to the wrong half of the contrast.
Choosing "amused by" because it plausibly describes a viewer's response, ignoring that it has no synonymous partner among the six choices.

concept.technique_name: explain the discrepancy (EXCEPT) via the 4-step Critical Reasoning process
concept.sub_category: Critical Reasoning — Evidence Family / Explain the Discrepancy

examples.problem_statement: Hunting Season. In an effort to reduce the number of deer, and therefore decrease the number of automobile accidents caused by deer, the government lengthened the deer hunting season earlier this year. Surprisingly, the number of accidents caused by deer has increased substantially since the introduction of the longer hunting season. All of the following, if true, help to explain the increase in traffic accidents caused by deer EXCEPT (A) The presence of humans in the woods causes the deer to move to new areas, which causes the deer to cross roads more frequently than normal. (B) In the area where the deer live, the lengthened hunting season attracted a significantly greater amount of traffic than usual this year. (C) Most automobile accidents involving deer result from cars swerving to avoid deer, and they leave the deer in question unharmed. (D) Deer tend to bolt when hearing gunshots or other loud sounds and are more likely to run across a road without warning. (E) A new highway was recently built directly through the state's largest forest, which is the primary habitat of the state's deer population.

solution.operation: Identify the question: the phrase "help to explain" plus "EXCEPT" marks this as a Discrepancy EXCEPT question.
solution.result: Question type: Explain the Discrepancy, EXCEPT format.
solution.description: Read the question stem before the argument and classify it, because the type determines what the right answer must do — here the wording tells you four choices will resolve the puzzle and one will not.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument into its causal chain: longer hunting season → fewer deer → fewer car accidents.
solution.result: Government plan: increased hunting season leads to decreased deer, which leads to decreased car accidents.
solution.description: Map the intended multi-level chain on paper so the surprising outcome can be placed against a specific expectation rather than a vague impression.

solution.operation: Add the surprising evidence: accidents caused by deer have increased substantially since the longer season began.
solution.result: Observed outcome is the exact opposite of the predicted one — the discrepancy to be explained.
solution.description: State the contradiction explicitly, because every answer choice will be judged by whether it accounts for more accidents, not for accidents in general.

solution.operation: State the goal: find the one choice that does NOT explain why accidents increased; cross off the four that do.
solution.result: Right answer = the odd one out that fails to fix the discrepancy.
solution.description: Set the elimination rule before touching the choices, so the EXCEPT format does not invert your instinct to keep whatever sounds reasonable.

solution.operation: Test (A): longer season means people in the woods longer, so deer cross roads more frequently than they otherwise would.
solution.result: Increases the likelihood of deer-caused accidents — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Check whether the choice supplies a mechanism that raises the accident count, and eliminate it when it does, since explaining choices are the wrong answers here.

solution.operation: Test (B): the lengthened season attracted significantly more traffic than usual to the area where the deer live.
solution.result: More cars where the deer are means more chances for collisions — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Note that this choice raises accidents through the other side of the collision (cars, not deer), which still resolves the puzzle, so it is eliminated.

solution.operation: Test (C): most deer-related accidents come from cars swerving to avoid deer, leaving the deer unharmed.
solution.result: Explains how accidents happen but says nothing about the number of accidents rising — does not resolve the discrepancy.
solution.description: Separate mechanism from magnitude: this choice describes the form accidents take, and because the discrepancy is about an increase in count, it is the one that fails and therefore the answer.

solution.operation: Test (D): deer bolt at gunshots and are more likely to run across a road without warning.
solution.result: A longer season means more gunshots over more time, so more sudden crossings — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Confirm the choice ties the change (a longer season) to more accident opportunities, which disqualifies it in an EXCEPT question.

solution.operation: Test (E): a new highway was built directly through the forest that is the deer's primary habitat.
solution.result: The situation changed from the prior year in a way that would raise deer-caused accidents — explains the discrepancy; cross off.
solution.description: Accept an alternative cause as an explanation — a Discrepancy answer need not involve the hunting season at all, only account for the rise — leaving (C) as the sole non-explainer.

key_reminders: On a Discrepancy EXCEPT question the four choices that resolve the puzzle are the wrong answers; the one that fails to resolve it is correct.
The discrepancy here is about the number of accidents increasing, so a choice must bear on quantity, not merely on how accidents occur.
An answer may explain the rise through an unrelated cause (a new highway) and still count as explaining.
common_mistakes: Reversing the EXCEPT format and selecting (A) or (D) because they explain the increase well.
Accepting (C) as an explanation because it describes deer accidents plausibly, without asking whether it shows the count going up.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion driven by a contrast connective

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Researchers trying to make it possible to trace counterfeit documents to the printer that produced them are (i) ______ the fact that the rotating drums and mirrors inside laser printers are imperfect devices that leave unique patterns of banding in their output. Although these patterns are (ii) ______ to the naked eye, they can be (iii) ______ and analyzed by computer programs that the researchers have spent the past year devising. Blank (i): A exploiting, B facing, C manipulating. Blank (ii): D invisible, E obvious, F unappealing. Blank (iii): G detected, H implemented, I generated.

solution.operation: Note the "although" that begins the second sentence and read it as a contrast between how the naked eye perceives the patterns and how computer programs view them.
solution.result: Blanks (ii) and (iii) must stand in opposition to each other.
solution.description: Start with the connective, since it is the only explicit logical signal in the passage and it links the two blanks in the same sentence — solving them as a pair is easier than solving either alone.

solution.operation: Search the columns for the (ii)/(iii) pairing that produces that eye-versus-computer contrast: invisible/obvious/unappealing against detected/implemented/generated.
solution.result: "Invisible" and "detected" are the only pairing that creates the contrast.
solution.description: Test the pairs jointly rather than the words separately; the eye fails to see the patterns while the programs pick them out, which only invisible-plus-detected expresses.

solution.operation: Characterize what Blank (i) must express: the relationship between the researchers and the inevitability of imperfections in printing technology.
solution.result: The blank names how the researchers treat an unavoidable flaw.
solution.description: Define the job of the remaining blank before scanning its column, so the choice is judged against the passage's logic instead of against which word sounds most sophisticated.

solution.operation: Apply the passage's assertion that the researchers use computers to analyze these imperfections to the Blank (i) column.
solution.result: "Exploiting" is the best choice, since the researchers turn the flaw to their advantage.
solution.description: Use the information already established in step 2 — the programs detect and analyze the banding — as the evidence that selects the first blank, which is why the blanks are solved out of order.

solution.operation: Rule out the other Blank (i) options: weigh "facing" and "manipulating" against that same assertion.
solution.result: "Facing" does not imply the level of engagement detailed in the passage; "manipulating" suggests changing the imperfections rather than analyzing them.
solution.description: Confirm the pick by naming the specific defect in each rival — too little engagement in one case, the wrong kind of action in the other — rather than dismissing them by feel.

examples.answer: Choice A: exploiting; Choice D: invisible; Choice G: detected

key_reminders: "Although" signals contrast: the two blanks it joins must oppose each other.
Solve the blank with the strongest textual signal first, then use what it establishes to fix the remaining blank — order of blanks need not be order of solving.
A wrong choice can fail on degree of engagement ("facing") or on direction of action ("manipulating"), not only on topic.
common_mistakes: Choosing "manipulating" for Blank (i) because researchers are working with the printer flaws, when the passage has them analyzing rather than altering those flaws.
Filling Blank (ii) with "obvious" and Blank (iii) with "detected," which destroys the contrast "although" demands.

concept.technique_name: solving a reciprocal-sum rational equation by splitting the right side into reciprocal fractions

examples.problem_statement: Using the Equation Solving with Reciprocals technique, work two algebraic equations: first a linear equation admitting two possible interpretations, then the rational equation \frac{x}{x+1} + \frac{x+1}{x} = \frac{169}{60}. Given the factor pairs of 60 (2 \times 30, 3 \times 20, 4 \times 15, 5 \times 12, 6 \times 10), the matching pair 5 and 12 with 5^2 + 12^2 = 169, and the decomposition \frac{169}{60} = \frac{12}{5} + \frac{5}{12}. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: x+2 = 4 \text{ or } x+2 = 1, \text{ denominator } x+3 \text{ in both cases}
solution.result: Two readings of the first equation: \frac{4}{x+3} = \frac{x+2}{1}\text{-style and its counterpart}
solution.description: Record that the printed first equation is ambiguous and admits two interpretations, both sharing the denominator x+3; each reading has to be carried through separately.
Cross-multiply each interpretation to clear the fraction, turning both readings into plain linear equations.
Distribute the 4 across each bracket so that the x-terms and constants stand separately and can be collected.

solution.result: x-terms on the left, constants on the right
solution.description: Rearrange each equation, moving the x-terms to one side and the constants to the other.
Combine like terms and divide by 3 to solve each interpretation, giving the two possible values for the first equation.

solution.result: The second equation, now to be solved
solution.description: Turn to the second problem and write out the rational equation that the reciprocal technique will handle.

solution.result: The left side is a sum of a fraction and its reciprocal
solution.description: Recognize the structural feature the whole method rests on: the two terms on the left invert each other, so the right side must decompose the same way.

solution.result: All factor pairs of the denominator 60
solution.description: Factorize the denominator 60 into every pair of factors, since a reciprocal split \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} has denominator ab.

solution.result: The pair 5 and 12 matches the numerator 169
solution.description: Test the factor pairs to find the one whose squares add to the numerator 169, because \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}.

solution.result: Right side written as a sum of reciprocal fractions
solution.description: Rewrite the right-hand side using the matched pair, so both sides of the equation now have the identical reciprocal-sum form.

solution.result: Two simple proportions replacing the rational equation
solution.description: Match the terms on the left to the terms on the right term by term; either assignment is admissible, which is why the technique yields corresponding pairs of values.
Cross-multiply whichever proportion you prefer and solve it for x — the book stops here, leaving the final arithmetic to the reader.

examples.answer: First equation has two possible solutions: x = -10/3 or x = -5/3. Second equation can be solved by equating x/(x+1)=12/5 or 5/12, giving corresponding x values.

key_reminders: \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab}: the denominator of the sum is the product of the pair and the numerator is the sum of their squares.
To split a target fraction into reciprocals, list the factor pairs of its denominator and test which pair's squares add to its numerator.
Once both sides are reciprocal sums, the terms can be equated pairwise, and either assignment is valid.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the first factor pair of 60 instead of testing pairs until 5^2 + 12^2 = 169 is reached.
Equating only one way (\frac{x}{x+1} = \frac{12}{5}) and missing that the reversed assignment is equally admissible.
Solving only one interpretation of the ambiguous first equation and reporting a single value instead of both -\frac{10}{3} and -\frac{5}{3}.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion using an explicit contrast between time periods

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. In stark contrast to his later (i) ______ , Simpson was largely (ii) ______ politics during his college years, despite the fact that the campus he attended was rife with political activity. Blank (i): A activism, B apathy, C affability. Blank (ii): D devoted to, E indifferent to, F shaped by.

solution.operation: Read "In stark contrast to his later ..." as setting Simpson's college-year relation to politics against his later relation to politics.
solution.result: The two blanks must contrast with each other.
solution.description: Identify the contrast frame first, because it is what ties the two blanks together and means neither can be chosen in isolation.

solution.operation: Read the "despite" clause: the campus was rife with political activity, yet Simpson's college-year stance is being singled out.
solution.result: In college, Simpson did not engage with the political activity around him.
solution.description: Use the concessive clause to pin down Blank (ii)'s direction — "despite" only makes sense if his behavior ran against the surrounding activity, i.e., nonengagement.

solution.operation: Test the Blank (ii) column for that nonengagement: devoted to, indifferent to, shaped by.
solution.description: Match each option against the requirement established in step 2; "devoted to" and "shaped by" both describe engagement and so contradict the "despite" clause.

solution.operation: Test the Blank (i) column for the required contrast with "indifferent to": activism, apathy, affability.
solution.description: Now that Blank (ii) is settled, pick the later-life quality that opposes indifference — "apathy" would repeat it rather than contrast, and "affability" is off the political topic entirely.

examples.answer: Choice A: activism; Choice E: indifferent to

key_reminders: "In stark contrast" requires the two blanks to oppose each other, not merely to be plausible on their own.
A "despite" clause tells you the subject behaved against the surrounding circumstance — here, disengagement amid campus political activity.
Solve the blank the text constrains most tightly first, then use it to fix the other.
common_mistakes: Selecting "apathy" for Blank (i), which echoes rather than contrasts with the college-year indifference the sentence describes.
Selecting "shaped by" or "devoted to" for Blank (ii) by reading the campus's political activity as something Simpson took part in, which the "despite" clause rules out.

concept.technique_name: telescoping infinite product via difference of squares

solution.description: Name the common base as x = -1/3 so the product becomes the generic form with exponents 1, 2, 4, 8, ... in x.
Multiply both sides by the extra factor (1-x), which is the trick that lets the product start collapsing.
Combine the first two factors by the difference of squares, replacing them with the single factor 1-x^2.
Apply the same difference of squares again; each pass doubles the exponent, so the collapsing continues indefinitely.
Since x is negative with absolute value less than 1, the repeatedly collapsing right-hand side settles at the value 1.
Solve for S by dividing by (1-x), then substitute x = -1/3 back in to get the numerical value.

key_reminders: Difference of squares: (1-a)(1+a) = 1-a^2, which is what makes exponents 1, 2, 4, 8, ... telescope.
Multiplying by the missing factor (1-x) is legitimate as long as x \neq 1 so it can be divided out at the end.
With |x| < 1, the repeatedly squared term dies away and the collapsing right-hand side equals 1.
common_mistakes: Treating the bracketed expression as a geometric series to be summed instead of a product to be telescoped.
Mis-signing the substitution and computing 1/(1 - 1/3) = 3/2 instead of 1/(1 + 1/3) = 3/4.

concept.technique_name: perimeter equation followed by the Pythagorean theorem

examples.problem_statement: What is the length of a diagonal of a rectangle that has width 5 and perimeter 34?

solution.description: Label the rectangle's length L, width W, and diagonal D, recording that only the width and the perimeter are given.
Write the perimeter as 2(L+W) and substitute the known width 5 and perimeter 34 to get an equation in L alone.
Divide both sides by 2 to strip off the factor multiplying the parenthesis.
Subtract the width from 17 to isolate L, giving the rectangle's length.
Draw the diagonal: it is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the width 5 and the length 12, so apply the Pythagorean theorem to those legs.
Take the positive square root to recover the diagonal's length.

key_reminders: The perimeter of a rectangle is 2(L+W), so one known side plus the perimeter determines the other side.
A rectangle's diagonal splits it into right triangles whose legs are the length and the width.
Pythagorean theorem: leg^2 + leg^2 = hypotenuse^2.
common_mistakes: Halving 34 to 17 and treating that as the length, forgetting that 17 is L + W and the width 5 still has to be removed.
Adding 5 and 12 to get 17 for the diagonal instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.

concept.technique_name: angle sum property with Pythagoras converse

examples.problem_statement: In \triangle ABC, \frac{\angle A}{\angle B} = 1 - \frac{\angle C}{\angle B}. Which of the following statements is true? (a) \triangle ABC is always an acute angled triangle (b) an angle exceeds 90^\circ (c) AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2 (d) None of these

solution.operation: \frac{\angle A}{\angle B} \cdot \angle B = \left(1 - \frac{\angle C}{\angle B}\right) \cdot \angle B
solution.description: Clear the denominators by multiplying the given relation through by \angle B, turning the fractional condition into a plain relation among the three angles.

solution.result: \angle B equals the sum of the other two angles
solution.description: Move \angle C to the left side, so the condition now says that angle B alone accounts for as much as angles A and C together.

solution.result: the three angles of the triangle total 180^\circ
solution.description: Bring in the angle sum property of a triangle, the second fact needed alongside the relation just derived.
Substitute \angle A + \angle C = \angle B into the angle sum, replacing that pair by a single \angle B.
Halve both sides to isolate \angle B, which shows the triangle is right angled at B.
Apply Pythagoras at the right angle B: the two sides enclosing B are AB and BC, so their squares add to the square of the hypotenuse AC.

key_reminders: The angles of a triangle sum to 180^\circ.
If one angle equals the sum of the other two, that angle is 90^\circ.
In a right triangle the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so the legs are the two sides meeting at it.
common_mistakes: Applying Pythagoras as AB^2 + AC^2 = BC^2, i.e. treating a leg as the hypotenuse instead of AC, which lies opposite the right angle at B.
Choosing (a) after seeing only that the relation is satisfiable, without deriving that \angle B is exactly 90^\circ, which rules out an acute triangle.

concept.technique_name: blank-by-blank synonym substitution and elimination

examples.problem_statement: The actress was desperate to (i) ___________ the part in the new Michel Gondry film. It was (ii) ___________ role, with lots of onscreen time and a number of long scenes that would allow the actress, usually cast as a vapid ingenue or bombshell, to truly show her dramatic range. Blank (i): land / ascertain / ensure. Blank (ii): a plum (among the choices offered).

solution.result: the target meaning for the first blank is fixed before looking at choices
solution.description: Read the first sentence and decide what the blank must mean: the actress is desperate to obtain the part, so the word has to be a synonym of get.
Substitute ascertain into the sentence and check the sense; it does not mean get, so it makes no sense here.

solution.operation: Test "ensure the part" against "ensure that she gets the part"
solution.result: ensure is rejected, leaving land for blank (i)
solution.description: Substitute ensure and notice it is used incorrectly: one can ensure that she gets the part, but not ensure the part itself, which eliminates the last rival.

solution.operation: Blank (ii) = a synonym of "good", matched to "a plum"
solution.result: a plum is chosen for blank (ii)
solution.description: Use the description that follows, lots of onscreen time and long showcase scenes, to set the second blank's target meaning as good, which is exactly what plum means.

key_reminders: Predict the meaning each blank needs from the sentence's own clues before evaluating the answer choices.
A choice must fit the exact grammatical object given, not a paraphrase you supply: ensure a clause is not ensure a noun.
The detail after the second blank (onscreen time, long scenes) is the clue that defines the required word.
common_mistakes: Picking ensure because the actress plausibly wants to ensure she gets the part, ignoring that the blank takes the part directly as its object.
Treating ascertain as a fancy synonym of obtain rather than of find out.

concept.technique_name: speed as distance over time with m/s to km/hr conversion

examples.problem_statement: How many km per hour does a man walk who passes through a street 600 m long in 5 minutes?

solution.description: Divide the distance in metres by the time expressed in seconds, converting the 5 minutes to 5 \times 60 seconds so that both quantities use base units.
Multiply the speed in m/s by 18/5, the standard factor that converts metres per second into kilometres per hour.
Write the improper fraction as a mixed number to state the walking speed in km/hr.

key_reminders: Speed = distance / time, with distance and time in matching units.
To convert m/s into km/hr multiply by 18/5.
common_mistakes: Dividing 600 by 5 and treating the result as m/s, forgetting to convert the 5 minutes into 300 seconds.
Multiplying by 5/18 instead of 18/5, which reverses the direction of the conversion.

concept.technique_name: fraction to percentage conversion

examples.problem_statement: What percentage is equivalent to \frac{3}{8}?

solution.description: Multiply the fraction by 100 to express it as a percentage, cancelling the 8 against the 100 to leave 75/2.
Convert the improper fraction into a mixed number and attach the percent sign.

key_reminders: A fraction becomes a percentage when multiplied by 100.
Cancel before multiplying: 100 divided by 8 gives 25/2, which keeps the arithmetic small.
common_mistakes: Reporting 37 % and dropping the leftover half, since 75/2 is not a whole number.

concept.technique_name: order of operations (PEMDAS)

examples.problem_statement: Quantity A: 14 - 3(4 - 6).  Quantity B: (4)(-3)(2)(-1).  Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Simplify inside the parentheses of Quantity A first, since parentheses come before every other operation in PEMDAS.
Multiply the coefficient by the value just found in the parentheses; multiplication is handled before the subtraction in front of it.
Perform the remaining addition last to finish Quantity A.
Multiply the four factors of Quantity B straight through; the two negative factors make the product positive.
Compare the two simplified values to pick the answer choice.

key_reminders: PEMDAS order: parentheses/exponents, then multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction.
Subtracting a negative product is the same as adding: 14 - 3(-2) = 14 + 6.
An even count of negative factors gives a positive product.
common_mistakes: Subtracting 3 from 14 before multiplying, giving 11(4-6) = -22 instead of 20.
Treating -3(-2) as -6 and getting 8 for Quantity A.
Losing track of the two negative signs in Quantity B and reporting -24.

concept.technique_name: units digit cyclicity and case enumeration

examples.problem_statement: If x, y, z and w are natural numbers, then what is the sum of all the possible remainders when 9^x + 6^y + 4^z + 11^z is divided by 10?

solution.description: Record the units digit of the first term; it alternates with the parity of x, which is why the cases are built on odd/even x.
Fix the second term's units digit as 6, since every power of 6 ends in 6 and y therefore never splits the cases.
Record the third term's units digit; it alternates with the parity of z, the second variable that splits the cases.
Fix the fourth term's units digit as 1, since every power of 11 ends in 1 regardless of the exponent.
Take the scenario with x and z both even and add the four units digits, then divide by 10 to read off the remainder.
Take the scenario with x and z both odd and add its four units digits, then reduce mod 10.
Take the mixed scenario with x odd and z even and reduce its digit sum mod 10.
Take the remaining mixed scenario with x even and z odd and reduce its digit sum mod 10.
Add the remainders produced by the four scenarios, as the question asks for the sum of all possible remainders.

key_reminders: A number's remainder on division by 10 is just its units digit.
Only x and z change the units digits here, so exactly four parity scenarios exist.
Powers of 6 always end in 6 and powers of 11 always end in 1.
common_mistakes: Adding the four distinct remainders again after they repeat, or dropping the repeated remainder 2 and answering 6.
Treating y and w as extra parity cases and enumerating more than four scenarios.
Reporting the digit sums (14, 20, 22, 12) rather than their remainders mod 10.

concept.technique_name: percentage increase over a base year

examples.problem_statement: A multiple bar diagram shows the student strength of a college in four faculties across 1990-91, 1991-92 and 1992-93. Arts: 600, 550, 500. Science: 400, 500, 600. Commerce: 200, 250, 250. Law: 150, 200, 250. How much percent was the increase in science students in 1992-93 over 1990-91? a) 50% b) 150% c) 66 2/3% d) 75%

solution.description: Read the two Science bars off the chart: 400 in the base year 1990-91 and 600 in 1992-93.
Subtract to get the actual increase in the number of science students.
Divide the increase by the 1990-91 figure, because 'over 1990-91' makes that year the base, and multiply by 100 to convert to a percent.
Match the computed percentage to the printed choices.

key_reminders: Percentage increase = (increase / original value) x 100.
'Increase in Y over X' makes year X the denominator, not year Y.
common_mistakes: Dividing 200 by the 1992-93 figure 600 and answering 33 1/3%.
Using 600/400 x 100 = 150% (choice b), which is the ratio, not the increase.

concept.technique_name: mean and median of a listed set

examples.problem_statement: For the list of numbers {4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 21}, how much greater is the mean than the median?

solution.description: Add all seven listed terms to get the sum that the mean is built from.
Divide that sum by the number of terms, which is the definition of the mean.
Take the middle number of the already-ordered list of seven values; with an odd count the median is a single term.
Subtract the median from the mean to answer how much greater the mean is.

key_reminders: Mean = sum of terms divided by the number of terms.
With an odd number of ordered terms the median is the single middle term.
common_mistakes: Letting the outlier 21 pull the median as well, instead of noting it only raises the mean.
Counting the repeated 5 once and dividing the sum by 6 terms.
Reporting the mean (8) or the median (6) instead of their difference.

concept.technique_name: fundamental counting principle

examples.problem_statement: A 10-student class is to choose a president, vice president, and secretary from the group. Assuming that no person can occupy more than one post, in how many ways can this be accomplished?

solution.description: Ask how many choices exist for the first post. Since no one has been chosen yet, all 10 students are available for president.
Move to vice president. One student is already committed as president, so only 9 students remain eligible for this post.
Move to secretary. Two students are now taken by the earlier posts, leaving 8 students to choose from.
Apply the fundamental counting principle: multiply the independent per-post choice counts together to get the total number of possible selections.

key_reminders: The fundamental counting principle: multiply the number of choices available at each stage to get the total number of outcomes.
Because no person can occupy more than one post, each selection reduces the pool available to the next post by one.
Order matters here, since the three posts are distinct roles rather than an unlabeled group.
common_mistakes: Treating the three posts as an unordered group and dividing by 3!, which gives 120 instead of 720.
Reusing 10 for every post (10^3 = 1000) by forgetting that a chosen student is removed from the pool.

concept.technique_name: combining inequalities by addition

examples.problem_statement: j + 2k > 0 and j - k < 3. Quantity A: k. Quantity B: -1. Choose (A) Quantity A is greater, (B) Quantity B is greater, (C) The two quantities are equal, or (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: \text{two inequalities whose signs point in opposite directions}
solution.description: Recognize the setup: two variables and two inequalities can often be combined by adding them, but adding is only legitimate once both inequality signs face the same direction, and here they do not.
Multiply everything in the second inequality by -1, which flips the inequality sign so that both inequalities now point the same way.
Add the two same-direction inequalities term by term; j cancels against -j, leaving a statement in k alone.
Divide both sides by the positive number 3, which leaves the inequality direction unchanged, to isolate k.
Compare the quantities: because k must be greater than -1 in every case allowed by the constraints, Quantity A is always greater.

key_reminders: Two inequalities may be added only when both signs face the same direction.
Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction; dividing by a positive number does not.
In quantitative comparison, choose (A) only if the derived relationship holds for every value permitted by the constraints.
common_mistakes: Adding j + 2k > 0 and j - k < 3 as printed, without first flipping the second sign, which yields the invalid conclusion k > -3 with j uncancelled.
Multiplying the second inequality by -1 but leaving the sign as < , producing -j + k < -3 and the reversed comparison.
Concluding (D) on the grounds that j and k are individually unknown, even though j cancels and k is fully bounded.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion by clue-and-trap elimination

examples.problem_statement: If anthropologists reveal too much of their culture to the subjects of their (i) _________, they risk the corruption of the sometimes fragile societies they seek to understand, as well as other (ii) _________ that may appear incongruous with their task. Blank (i): objectivity / society / scrutiny. Blank (ii): sequelae / inconsistencies / paradoxes.

solution.operation: Ask what anthropologists do to the people called 'the subjects of their (i) _____'
solution.result: Blank (i) must name the act of examining or studying another society
solution.description: The learner reads the phrase around blank (i) and fixes the meaning it has to carry: anthropologists are attempting to understand or examine other societies, so the blank names that examining.

solution.operation: Test 'objectivity' and 'society' against the phrase 'subjects of their _____'
solution.description: The learner eliminates the two decoys: anthropologists may be objective scientists, but objectivity does not have 'subjects'; and the societies being studied are not theirs. 'Scrutiny' is what survives.

solution.operation: Ask what 'other _____ that may appear incongruous with their task' must mean
solution.result: Blank (ii) must mean unintended or secondary consequences
solution.description: The learner reads blank (ii) as a second item in the list of risks, parallel to corrupting fragile societies, so it must name further consequences of revealing too much.

solution.operation: Test 'inconsistencies' and 'paradoxes' against the word 'incongruous' already in the sentence
solution.description: The learner eliminates the remaining two choices because they are close in meaning to 'incongruous' and would be redundant in the sentence, leaving 'sequelae', the word for secondary consequences.

key_reminders: The blank must fit the exact grammatical frame around it, not merely the general topic ('subjects of their _____' rules out abstractions like objectivity).
A choice that merely repeats a word already in the sentence ('incongruous') is redundant and therefore wrong.
Possessives matter: 'their culture' belongs to the anthropologists, so the studied societies cannot be 'their society'.
common_mistakes: Picking 'objectivity' because anthropologists are associated with being objective, ignoring that objectivity cannot have subjects.
Picking 'inconsistencies' or 'paradoxes' for blank (ii) because they echo 'incongruous', when that echo is exactly what makes them redundant.

concept.technique_name: threshold comparison on a chart (double a reference value, then count)

examples.problem_statement: In how many of the time periods shown was the average duration of visits to Aquarium A more than twice as much as the average in 1985 ? (A) Four (B) Three (C) Two (D) One (E) Zero

solution.operation: Scan the chart set for the one whose vertical axis is average duration of visits
solution.result: The bottom chart is the relevant one
solution.description: The learner first identifies which of the displayed charts actually reports average visit duration, since only that chart can answer the question.

solution.operation: Read the 1985 value for average duration of a visit to Aquarium A
solution.description: The learner locates the reference year named in the question and reads its average visit duration off the bottom chart.
The learner doubles the 1985 reference value to turn 'more than twice as much' into a single numeric cutoff to compare every other year against.

solution.operation: Scan every time period for an average visit duration greater than 90 minutes and count the hits
solution.description: The learner sweeps the bottom chart against the 90-minute cutoff, finds that only 1995 and 2000 exceed it, and counts them to get the answer.

key_reminders: 'More than twice as much as' becomes a single threshold once you double the reference value.
Read the reference figure from the chart that plots the quantity actually asked about, not a neighbouring chart of the same data set.
The comparison is strict: a period must exceed the doubled value, not merely equal it.
common_mistakes: Reading 1985 off the wrong chart in the set (e.g. number of visits instead of average duration).
Comparing years against the raw 45 minutes instead of the doubled 90-minute cutoff, which inflates the count.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence by contrast signal plus synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Notwithstanding their ______ regarding other issues, township residents have consistently passed the board of education's annual budget. Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. (A) accord (B) indecision (C) consensus (D) disagreement (E) divergence (F) enthusiasm

solution.operation: Identify the function of the opening word 'Notwithstanding'
solution.result: The sentence sets up a contrast between two behaviours
solution.description: The learner registers the contrast signal, which means the blank must describe behaviour that runs against what the rest of the sentence reports.

solution.operation: Read the behaviour on the other side of the contrast: residents have 'consistently passed' the annual budget
solution.result: The blank must name a lack of agreement on other issues
solution.description: The learner fixes the required meaning by contrasting it with the residents' consistent agreement on the budget.

solution.operation: Test 'accord' and 'consensus' against the required contrast
solution.description: The learner discards this synonym pair because, although the two words are alike in meaning, they express agreement and so supply no contrast with the consistently passed budget.

solution.operation: Test 'indecision' for a partner of matching meaning among the remaining choices
solution.result: Eliminated for lack of a match
solution.description: The learner notes that 'indecision' fits the context but discards it because no other choice matches it closely, and the task requires two words that yield sentences alike in meaning.

solution.result: The pair supplies the contrast and yields two sentences nearly alike in meaning
solution.description: The learner selects the surviving pair, which both provides the necessary contrast with consistent budget approval and satisfies the requirement that the two completions be alike in meaning.

examples.answer: Choice D: disagreement AND Choice E: divergence

key_reminders: 'Notwithstanding' signals contrast: the blank opposes the behaviour described in the main clause.
A correct sentence-equivalence answer needs both a contextual fit and a partner choice of matching meaning.
A synonym pair that fails the context (accord/consensus) is eliminated as a pair, not one word at a time.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'accord' and 'consensus' because they form a clean synonym pair, while ignoring that 'Notwithstanding' demands the opposite meaning.
Choosing 'indecision' on contextual fit alone, when no second choice matches it closely enough to produce equivalent sentences.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence pair elimination

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. If researchers can determine exactly what is wrong with people who suffer from this condition, they may be able to suggest drug therapies or other treatments that could ______ the effects of the damage.

solution.operation: Read the sentence for its overall sense: better information about a damaging condition lets researchers act on the effects of that damage.
solution.result: Target meaning for the blank: to lessen the future negative effects.
solution.description: Before touching the choices, extract from the sentence itself what the blank must mean, so that every later choice is tested against a fixed target rather than against the other choices.

solution.operation: Test the pair 'specify' (C) and 'identify' (D), which do produce sentences alike in meaning, against the sentence's logic.
solution.result: Eliminated: the researchers are seeking to control effects already known, not to gain further specificity or identification.
solution.description: Reject this pair even though the two words are near-synonyms, because sentence equivalence requires the pair to fit the sentence's meaning as well as match each other.

solution.operation: Test 'exacerbate' (B), which means to increase the negative effects.
solution.result: Eliminated: it is unreasonable that researchers would wish to increase the damage, and no other choice creates the same meaning.
solution.description: Discard this word on two counts at once - it contradicts the sentence's sense, and it is left with no partner word to form a matching pair.

solution.operation: Test 'stabilize' (F) against the target meaning of lessening.
solution.result: Eliminated: it implies the negative effects are merely held steady rather than reduced, and again no other choice matches it.
solution.description: Separate holding effects constant from reducing them; the sentence calls for reduction, so this word misses the target and also lacks a partner.

solution.operation: Check the remaining words 'mitigate' (A) and 'ameliorate' (E) against the target meaning and against each other.
solution.result: Both mean to lessen the effects and produce sentences alike in meaning.
solution.description: Confirm the surviving pair satisfies both requirements of the question type - each word fits the sentence, and the two completed sentences are equivalent.

examples.answer: Choice A: mitigate; AND Choice E: ameliorate

key_reminders: A sentence equivalence answer must be a pair: each word fits the sentence AND the two completed sentences mean the same thing.
A word with no synonym among the choices cannot be correct, however well it fits.
Derive the required meaning of the blank from the sentence before evaluating any choice.
common_mistakes: Picking 'specify' and 'identify' because they are obvious synonyms of each other, without checking that the sentence wants effects lessened rather than named.
Accepting 'stabilize' as close enough to 'mitigate', treating controlling the effects as the same as reducing them.

concept.technique_name: weaken the argument (4-step critical reasoning process)

examples.problem_statement: The Smithtown Theatre, which stages old plays, has announced an expansion that will double its capacity along with its operating costs. The theatre is only slightly profitable at present. In addition, all of the current customers live in Smithtown, and the population of the town is not expected to increase in the next several years. Thus, the expansion of the Smithtown Theatre will prove unprofitable. Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument?

solution.operation: Identify the question: the stem says 'if true, would most seriously weaken the argument'.
solution.description: Read the question stem first; the phrases 'if true' and 'weaken' fix the task before any answer choice is considered.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument: expansion doubles capacity and operating costs; the theatre is only slightly profitable now; all customers live in Smithtown and the town's population is not expected to grow. Conclusion: the expansion will prove unprofitable.
solution.result: Premises mapped, with the final sentence marked as the conclusion the author is defending.
solution.description: Separate the facts and the future prediction from the claim they support, so the conclusion under attack is explicit.

solution.operation: State the goal: find a statement that undercuts the claim that the expansion will fail, i.e. one that shows the expansion may work.
solution.result: Target answer type: new evidence that the expanded theatre can draw enough additional audience.
solution.description: Fix the direction of attack carefully - the task is to weaken the author's prediction of failure, not to weaken the theatre's plan itself.

solution.operation: Evaluate (A): a large movie chain plans to open a multiplex in Smithtown this year.
solution.result: Eliminated as Reverse Logic - new competition would take business away, strengthening the prediction of failure.
solution.description: Check the direction of each choice's effect; a choice that supports the conclusion is the trap the directions warn about, not the answer.

solution.operation: Evaluate (B): concession sales make up a substantial proportion of the theatre's revenues.
solution.result: Eliminated - profitability after expansion still depends on attracting more people, so this adds nothing new.
solution.description: Ask whether the fact changes once the theatre expands; a revenue mix that hinges on the same unresolved attendance question leaves the argument untouched.

solution.operation: Evaluate (C): many recent arrivals to Smithtown are students, less likely than older residents to attend.
solution.result: Eliminated as Reverse Logic - the new residents are unlikely theatregoers, strengthening the prediction of failure.
solution.description: Note that added population only helps if it converts to audience; here it does not, so the choice pushes the argument the wrong way.

solution.operation: Evaluate (D): the expansion would let the theatre stage larger, more popular shows attracting customers from neighboring towns.
solution.result: Weakens the argument - a new audience beyond Smithtown can fill the doubled capacity and cover the doubled costs.
solution.description: Match this choice to the goal from step 3: it supplies the additional customers the author assumed were unavailable, so the prediction of failure loses its support.

solution.operation: Evaluate (E): the Board often solicits input from town residents when choosing shows.
solution.result: Eliminated - this describes current practice with no indication of what happens after the expansion.
solution.description: Discard a choice that gives no information about the post-expansion situation the conclusion is about.

key_reminders: A weakener attacks the conclusion, which here is the author's prediction of failure - so the right answer makes the plan look better.
Reverse Logic choices support the conclusion instead of undermining it; every problem in this set contains at least one.
The argument's weak point is the assumption that no additional customers are available; the answer supplies them.
common_mistakes: Weakening the theatre's expansion plan instead of the author's claim that it will fail, which makes (A) or (C) look attractive.
Choosing (B) because concessions sound like extra profit, without noticing that concession revenue still scales with attendance, the very thing in doubt.
Treating the fixed Smithtown population as a hard limit on audience and overlooking customers from neighboring towns.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal text completion across linked blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. That today's students of American culture tend to (i) ______ classical music is understandable. In our own time, America's musical high culture has degenerated into a formulaic entertainment divorced from the contemporary moment. Thus, to miss out on what our orchestras are up to is not to (ii) ______ much. In the late Gilded Age, however, music was widely esteemed as the 'queen of the arts.' Classical music was in its American heyday, (iii) ______ the culture at large.

solution.operation: Locate the pivot word 'however' in the next-to-last sentence and read what it contrasts.
solution.result: The Gilded Age esteem for music is set against the present state of affairs, so the present must involve music being viewed negatively or disregarded.
solution.description: Use the contrast signal to establish the passage's two-era structure, which fixes the required sense of the present-day blanks before any choice is weighed.

solution.operation: Apply that required sense to Blank (i), comparing 'promote' (A), 'reinterpret' (B) and 'ignore' (C).
solution.result: 'Ignore' is selected; 'promote' connotes the opposite, and 'reinterpret' suggests a different, positive engagement not mentioned in the passage.
solution.description: Choose the only word conveying disregard, rejecting the one that reverses the sense and the one that imports an idea the passage never raises.

solution.operation: Gather the context for Blank (ii): the author calls the present disconnection understandable and describes current classical music with the pejoratives 'degenerated' and 'formulaic'.
solution.result: The blank must carry a dismissive attitude toward what a concert-skipper forgoes.
solution.description: Read the author's own loaded vocabulary to determine the attitude the second blank has to express, rather than guessing from the blank's sentence alone.

solution.operation: Test the Blank (ii) choices 'sacrifice' (D), 'appreciate' (E) and 'malign' (F) against that dismissive attitude.
solution.result: 'Sacrifice' is selected; 'appreciate' would imply something worthwhile is being missed, and 'malign' overstates the feeling of someone who simply does not attend concerts.
solution.description: Reject one choice for reversing the author's dismissiveness and the other for exceeding the intensity that mere non-attendance warrants.

solution.operation: Return to the contrast for Blank (iii): the present lack of connection between culture and classical music must be opposed by the Gilded Age relationship.
solution.result: 'Centrally embedded in' (I) is selected; 'generally rejected by' (H) would provide no contrast, and 'antagonistic toward' (G) would not explain why music was so widely esteemed.
solution.description: Complete the contrast established in step 1 by choosing the phrase that makes the Gilded Age the opposite of today, and discard the two that either repeat the present or clash with the stated esteem.

examples.answer: Choice C: ignore; Choice D: sacrifice; Choice I: centrally embedded in

key_reminders: 'However' marks a contrast: the two eras described must be opposites, and that fixes the sense of every blank.
The author's evaluative vocabulary ('degenerated', 'formulaic') supplies the attitude a blank must carry.
Reject choices that introduce ideas the passage never mentions or that overstate the intensity of the described behavior.
common_mistakes: Reading 'not to ______ much' too quickly and selecting 'appreciate', which reverses the author's dismissal of today's orchestras.
Choosing 'generally rejected by' for Blank (iii), which restates the present-day situation instead of contrasting with it as 'however' requires.
Taking 'malign' as the strong dismissive word when the sentence describes only someone who skips concerts.

concept.technique_name: irony-signal text completion from sentence evidence

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Ironically, the writer so wary of (i) ______ was (ii) ______ with ink and paper, his novel running to 2,500 shagreen-bound folio pages - a fortune in stationery at the time.

solution.operation: Mine the last part of the sentence for evidence: a novel of 2,500 folio pages costing a fortune in stationery.
solution.result: The writer used vast amounts of material, showing a lack of restraint with ink and paper.
solution.description: Start with the concrete detail after the dash, since it is the only descriptive evidence in the sentence and it characterizes the writer's actual behavior.

solution.operation: Match that lack of restraint against the Blank (ii) choices 'acquisitive' (D), 'illiberal' (E) and 'profligate' (F).
solution.result: 'Profligate' is selected as the only choice meaning wastefully unrestrained in spending material.
solution.description: Fill the blank the evidence directly supports first, eliminating the choices about acquiring and about stinginess, neither of which describes lavish expenditure.

solution.operation: Read the signal word 'Ironically' to relate Blank (i) to the established behavior, then test 'probity' (A), 'extravagance' (B) and 'disapprobation' (C).
solution.result: 'Extravagance' is selected as the choice closest to profligacy, making the writer wary of the very quality he displays.
solution.description: Use the irony marker to require that what the writer feared resembles his own profligacy, and pick the first-blank word nearest in meaning to the one just chosen.

examples.answer: Choice B: extravagance; Choice F: profligate

key_reminders: Fill the blank that the sentence's concrete evidence supports first, then use it to constrain the other blank.
'Ironically' means the two blanks describe similar qualities held in tension, not opposite ones.
common_mistakes: Reading 'Ironically' as a contrast marker and choosing a first-blank word opposed to 'profligate', such as 'probity'.
Selecting 'acquisitive' for Blank (ii), which describes wanting to obtain things rather than spending them lavishly.

concept.technique_name: counting trailing zeros by successive division (Legendre's formula for the power of 5)

examples.problem_statement: If X is a natural number and X! ends with Y zeros then number of zeros at the end of (5X)! is

solution.description: Write the count of trailing zeros of X! as the sum of the successive quotients of X by 5, 25, 125, ...; the book names this whole sum Y.
Apply the same successive-division sum to (5X)!, dividing 5X in turn by 5, 25, 125, and so on.
Simplify each term of the (5X)! sum: it becomes X followed by exactly the sum written in step 1, so the total is X plus Y.
Check the relationship by trial with concrete values, as the book does: for X = 10 and for X = 20 the zero count of (5X)! equals X + Y in both cases.

key_reminders: Trailing zeros of a factorial are counted by the successive quotients [N/5] + [N/25] + [N/125] + ... , keeping only the integer part of each division.
Dividing 5X by 5, 25, 125, ... reproduces the term list for X shifted by one place, with the leading term equal to X itself.
The book verifies the general result by substituting concrete natural numbers for X.
common_mistakes: Stopping the successive-division sum at [N/5] and missing the higher powers 25, 125, ... that also contribute zeros.
Assuming the zero count scales by a factor of 5 (giving 5Y) instead of shifting the term list to give X + Y.

concept.technique_name: work equation W = RT applied twice to a shared job size

examples.problem_statement: Machine A, which produces 15 golf clubs per hour, fills a production lot in 6 hours. Machine B fills the same production lot in 1.5 hours. How many golf clubs does Machine B produce per hour?

solution.operation: W = RT = (15 \text{ clubs per hour})(6 \text{ hours})
solution.description: Put Machine A's rate and time into the work formula W = RT to find how much work one production lot represents.
Carry the lot size of 90 clubs over to Machine B, which fills the same lot, and rewrite its 1.5 hours as 3/2 to make the division easier, as the book directs.
Use W = RT a second time for Machine B, dividing its work by its time to get its hourly rate.

key_reminders: W = RT: with any two of work, rate and time known, the third follows.
Both machines fill the same production lot, so the work value found from Machine A is reused for Machine B.
Converting 1.5 hours to 3/2 turns the division into a multiplication by 2/3's reciprocal and keeps the arithmetic exact.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 1.5 as though it were a rate rather than a time, or multiplying 90 by 1.5 instead of dividing.
Reporting the lot size 90 as the answer instead of continuing to Machine B's per-hour rate.

concept.technique_name: mean of a frequency distribution (weighted sum divided by total frequency)

examples.problem_statement: The table above shows the frequency distribution of the values of a variable Y. What is the mean of the distribution? Give your answer to the nearest 0.01.

solution.description: Rather than writing each repeated value out one at a time, multiply every value of Y by the frequency next to it in the table and add the products; the book's total is 44.
Add down the Frequency column to get how many values of Y there are in all.
Divide the summed values by the number of values, which is what the mean of the distribution means.
Round the decimal quotient to two decimal places, as the question's instruction requires.

key_reminders: The mean of a distribution is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
In a frequency table, a value repeated f times contributes value times f to the sum, and f to the count.
The number of values is the sum of the Frequency column, not the number of table rows.
common_mistakes: Dividing 44 by the number of distinct rows (5) instead of by the total frequency 34.
Truncating 1.2941... to 1.294 or 1.30 instead of rounding to the required nearest 0.01.

concept.technique_name: man-days work equivalence

examples.problem_statement: 15 men could finish a piece of work in 210 days. But at the end of 100 days, 15 additional men are employed. In how many more days will the work be complete?

solution.description: Convert the whole job into man-days by multiplying the original 15 men by the 210 days they would have needed.
Measure the work finished in the first phase: 15 men worked for the first 100 days.
Subtract the man-days already spent from the total man-days to get the work still outstanding.
Divide the remaining man-days by the new daily strength of 30 men (the original 15 plus the 15 additional men) to get the number of further days needed.

key_reminders: Total work can be expressed as (number of men) \times (number of days) in man-days.
Man-days already spent are subtracted from total man-days to get work remaining.
Days remaining = work remaining in man-days divided by the men now working each day.
common_mistakes: Dividing the remaining 1650 man-days by 15 instead of by the enlarged workforce of 30.
Reporting the total elapsed time rather than the additional days asked for.

concept.technique_name: predict-the-blank then eliminate

examples.problem_statement: After the US Civil War, “carpetbaggers”—so-called because they carried suitcases made of inexpensive carpeting material— _________ the South, hoping to turn a quick profit.

solution.operation: Fill the blank with your own words before looking at the choices: “went to”
solution.result: A working prediction of movement into the South
solution.description: Read the sentence and supply your own filler for the blank, so the answer choices are judged against your prediction rather than against each other.

solution.operation: Locate the clue: the carpetbaggers carried suitcases
solution.description: Identify the detail in the sentence that supports the prediction — people carrying suitcases were probably on the move.
Strike out each option that introduces an idea the sentence never indicates, since none of conquering, blacklisting, boycotting or scolding is supported here.

solution.operation: Check the survivor: inundated = flooded, overwhelmed
solution.description: Confirm the one remaining choice by substituting its meaning back into the sentence, where flooding into the South matches the prediction.

key_reminders: Predict a filler for the blank from the sentence itself before reading the options.
The clue for the blank is stated in the sentence — here, the suitcases.
Reject any choice that adds an idea the sentence does not indicate.
common_mistakes: Picking a hostile-sounding word such as vanquished or berated because the passage's subject feels negative, though the sentence itself indicates only arrival.

concept.technique_name: common-multiple profit percentage (with cross-method shortcut)

examples.problem_statement: A boy buys oranges at 9 for Rs 16 and sells them at 11 for Rs 20. What does he gain or lose per cent?

solution.result: A quantity divisible by both 9 and 11
solution.description: Choose 99 as the working number of oranges so that both the buying lot of 9 and the selling lot of 11 divide it exactly and no fractions appear.
Scale the buying rate of Rs 16 per 9 oranges up to 99 oranges to get the total cost price.
Scale the selling rate of Rs 20 per 11 oranges up to the same 99 oranges to get the total selling price.

solution.result: Profit of Rs 4 on a cost of Rs 176
solution.description: Subtract cost price from selling price to get the absolute profit on the 99 oranges.
Express the profit as a percentage of the cost price, which is the base for gain per cent.

solution.result: Same 2 3/11 per cent, positive so it is a gain
solution.description: Apply the book's quicker cross method directly to the four given numbers, cross-multiplying the rates and dividing by the cost cross-product; the positive sign marks it a gain.

key_reminders: Work with a quantity that is a common multiple of the buying and selling lot sizes.
Gain per cent is computed on the cost price, not the selling price.
