Cross method: profit per cent = (buy-quantity \times sell-price - buy-price \times sell-quantity) / (buy-price \times sell-quantity) \times 100, positive meaning gain.
common_mistakes: Comparing the rates Rs 16 and Rs 20 directly without equalising the number of oranges (9 versus 11).
Dividing the Rs 4 profit by the selling price 180 instead of the cost price 176.

concept.technique_name: linear equation from a divide-instead-of-multiply error

examples.problem_statement: A boy was asked to find 7/9 of a fraction. He made a mistake of dividing the fraction by 7/9 and so got an answer which exceeded the correct answer by 8/21. Find the correct answer.

solution.operation: Let the fraction be x; \frac{x}{7/9} - x \times \frac{7}{9} = \frac{8}{21}
solution.description: Name the unknown fraction x and set the wrong result (x divided by 7/9) minus the correct result (7/9 of x) equal to the stated excess of 8/21.

solution.result: Both terms written with x as a coefficient
solution.description: Rewrite the division by 7/9 as multiplication by 9/7 so the left side is two like terms in x.
Combine the two terms over the common denominator 63, subtracting the numerators 81 and 49 to leave 32.
Solve for x by multiplying both sides by the reciprocal of the coefficient 32/63, giving the original fraction.
Take 7/9 of the recovered fraction, which is what the question originally asked for, to get the correct answer.

key_reminders: Dividing by 7/9 is the same as multiplying by 9/7.
“Of” means multiply, so the correct answer is 7/9 \times x.
The question asks for the correct answer, not the fraction x itself — one further multiplication is needed after solving.
common_mistakes: Stopping at x = 3/4 and reporting it instead of taking 7/9 of it.
Reversing the difference and writing the correct answer minus the wrong one, since 9x/7 is the larger of the two.

concept.technique_name: constant percentage profit implies income proportional to expenditure

examples.problem_statement:
Refer to the line chart of percentage profit earned by companies A and B over the years 2003-2008 (B: 2003 = 30, 2004 = 60, 2005 = 80, 2006 = 80, 2007 = 70, 2008 = 100). If the expenditure of company B increases by 20% from 2005 to 2006, the income in 2006 will be how many times the income in 2005?
(a) 2.16 times (b) 1.2 times (c) 1.8 times (d) None of these

solution.operation: Read company B's percentage profit for 2005 and 2006 from the chart
solution.result: Both years show the same percentage profit
solution.description: Compare B's two plotted points on the chart and note that the profit percentage does not change between 2005 and 2006.

solution.operation: Equal profit per cent \Rightarrow income rises in the same proportion as expenditure, i.e. by 20\%
solution.result: Income in 2006 is 120 for every 100 in 2005
solution.description: Since profit per cent is fixed, income is a fixed multiple of expenditure, so a 20% rise in expenditure carries a 20% rise in income.
Form the ratio of the 2006 income to the 2005 income from those proportional figures to get how many times larger it is.

key_reminders: Percentage profit = (income - expenditure) / expenditure \times 100, so a constant profit per cent fixes the income-to-expenditure ratio.
When that ratio is fixed, income scales by exactly the same percentage as expenditure.
common_mistakes: Combining the 20% expenditure rise with the 80% profit figure (e.g. 1.2 \times 1.8 = 2.16) even though the profit per cent is unchanged between the two years.

concept.technique_name: percentile interpretation on a non-linear scale

examples.problem_statement: The 75th percentile on a test corresponded to a score of 700, while the 25th percentile corresponded to a score of 450. Quantity A: 800. Quantity B: A 95th percentile score.

solution.operation: Record the two given anchors: 25\text{th percentile} = 450,\ 75\text{th percentile} = 700
solution.result: Two fixed points on the percentile-to-score mapping, 50 percentile points apart
solution.description: Write down the only two percentile-score pairs the problem supplies, so it is clear what is actually known before any comparison is attempted.

solution.operation: Test whether the 250\text{-point gap over }50\text{ percentile points} may be extended to other percentiles
solution.result: It may not: scoring scales on a test are not necessarily linear
solution.description: Check the hidden assumption behind lining up percentile differences with score differences; because test scales need not be linear, that extrapolation is not licensed.

solution.operation: State the full information the two anchors give about the distribution: 25\% \le 450,\ 50\% \text{ between } 450 \text{ and } 700,\ 25\% > 700
solution.result: The only certain facts are these three population shares
solution.description: Convert the percentile statements into the distribution facts they guarantee, so nothing beyond them is smuggled into the comparison.

solution.operation: Compare 800 against candidate 95th percentile scores such as 750 \text{ and } 963
solution.result: Quantity B can be below 800 (750) or above 800 (963)
solution.description: Since any score above 700 is consistent with the 95th percentile, try one candidate under 800 and one over it to see that Quantity B is not pinned down.

solution.operation: Select the comparison verdict consistent with both candidates
solution.description: Because two admissible scenarios give opposite comparisons, no single relationship holds, which is the choice for an undetermined comparison.

key_reminders: A percentile tells you the share of scores above and below a value, not the spacing between scores.
Test scoring scales are not necessarily linear, so percentile gaps cannot be converted into score gaps.
In a quantitative comparison, one admissible case each way forces the undetermined answer.
common_mistakes: Treating 450 to 700 across 25th to 75th percentile as a constant 5 points per percentile and extrapolating a 95th percentile score of 800.
Assuming the scores are normally distributed and reading the 95th percentile off a bell curve, when no distribution is given.

concept.technique_name: simultaneous linear equations in digits

examples.problem_statement: A four digit number wxyz is such that x + y = 2w, y + 6z = 2(w + x) and w + 5z = 2y. Find the sum of such four digit numbers which satisfy the given conditions.

solution.operation: Number the constraints: x + y = 2w \ (1),\quad y + 6z = 2(w + x)\ (2),\quad w + 5z = 2y\ (3)
solution.result: Three linear equations in the four digits w, x, y, z
solution.description: Label each printed condition so the eliminations that follow can refer to them by number.
Subtract the first equation from the second; the y terms cancel and the right side leaves 2x, giving x directly in terms of z.
Put the relation just found back into equation (1) to get a new equation (4) in w, y and z only.
Combine the two remaining equations to express w and y as multiples of z, so every digit is now a multiple of z.

solution.operation: Read off z : y : x : w = 1 : 4 : 2 : 3 and take the admissible digit multiples
solution.description: Scale the ratio by z; only z = 1 and z = 2 keep every digit in range, producing the two four-digit numbers that satisfy all three conditions.
Add the two qualifying numbers, since the question asks for the sum of all such four-digit numbers.

key_reminders: Subtracting one condition from another to cancel a shared digit term is the fastest route into these digit puzzles.
Once all digits are multiples of z, only the values of z that keep every digit a single digit are admissible.
The question asks for the sum of all qualifying numbers, not for one number.
common_mistakes: Stopping at one solution (3241 or 6482) and reporting it instead of their sum.
Accepting z = 3, which forces y = 12 and is not a digit.

concept.technique_name: data sufficiency on dividend rate

examples.problem_statement: Mahesh got Rs 1200 as dividend from a finance co. What is the rate of interest given by the company? Which of the given statements is/are sufficient/necessary? A. Mahesh has 960 shares of Rs 10 denomination. B. The dividend paid last year was 9.5%.

solution.description: Multiply the number of shares by the face value given in statement A to obtain the capital on which the dividend was paid.

solution.operation: Form the rate from the dividend and that capital: \dfrac{1200}{9600}
solution.result: The rate is determined, so A alone is sufficient
solution.description: Divide the known dividend by the capital just computed; because both quantities are now known, statement A settles the rate on its own.

solution.operation: Test statement B: last year's dividend rate of 9.5\% against this year's rate
solution.result: Last year's dividend need not equal this year's, so B is not sufficient
solution.description: Check whether the prior year's rate constrains the current year; it does not, so statement B contributes nothing to the required rate.

solution.operation: Match the finding (A sufficient, B not) to the printed options
solution.description: Pick the option that says A alone suffices, since one statement worked and the other did not.

key_reminders: Dividend rate is computed on the face value of the holding: capital = number of shares x denomination.
A rate from a previous year is not evidence about the current year's rate.
common_mistakes: Reading 'rate of interest' as needing a market price and declaring A insufficient, when the Rs 10 denomination already fixes the capital.
Assuming the 9.5% of statement B carries over to this year and calling B sufficient.

concept.technique_name: average table (average x number = sum)

examples.problem_statement: Grace's average bowling score over the past 6 games is 150. If she wants to raise her average score by 10%, and she has two more games remaining in the season, what must her average score on the last two games be?

solution.description: Take 10 percent of the current average, because the target is an average raised by that percentage.
Add the increase to the current average to get the average Grace must hold across the whole season.
Fill the first row of the average table, converting the known average and game count into the points already scored.

solution.operation: Final two games row: A \times 2 = 2A;\ targeted outcome row: 165 \times 8 = 900 + 2A
solution.description: Write the last two games with unknown average A, then set the eight-game total from the target average equal to the old sum plus those two games.
Solve the last row of the table for A by isolating the two-game sum and halving it, giving the required average for the final two games.

key_reminders: Average x number of terms = sum; build a row per scenario and keep the sums consistent.
A percentage increase in an average is taken on the original average, here 10% of 150.
The target average applies to all 8 games, not just the remaining 2.
common_mistakes: Raising the target only over the 2 remaining games, i.e. answering 165 instead of 210.
Using 6 games instead of 8 in the target row and getting a sum of 990.

concept.technique_name: conditional rule application in a basic grouping game

examples.problem_statement: On a field trip to the Museum of Natural History, each of six children - Juana, Kyle, Lucita, Salim, Thanh, and Veronica - is accompanied by one of three adults - Ms. Margoles, Mr. O'Connell, and Ms. Podorski. Each adult accompanies exactly two of the children, consistent with the following conditions: If Ms. Margoles accompanies Juana, then Ms. Podorski accompanies Lucita. If Kyle is not accompanied by Ms. Margoles, then Veronica is accompanied by Mr. O'Connell. Either Ms. Margoles or Mr. O'Connell accompanies Thanh. Juana is not accompanied by the same adult as Kyle; nor is Lucita accompanied by the same adult as Salim; nor is Thanh accompanied by the same adult as Veronica. Mr. O'Connell CANNOT accompany which one of the following pairs of children?

solution.operation: Classify the answer choices: four pairs CAN be assigned to O, exactly one CANNOT
solution.result: The task is to find the single pair that breaks a rule when placed in O's column
solution.description: Read the question as an exception question so the search is for the one violating pair rather than for a full valid arrangement.

solution.operation: Identify the rule that governs O's column: \text{not } V_O \rightarrow K_M
solution.result: Whenever V is not with O, K must be with M
solution.description: Since the question is about O's column, isolate the conditional that fires on O, and note it triggers precisely for choices that do not contain V.

solution.operation: Test (A): place J and L with O
solution.result: K can go to M, and T and V can be kept apart - no violation
solution.description: Try the first V-free choice and check the conditional and the separation rules; an arrangement exists, so (A) is not the answer.

solution.operation: Test (C): place K and T with O, which also omits V
solution.result: V not with O forces K into M, yet (C) puts K with O - contradiction
solution.description: Apply the same conditional to the other V-free choice; the trigger demands K in M while the choice itself places K with O, so the pair is impossible.

solution.operation: Select the pair shown to be impossible in O's column
solution.result: Kyle and Thanh cannot both be with Mr. O'Connell
solution.description: Report the choice whose placement was contradicted, since it is the only pair that cannot be assigned to O.

key_reminders: In a CANNOT question, one choice must break a rule while the other four are constructible.
Target the conditional whose trigger involves the group the question asks about, here the rule firing when V is not with O.
The contrapositive matters: V not in O's column forces K into Margoles' column.
common_mistakes: Skipping the V-free choices and testing (B) or (E), where the conditional never fires and no contradiction appears.
Reading the rule as 'V must be with O' rather than as the conditional that forces K into M.

concept.technique_name: elimination by subtracting one equation from another

examples.problem_statement:
4x + y + 3z = 34
4x + 3z = 21
What is the value of y?

solution.operation: Count what is given: 2 equations, 3 unknowns x, y, z
solution.result: The system is underdetermined, so x, y and z cannot each be solved for individually
solution.description: Before manipulating anything, take stock of the system: there are only two equations for three variables, so the usual solve-for-every-variable route is closed and y has to be isolated some other way.

solution.operation: Compare coefficients across the two equations: 4x and 3z appear in both
solution.result: The x and z terms are identical in the two equations, so a subtraction will cancel both at once
solution.description: Look at the coefficients rather than the variables: because x carries 4 and z carries 3 in each equation, the two unwanted terms are already matched and can be removed together instead of one at a time.

Subtract the second equation from the first, term by term on the left and value by value on the right; 4x - 4x and 3z - 3z both vanish, leaving y alone on the left and the difference of the constants on the right.

key_reminders: Two equations cannot pin down three variables individually, but a single combined variable can still be determined.
Subtracting equations eliminates any term whose coefficient is identical in both.
Subtract both sides: the left sides combine term by term and the right sides combine as numbers.
common_mistakes: Adding the equations instead of subtracting, which doubles 4x and 3z instead of cancelling them.
Declaring the problem unsolvable because there are three variables and only two equations, without checking that x and z share coefficients.
Subtracting the left sides but forgetting to subtract 21 from 34 on the right.

concept.technique_name: evidence-function identification with answer-choice elimination
concept.sub_category: Reading Comprehension - function of cited detail

examples.problem_statement:
The fact that "adjacent agricultural fields can produce significantly different yields" (lines 16-17) is offered as evidence of the
(A) unpredictability of the climate and environment of the southwestern United States
(B) difficulty of producing a consistent food supply for a large population in the Western Pueblo region
(C) lack of water and land suitable for cultivation in central Arizona
(D) local climatic variation in the environment of the southwestern United States
(E) high-frequency environmental processes at work in the southwestern United States

solution.operation: Return to the second paragraph, where the quoted lines sit, and read what surrounds them
solution.result: The paragraph attributes the differing yields of adjacent fields to rainfall variations between local valleys
solution.description: Go back to the cited lines in their own paragraph rather than judging them in isolation, because the question asks what the detail is being used to support, and only the surrounding sentences say so.

solution.operation: State the claim the detail is illustrating: climate in the Southwest is not uniform but varies significantly from place to place
solution.result: The detail functions as an example of local climatic variation, which is choice D
solution.description: Name the larger point the example serves; the passage offers the yield difference precisely as an instance of place-to-place climatic difference, which matches choice D word for word in substance.

solution.operation: Test choice A against how the detail is actually used
solution.result: A is rejected: variability could imply unpredictability, but that is not the use the passage makes of the yield difference
solution.description: Reject A by distinguishing an inference someone might draw from the evidence's stated purpose; the passage deploys the fact to show variation across places, not to argue that the climate is unpredictable.

solution.operation: Check choices B and C for support anywhere in the passage
solution.result: B and C are rejected: the passage neither claims nor reports a claim about feeding large populations, nor asserts that central Arizona lacks cultivable land
solution.description: Eliminate B and C on the ground that their content is simply absent from the passage, so neither can be what the cited fact is evidence for.

solution.operation: Locate where high- and low-frequency processes are discussed and compare with the cited lines
solution.result: E is rejected: that discussion is in the third paragraph, and the author never labels the rainfall and yield differences as a high-frequency process
solution.description: Eliminate E by checking paragraph placement and wording; the high-frequency terminology belongs to a different paragraph and is never applied to the geographic differences in rainfall and yield, leaving D as the answer.

examples.answer: Choice D: local climatic variation in the environment of the southwestern United States

key_reminders: A cited-detail question asks what the detail is used to prove, not merely what the detail says.
The paragraph containing the citation supplies the claim the detail supports.
A choice that is plausible in the world but unsupported in the passage is still wrong.
common_mistakes: Choosing A because unpredictability sounds like a natural consequence of varying yields, though the passage uses the fact to show variation, not unpredictability.
Choosing E by matching the phrase 'high-frequency environmental processes' to the passage's third paragraph, which discusses a different point.
Importing outside knowledge about food supply or Arizona farmland to justify B or C.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal prediction for double-blank completion

examples.problem_statement:
Anne could have made a larger salary elsewhere, but such (i) _________ as ample vacation time and excellent insurance persuaded her to (ii) _________.

Blank (i): perquisites / remuneration / disincentives
Blank (ii): negotiate / abscond / abide

solution.operation: Read the pivot word "but" joining the larger-salary clause to the rest of the sentence
solution.result: Anne did not leave for the larger salary; she stayed
solution.description: Use the contrast signal "but" to fix the sentence's direction: whatever follows must explain why Anne stayed rather than chased the higher pay.

solution.operation: Predict blank (i) from its own appositive list — ample vacation time and excellent insurance — as "non-salary rewards"
solution.description: Let the examples given after "such ... as" define the blank: vacation time and insurance are benefits that come on top of salary, so write that plain-language prediction before touching the choices.

solution.operation: Match the prediction "non-salary rewards" against perquisites, remuneration, disincentives
solution.description: Pick the only choice that carries the predicted meaning: perquisites (informally "perks") are exactly non-salary rewards, so it fills blank (i).

solution.operation: Predict blank (ii) as "stay" and match it against negotiate, abscond, abide
solution.description: Since step 1 established that Anne stayed, the second blank needs a word meaning "stay"; only abide can carry that sense, so it fills blank (ii).

solution.operation: Check abide's secondary senses "tolerate" and "wait for" against the sentence
solution.result: abide still fits; it is the only candidate meaning stay
solution.description: Confirm the choice by noting that abide more commonly means tolerate or wait for, yet its "stay" sense is available and no other option offers it.

key_reminders: The word but reverses direction: it signals Anne stayed instead of taking the larger salary.
Predict each blank in your own words from the sentence's own clues before reading the answer choices.
"such ___ as X and Y" makes X and Y the definition of the blank.
common_mistakes: Choosing remuneration for blank (i) — it means payment, i.e. the salary the sentence explicitly says she gave up, not the non-salary benefits.
Reading abide only as "tolerate" and rejecting it, missing the "stay" sense the sentence needs.
Choosing abscond, which means to leave secretly — the opposite of the direction "but" establishes.

concept.technique_name: percentage part-to-whole translation

examples.problem_statement:
Geoff used $630 to buy a new guitar. This amount was 15 percent of his earnings last summer.

Quantity A: The amount of Geoff's earnings last summer not used to buy the new guitar
Quantity B: $3,570

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

solution.operation: State what Quantity A asks for: earnings last summer minus the 630 spent on the guitar
solution.description: Name the target before computing: Quantity A is the leftover earnings, so the unknown you must find first is total earnings last summer.

solution.operation: Translate the given percent relationship into an equation: 0.15 \times (\text{earnings last summer}) = 630
solution.description: Turn the words "this amount was 15 percent of his earnings" into an arithmetic statement, with the 630 as the part and the earnings as the whole.
Solve the equation for the whole by dividing the part by the decimal form of the percent, giving Geoff's total earnings last summer.
Subtract the guitar's cost from the total earnings to get the amount he did not spend, which is Quantity A.

solution.operation: Compare Quantity A = 3570 with Quantity B = 3570
solution.description: Set the computed value of Quantity A beside the stated Quantity B; they match, so the comparison resolves to equality.

examples.answer: Choice C: The two quantities are equal.

key_reminders: Translate "A is P percent of B" directly into the equation (P/100) \times B = A.
Find the whole by dividing the part by the decimal percent, not by multiplying.
Quantity A here is the remainder after the purchase, so the subtraction step is mandatory before comparing.
common_mistakes: Comparing the whole 4200 against 3570 and answering A, forgetting that Quantity A is earnings minus the 630 spent.
Multiplying 630 by 0.15 instead of dividing, which treats the part as the whole.
Taking 630 as 15 percent of the leftover rather than of total earnings.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence pair matching

examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

That people ______ the musical features of birdsongs suggests that despite the vast evolutionary gulf between birds and mammals, songbirds and humans share some common auditory perceptual abilities.

A mimic
B recognize
C relish
D are confounded by
E can make out
F are puzzled by

solution.operation: Read what the sentence claims: some human ability toward the musical features of birdsongs suggests that humans share a perceptual ability with songbirds.
solution.result: The blank must name an ability that humans actually possess, and it must be perceptual.
solution.description: Trace the logic of the sentence first: because the main clause concludes that humans and songbirds share an auditory perceptual ability, whatever fills the blank has to be evidence that humans have that ability.

solution.operation: Test 'are confounded by' (D) and 'are puzzled by' (F) against that requirement.
solution.description: Insert each of these two choices and check them against the requirement from step 1: they describe a failure to perceive, so they do not allow for the existence of the ability the sentence needs, and both drop out.

solution.result: Both make sense in the blank but are eliminated: each designates more than just perception, and neither has a partner among the choices that would produce a similar sentence.
solution.description: Check the remaining tempting choices on two counts at once. They read acceptably, but each carries meaning beyond perception, and Sentence Equivalence needs a matching second word, which neither one has.

solution.result: The two completed sentences are alike in meaning and both express plain perception.
solution.description: Confirm the surviving pair: these two are the only choices that both stay within perception and mean the same thing as each other, satisfying the requirement that the two completed sentences be alike in meaning.

examples.answer: Choice B: recognize; AND Choice E: can make out

key_reminders: The two correct choices must produce completed sentences alike in meaning, not merely two sentences that each make sense.
The word in the blank has to be consistent with the claim the rest of the sentence draws from it.
A choice that designates more than the sentence needs is weaker than one that names exactly the required idea.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'are confounded by' and 'are puzzled by' as a synonym pair, ignoring that they contradict the sentence's conclusion that humans share the perceptual ability.
Selecting 'mimic' or 'relish' because it reads well in the blank, without checking that a second choice creates a sentence similar in meaning.

concept.technique_name: evaluate the argument (two-path test)

examples.problem_statement:
Recently, the tuition at most elite private high schools has been rising more quickly than inflation. Even before these increases, many low- and middle-income families were unable to afford the full tuition costs for their children at these schools. With the new tuition increases, these schools will soon be attended solely by students from affluent families.

Which of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the argument?

(A) Whether students from affluent families are more likely to prefer public or private high schools
(B) Whether most students from low- and middle-income families are academically qualified to attend elite private high schools
(C) Whether low-income families are less likely to be able to afford tuition costs than middle-income families
(D) Whether graduates of elite private high schools typically earn higher salaries as adults than do people who did not graduate from these schools
(E) Whether grants or scholarships are available for students from economically disadvantaged families

solution.operation: Identify the question type from the words 'evaluate' and 'most useful to determine'.
solution.description: Read the question stem before the argument and classify it: the phrases 'evaluate' and 'useful to determine' mark this as an Evaluate the Argument question, which sets what the right answer must do.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument into its parts: tuition rising faster than inflation (fact); many low- and middle-income families already could not afford it (fact); these schools will soon be attended solely by affluent students (prediction).
solution.result: Conclusion: private high schools will have only rich students.
solution.description: Separate facts from conclusion by labeling each sentence. The first two are stated facts, so the third, a prediction about the future, is the conclusion the answer must bear on.

solution.operation: State the goal and surface the assumption: the author assumes there is no way for lower-income students to attend, that is, no loans, no scholarships.
solution.result: The right answer must have two paths, one making the conclusion more likely valid and one making it less likely valid.
solution.description: Before touching the choices, fix the target. Name the gap the conclusion depends on, and note that a correct Evaluate answer must be a question whose two possible answers push the conclusion in opposite directions.

solution.operation: Eliminate (A), (B), (C), and (D) against the two-path test.
solution.result: (A) out: the conclusion is that private schools have only wealthy students, not that all wealthy students attend private schools. (B) out: qualified or not, these students still cannot afford the schools, so the conclusion holds either way. (C) out: the argument combines low- and middle-income families rather than distinguishing them. (D) out: it addresses the consequences of attending, not whether students can afford to attend.
solution.description: Work from wrong to right, checking each of the four choices for whether its two possible outcomes actually move the conclusion in opposite directions. Each of these fails, either by reversing the conclusion's direction, by leaving it equally strong both ways, or by addressing something outside it.

solution.operation: Apply the two-path test to (E): if grants and scholarships exist, lower-income students may afford these schools; if they do not exist, those students cannot attend.
solution.result: (E) can either weaken or strengthen the conclusion, so it is correct.
solution.description: Run both branches of the surviving choice explicitly. One branch hurts the conclusion and the other supports it, which is exactly the behavior an Evaluate answer must show.

key_reminders: An Evaluate answer must have two paths: one answer to it makes the conclusion more likely valid, the other less likely valid.
Sort each sentence into fact or conclusion before evaluating answers; the prediction about the future is the conclusion here.
A choice that leaves the conclusion equally strong whichever way it resolves is wrong.
common_mistakes: Picking (B) because qualification feels relevant, missing that unqualified and unaffordable both lead to the same conclusion.
Picking (C) by splitting low- from middle-income families when the argument treats them as one group.
Reversing the conclusion into 'all wealthy students attend private schools' and so being drawn to (A).

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via tone and contrast cues

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

It is a sad but just indictment of some high school history textbooks that they frequently report as (i) ______ claims that historians hotly debate or that are even completely (ii) ______ by (iii) ______ primary sources.

Blank (i): A factual, B controversial, C sensational
Blank (ii): D resolved, E corroborated, F contradicted
Blank (iii): G dubious, H incomplete, I reliable

solution.operation: Read the word 'indictment', meaning a charge of wrongdoing.
solution.result: The sentence sharply criticizes the textbooks, so every blank must support that critique.
solution.description: Start from the tone word that governs the whole sentence. Because 'indictment' signals a charge of wrongdoing, each blank has to be filled with a word that keeps the criticism intact.

solution.operation: For Blank (i), test 'controversial' against the phrase 'claims that historians hotly debate'.
solution.description: Try the choice that merely restates the context. Reporting hotly debated claims as controversial would be neither surprising nor inaccurate, so it produces no criticism and cannot be right.

solution.operation: Weigh 'sensational' against 'factual' for Blank (i), then check against the rest of the sentence, which concerns the textbooks' relationship to primary sources.
solution.result: 'factual' (Choice A) is chosen, since it implies gross inaccuracies and the critique centers on accuracy rather than tone.
solution.description: Compare the two remaining candidates on what kind of fault each alleges. 'Sensational' charges melodramatic tone while 'factual' charges inaccuracy, and the rest of the sentence, about primary sources, shows the critique is about accuracy.

solution.operation: For Blank (ii), use the 'even' preceding it, which demands a word further from factual than 'hotly debated'.
solution.result: 'contradicted' (Choice F) fits; 'resolved' and 'corroborated' are the opposite of what is needed.
solution.description: Let the escalating 'even' set the requirement for this blank: it needs something stronger against factuality than mere debate. Only 'contradicted' escalates that way, while the other two point the opposite direction.

solution.operation: For Blank (iii), determine what the primary sources must be, given that the accuracy critique rests on the textbooks' divergence from them.
solution.result: The sources must be authoritative, so 'reliable' (Choice I) fits; 'dubious' and 'incomplete' suggest the opposite.
solution.description: Ask what quality the sources need for the criticism to land. Since the textbooks are faulted for diverging from these sources, the sources must be authoritative, which 'reliable' supplies and the other two undercut.

examples.answer: Choice A: factual; Choice F: contradicted; Choice I: reliable

key_reminders: 'Indictment' marks the sentence as criticism, so every blank must sustain the critique.
'even' before a blank signals escalation: the word must go further than the idea just stated.
The primary sources must be authoritative for a divergence from them to count as an error.
common_mistakes: Filling Blank (i) with 'controversial' because it echoes 'hotly debate', producing an accurate report rather than an indictment.
Choosing 'sensational' for Blank (i), shifting the charge to tone when the rest of the sentence makes it about accuracy.
Putting 'corroborated' or 'resolved' in Blank (ii), which reverses the escalation that 'even' demands.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion via paragraph theme

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

Richard M. Russell said 52 percent of the nation's growth since the Second World War had (i) ______ invention. He said, (ii) ______ research, the government's greatest role in assuring continuing innovation is promoting a strong, modern patent office. "Unless we can (iii) ______ original ideas, we will not have invention," Mr. Russell said. Speculating on the state of innovation over the next century, several inventors agreed that the future lay in giving children the tools to think creatively and the motivation to invent.

Blank (i): A been at the expense of, B no bearing on, C come through
Blank (ii): D in addition to restricting, E aside from supporting, F far from
Blank (iii): G evaluate, H protect, I disseminate

solution.operation: Take a quick overview of the paragraph to fix its topic.
solution.result: The topic is the encouragement of invention and innovation.
solution.description: Read the whole paragraph before filling anything in, so that a single controlling theme, here the encouragement of invention and innovation, can govern all three choices.

solution.operation: For Blank (i), apply that theme to the claim about 52 percent of the nation's growth.
solution.result: 'come through' (Choice C) is chosen because it emphasizes the importance of invention; the other choices suggest invention is irrelevant to growth or harmed by it.
solution.description: Match this blank to the theme from step 1. Only a phrase crediting invention for the growth emphasizes its importance, while the alternatives make invention irrelevant or damaged.

solution.operation: For Blank (ii), check which choice continues the theme of encouraging invention.
solution.result: 'aside from supporting' (Choice E) is the only one that does.
solution.description: Screen this blank's three options by the same encouragement theme rather than by grammar alone, since only one of them keeps the government in a supporting role toward invention.

solution.operation: For Blank (iii), carry over the second sentence's emphasis on a strong patent office into Mr. Russell's quotation, which reaffirms it.
solution.description: Link the quotation back to the sentence before it. Since that sentence stresses the patent office and the quotation restates the same thought, the blank needs the verb that names what a patent office does for original ideas.

examples.answer: Choice C: come through; Choice E: aside from supporting; Choice H: protect

key_reminders: Establish the paragraph's overall theme first; in a multi-blank text all blanks must serve it.
A quotation that reaffirms the preceding sentence must be filled with a word consistent with that sentence.
Reject choices that reverse the passage's stance, such as those making invention irrelevant or restricted.
common_mistakes: Filling Blank (i) with 'been at the expense of' or 'no bearing on', which contradicts the paragraph's praise of invention.
Choosing 'evaluate' or 'disseminate' for Blank (iii) instead of the verb that matches the patent-office emphasis of the preceding sentence.

concept.technique_name: counting multiples in an interval

examples.problem_statement: The difference between two numbers is 16. What can be said about the total numbers divisible by 7 that can lie in between these two numbers.

solution.result: at least 2 multiples of 7 always lie inside the gap
solution.description: Note that a gap of 16 always contains two multiples of 7, so the count is definitely at least two.

solution.result: the case that pushes the count to 3
solution.description: Take the first number in the form one less than a multiple of 7, since that placement squeezes an extra multiple into the interval.
Use the book's instance of that form: 27 is one less than 28, and adding the difference 16 gives the other number 43.
List the multiples of 7 lying between 27 and 43 to see this case yields three, not two.

examples.answer: may be 2 or 3 depending upon the numbers

key_reminders: A fixed difference of 16 guarantees two multiples of 7 in between, never fewer.
Starting the interval at a number of the form 7n - 1 is what admits a third multiple.
common_mistakes: Dividing 16 by 7 and answering a single fixed count of 2, missing the 7n - 1 starting position that gives 3.
Counting the endpoints themselves as numbers lying in between.

concept.technique_name: prime factorization divisibility test

examples.problem_statement: If a is a multiple of 18 and b is a multiple of 12, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) a - b is divisible by 6. (B) a + b is divisible by 12. (C) a \times b is divisible by 18. (D) a \div b is divisible by 6.

solution.result: prime factor sets for a and b
solution.description: Build a factor tree for each multiple so every guaranteed prime factor of a and of b is visible before testing any statement.

solution.result: both a and b are divisible by 6, so a - b is too; select (A)
solution.description: Check (A): 6 needs a 2 and a 3, and both a and b carry both, so each is a multiple of 6 and their difference is as well.

solution.result: 30 is not a multiple of 12; eliminate (B)
solution.description: Check (B): b is a multiple of 12 but a need not be, so test the counterexample a = 18, b = 12 and see the sum fails.

solution.result: contains a 2 and two 3s, so it is divisible by 18; select (C)
solution.description: Check (C): pool the prime factors of a and b, then confirm the pool contains the 2, 3, 3 that 18 requires.

solution.result: not even known to be an integer; eliminate (D)
solution.description: Check (D): dividing the factor sets leaves an unknown quotient, so divisibility by 6 cannot be guaranteed.

examples.answer: (A) a − b is divisible by 6; (C) a × b is divisible by 18

key_reminders: A multiple of n is guaranteed to carry every prime factor of n, and nothing more.
If two numbers are each divisible by d, their sum and difference are divisible by d.
The prime factors of a product include all prime factors of both operands.
common_mistakes: Assuming a is a multiple of 12 because b is, which wrongly validates (B).
Treating a \div b as an integer when nothing forces b to divide a, which wrongly validates (D).

concept.technique_name: standard deviations from the mean
concept.sub_category: Descriptive statistics: mean and standard deviation

examples.problem_statement: A list of numbers has a mean of 8 and a standard deviation of 2.5. If x is a number in the list that is 2 standard deviations above the mean, what is the value of x ?

solution.description: Read off the given mean and standard deviation and restate the position of x relative to the mean.
Convert the distance from standard-deviation units into actual units by multiplying 2 by the standard deviation 2.5.
Add that 5-unit distance to the mean of 8, since x lies above the mean.

key_reminders: A value k standard deviations above the mean equals mean + k \times (\text{standard deviation}).
Above the mean means add the distance; below the mean would subtract it.
common_mistakes: Adding 2 instead of (2)(2.5), giving 10 rather than 13.
Multiplying the mean by the standard deviation instead of offsetting it.

concept.technique_name: compound interest year-by-year multiplication

examples.problem_statement: The number of years it would take for the value of an investment to double, at 26% interest compounded annually, is approximately

solution.result: 1 grows by a factor of 1.26 each year and must reach 2
solution.description: Set up the model the book uses: begin with one dollar and multiply by 1.26 for each year that passes, since doubling means reaching two dollars.
Apply the multiplier once to get the end-of-Year-1 value; it is still below the doubling target.
Multiply the Year 1 value by 1.26 again to get the end-of-Year-2 value, which is still short of 2.

solution.result: 2.000376 at the end of Year 3, which is about 2.00
solution.description: Multiply the Year 2 value by 1.26 a third time; the result is approximately 2.00, so the doubling target is reached here.
Read off the first year whose ending value meets the target: the investment takes 3 years to double.

key_reminders: Compounding multiplies the previous year's amount by 1 + r each year, so carry the running value forward.
Doubling means the running value reaches 2 times the starting amount.
Compounded growth earns interest on the interest, so it doubles faster than simple interest suggests.
common_mistakes: Treating 26% as simple interest and reasoning that 26% is a bit more than 25% = 1/4, which wrongly gives about 4 years instead of 3.
Stopping at Year 2 because 1.5876 looks close to 2, when the target is not yet reached.

concept.technique_name: HCF of quantities after unit conversion

examples.problem_statement: Find the greatest weight which can be contained exactly in 1 kg 235 gm and 3 kg 430 gm.

solution.description: Reduce the first quantity to a single unit by converting the kilogram part to grams and adding the gram part.
Reduce the second quantity to grams the same way, so both weights are expressed in the same unit.
Take the HCF of the two gram values, because the greatest weight contained exactly in both must divide both.

key_reminders: Both quantities must be expressed in the same unit before any HCF is taken.
The greatest measure contained exactly in two quantities is their HCF.
common_mistakes: Taking the HCF of 235 and 430 alone and ignoring the kilogram parts, instead of using 1235 and 3430.
Taking the LCM instead of the HCF, which asks for the smallest common multiple rather than the greatest common measure.

concept.technique_name: unit conversion then ratio comparison

examples.problem_statement: Compare the rates of two trains, one travelling at 45 km an hour and the other at 10 m a second.

solution.description: Convert the second train's speed from metres per second to kilometres per hour by multiplying by the factor 18/5.

solution.result: the two speeds are 45 km/hr and 36 km/hr
solution.description: State both rates in the same unit so they can be compared directly.
Form the ratio of the two km/hr figures and reduce it by dividing both terms by 9.

key_reminders: Multiply by 18/5 to convert metres per second into kilometres per hour.
Rates can only be compared as a ratio once both are in the same unit.
Reduce the resulting ratio to lowest terms.
common_mistakes: Using 5/18 instead of 18/5 and converting in the wrong direction, turning 10 m/s into a much smaller km/hr figure.
Comparing 45 with 10 directly and reporting 9 : 2 without converting units.

concept.technique_name: absolute value inequality case split

examples.problem_statement: |x^3| < 64. Quantity A: -x. Quantity B: -|x|. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Apply the absolute value identity to |x^3| < 64, splitting it into the two cases the book uses: the inside taken as positive, and the inside taken as negative.
Take the cube root of the positive case to get the upper bound on x.
Multiply the negative case by -1, flipping the inequality sign as the book notes, then take the cube root to get the lower bound on x.

solution.result: x \text{ may be positive, negative, or zero}
solution.description: Combine the two bounds into a single interval, and observe that this interval does not fix the sign of x.

solution.operation: \text{compare } -x \text{ and } -|x| \text{ for } x \ge 0 \text{ and for } x < 0
solution.result: \text{equal when } x \ge 0; \ \text{Quantity A greater when } x < 0
solution.description: Test both sign cases in the two quantities: with x positive or zero the quantities match, with x negative Quantity A is larger, so no single relationship holds.

key_reminders: |a| = a when a is positive or zero, and |a| = -a when a is negative
Multiplying an inequality by -1 flips the inequality sign
A quantitative comparison is (D) whenever two allowed values of the variable give different relationships
common_mistakes: Dropping the negative case and concluding only x < 4, which would hide the negative values that make Quantity A greater
Forgetting to flip the sign when multiplying x^3 > -64 through by -1
Assuming -x is always negative, which makes the two quantities look permanently equal

concept.technique_name: unit digit pairing for divisibility by 10

examples.problem_statement: If n is a natural number, then what is the sum of all the possible distinct remainders when 9^n + 6^n + 4^n + 11^n is divided by 10?

solution.result: 0 \ \text{when } n \text{ odd}; \ 2 \ \text{when } n \text{ even (last digit of } 9^2 + 11^2)
solution.description: Pair the first and last terms and check their combined last digit: the pair is divisible by 10 for odd n, and leaves 2 for even n.

solution.result: 0 \ \text{when } n \text{ odd}; \ 2 \ \text{when } n \text{ even (last digit of } 6^2 + 4^2)
solution.description: Pair the middle two terms the same way: divisible by 10 for odd n, leaving 2 for even n.
Add the two pair remainders for odd n, giving no remainder when 10 divides the whole expression.
Add the two pair remainders for even n to get the remainder in that case.
Sum the distinct remainders found across the two cases to answer what the question asks for.

key_reminders: A remainder on division by 10 is just the last digit of the expression
Terms can be grouped in pairs whose last digits cancel to 0
Powers of 9, 11, 6 and 4 behave differently for odd and even exponents, so both parities must be checked
common_mistakes: Reporting 4 as the only remainder and ignoring the odd-n case that contributes remainder 0
Summing the remainders 2 and 2 as the final answer without first separating the odd and even cases
Pairing the terms as 9^n + 6^n and 4^n + 11^n, whose last digits do not combine to a multiple of 10

concept.technique_name: ratio proportion in data sufficiency
concept.sub_category: Data Sufficiency on income, expenditure and savings ratios

examples.problem_statement: Directions: The following question is accompanied by three statements A, B and C. You have to determine which statement(s) is/are sufficient/necessary to answer the question. Income of P is 1 2/3 of the income of Q. The expenses of P, Q and R are in the ratio of 6 : 4 : 5. Find the expenses of Q. A. Expenses of R is Rs 2000 less than that of P. B. P's saving is Rs 3000. C. Income of R is one-third of the total incomes of P, Q and R of Rs 36000. 1) Only B and C together are sufficient 2) Only A alone is sufficient 3) All together are necessary 4) Either B and C together or A alone is sufficient 5) All even together are not sufficient

solution.description: Use statement A: the gap between P's and R's expense ratio shares is one unit, and that gap is stated to be Rs 2000, which fixes the value of a single ratio unit.
Multiply Q's four ratio units by the unit value found, giving Q's expense from statement A alone, so A alone is sufficient.
Use statement C: R's income is one-third of the Rs 36000 total, so divide the total by 3.
Subtract R's income from the total to isolate the combined income of P and Q.
Substitute the given income relation between P and Q into the combined income to solve for P's income.
Use statement B: subtract P's saving from P's income to get P's expense.
Convert P's expense into one ratio unit and scale it to Q's four units, so B and C together also give Q's expense; either route works, giving option 4.

key_reminders: A difference between two ratio shares can be equated to a stated rupee difference to fix one ratio unit
Income minus savings equals expense
In data sufficiency, once one route answers the question, keep testing the other statements before choosing a combination option
common_mistakes: Reading 'income of P is 1 2/3 of Q' as P = 1.23Q or as a 1 : 3 relation instead of P = 5/3 Q
Stopping after statement A works and choosing option 2, missing that B and C together also suffice
Applying the Rs 2000 difference to Q's share instead of to the single unit gap between P and R

concept.technique_name: equivalent rule substitution in an ordering game

examples.problem_statement: Detectives investigating a citywide increase in burglaries questioned exactly seven suspects - S, T, V, W, X, Y, and Z - each on a different one of seven consecutive days. Each suspect was questioned exactly once. Any suspect who confessed did so while being questioned. The investigation conformed to the following: T was questioned on day three. The suspect questioned on day four did not confess. S was questioned after W was questioned. Both X and V were questioned after Z was questioned. No suspects confessed after W was questioned. Exactly two suspects confessed after T was questioned. Which of the following, if substituted for the rule that exactly two suspects confessed after T was questioned, would have the same effect both in determining the order in which suspects were questioned and in identifying which suspects confessed during questioning? (A) The final suspect to confess was the sixth suspect questioned. (B) W and the suspect questioned immediately before W were the last two suspects to confess. (C) W was the last suspect to confess. (D) The suspects questioned fifth and sixth both confessed. (E) S was questioned last and immediately after W.

solution.operation: T \ \text{in slot } 3, \ \text{exactly two C's after T}
solution.description: Unpack the original rule: since T sits third, the two confessions after T and the two non-confessions must all fall in slots four through seven.
Apply the separate rule that the fourth suspect did not confess, removing one N from the block and leaving the rest for slots five to seven.
Order the remaining letters using the rule that nobody confesses after W, which forces the N to the end and places W and S in the last two slots.
Check answer (A) against the chain: it puts a C in slot six but leaves slot five unfixed, so it does not reproduce the full effect.

solution.operation: \text{test (B): } W \ \text{and the suspect before } W \ \text{are the last two C's}
solution.result: W \ \text{could sit in slot } 2 \ \text{with N's in } 3\text{-}7
solution.description: Check answer (B): it looks like it forces W into slot six, but it also permits W in slot two with every later suspect not confessing, an arrangement the original diagram forbids.

solution.result: W \ \text{could sit in slot } 1 \ \text{or } 2; \ \text{slot } 5 \ \text{not forced to } C
solution.description: Check answer (C): it has the same defect as (B) plus the defect of (A), since it neither pins W late nor forces a confession in slot five.
Check answer (D): a confession in slot six plus the no-confession-after-W rule pushes W and S into slots six and seven, rebuilding exactly the same consequences as the original rule.
Check answer (E): it fixes an order but says nothing about who confessed, so it fails to reproduce the confession pattern and (D) stands.

key_reminders: An equivalent rule must reproduce every downstream inference of the original, not just one of them
The chain here runs: two C's after T, then two C's and one N in slots 5-7, then C C N with W and S in 6 and 7
Because no one confesses after W, any confession late in the order pins W's position
common_mistakes: Choosing (B) because W confessing alongside the prior suspect feels like it forces W into slot six, when W in slot two also satisfies it
Accepting (A) on the strength of slot six alone without checking that slot five must also be a confession
Treating (E) as equivalent because it fixes W and S at the end, overlooking that it never establishes any confession

concept.technique_name: prime factorization to test divisibility

examples.problem_statement: If a is divided by 7 or by 18, an integer results. Is a/42 an integer?

solution.result: the prime factors of a include 2, 3, 3, and 7
solution.description: Because a is divisible by both 7 and 18, break each divisor into primes and collect them; those primes must all sit in a's factor tree.

solution.result: every such product is itself a factor of a
solution.description: Apply the rule the book uses here: any integer assembled as a product of a's known prime factors is also a factor of a.

solution.result: 42 is built entirely from the available primes 2, 3, and 7
solution.description: Factor 42 and check that each of its primes is drawn from the pool of 2, 3, 3, 7 found in step 1.
Since 42 is a product of a's prime factors, it is a factor of a, so dividing a by 42 leaves an integer.

key_reminders: If a is divisible by two numbers, its prime factorization contains the primes of both.
Any product formed from an integer's prime factors is itself a factor of that integer.
common_mistakes: Multiplying 7 and 18 to get 126 and testing that instead of noticing 42 = 2 x 3 x 7 already fits inside the prime pool.
Forgetting that 18 supplies two 3s, so a repeated prime is available for products such as 63 as well.

concept.technique_name: units digit cycles

examples.problem_statement: What is the remainder when 13^{17} + 17^{13} is divided by 10?

solution.result: the problem becomes a units-digit question
solution.description: Replace the division by 10 with the equivalent question about the units digit, since dividing an integer by 10 always leaves its units digit as the remainder.

solution.result: only the units digits 3 and 7 matter
solution.description: Drop every digit except the units digit of each base, because only units digits affect the units digit of a power or a sum.
Write out the four-term repeating cycle for powers of 3 and locate the 17th power one step past the end of the fourth repeat, landing on the first entry.
Do the same for powers of 7: the cycle repeats every four terms, and the 13th power is one past the third repeat, so it takes the first entry.
Add the two units digits found above; the units digit of that total is the units digit of the whole expression, and hence the remainder.

key_reminders: The remainder on division by 10 is the units digit.
Only the units digit of a base determines the units digit of its powers.
Units digits of 3 and of 7 both repeat in cycles of length 4.
common_mistakes: Counting the cycle position from 1 instead of subtracting the largest multiple of 4 (using 17 - 16 = 1, not the 17th slot directly).
Reporting 10 as the remainder instead of the units digit 0 after adding 3 + 7.

concept.technique_name: plugging in numbers for rectangle area scaling

examples.problem_statement: The length of a rectangle increased by a factor of 2, and at the same time its area increased by a factor of 6. Quantity A: The factor by which the width of the rectangle increased. Quantity B: 3. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: an original rectangle with length 2, width 1, area 2
solution.description: Pick easy numbers for the original rectangle and record them in the Old column of the table.
Apply the given factor of 2 to the original length and enter the result in the New column.
Apply the given factor of 6 to the original area of 2 and enter that in the New column as well.
Recover the new width from the completed table by dividing the new area by the new length.

solution.result: the width increased by a factor of 3, matching Quantity B
solution.description: Compare the new width to the original width to get the growth factor, then set that factor against Quantity B's value of 3.

key_reminders: Area of a rectangle is length times width, so width equals area divided by length.
Quantitative comparison questions about scaling factors can be settled by plugging in convenient numbers.
common_mistakes: Dividing the area factor 6 by the length factor 2 incorrectly, or subtracting them, instead of tracking actual values in the table.
Comparing the new width 3 against the old length 2 rather than against the old width 1 when forming the factor.

concept.technique_name: context-driven vocabulary in context with answer elimination

examples.problem_statement: In the passage, the sentence containing "shades" (line 2) describes multiple definitions, each subtly different from all the others. In the context in which it appears, "shades" (line 2) most nearly means: A reminders  B nuances  C obscurities  D coverings  E degrees

solution.operation: \text{read "shades" against the phrase about multiple definitions that differ subtly}
solution.result: "shades" refers to subtle distinctions in meaning
solution.description: Fix the intended sense from the surrounding sentence, which is about several definitions each differing slightly from the others.
Rule out the choice that implies unclearness and the literal physical sense, since the sentence is about definitions conveying meaning, not about hiding or covering.

solution.result: the sentence is about slight differences in meaning, not differing degrees of one meaning
solution.description: Weigh the two survivors by asking whether the passage varies the meaning itself or merely the emphasis given to a single meaning.
Choose the word that captures slight variations in meaning, which is what the passage's subtly different definitions produce.

key_reminders: A vocabulary-in-context question asks for the sense the passage actually uses, not the word's most common meaning.
Eliminate literal or off-tone senses first, then separate the remaining near-synonyms on a single distinguishing feature.
common_mistakes: Picking "degrees," which fits variation in amount or emphasis rather than the passage's variation in meaning itself.
Falling for "coverings," the literal everyday sense of "shades," instead of the figurative one the sentence requires.

concept.technique_name: clue-and-contrast blank filling

examples.problem_statement: It was a fact that the region was both quiet and rural, but what the typically impoverished residents considered (i) _________ refuge was considered by the well-heeled visitors to be an intolerable (ii) _________, and its residents' lifestyles unpleasantly (iii) _________. Blank (i): a parochial / an arcadian / a squalid. Blank (ii): penumbra / utopia / hinterland. Blank (iii): tony / spartan / apollonian.

solution.operation: Mark the clue words "quiet and rural" and note that "refuge" carries positive charge for the residents.
solution.result: Blank (i) needs a positive word about rural life; blanks (ii) and (iii) sit on the visitors' contrasting negative side.
solution.description: Before testing any choice, pull the sentence's own signals: the region is described as quiet and rural, and the residents call it a refuge, which is a positive label. That fixes the charge each blank must carry.

solution.operation: Match blank (i) to the positive-rural requirement: test parochial, arcadian, squalid.
solution.description: Choose the word that conveys a positive view of rural life. Arcadian does exactly that, while the other two options do not carry that favorable rural sense.

solution.operation: Apply the contrast signaled by the visitors' "intolerable" judgment to blank (ii): test penumbra, utopia, hinterland.
solution.description: Fill the second blank with the word that flips the residents' positive view into the visitors' negative one. Hinterland conveys a backwater or undesirable, far-out place, which is the contrast the sentence demands.

solution.operation: Apply the negative requirement carried by "unpleasantly" to blank (iii): test tony, spartan, apollonian.
solution.description: Pick the only choice that can be read as negative in this slot. Of the three offered words, only spartan can carry that negative sense, so it completes the sentence.

key_reminders: A word like "refuge" is itself a charge clue: it tells you the blank beside it must be positive.
When a sentence contrasts two groups' views of the same place, the blanks on opposite sides must take opposite charges.
In a three-blank question, a blank whose choice set offers only one word of the required charge is settled by charge alone.
common_mistakes: Reading "quiet and rural" as inherently negative and choosing parochial or squalid for blank (i), ignoring that the residents call the place a refuge.
Filling blank (ii) with utopia, which repeats the residents' positive view instead of delivering the visitors' "intolerable" verdict.
Treating spartan as merely descriptive and picking tony for blank (iii), which contradicts "unpleasantly".

concept.technique_name: synonym-pair elimination from sentence context

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The plan, which the engineers said would save the aquifer by reducing pumping to _________ levels, has passed a governmental environmental review but faces opposition from outdoor and environmental groups. Choices: (A) innocuous, (B) feasible, (C) practicable, (D) minimal, (E) remedial, (F) benign.

solution.operation: Read the engineers' claim that the reduced pumping levels would save the aquifer, and ask what kind of levels that implies.
solution.result: The blank must describe levels that do no harm to the aquifer.
solution.description: Start from the sentence's own logic rather than the choices: if the engineers believe the reduced levels will save the aquifer, the blank has to characterize those levels as harmless or curative.

solution.operation: Collect every choice that fits that sense: innocuous, minimal, remedial, benign.
solution.result: A four-word shortlist of contextually acceptable words.
solution.description: Sweep the six options and keep each one an engineer could plausibly use for levels that save the aquifer. Four words survive this contextual filter.

solution.operation: Within the shortlist, look for two words that produce sentences alike in meaning.
solution.result: innocuous and benign pair; minimal and remedial each stand alone.
solution.description: Sentence Equivalence requires a matched pair, not just two workable words. Among the four survivors, only innocuous and benign mean the same thing, so the other two shortlisted words cannot be part of the answer.

solution.operation: Check the remaining near-synonym pair, feasible and practicable, against the context.
solution.result: Rejected: they imply the current levels are not feasible or practicable.
solution.description: Confirm the discarded pair really fails on meaning, not just on charge. These two words are similar to each other, but using them implies the current pumping levels are not feasible, which conflicts with the sentence's implication that the current levels, though perhaps undesirable, are entirely feasible.

examples.answer: Choice A: innocuous AND Choice F: benign

key_reminders: The answer must be a pair of words that are alike in meaning, not merely two words that each fit the blank.
A word can fit the blank's sense and still be wrong if no second choice matches it in meaning.
Rejecting a choice requires showing it distorts what the sentence implies, not just that another choice reads better.
common_mistakes: Selecting feasible and practicable because they form an obvious synonym pair, without testing whether that meaning fits a sentence about saving the aquifer.
Picking minimal and remedial together as though they were synonyms, when each fits the context but neither matches the other in meaning.
Stopping at innocuous alone and treating the question as single-answer rather than finding its benign partner.

concept.technique_name: contrast-connector sentence equivalence

examples.problem_statement:
Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning.

Biologists agree that snakes descended from lizards, but exactly where this first happened has been a matter of debate since the 1800s, when two ______ theories emerged.

A complex   B competing   C dubious   D conclusive   E contending   F irrefutable

solution.operation: Read the connector "but" joining the two halves of the sentence
solution.result: the second half must contrast in some way with the first half
solution.description: Locate the pivot word before choosing anything: "but" signals that whatever follows it stands opposed to the clause before it, so the blank has to serve that opposition.

solution.operation: Name the two sides of the contrast: agreement on the central fact (snakes descended from lizards) versus a long-standing debate over the detail (exactly where)
solution.result: the blank must emphasize the biologists' disagreement about the two theories
solution.description: Spell out what is being contrasted so the requirement on the blank becomes concrete — the word must foreground disagreement, not merely describe a theory.

solution.result: both imply the two theories are what the long-running debate has centered upon
solution.description: Check the candidate pair: each word casts the two theories as rivals, which is exactly the disagreement the sentence needs, and the two are alike in meaning as the question type demands.

solution.operation: Test the other synonym pair, "conclusive" (D) and "irrefutable" (F)
solution.result: roughly synonymous, but neither suggests a matter worthy of a long-running debate
solution.description: Reject this pair on sense rather than on form: theories described as settled beyond dispute could not have fueled debate since the 1800s.

solution.result: neither has a near-synonym among the choices; "dubious" would not explain why the two theories triggered the debate, and "complex" does not foreground the biologists' disagreement
solution.description: Eliminate the singletons: sentence equivalence requires a matching pair, and on meaning alone each of these fails to account for the debate the sentence describes.
Commit to the one pair that both matches in meaning and satisfies the contrast set up by "but".

examples.answer: Choice B: competing; AND Choice E: contending

key_reminders: "but" marks a contrast, so the blank must carry the opposition between the two clauses.
Sentence equivalence needs two choices that are alike in meaning AND fit the sentence — a synonym pair that misfits the sense is still wrong.
A choice with no near-synonym among the options cannot be part of the answer.
common_mistakes: Picking "conclusive" and "irrefutable" just because they form a clean synonym pair, without checking that settled theories could not sustain a debate since the 1800s.
Choosing "complex" because it plausibly describes a theory, ignoring that it has no partner among the choices and does not express disagreement.

concept.technique_name: critical reasoning inference (must-be-true) elimination

examples.problem_statement:
Mycenaean Vase. Museum A will display only objects that are undamaged and that have been definitively proven to be authentic. Doubts have been raised about the origins of a supposedly Mycenaean vase currently on display in the museum's antiquities wing. The only way to establish this vase's authenticity would be to pulverize it, then subject the dust to spectroscopic analysis.

The claims above, if true, most strongly support which of the following conclusions?

(A) Authentic Mycenaean vases are valuable and rare.
(B) Museum A was not sufficiently diligent in establishing the authenticity of the vase before displaying it.
(C) The vase in question will no longer be displayed in Museum A.
(D) Spectroscopic analysis is the only method used by Museum A to establish the authenticity of objects.
(E) Many of the world's museums unknowingly display forgeries.

solution.operation: Identify the question from the stem wording "most strongly support which of the following conclusions"
solution.result: an Inference question — the conclusion sits in the answer choices, not in the argument
solution.description: "Strongly support" alone could mean Inference or Strengthen; the phrase "which of the following conclusions" settles it, because it places the conclusion among the answers.

solution.operation: Deconstruct claim 1: Museum A displays only objects that are undamaged and definitively proven authentic
solution.description: Record the museum's display rule as a fact — both conditions, undamaged and authenticated, must hold for anything on display.

solution.operation: Deconstruct claim 2: doubts have been raised about the origins of the vase now on display
solution.description: Note the second fact: the vase's authenticity is currently unsettled.

solution.operation: Deconstruct claim 3: the only way to establish authenticity is to pulverize the vase and analyze the dust
solution.result: To authenticate, the museum must destroy the vase
solution.description: Capture the trap built into the third fact — the sole authentication route destroys the object it would authenticate.

solution.operation: State the goal by chaining the three facts
solution.result: they cannot display a vase not proven authentic, and cannot display a pulverized one — so it cannot be displayed at all
solution.description: An Inference answer must be provable from the given information; combining the display rule with the destructive test forces the outcome before you read the choices.

solution.operation: Test (A): authentic Mycenaean vases are valuable and rare
solution.result: eliminated — might be true, but unprovable from the argument
solution.description: Value and rarity are never mentioned, and outside plausibility is not proof, so this fails the must-be-true standard.

solution.operation: Test (B): the museum was not sufficiently diligent before displaying the vase
solution.result: tempting but eliminated — it is a value judgment, not something the facts establish
solution.description: It feels reasonable to ask why an unauthenticated vase was on display, but "not sufficiently diligent" is a judgment the argument never supports.

solution.operation: Test (C): the vase will no longer be displayed in Museum A
solution.result: provable — this matches the chain built in step 5
solution.description: Either they leave it unauthenticated (barred by the display rule) or they authenticate it by destroying it (nothing left to display); either way it comes off display, and unlike (B) this rests on logic rather than judgment.

solution.operation: Test (D) and (E): spectroscopy is the museum's only authentication method; many museums unknowingly display forgeries
solution.result: both eliminated — overreach beyond the given information
solution.description: The argument requires spectroscopy only for this vase, leaving other methods possible for other objects, and it describes one museum and one object, never many of the world's museums.

key_reminders: On an Inference question the correct answer must be provable from the stated facts alone.
"Which of the following conclusions" means the argument has no conclusion — it is in the answer choices.
A conditional rule plus a fact that makes the condition unsatisfiable forces the negative outcome.
common_mistakes: Choosing (B) because blaming the museum feels reasonable — it is a value judgment the three claims do not prove.
Choosing (D) by generalizing "the only way to establish this vase's authenticity" into the museum's only method for every object.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion by easiest-blank-first anchoring

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

When the normally (i) ______ film director was interviewed, it was only the topic of her next movie that (ii) ______ her flow of words. Her (iii) ______ on that subject suggested that it was an unwelcome one.

Blank (i): A assiduous, B loquacious, C diffident
Blank (ii): D diverted, E stanched, F accentuated
Blank (iii): G taciturnity, H alacrity, I rhapsody

solution.operation: Start at Blank (iii), where the sentence supplies its own gloss: the director's reaction shows the topic is unwelcome
solution.result: Blank (iii) must name a reaction that signals the subject is unwelcome
solution.description: Anchor on the blank whose meaning the sentence states outright, so the other two can be resolved against a fixed point.

solution.result: both eliminated — each indicates excitement or eagerness to talk about the topic
solution.description: Eagerness contradicts the sentence's own statement that the subject is unwelcome, so both choices are implausible.

solution.result: taciturnity indicates unwillingness or reserve about speaking — the correct choice
solution.description: The surviving word denotes silence or reserve, exactly the reaction that would mark the topic as unwelcome.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (i), which must contrast with that taciturnity because it describes the director's normal conversational style
solution.result: loquacious (B); "diffident" means reserved and "assiduous" means diligent, so neither supplies the contrast
solution.description: The word "normally" sets the usual behavior against the exceptional reaction, so Blank (i) needs a ready willingness to converse — "diffident" would echo taciturnity instead of opposing it, and "assiduous" is off the axis of talkativeness entirely.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (ii), the verb describing what the unwelcome topic did to the flow of words of a normally talkative person
solution.result: stanched (E); "accentuated" indicates the opposite, and "diverted" implies a change of topic unsupported by the passage
solution.description: The topic checked her conversation, so the verb must stop the flow — "accentuated" would increase it, and "diverted" smuggles in a redirection the rest of the sentence never mentions.
Read the completed sentence back to confirm the normally talkative director fell silent on the one unwelcome subject.

examples.answer: Choice B: loquacious; Choice E: stanched; Choice G: taciturnity

key_reminders: Fill the blank the sentence explains first, then use it as the anchor for the others.
"Normally" signals a contrast between habitual behavior and the exceptional reaction described.
Reject a choice that adds information the rest of the sentence does not support.
common_mistakes: Working Blank (i) first, before the sentence's own gloss on Blank (iii) has fixed the direction of the contrast.
Choosing "diverted" for Blank (ii) because interrupting speech sounds plausible, though nothing in the sentence indicates a change of topic.
Reading "diffident" as merely quiet-mannered and letting it stand as the director's normal style, which erases the required contrast with taciturnity.

concept.technique_name: All from 9 and the last from 10 (Nikhilam) subtraction

examples.problem_statement: Using the Vedic subtraction technique built on the sutra "All from 9 and the last from 10", evaluate 459876 - 389924. Work column by column from right to left across all 6 columns, using ordinary subtraction where the minuend digit is larger and the complement rule where it is not. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.operation: Scan right to left; where the minuend digit exceeds the subtrahend digit (6 > 4, 7 > 2) subtract normally: 6 - 4 and 7 - 2
solution.description: Begin at the right and handle the easy columns first — when the top digit is the larger one, no complement is needed and plain subtraction gives the digit.

solution.operation: At the hundreds column the minuend digit is smaller (8 < 9), so apply the sutra: 10 - (9 - 8)
solution.description: This is the column that triggers the rule: take the shortfall of the minuend below the subtrahend, then complete it from 10 to get the digit.

solution.operation: At the thousands column the digits are equal (9 and 9), so subtract the difference from 9: 9 - (9 - 9)
solution.description: An equal-digit column sits inside the complement run, so it takes the "all from 9" form rather than plain subtraction, and the zero difference leaves 9.
