solution.operation: At the ten thousands column the minuend digit is again smaller (5 < 8): 9 - (8 - 5)
solution.description: Another shortfall column, still inside the complement run, so subtract the difference from 9 rather than from 10.

solution.operation: At the hundred thousands column the minuend digit is larger (4 > 3) but a complement was used in the previous column, so subtract an extra 1: 4 - 3 - 1
solution.description: Pay back the borrow created by the complement run — the leading column returns to normal subtraction but must give up one unit to the column on its right.

solution.operation: Read the digits back from the hundred thousands column down to the units: 0, 6, 9, 9, 5, 2
solution.description: Assemble the per-column digits in place-value order to state the difference.

examples.answer: 459876 - 389924 = 069952 using Vedic subtraction with complement method

key_reminders: Work right to left, deciding column by column whether the minuend digit is larger.
Where the minuend digit is smaller, the first such column completes from 10 and the columns continuing the run take all from 9.
A column that follows a complement column loses an extra 1 when it reverts to normal subtraction.
common_mistakes: Treating the 9 - 9 thousands column as plain subtraction and writing 0 instead of the 9 the complement run requires.
Forgetting the extra -1 in the leading 4 - 3 column, which turns the leading digit into 1 and inflates the answer by 100000.

concept.technique_name: three-blank text completion by internal-contrast cues

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text.

The most striking thing about the politician is how often his politics have been (i) ______ rather than ideological, as he adapts his political positions at any particular moment to the political realities that constrain him. He does not, however, piously (ii) ______ political principles only to betray them in practice. Rather, he attempts in subtle ways to balance his political self-interest with a (iii) ______, viewing himself as an instrument of some unchanging higher purpose.

Blank (i): A quixotic, B self-righteous, C strategic
Blank (ii): D brandish, E flout, F follow
Blank (iii): G profound cynicism, H deeply felt moral code, I thoroughgoing pragmatism

solution.operation: Fill Blank (i) from the clause "adapts his political positions ... to the political realities that constrain him", and check it against "rather than ideological"
solution.result: strategic (C) — the only choice that also provides the required contrast with "ideological"
solution.description: The sentence both defines the blank and opposes it to "ideological", so the word must name politics driven by circumstance rather than doctrine; "strategic" is the only choice that does both.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (ii) with the verb that a politician might do piously to political principles before betraying them in practice
solution.description: The adverb "piously" and the follow-on "only to betray them in practice" require a showy public display of principles, which is what brandishing them means.

solution.operation: Test the rival choices "flout" (E) and "follow" (F) for Blank (ii)
solution.result: both eliminated — flouting is not pious, and following principles does not fit with betraying them in practice
solution.description: Check each against the two cues separately: "flout" fails the "piously" cue, and "follow" contradicts the betrayal that the sentence says comes next.

solution.operation: Fill Blank (iii) with something that must be balanced against "political self-interest" and embraced in service of an "unchanging higher purpose"
solution.result: deeply felt moral code (H) — the only viable choice
solution.description: The blank sits on the opposite side of a balance from self-interest and is glossed by the higher-purpose clause, so it needs a genuine moral commitment; cynicism and pragmatism would sit with self-interest, not against it.

solution.result: strategic (C), brandish (D), deeply felt moral code (H)
solution.description: Read the completed passage back: a politician who is strategic rather than ideological, who does not merely parade principles, and who still answers to a genuine moral code.

examples.answer: Choice C: strategic; Choice D: brandish; Choice H: deeply felt moral code

key_reminders: "Rather than" marks a contrast: the blank must oppose the word on the other side of the phrase.
"However" and "Rather" reverse the direction of the argument between sentences — track that reversal when filling the later blanks.
A blank balanced against a stated quality must contrast with it, not restate it.
common_mistakes: Choosing "flout" for Blank (ii) because the sentence is about betrayal, overlooking that "piously" demands a display of devotion, not defiance.
Choosing "thoroughgoing pragmatism" for Blank (iii) by carrying over the adaptability of Blank (i), when the blank must be balanced against self-interest rather than aligned with it.

concept.technique_name: unrolled cylinder turn as right-triangle hypotenuse

examples.problem_statement: A thread is wound on a cylinder such that it makes exactly twenty-four complete turns around the cylinder. The two ends of thread touch the top and bottom of cylinder. If cylinder has a radius of 15 cm and its curved surface area is 2880 cm^2 then find the length of the string:

solution.description: Divide the given curved surface area by 15, the value the book divides by, to recover the height of the cylinder.
Split that height across the twenty-four complete turns, giving the vertical rise of one turn; this is the 8 the book carries into its next line.
Treat one unrolled turn as the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 15, and take the square root of the sum of their squares to get the length of a single turn.
Multiply the length of one complete turn by the twenty-four turns to obtain the total length of the thread.

key_reminders: Curved surface area of a cylinder divided by its circumference term gives the height.
Each unrolled turn of a helically wound thread is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the rise per turn and the horizontal run per turn.
Total thread length is the length of one turn times the number of turns.
common_mistakes: Reporting the height 192 cm or the single-turn length 17 cm as the final answer instead of multiplying by the 24 turns.
Using the full height 192 rather than the per-turn rise 8 as the vertical leg of the right triangle.

concept.technique_name: chaining two ratios through a common term using least common multiples

examples.problem_statement: At a certain fruit stand, there is a 2 to 5 ratio of pomelos to quinces and a 2 to 7 ratio of quinces to raspberries. Which of the following could be the number of pomelos at the stand? Select all that apply. (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 8 (E) 10

solution.description: Multiply both values of the first ratio by 2, the multiplier the book prescribes, so that the quince term becomes the least common multiple 10.
Multiply both values of the second ratio by 5, the book's second multiplier, so its quince term also becomes 10.
Join the two scaled ratios on their now-common number of quinces to read off the single combined ratio, whose pomelo term is 4.
Conclude that the actual number of pomelos must be a multiple of 4, then keep only the answer choices that are multiples of 4.

key_reminders: To chain two ratios, scale each so the shared quantity takes the same value, using the least common multiple of its two terms.
Scaling a ratio means multiplying every term in it by the same factor.
In a combined ratio, an actual count must be a whole-number multiple of its ratio term.
common_mistakes: Reading the pomelo term as 2 from the unscaled first ratio and selecting 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 as all possible.
Selecting only 4 and forgetting that any multiple of 4, including 8, also qualifies.

concept.technique_name: percent change formula

examples.problem_statement: What is the percent increase from 50 to 60? %

solution.description: Subtract the original value from the new value to get the difference called for by the percent change formula.
Divide that difference by the original value 50, reducing the fraction to one fifth, which is 0.2.
Multiply the decimal by 100 to express the change as a percent.

key_reminders: Percent change equals the difference divided by the original value.
The original value is the one you start from, here 50, not the new value 60.
A decimal becomes a percent when multiplied by 100.
common_mistakes: Dividing the difference 10 by the new value 60 instead of the original 50, which gives about 16.7% rather than 20%.

concept.technique_name: congruent alternate angles across a transversal of parallel lines

examples.problem_statement: In the figure above, line k is parallel to line m. What is the value of y ? y =

solution.operation: (2y)^\circ \text{ and } 35^\circ \text{ lie between } k \parallel m \text{ on opposite sides of the transversal}
solution.description: Locate the two marked angles in the figure: both sit between the parallel lines k and m and on opposite sides of the line crossing them, so they are congruent.
Translate that congruence from the figure into an equation setting the two angle measures equal.
Divide both sides of the equation by 2 to isolate y.

key_reminders: Angles between two parallel lines and on opposite sides of a transversal are congruent.
Translate a figure into an algebraic equation before solving.
The variable y is half the angle expression (2y), so the angle measure is not the answer itself.
common_mistakes: Answering 35 by reporting the angle measure instead of dividing by 2 to get y.
Treating the two angles as supplementary and writing 2y = 145 instead of congruent.

concept.technique_name: linear equation in one unknown

examples.problem_statement: Two forest officials in their respective divisions were involved in the harvesting of tendu leaves. One division had an average output of 21 tons from a hectare and the other division, which had 12 hectares of land less, dedicated to tendu leaves, got 25 tons of tendu from a hectare. As a result, the second division harvested 300 tons of tendu leaves more than the first. How many tons of tendu leaves did the first division harvest?

solution.operation: n = \text{hectares of the first division},\; n - 12 = \text{hectares of the second division}
solution.result: first division area n, second division area n - 12
solution.description: Name the first division's area n; the second division has 12 hectares less, so its area is n - 12.
Write the second division's output 25(n-12) as the first division's output 21n plus the stated excess of 300 tons.
Expand, collect the n terms on one side and the constants on the other, and divide to get the first division's area.
Multiply the first division's 150 hectares by its per-hectare output of 21 tons to get the tonnage asked for.

key_reminders: Total output = yield per hectare x number of hectares.
"300 tons more than the first" becomes an equation by adding 300 to the first division's total, not to the second's.
common_mistakes: Letting n be the second division's area and then writing 25n = 21(n-12) + 300, which shifts the 12 hectares onto the wrong division.
Stopping at n = 150 and reporting hectares instead of multiplying by 21 for the tonnage.

concept.technique_name: clue-and-reversal contrast reading

examples.problem_statement: The danger of giving too many long and bombastic speeches while on the campaign trail is that a politician can come off as __________ rather than eloquent.

solution.description: Find the word in the sentence that the blank is being measured against; here the only descriptive anchor is eloquent.

solution.operation: Apply the reversal signalled by "rather than" to the clue
solution.description: Because "rather than" sets the blank against the clue, flip the clue: the blank needs a negative word about the way someone speaks.

solution.operation: Test unscrupulous, inane, voluble against that requirement
solution.description: Rule out unscrupulous and inane because they are negative but not really about speech, and voluble because it carries no negative connotation.

solution.operation: Check glib = "fluent and talkative, but insincere and shallow"
solution.description: Confirm the survivor: glib is both about speech and negative, so it fits the flipped clue perfectly.

key_reminders: "Rather than" is a reversal pivot: the blank takes the opposite charge of the clue it is paired with.
A candidate must match both the topic (speech) and the charge (negative), not just one of them.
common_mistakes: Picking voluble because it means talkative, ignoring that it lacks the negative connotation the reversal demands.
Picking unscrupulous or inane on negative charge alone, though neither describes a manner of speaking.

concept.technique_name: percentage change via assumed value

examples.problem_statement: A positive no. is by mistake multiplied by 5 instead of being divided by 5. By what per cent more or less than the correct answer is the result obtained?

solution.description: Assume the number is 1, since the percentage comparison does not depend on which positive number is chosen.
Compute what the intended operation gives: divide the assumed number by 5.
Compute what the mistaken operation gives: multiply the assumed number by 5.
Subtract the correct answer from the incorrect one to get how much the result exceeds it.
Divide that excess by the correct answer (the base of the comparison) and multiply by 100 to express it as a percentage.

key_reminders: Percentage more or less is always measured against the correct value as base.
With only ratios involved, assuming the number equals 1 loses nothing.
common_mistakes: Dividing the excess 24/5 by the wrong base (the incorrect answer 5), which gives 96% instead of 2400%.
Answering 2500% by dividing the incorrect answer 5 by 1/5 without first subtracting the correct answer.

concept.technique_name: componendo-dividendo

examples.problem_statement: If x/y = 3/4, then the value of 6/7 + (y-x)/(y+x) is _____.

solution.description: Apply componendo-dividendo: with x and y in the ratio 3 : 4, substitute 3 for x and 4 for y in the expression (y-x)/(y+x).
Evaluate the numerator and denominator of that fraction.
Add the result to the given 6/7; the like denominators combine to a single whole.

key_reminders: A ratio x/y = 3/4 lets you use x = 3 and y = 4 directly in any expression that is homogeneous in x and y.
In (y-x)/(y+x) the larger term y comes first in both numerator and denominator, so the value stays positive.
common_mistakes: Substituting the ratio backwards as x = 4, y = 3, which turns (y-x)/(y+x) into -1/7 and gives 5/7.

concept.technique_name: substitution by scaling an equation

examples.problem_statement: Given 3x + 6y = 27 and x + 2y + z = 11, compare Quantity A: z + 5 with Quantity B: x + 2y - 2. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Rather than solving for three variables from two equations, divide the first equation through by 3 to expose the compound quantity x + 2y.

solution.result: The second equation is regrouped around the block x + 2y
solution.description: Rewrite the second equation so that x + 2y appears as a single block, which is what the first equation has just evaluated.
Substitute the value 9 for the block x + 2y inside the regrouped second equation.
Isolate z by subtracting 9 from both sides, giving the single unknown the comparison needs.
Evaluate Quantity A by putting the value of z just found into z + 5.
Evaluate Quantity B by reusing x + 2y = 9 from step 1 in place of the block x + 2y.
Compare the two numeric values obtained and see that neither quantity exceeds the other.

key_reminders: Dividing an entire equation by a common factor is legal and often reveals a reusable compound block such as x + 2y.
Three variables with two equations is still solvable when the extra variables only ever appear as one fixed block.
A quantitative comparison only needs each quantity's value, not the individual values of x and y.
common_mistakes: Declaring the answer (D) because there are three variables and only two equations, without first dividing 3x + 6y = 27 by 3.
Trying to solve separately for x and y, which is impossible and unnecessary here.

concept.technique_name: cyclicity of unit digits

examples.problem_statement: Find the unit's digit of 7^{51!^{31!}}.

solution.result: The exponent is a multiple of 4
solution.description: Test the exponent for divisibility by 4: 51! already carries the factors 2 and 4, so any power of it is divisible by 4.

solution.result: 7 raised to any multiple of 4 ends in 1
solution.description: Apply the known unit-digit rule for powers of 7, whose cycle closes every 4 steps at 1.
Match this power to the 7^{4k} form established in step 2, since step 1 showed its exponent is a multiple of 4.

key_reminders: The unit digit of powers of 7 repeats with period 4, ending in 1 at every exponent that is a multiple of 4.
Only the exponent's remainder on division by 4 matters, never its actual size.
A factorial of 4 or more is automatically divisible by 4, and so is any power of it.
common_mistakes: Attempting to evaluate or estimate the astronomically large exponent 51!^{31!} instead of testing it modulo 4.
Using remainder 0 as if it meant the first term of the cycle (7) rather than the fourth term (1).

concept.technique_name: laws of indices with prime factorisation

examples.problem_statement: Find the value of \frac{2^{n} \times 6^{m+1} \times 10^{m-n} \times 15^{m+n-2}}{4^{m} \times 3^{2m+n} \times 25^{m-1}}. Options: 1) 2  2) 2/3  3) 1/3  4) 3  5) None of these

solution.description: Break every composite base in the numerator into its prime factors so the whole expression is written over the primes 2, 3 and 5 only.
Do the same prime-factor rewrite for the composite bases in the denominator, leaving 3^{2m+n} unchanged since it is already prime-based.
Collect the numerator's like bases by adding their exponents, which is what the product rule for indices permits.
Divide base by base, subtracting each denominator exponent from the matching numerator exponent.
Simplify the surviving exponents: the 5s cancel entirely, one factor of 2 remains on top and one factor of 3 remains below.

key_reminders: Reduce every base to primes before combining; only like bases may have their exponents added or subtracted.
a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m+n} and a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m-n}.
A base whose net exponent is 0 cancels out of the expression entirely.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that 6 and 10 and 15 each split into two different primes, so their exponents must be distributed to both.
Mis-signing the exponent of 3, where (2m+n-1) - (2m+n) = -1 gives a denominator factor, not a numerator one.

concept.technique_name: sum of an evenly spaced set via its middle term

examples.problem_statement: If x = 3, what is the sum of 2x, (2x + 1), (2x + 2), (2x + 3), and (2x + 4)?

solution.result: An evenly spaced sequence with common difference 1
solution.description: Instead of substituting x into all five terms, notice each term is exactly one more than the one before it.
Identify the middle term of the five, which for an evenly spaced set is also the set's average.
Plug x = 3 into that middle term alone to get the numeric average.
Multiply the average by the number of terms, since sum equals average times count.

key_reminders: In an evenly spaced set the average equals the middle term.
Sum = average \times number of terms.
With an odd count of terms there is a single true middle term to read off.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = 3 into all five terms and adding, which works but wastes time and invites an arithmetic slip.
Taking 2x + 2 as the answer itself rather than as the average that still has to be multiplied by 5.

concept.technique_name: conditional ordering with constraint elimination

examples.problem_statement: During a single week, from Monday through Friday, tours will be conducted of a company's three divisions - Operations, Production, Sales. Exactly five tours will be conducted that week, one each day. The schedule must conform to these restrictions: each division is toured at least once; Operations is not toured on Monday; Production is not toured on Wednesday; Sales is toured on two consecutive days and on no other days; if Operations is toured on Thursday, then Production is toured on Friday. If in the week's tour schedule the division that is toured on Tuesday is also toured on Friday, then for which one of the following days must a tour of the Production division be scheduled? (A) Monday (B) Tuesday (C) Wednesday (D) Thursday (E) Friday

solution.result: One division occupies both Tuesday and Friday
solution.description: Take on the question's extra condition and ask which of the three divisions could occupy both Tuesday and Friday.
Rule out Sales, since Sales must be toured on two consecutive days only, and Tuesday and Friday are not consecutive.

solution.operation: P \text{ on Tue and Fri} \Rightarrow \text{two P and two S fill Tue-Fri} \Rightarrow O \text{ on Mon}
solution.result: Illegal, so P is ruled out
solution.description: Rule out Production too: two Ps plus the two consecutive Sales days would fill Tuesday through Friday, forcing Operations onto Monday, which the rules forbid.

solution.operation: \text{Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri} = P\; O\; S\; S\; O
solution.description: With Sales and Production eliminated, Operations takes Tuesday and Friday, and the book states the resulting arrangement is P O S S O - putting Production on Monday.

key_reminders: Sales occupies exactly two consecutive days, so it can never be the division repeated on two non-adjacent days.
Operations is never toured on Monday, which is the constraint that kills the Production-on-Tuesday-and-Friday branch.
Every division must appear at least once across the five days.
common_mistakes: Assuming the repeated Tuesday/Friday division could be Sales, forgetting that Sales' two days must be consecutive.
Missing that placing Production on both Tuesday and Friday leaves only Monday for Operations, which is barred.

concept.technique_name: average rate via total distance over total time (Smart Numbers)

examples.problem_statement: A car travels from Town A to Town B at an average speed of 40 miles per hour, and returns along the same route at an average speed of 50 miles per hour. What is the approximate average speed in miles per hour for the entire trip?

solution.result: the quantity to build is total distance divided by total time
solution.description: Set up the average-rate relationship the book uses: on average rate problems you do not average the two speeds, you find the total distance and divide by the total time.
Choose a Smart Number for the one-way distance d. The book picks 200 miles because it is a common multiple of the two rates, 40 and 50, so both leg times come out whole.
Find the time for the outbound leg by dividing the chosen distance by the outbound rate of 40 miles per hour.
Find the time for the return leg by dividing the same distance by the return rate of 50 miles per hour.
Add the two leg times to get the total time for the two trips, exactly as the book totals them.
Add the two equal one-way distances to get the total distance for the two trips, which the book states as 400 miles.

Divide the total distance by the total time to get the average rate for the entire trip. Note it lands below the midpoint 45, because with equal distances the average rate is always weighted toward the slower rate, where more time is spent.

key_reminders: Average rate is total distance divided by total time, never the plain average of the two rates.
When the distance is unknown but the rates are fixed, pick a Smart Number for the distance that is a common multiple of the rates.
With equal distances the average rate is always pulled toward the slower rate, since more time is spent at that rate.
common_mistakes: Averaging 40 and 50 to get 45, which ignores that more time is spent at 40 miles per hour.
Adding the distances but forgetting the trip covers 400 miles, not 200, when dividing by the 9-hour total.

concept.technique_name: standard deviation from squared differences about the mean

examples.problem_statement: Set S = \{-1, 4, 30, -21\}. If the mean = 4, then the standard deviation, rounded to the nearest tenth, is equal to

solution.description: Take the difference between the mean, 4, and the first term, -1, and square it. The book works this one out explicitly as the model for the rest.
Repeat the squared-difference computation for the term 4; the printed solution records this term's contribution as 16.
Take the difference between the mean and the term 30, giving -26, and square it. Squaring removes the sign, so the negative difference contributes a positive amount.
Take the difference between the mean and the term -21, giving 25, and square it. Subtracting a negative widens the gap, which is why this term contributes so heavily.
Add all four squared differences together to get the single total the book carries forward.
Take the square root of that total, using the on-screen calculator as the book directs.
Round the square root to the nearest tenth, because the question asked for that precision.

key_reminders: Work from differences about the mean, and square each difference so signs do not cancel.
Subtracting a negative term from the mean widens the difference: 4 - (-21) = 25, not -17.
Round only at the end, to the precision the question names.
common_mistakes: Mishandling 4 - (-1) and 4 - (-21) as subtraction of positives, losing the two largest contributions.
Rounding \sqrt{1342} to 36.7 or truncating to 36.6 without checking the digit after the tenths place.

concept.technique_name: combinations with the multiplication principle across two independent picks

examples.problem_statement: Lothar has 6 stamps from Utopia and 4 stamps from Cornucopia in his collection. He will give two stamps of each type to his friend Peggy Sue. Quantity A: the number of ways Lothar can give 4 stamps (two of each type) to Peggy Sue. Quantity B: 100. Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: \text{two successive pick-a-group problems: choose 2 of 6, then 2 of 4}
solution.result: one Utopian selection and one Cornucopian selection
solution.description: Frame the task the way the book does: Lothar picks 2 out of his 6 Utopian stamps, and then separately picks 2 out of his 4 Cornucopian stamps.
Apply the combinations formula to the Utopian stamps to count the groups of size 2 that can be drawn from 6; order within the group does not matter.
Apply the same combinations formula to the Cornucopian stamps to count the groups of size 2 drawn from 4.
Multiply the Utopian result by the Cornucopian result, since each Utopian pair can be paired with any Cornucopian pair, giving Quantity A.
Compare Quantity A, 90, against Quantity B, 100, and select the choice stating that Quantity B is greater.

key_reminders: Use combinations, not permutations: the two stamps handed over form a group, so order does not matter.
Two independent selections combine by multiplying their counts, not adding them.
common_mistakes: Adding 15 + 6 = 21 instead of multiplying, which would flip the comparison the wrong way.
Treating the picks as ordered (6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3) and getting a count above 100, leading to choice (A).

concept.technique_name: clue-and-contrast word matching in a two-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: While some feel that the author’s (i) _________ late in his life (ii) _________ his reputation, others felt that his dissolution added a certain glamour to his biography and credibility to his libertinous tales. Blank (i): vitiation / debauchment / deterioration. Blank (ii): derogated from / bedizened / aggrandized.

solution.operation: Locate the sentence's clue words: “dissolution” and “libertinous”
solution.result: The clue describes a life falling apart — drugs, promiscuity, crime, or general dissipation
solution.description: Read the second half of the sentence and pull out the words that describe the author's late-life conduct; these are the clue the blanks must agree with.

solution.operation: Match blank (i) to the meaning of “dissolution” / “libertinous”
solution.description: Choose for the first blank the option whose meaning is the same kind of moral dissipation the clue describes, since blank (i) simply names what “dissolution” refers to.

solution.operation: Read the contrast set up by “while some feel … others felt … added a certain glamour” to fix the charge of blank (ii)
solution.description: Because the “others” hold the positive view that the dissolution added glamour, the first group's view must be the opposite, so the word going into blank (ii) has to act negatively on his reputation.

solution.operation: Select the negative option among “derogated from,” “bedizened,” and “aggrandized”
solution.description: Apply the negative requirement from the previous step to the second blank's choices and keep the only one that means to detract from something.

key_reminders: The blank must agree with the sentence's own clue word; here “dissolution” and “libertinous” point to the same idea as the answer.
A “while some … others …” frame signals contrast: if one side's view is positive, the blank on the other side must be negative.
common_mistakes: Taking “deterioration” or “vitiation” for blank (i): both mean a general worsening or spoiling, but neither carries the specific moral dissipation that “dissolution” and “libertinous” signal.
Choosing “aggrandized” for blank (ii), which points the wrong way — it matches the “others” who saw glamour rather than the “some” whose view the blank expresses.

concept.technique_name: algebraic translation of a comparison into an inequality

examples.problem_statement: Translate the following statement into a mathematical relationship: Jean has more than twice as many CDs as Kim.

solution.operation: Let J = Jean's number of CDs and K = Kim's number of CDs
solution.result: J and K stand for the two counts being compared
solution.description: Give each person's CD count a letter so the sentence's comparison can be written symbolically.

solution.operation: Multiply Kim's number by 2 to represent “twice as many as Kim”
solution.description: Turn the phrase “twice as many CDs as Kim” into an expression by doubling the quantity that belongs to Kim.

solution.operation: Join J to 2K with an inequality sign rather than an equals sign: J > 2K
solution.description: Since the sentence says more than twice, not exactly twice, connect Jean's count to the doubled amount with a greater-than sign instead of equality.

key_reminders: “Twice as many as X” multiplies X itself by 2, so the doubling attaches to Kim's count, not Jean's.
“More than” makes the statement an inequality; only “exactly” or “as many as” would justify an equals sign.
common_mistakes: Writing 2J > K, doubling the wrong person because Jean is named first in the sentence.
Writing J = 2K, dropping the “more than” and turning a strict inequality into an equation.

concept.technique_name: sentence-equivalence selection by matching the sentence's implied reaction

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole: Because they had expected the spacecraft Voyager 2 to be able to gather data only about the planets Jupiter and Saturn, scientists were ______ the wealth of information it sent back from Neptune twelve years after leaving Earth. (A) anxious for (B) confident in (C) thrilled about (D) keen on (E) elated by (F) eager for

solution.operation: Note the words “expected” and “only” in the opening clause
solution.result: The data received exceeded what the scientists had expected
solution.description: Read the “Because” clause and see that the scientists had anticipated far less, so the information from Neptune was more than they had counted on.

solution.operation: State what the blank must therefore mean
solution.result: A reaction to results that are better than hoped for
solution.description: Convert the finding from the previous step into a requirement on the blank: it has to describe how one responds to an unexpectedly good outcome.

solution.operation: Test each choice against “reaction to better-than-hoped-for results”
solution.result: “thrilled about” and “elated by” both express such a reaction
solution.description: Check the options one at a time and keep the two that name delight at an outcome that surpassed expectation.

solution.result: Eagerness is not explained by the unexpectedness of the information
solution.description: Discard the two words that describe anticipation rather than response, since the sentence's causal “Because” clause gives no reason for the scientists to have been eager for data they never expected.

examples.answer: Choice C: thrilled about AND Choice E: elated by

key_reminders: A “Because” clause states the cause of the blank; the chosen words must be explained by that cause.
“Expected … only” signals that what actually happened went beyond expectation.
common_mistakes: Picking “eager for” and “keen on” as the pair — they form a plausible synonym pair, but they describe anticipation before the fact, which the unexpectedness in the sentence does not support.
Choosing “confident in” or “anxious for,” which contradict the scientists' stated low expectation of the Neptune data.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal blank prediction with synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. A recent study suggests that vitamin E supplements, despite widespread belief in their ______ , are no better than sugar pills for delaying the onset of the degenerative disease.

solution.operation: Read the main clause: the supplements are "no better than sugar pills" for delaying the disease.
solution.result: The sentence establishes that vitamin E supplements are ineffective against the disease.
solution.description: Extract the factual claim the sentence makes about the supplements before looking at any choice, so you know what the blank must be measured against: they do not work.

solution.operation: Register the pivot word "despite" joining the blank phrase to that main clause.
solution.result: The belief named in the blank contrasts with the established ineffectiveness.
solution.description: Use the contrast signal to fix the direction of the blank: whatever people widely believe must stand opposed to the ineffectiveness just identified.

solution.operation: Predict the blank as the opposite of "ineffectiveness".
solution.result: The blank needs a word meaning effectiveness, and it needs a near-synonym partner among the choices.
solution.description: Convert the contrast into a prediction, remembering that this format requires two choices that yield sentences alike in meaning, so the target word must have a match.

solution.operation: Match the prediction against the choices: efficacy, usefulness.
solution.result: "Efficacy" and "usefulness" both mean effectiveness and pair as near-synonyms.
solution.description: Select the pair that satisfies both requirements at once - opposite of ineffectiveness, and alike in meaning to each other.

solution.result: "Potential" contrasts less directly with ineffectiveness and has no near-synonym partner among the choices.
solution.description: Eliminate the tempting choice by checking it on the weaker of its two duties: even granting a loose contrast, it is left without a partner, so it cannot be one of two correct answers.

solution.operation: Test "prevalence" and "popularity" against what the blank must characterize.
solution.result: Both describe how widely the supplements are used, not how they are viewed as working.
solution.description: Reject this attractive pair by noting the blank sits inside "belief in their ______", which calls for a word about the supplements' assumed effectiveness rather than their extent of use.

examples.answer: Choice D: efficacy; AND Choice F: usefulness

key_reminders: "Despite" forces the blank to contrast with the main clause's claim.
Sentence Equivalence requires two choices producing sentences alike in meaning, so a correct word must have a near-synonym among the options.
Read what the blank grammatically modifies - here a belief about the supplements, not their usage.
common_mistakes: Choosing "potential" because it sounds positive, without checking that it has no synonym partner.
Choosing the "prevalence"/"popularity" pair because they are synonyms of each other, ignoring that they describe use rather than assumed effectiveness.

concept.technique_name: four-step Weaken the Argument process

examples.problem_statement:
The owners of a book store and a nearby coffee shop have decided to combine their businesses. Both owners believe that this merger will increase the number of customers and therefore the gross revenue, because customers who come for one reason may also decide to purchase something else. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the owners' conclusion that a merger will increase revenue?
(A) Books and drinks can both be considered impulse purchases; often, they are purchased by customers without forethought.
(B) Profit margins at a coffee shop are generally significantly higher than profit margins at a book store.
(C) People who are able to read the first chapter of a book before buying are more likely to decide to buy the book.
(D) A large majority of the book store's current customer base already frequents the coffee shop.
(E) A combination book store and coffee shop that opened in a neighboring city last year has already earned higher than expected profits.

solution.operation: Identify the question from the words "if true" and "most weakens".
solution.result: This is a Weaken question, and the stem names the conclusion: the merger will increase revenue.
solution.description: Classify the question type first, because the stem hands you the conclusion outright: merger leads to increased revenue.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument, labelling the first sentence as fact.
solution.result: Fact: the book store and coffee shop are combining.
solution.description: Separate what has already been decided from what is being claimed - the combining itself is not in dispute.

solution.operation: Map the owners' claim and its support: merger raises customer count and therefore gross revenue, because customers who come for one reason may buy something else.
solution.result: Conclusion: merger leads to more customers and more revenue, supported by cross-selling.
solution.description: Write out the conclusion with its premise so the cross-sell reasoning is visible as the load-bearing support.

solution.operation: State the goal by surfacing the assumption behind the cross-sell premise.
solution.result: The argument assumes the same customers were not already visiting both stores; the right answer must make increased revenue less likely.
solution.description: Turn the argument into a target: find the choice showing revenue might not rise, most likely by attacking the assumption of newly gained customers.

solution.operation: Evaluate (A): books and drinks are impulse purchases.
solution.result: Reverse logic - it makes cross-selling more likely, strengthening the merger.
solution.description: Eliminate (A) as the classic reverse-logic trap: it helps the plan when the task is to hurt it.

solution.operation: Evaluate (B): coffee profit margins exceed book store margins.
solution.result: It concerns profits, not revenues, and does not touch the revenue claim.
solution.description: Eliminate (B) on scope: it might discourage one owner, but the conclusion is about revenue, and margins are a profit issue.

solution.operation: Evaluate (C): reading a first chapter makes people likelier to buy the book.
solution.result: Reverse logic - sitting with coffee while reading would raise purchases and revenue.
solution.description: Eliminate (C) as a second reverse-logic answer: it supplies another reason the merger would raise revenue.

solution.operation: Evaluate (D): a large majority of the book store's customers already frequent the coffee shop.
solution.result: The merger would gain far fewer new customers than assumed, so revenue may not increase.
solution.description: Keep (D) because it attacks the assumption stated in step 4 - the customer bases already overlap, so the cross-sell cannot add the new customers the owners are counting on.

solution.operation: Evaluate (E): a combined store in a neighboring city beat profit expectations.
solution.result: Wrong store and wrong measure - it addresses profits, not this pair's revenue.
solution.description: Eliminate (E) on two counts: a different business is not evidence about these owners, and it again reports profits rather than revenues.

key_reminders: A Weaken answer must make the stated conclusion less likely - it need not disprove it.
Revenue and profit are different claims; a choice about margins or profits does not touch a revenue conclusion.
Attack the argument's assumption - here, that the two stores' customers are largely different people.
common_mistakes: Picking (A) or (C), which are reverse-logic choices that strengthen the merger case.
Picking (B) or (E) by treating higher profits as evidence about gross revenue.
Treating (E)'s neighboring-city store as evidence about these particular businesses.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion via contrast clause

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. That the artist chose to remain in his hometown does not mean that he remained (i) ______ ; on the contrary, he (ii) ______ the international artistic movements of his day.
Blank (i): A provincial, B capricious, C obstinate
Blank (ii): D knew nothing about, E made light of, F kept abreast of

solution.operation: Read the first clause: staying in one's hometown "does not mean" the artist remained (i).
solution.result: Blank (i) must name a quality one would stereotypically expect of someone who never leaves home.
solution.description: Establish what kind of word the first blank takes - the sentence denies a quality that staying home would normally suggest.

solution.operation: Read the second clause, which concerns the artist and "the international artistic movements of his day".
solution.result: The denied quality has to do with the person's attitude toward the wider world.
solution.description: Narrow the first blank further using the second clause, which shows the contrast is specifically about engagement beyond one's own locality.

solution.operation: Match those two conditions against A provincial, B capricious, C obstinate.
solution.result: "Provincial" fits both conditions, so Blank (i) is provincial.
solution.description: Choose the word that names the narrow-horizons quality the sentence is denying, since that is the only choice satisfying both the hometown expectation and the wider-world dimension.

solution.operation: Apply "on the contrary" to Blank (ii), which must describe the opposite of being provincial.
solution.result: Someone the opposite of provincial is interested in what happens outside his narrow domain, so "kept abreast of" is correct.
solution.description: Use the reversal signal to set the second blank against the first: the artist must be shown engaging with, not ignoring or belittling, the international movements.

solution.result: "Obstinate" implies no particular attitude toward the world beyond one's environment.
solution.description: Eliminate the plausible alternative: although provincial people are often stubborn, obstinacy alone fails the wider-world condition, since one can cling to one's opinions while still following outside opinion.

examples.answer: Choice A: provincial; Choice F: kept abreast of

key_reminders: "On the contrary" makes the second blank reverse the quality named in the first.
A two-blank Text Completion answer must satisfy every condition in the sentence, not merely sound plausible.
Anchor each blank to the specific noun phrase it governs - here, attitude toward international movements.
common_mistakes: Choosing "obstinate" from the stereotype of the stay-at-home artist, though it says nothing about the wider world.
Choosing "knew nothing about" or "made light of" for Blank (ii) by ignoring the reversal that "on the contrary" requires.

concept.technique_name: cross-multiplication and reciprocal-difference decomposition

examples.problem_statement: Using the Equation Solving Techniques of Vedic mathematics, solve two algebraic equations: first the simple linear equation \frac{x}{x+1} = \frac{5}{12} by cross-multiplication and isolation of the variable, then the reciprocal difference equation \frac{3x+7}{2x-9} - \frac{2x-9}{3x+7} = \frac{56}{45} by decomposing the right-hand side into a difference of two fractions with matching numerator patterns. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.description: Clear the two fractions in the first equation by cross-multiplying, sending each denominator across to multiply the opposite numerator.
Expand the bracket, collect the x terms on one side and the constant on the other, then divide to isolate x.

solution.operation: Recognize \frac{3x+7}{2x-9} - \frac{2x-9}{3x+7} = \frac{56}{45} as a difference of a fraction and its reciprocal.
solution.result: The left-hand side has the form t - \frac{1}{t}, so it is enough to find the value of t.
solution.description: Read the structure of the second equation before expanding anything: the two terms are reciprocals of one another, which is what makes the decomposition method apply.

solution.result: The candidate factor pairs of the denominator are 3 and 15, and 9 and 5.
solution.description: Factor the right-hand denominator, since the target form \frac{a}{b} - \frac{b}{a} has denominator ab, so a and b must be a factor pair of 45.

solution.result: The pair 9 and 5 is the one whose squared difference equals the numerator 56.
solution.description: Test each factor pair against the numerator, because \frac{a}{b} - \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2 - b^2}{ab}; the pair 3 and 15 overshoots, while 9 and 5 matches exactly.

solution.result: The right-hand side is rewritten in the same reciprocal-difference form as the left-hand side.
solution.description: Write the right-hand side using the pair found in the previous step so that both sides of the equation now share one structure.

solution.result: The reciprocal-difference equation reduces to simple linear equations in x.
solution.description: Equate the corresponding terms on the two sides, taking both matchings the structure allows, and solve each as an ordinary cross-multiplication problem like the first equation.

examples.answer: First equation solution: x = 5/7. Second equation approach: Decompose 56/45 into 9/5 - 5/9, then equate corresponding terms from LHS to solve for x.

key_reminders: Cross-multiplication turns \frac{p}{q} = \frac{r}{s} into ps = qr.
\frac{a}{b} - \frac{b}{a} = \frac{a^2 - b^2}{ab}, so a and b must be a factor pair of the target denominator whose squared difference is the target numerator.
When both sides share the reciprocal-difference form, the corresponding terms can be equated directly instead of expanding.
common_mistakes: Taking the factor pair 3 and 15 of 45 without checking the squared difference, which gives 216 rather than 56.
Cross-multiplying the second equation out into a quadratic instead of exploiting the reciprocal structure.
Keeping only the \frac{9}{5} matching and missing the -\frac{5}{9} case.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion via myth-versus-reality contrast

examples.problem_statement:
Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. Everyone has routines that govern their work. The myth is that artists are somehow different, that they reject (i) ______ , but of course that's not true: most artists work as the rest of us do, (ii) ______ , day by day, according to their own customs.
Blank (i): A latitude, B habit, C materialism
Blank (ii): D impetuously, E ploddingly, F sporadically

solution.operation: Identify the passage's controlling idea: artists are like everyone else in having "routines that govern their work".
solution.result: Routine, not exception, is the theme both blanks must serve.
solution.description: Fix the sentence's main point first, since the passage ends by reaffirming that artists work by their own customs day by day.

solution.operation: Locate the contrast: the myth that artists are "somehow different" and reject (i).
solution.result: Blank (i) must name something whose rejection would contrast with being governed by work routines.
solution.description: Set up the first blank as part of the myth being denied - the thing artists supposedly reject must be exactly what routine-governed work consists of.

solution.operation: Test A latitude, B habit, C materialism against that condition.
solution.result: Only "habit" works: rejecting latitude would match being governed by routines rather than contrast with it, and materialism is irrelevant to work routines.
solution.description: Eliminate on the contrast requirement - latitude fails because rejecting freedom is consistent with routine, and materialism fails because it has no bearing on how one works.

solution.operation: Read Blank (ii) as describing how artists "work as the rest of us do", alongside "day by day".
solution.result: Blank (ii) must be consistent with steady, routine-bound work.
solution.description: Anchor the second blank to the phrase it modifies, which restates the routine idea rather than the myth.

solution.operation: Test D impetuously, E ploddingly, F sporadically against that emphasis.
solution.result: Only "ploddingly" is consistent with routines and day-by-day work.
solution.description: Choose the adverb of plodding regularity, since impetuous and sporadic work would describe the mythical artist the passage has already rejected.

examples.answer: Choice B: habit; Choice E: ploddingly

key_reminders: When a sentence states a myth and denies it, the blanks inside the myth take the words the denial reverses.
The second blank must agree with the nearby restatement "day by day, according to their own customs".
A choice is wrong if rejecting it would be consistent with, rather than contrary to, the passage's stated routine.
common_mistakes: Choosing "latitude" for Blank (i) without noticing that rejecting latitude fits routine-governed work instead of contrasting with it.
Choosing "materialism" from a general stereotype about artists, though it is unrelated to work routines.
Choosing "impetuously" or "sporadically" for Blank (ii), which describe the myth rather than the day-by-day reality.

concept.technique_name: perimeter partition and area comparison

examples.problem_statement: A wire, if bent into a square, encloses an area of 484 cm^2. This wire is cut into two pieces with the bigger piece having a length three-fourth of the original wire's length. Now, if a circle and a square are formed with the bigger and the smaller piece respectively, what would be the area enclosed by the two pieces?

solution.result: side of the original square = 22 cm
solution.description: Take the square root of the enclosed area to recover the side of the square the whole wire was bent into.
Multiply that side by 4, since the wire's full length is the perimeter of that square.

solution.result: longer piece = 66 cm, which becomes the circumference of the circle
solution.description: Take three-fourths of the wire to get the bigger piece, the one bent into the circle.
Set the longer piece equal to the circumference 2\pi r and solve for the radius.

solution.result: shorter piece = 22 cm, so the small square has side \frac{11}{2} cm
solution.description: Take the remaining quarter of the wire and divide it by 4, because that piece is bent into a square.
Substitute the radius into \pi r^2, using \pi = \frac{22}{7} as the book does, to get the circle's area.

solution.result: area of the small square = \frac{121}{4} cm^2
solution.description: Square the side found in step 5 to get the area enclosed by the shorter piece.
Add the two areas together, since the question asks for the area enclosed by both pieces.

key_reminders: The wire's length is conserved: it is the perimeter of the original square and is then split into a circumference and a new perimeter.
For a circle formed from a piece of wire, that piece is the circumference, so r = \frac{\text{length}}{2\pi}.
Use \pi = \frac{22}{7} here, as the book does, so the circle's area comes out as an exact fraction.
common_mistakes: Treating the 66 cm piece as the circle's diameter or radius instead of its circumference.
Forgetting to divide the 22 cm shorter piece by 4 before squaring, and using 22^2 as the square's area.

concept.technique_name: three-part inequality isolation

examples.problem_statement: If -13 < 3 - 2a < 10, which of the following could be the value of a? Indicate all possible values. Choices: (A) -9, (B) -3, (C) 0, (D) 5, (E) 8, (F) 10

solution.result: the given three-part inequality, to be handled either as two separate inequalities or by operating on all three parts at once
solution.description: Start from the compound inequality and decide to isolate a by doing the same thing to all three parts.
Subtract 3 from all three parts of the inequality to strip the constant off the middle.
Divide all three parts by -2 and flip both inequality signs, because dividing by a negative reverses the direction.

solution.result: -3, 0 and 5 fall inside the range; -9, 8 and 10 do not
solution.description: Check each answer choice against the range just derived and keep every value strictly inside it.

key_reminders: Whatever you do to one part of a three-part inequality, do to all three parts.
Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number flips the inequality signs.
common_mistakes: Dividing by -2 without flipping the signs, which produces a < -3.5 or a > 8 and selects the wrong choices.
Including 8, which is an endpoint of a strict inequality and therefore excluded.

concept.technique_name: smart numbers (plugging values) for related fractions

examples.problem_statement: 4/5 of the women and 3/4 of the men speak Spanish. If there are 40% as many men as women, what fraction of the group speaks Spanish?

solution.description: Because the fractions apply to two groups that are themselves related by a percent, plug in easy numbers that satisfy 'men are 40% as many as women'.
Apply the women's fraction to the number of women you chose.
Apply the men's fraction to the number of men you chose.

solution.result: 140 people in the group, 110 of them Spanish speakers
solution.description: Add the two groups to get the total headcount, and add the two speaker counts to get the total speakers.
Divide speakers by total people to get the fraction of the group that speaks Spanish, reducing if you like.

key_reminders: When fractions are taken of two quantities that are themselves related by a fraction or percent, plugging numbers is faster than algebra.
Choose the base quantity (here women = 100) so that both the percent relation and the fractions give whole numbers.
The fraction of the whole group is total speakers over total people, not the average of the two fractions.
common_mistakes: Averaging \frac{4}{5} and \frac{3}{4} instead of weighting them by the 100-to-40 group sizes.
Dividing 110 by 100 (the women only) instead of by the 140-person total.

concept.technique_name: bounding a radius by distances to interior and exterior points

examples.problem_statement: In the xy-plane, the point with coordinates (-6, -7) is the center of circle C. The point with coordinates (-6, 5) lies inside C, and the point with coordinates (8, -7) lies outside C. If m is the radius of C and m is an integer, what is the value of m?

solution.operation: plot (-6, -7) as the center, (-6, 5) inside C, and (8, -7) outside C
solution.result: a figure showing one point directly above the center and one directly to its right
solution.description: Draw the given information as accurately as possible, the standard strategy of translating words into a figure.

solution.result: the interior point is 12 units from the center, so m > 12
solution.description: Measure the vertical distance to the interior point; since that point lies inside the circle, the radius must exceed it.

solution.result: the exterior point is 14 units from the center, so m < 14
solution.description: Measure the horizontal distance to the exterior point; since that point lies outside the circle, the radius must be less than it.
Combine the two bounds and use the fact that m is an integer, leaving exactly one value strictly between 12 and 14.

key_reminders: A point inside the circle is nearer the center than the radius; a point outside is farther, giving a lower and an upper bound on m.
Two points sharing an x-coordinate (or a y-coordinate) are separated by the difference of the other coordinates, so no distance formula is needed.
The integer restriction is what pins a range down to a single value.
common_mistakes: Mis-signing the coordinate differences and getting 2 instead of 12, or 2 instead of 14, from the negative center coordinates.
Reversing the roles and assuming the radius is greater than 14 or less than 12.

concept.technique_name: sector area as a fraction of the full circle

examples.problem_statement: The minute hand of a clock is 10 cm long. Find the area of the face of the clock described by the minute hand between 9 a.m. and 9 : 35 a.m.

solution.description: Start from the fact the book's solution opens with: one complete sweep of the minute hand covers the whole dial, which is 360 degrees.
Convert the 35 minutes of travel into the angle the hand traverses on that dial; the book records this sweep as 210 degrees.
Take the swept angle as a fraction of the full turn and apply that fraction to the area of the circle of radius 10 cm (the hand length), giving the area described.

key_reminders: The full clock dial is 360 degrees, and the minute hand sweeps all of it in 60 minutes.
A sector's area is the fraction (angle / 360) of the whole circle's area \pi r^2.
The radius of the swept sector is the length of the minute hand, 10 cm.
common_mistakes: Using 35 directly as the angle instead of converting 35 minutes into the 210 degrees the hand traverses.
Computing arc length (a fraction of 2 \pi r) instead of sector area (a fraction of \pi r^2).

concept.technique_name: multiplication by 12 (double each digit and add its neighbour)

examples.problem_statement: Multiplication by 12 — rule: double each digit in turn and add its neighbour (the digit to its right). Solve: 5324 x 12

solution.description: Write a leading zero in front of the number so the left-most digit also has a digit to double when the sweep reaches it.
Start at the right-most digit, 4: double it. There is no neighbour to its right, so 8 is written as the units digit of the answer.
Move left to 2: double it and add its right neighbour 4, giving 8, which is placed in the tens position.
Move left to 3: double it and add its right neighbour 2, giving 8, placed in the hundreds position.
Move left to 5: double it and add its right neighbour 3, giving 13; write the 3 and carry the 1 into the next position.
Finish on the leading zero: double it, add its right neighbour 5 and the carried 1, giving 6 as the left-most digit of the product.

key_reminders: Each output digit is (2 x current digit) + (digit immediately to its right).
Prefix a zero so the left-most real digit is processed like every other digit.
Any two-digit intermediate result leaves its units digit in place and carries the tens digit leftwards.
common_mistakes: Dropping the leading-zero step and stopping at 3888, losing the leading 6.
Forgetting to add the carry of 1 from the 2 x 5 + 3 = 13 step into the final position.

concept.technique_name: disjunctive syllogism (either-or elimination)

examples.problem_statement: Either Raghav is sick or he is stoned. (i) Raghav is sick. (ii) Raghav is not sick. (iii) Raghav is stoned. (iv) Raghav is not stoned. Which pair is such that the second statement follows logically from the first?

solution.result: at least one of the two holds
solution.description: Take the given statement at face value: it asserts that Raghav is sick or he is stoned, so the two possibilities cannot both fail.
Eliminate one branch: if he is not stoned, the remaining option must hold, so he must be sick — that is, statement (i) follows from statement (iv).
Match that ordered pair, (iv) leading to (i), against the answer choices and pick the option listing iv-i.

key_reminders: An inclusive 'either A or B' guarantees that denying one alternative forces the other.
The listed pair is ordered: the second statement must follow from the first.
common_mistakes: Choosing i-iii, treating the two alternatives as implying each other rather than as alternatives.
Getting the pair's direction backwards and picking a pair that reads (i) then (iv).

concept.technique_name: slope-intercept form conversion

examples.problem_statement: A line has the equation 2y - 4x - 8 = 0. Quantity A: The slope of the line. Quantity B: 4. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Move the constant term to the right side so the variable terms stand alone, the first move toward slope-intercept form y = mx + b.
Add 4x to both sides so that y is isolated on the left with the x-term on the right.
Divide every term by 2 to finish putting the line in the form y = mx + b.

solution.result: slope 2 < 4, so Quantity B is larger
solution.description: Read the coefficient of x as the slope, m = 2, and compare it to Quantity B's 4; note the y-intercept is 4, which is the trap value Quantity B echoes.

key_reminders: In y = mx + b the slope is m, the coefficient of x, and b is the y-intercept.
Divide the whole equation by the coefficient of y before reading off the slope.
The y-intercept is not the slope, even when the problem dangles its value as an answer choice.
common_mistakes: Comparing the y-intercept 4 with Quantity B's 4 and concluding the quantities are equal.
Reading the slope as 4 straight off 2y - 4x - 8 = 0 without dividing by the coefficient 2 of y.

concept.technique_name: percentage change on ratio terms

examples.problem_statement: The temperatures of Delhi and Lucknow were in the ratio 3 : 5 in July and 2 : 3 in August. The percentage increase in temperature from August to September is twice that from July to August for Delhi, and the same as that from July to August for Lucknow. The ratio of the sum of the temperatures of these two cities in August to that in July was 5 : 4. What was the percentage increase in temperature of Lucknow from July to August?

solution.description: Write Lucknow's July temperature as the second term of the July ratio 3 : 5 scaled by a common multiplier x.
Take the August ratio 2 : 3 with the multiplier 2x that the printed solution uses, so Lucknow's August temperature is the third term of that ratio, 3 times 2x.
Set up the percentage increase as (August value minus July value) divided by the July value, times 100, using the two expressions just written.
Cancel the common x in numerator and denominator and evaluate one-fifth of 100 to get the percentage increase.

key_reminders: Percentage increase = (new value - old value) / old value x 100, always divided by the earlier value.
Ratio terms only become temperatures once multiplied by a common factor; July uses x and August uses 2x here.
The common factor cancels in a percentage change, so the answer does not depend on x.
common_mistakes: Dividing the change by the August value 6x instead of the July value 5x.
Comparing the ratio terms 5 and 3 directly and reporting a decrease, ignoring that July and August carry different multipliers.

concept.technique_name: symbolic function substitution

examples.problem_statement: If A \diamond B = 4A - B, what is the value of (3 \diamond 2) \diamond 3 ?

solution.description: Work the operation inside the parentheses first, since its output becomes the left input of the outer operation.
Substitute A = 3 and B = 2 into the rule 4A - B and evaluate to get the inner value.
Replace the parenthesised expression with its output 10, leaving a single application of the operation to solve.
Substitute A = 10 and B = 3 into 4A - B and evaluate to reach the final value.

key_reminders: A custom symbol is just a rule: substitute the left operand for A and the right operand for B.
Evaluate the innermost parentheses first, then feed that output into the outer operation.
The rule 4A - B is not symmetric, so operand order matters.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the second operand by 4 as well, computing 4(3) - 4(2) instead of 4(3) - 2.
Using 10 as the right operand, computing 4(3) - 10 rather than 4(10) - 3, after the inner value is found.

concept.technique_name: ordering-diagram elimination

examples.problem_statement: A radio talk show host airs five telephone calls sequentially. The calls, one from each of Felicia, Gwen, Henry, Isaac, and Mel, are each either live or taped (but not both). Two calls are from Vancouver, two are from Seattle, and one is from Kelowna. The following conditions must apply: Isaac's and Mel's calls are the first two calls aired, but not necessarily in that order. The third call aired, from Kelowna, is taped. Both Seattle calls are live. Both Gwen's and Felicia's calls air after Henry's. Neither Mel nor Felicia calls from Seattle. Which one of the following could be an accurate list of the calls, listed in the order in which they are aired? (A) Isaac's, Henry's, Felicia's, Mel's, Gwen's (B) Isaac's, Mel's, Gwen's, Henry's, Felicia's (C) Mel's, Gwen's, Henry's, Isaac's, Felicia's (D) Mel's, Isaac's, Gwen's, Henry's, Felicia's (E) Mel's, Isaac's, Henry's, Felicia's, Gwen's

solution.result: \text{Isaac and Mel in slots 1-2, Henry in slot 3, Gwen and Felicia in slots 4-5}
solution.description: Read the ordering frame off the diagram: because the answer choices concern order only and not the live/taped or city subsets, the diagram alone settles which sequences are possible.
Check choice (A) against the frame: it places Henry second, but slots 1 and 2 are reserved for Isaac and Mel.
Check choice (B): it places Gwen third, but the third slot belongs to Henry.
Check choice (C): it places Gwen second, inside the pair of slots that Isaac and Mel must occupy.
Check choice (D): it places Gwen third, where the frame requires Henry.
With (A) through (D) each violating the frame, the one surviving list is the accurate ordering.

key_reminders: The deduced frame is (I M) H (G F): Isaac and Mel fill slots 1-2 in either order, Henry is third, Gwen and Felicia fill slots 4-5.
On an acceptability question, test each answer choice against the constraints and eliminate on the first violation.
When the choices list order only, the live/taped and city constraints need not be checked.
common_mistakes: Checking the Seattle, Kelowna, and live/taped conditions choice by choice when every wrong answer here fails on order alone.
Reading the Henry constraint as fixing Henry first rather than only ahead of both Gwen and Felicia, which combined with Isaac and Mel in slots 1-2 forces Henry into slot 3.

concept.technique_name: slope-intercept form and plotting a line through the origin

examples.problem_statement: Which quadrants, if any, do not contain any points on the line represented by x = 10y ?

solution.description: Rewrite the given equation in slope-intercept form; an equation of the form y = mx is the same as y = mx + 0.

Read the constant term off the slope-intercept form: because it is 0, the y-intercept is the origin, and whenever a line passes through the origin that single point serves as both the x-intercept and the y-intercept.
Substitute a convenient value for x to get a second point; 10 is the smart choice here because it divides evenly by the denominator, giving y = 1.
Plot the two points found and draw the line through them; it rises to the upper right from the origin and falls to the lower left.
Compare the drawn line against the four quadrants and name the ones it never enters.

key_reminders: y = mx is the same as y = mx + 0, so its y-intercept is the origin.
A line through the origin has the same point as both its x-intercept and its y-intercept.
Two plotted points are enough to draw a line and read off which quadrants it occupies.
common_mistakes: Reading x = 10y as y = 10x and getting a steep line instead of a shallow one (the slope is 1/10, not 10).
Picking x = 1 instead of x = 10, producing the awkward point (1, 0.1) that is hard to plot accurately.

concept.technique_name: probability as favorable outcomes over total outcomes, with inclusive counting

examples.problem_statement: An integer is randomly chosen from 2 to 20 inclusive. What is the probability that the number is prime?

solution.description: List every prime between 2 and 20 inclusive and count them; there are 8 of them, and these are the favorable outcomes.
Count the total integers in the inclusive range by subtracting the endpoints and adding one before you are done, so that both 2 and 20 are counted.
Check the count a second way: there are 20 integers from 1 to 20 inclusive, so dropping the number 1 must leave 19 integers from 2 to 20.
Apply the definition of probability, dividing the 8 desired outcomes by the 19 total equally likely choices.

key_reminders: Probability equals the number of desired items divided by the total number of choices.
For an inclusive range, count is last minus first plus one: add one before you're done.
1 is not prime and 2 is, so the list of primes starts at 2.
common_mistakes: Using 20 - 2 = 18 as the denominator and losing an endpoint, giving 8/18.
Counting 1 as prime or omitting 2, which shifts the numerator off 8.
Using 20 as the total because the numbers 'go up to 20', ignoring that the range starts at 2.

concept.technique_name: slope from two points read off a figure

examples.problem_statement: In the xy-plane shown, line k crosses the x-axis at (5, 0) and the y-axis at (0, -5). What is the slope of line k? (A) -5  (B) -1  (C) 0  (D) 1  (E) 5

solution.description: Recall the rule that for a line through two points, the slope is the difference of the y-coordinates divided by the difference of the x-coordinates.
Translate the figure into coordinates by reading where line k crosses the x-axis.
Read the second usable point off the same figure, where line k crosses the y-axis.
Substitute the two intercepts into the slope formula and simplify the resulting fraction.
Match the computed slope against the listed options to select the correct choice.

key_reminders: Slope between two points is (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1), valid whenever the x-coordinates differ.
A figure's intercepts are the easiest two points to translate into coordinates.
Subtracting a negative y-coordinate adds, so 0 - (-5) = 5.
common_mistakes: Mishandling 0 - (-5) as -5 and reporting a slope of -1 (choice B).
Inverting the formula to (x2 - x1) / (y2 - y1); here it happens to give the same value, hiding the error for later problems.
Grabbing the intercept value -5 straight from the figure as the slope (choice A).

concept.technique_name: context clue matching

examples.problem_statement: The (i) _________ child approached the diving board; (ii) _________ water in the first place, he found the prospect of jumping into it from some height even more frightening. Blank (i): tremulous / coltish / cumbersome. Blank (ii): beguiled by / chary of / repulsed by.

solution.operation: Collect the sentence's clue words about the child's state: "frightening", "even more frightening"
solution.result: Every clue in the sentence points to fear
solution.description: Gather the descriptive clues the sentence gives about the child before touching either blank, so both blanks are filled from the same established direction: fear.

solution.operation: Match blank (i) against the fear direction: tremulous vs. coltish vs. cumbersome
solution.description: Choose the blank (i) word that expresses fear; tremulous matches the fear clues best, while coltish and cumbersome describe something other than being scared.

solution.operation: Gauge the intensity blank (ii) needs: diving is "even more frightening" than the water itself, so the water feeling must be a milder fear
solution.result: Blank (ii) = chary of, meaning suspicious or slightly scared of
solution.description: Set the strength of blank (ii) from the comparison: because jumping is described as more frightening than the water, the child's feeling toward water must be a less extreme version of frightened, which is chary of.

key_reminders: Fill both blanks from the same clue direction the sentence establishes.
A comparative like "even more frightening" fixes the relative intensity of the two blanks: the earlier feeling must be the milder one.
common_mistakes: Taking "repulsed by" for blank (ii): it is a fear/aversion word but too extreme to be outranked by "even more frightening".
Reading "beguiled by" as fitting the fear direction when it points the opposite way, toward attraction.

concept.technique_name: extreme-case testing in quantitative comparison

examples.problem_statement: In the figure above, points A, B, C, and D lie in that order on a circle whose diameter is 10, and ABCD is the quadrilateral they form. Quantity A: the area of quadrilateral ABCD. Quantity B: 40. Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: List what is actually given: circle diameter = 10, and A, B, C, D lie on the circle in the order shown
solution.result: Only the diameter and the cyclic order of the four points are fixed
solution.description: Separate the given information from what the picture merely looks like, so you know exactly which facts you are allowed to use.

solution.operation: Apply the rule that figures are not necessarily drawn to scale, and redraw the circle with A, B, C, D still in the same order but spaced differently
solution.result: The positions of the four points may vary freely as long as their order is preserved
solution.description: Because the figure is not to scale, deliberately vary the point positions to see how much the area of ABCD can move while the given information stays true.

solution.operation: Place A and C opposite each other with B and D very close to C
solution.result: Quadrilateral ABCD collapses and its area is very close to 0, so the area can be less than 40
solution.description: Test the first extreme arrangement by crowding three vertices together, which squeezes the quadrilateral flat and drives its area below Quantity B.

solution.operation: Place A, B, C, D evenly spaced around the circle and draw the diameters AC and BD
solution.result: AC and BD are perpendicular bisectors of each other, cutting ABCD into four right triangles
solution.description: Test the opposite extreme by spreading the points evenly, then add the two diagonals, which for evenly spaced points are perpendicular diameters that split the quadrilateral into four congruent right triangles.

solution.operation: Each right triangle has legs equal to the radius: \frac{1}{2}(5)(5)
solution.description: Find the area of one of the four right triangles, whose two legs are each half of the diameter 10, that is, the radius 5.
Total the four congruent triangles to get the area of the evenly spaced quadrilateral, which exceeds Quantity B's 40.

solution.operation: Compare the two cases against Quantity B: one area is near 0 (less than 40), the other is 50 (greater than 40)
solution.result: No single relationship holds for every allowed figure
solution.description: Conclude from the two valid arrangements straddling 40 that Quantity A can be either smaller or larger, so the comparison cannot be settled.

examples.answer: Choice D: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

key_reminders: GRE figures are not necessarily drawn to scale; only the stated facts and the drawn order of points may be assumed.
In a quantitative comparison, one arrangement below the benchmark and one above it forces Choice D.
Diagonals joining diametrically opposite points are diameters, and for evenly spaced points they are perpendicular bisectors of each other.
common_mistakes: Trusting the drawn shape and computing a single area for ABCD instead of varying the point positions.
Stopping after finding the near-zero case and answering Choice B, without checking the evenly spaced case that gives 50.

concept.technique_name: sentence equivalence synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. It would have been disingenuous of the candidate to appear ______ when her opponent won the election, but she congratulated the victor nonetheless. (A) gracious (B) ecstatic (C) crestfallen (D) indifferent (E) euphoric (F) disgruntled

solution.operation: Interpret the key word: what reaction by a losing candidate would appear "disingenuous"?
solution.result: A show of delight at her own defeat would be insincere
solution.description: Decide what the blank must mean by reasoning from "disingenuous": the reaction has to be one that would be plainly insincere coming from the loser.

solution.operation: Test the choices against that requirement: ecstatic, euphoric
solution.result: Both would be highly disingenuous, and they are alike in meaning
solution.description: Pick out the choices that satisfy the insincerity requirement and also match each other, since the completed sentences must be alike in meaning.

solution.operation: Check the remaining tempting choice, gracious
solution.result: It fits the blank, but no other offered word is nearly alike in meaning to it, so it is rejected
solution.description: Rule out gracious by the pairing requirement: a word that fits the sentence but has no near-synonym among the choices cannot be part of the answer.

examples.answer: Choice B: ecstatic AND Choice E: euphoric

key_reminders: Sentence equivalence requires two choices that both fit the sentence and are alike in meaning to each other.
A choice that fits the blank but has no near-synonym among the options is automatically out.
common_mistakes: Selecting gracious because it reads naturally in the sentence, even though it is left without a matching partner.
Pairing crestfallen with disgruntled: those describe a sincere reaction to losing, which would not be disingenuous.
