concept.technique_name: definitional clue matching for equivalent word pairs

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Mr. Hirsch says he will aim to preserve the foundation's support of ______ thinkers, individuals who are going against the trends in a field or an acknowledged set of opinions.

solution.operation: Read the clause after the comma as the definition of the blank: "individuals who are going against the trends in a field or an acknowledged set of opinions"
solution.result: The blank must be filled by words meaning "opposed to established trends or opinions"
solution.description: Treat the appositive following the comma as a built-in definition of the type of thinkers being described, so the sentence tells you outright what meaning the blank needs.

solution.operation: Match that required meaning against "iconoclastic" and "heterodox"
solution.result: Both describe people whose opinions run counter to established norms
solution.description: Check the two candidates that carry the required sense; because both describe opinions running counter to established norms, they satisfy the definition and are also alike in meaning as the format demands.

solution.operation: Test "doctrinaire" and "dogmatic" against the required meaning
solution.result: Both mean the opposite: adhering to established principles
solution.description: Eliminate this pair by noting that adhering to established principles is the reverse of going against them, so they contradict the definition given after the comma.

solution.operation: Test "integrative" and "synthesizing" against the required meaning
solution.result: Both refer to a willingness to bring together disparate points of view
solution.description: Eliminate this pair as well: bringing together disparate viewpoints is a different idea from opposing prevailing ones, so neither fits the defined sense.

examples.answer: Choice A: iconoclastic; AND Choice D: heterodox

key_reminders: An appositive phrase set off by a comma often defines the blank outright.
In Sentence Equivalence the two correct choices must both fit the sentence and be alike in meaning.
Wrong pairs frequently cluster as opposites or as an unrelated but internally matched pair.
common_mistakes: Picking the doctrinaire/dogmatic pair because they form a matched pair, ignoring that they mean the opposite of going against established opinion.
Picking integrative/synthesizing on the strength of their pairing alone, though bringing viewpoints together is not opposing them.

concept.technique_name: subject-verb agreement by eliminating middlemen

examples.problem_statement: Choose the better version of the underlined portion; choice (A) repeats the original sentence. The recent string of burglaries, in addition to poor building maintenance, have inspired the outspoken resident to call a tenants' meeting. (A) The recent string of burglaries, in addition to poor building maintenance, have  (B) Recently, the string of burglaries, along with the poor building maintenance, has

solution.operation: Strike out the middleman modifier "in addition to poor building maintenance"
solution.result: The recent string of burglaries ... have inspired the outspoken resident
solution.description: Remove the interrupting phrase that sits between the subject and the verb; such modifiers never change the number of the subject, and cutting them makes the true pairing visible.

solution.operation: Identify the subject of the stripped sentence
solution.result: The subject is string, which is singular
solution.description: With the middleman gone, read off the head noun that actually governs the verb: it is string, not burglaries, and string is singular.

solution.operation: Apply subject-verb agreement in number to string
solution.result: The singular has is correct, so have is wrong
solution.description: Because subject and verb must agree in number, a singular subject requires the singular verb form, which rules out the plural have of the original.

solution.operation: Select the choice that supplies the singular verb
solution.description: Pick the option whose verb matches the singular subject identified in the previous step.

key_reminders: Eliminate the middlemen: modifiers between subject and verb do not affect agreement.
Phrases like "in addition to" or "along with" do not make a singular subject plural.
Subject and verb must agree in number.
common_mistakes: Taking the nearby plural burglaries as the subject and accepting the plural have.
Treating "in addition to poor building maintenance" as a compound subject that pluralizes string.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal reasoning across two blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The setting in which the concert took place (i) ______ : the group's performance was elegant and polished, but the sound, which seeped across the cold, unresonant high school auditorium, was oddly (ii) ______ , given the energy the players seemed to be putting into it. Blank (i): A exacted a toll, B encouraged nervousness, C solved a dilemma. Blank (ii): D clangorous, E tepid, F inviting.

solution.operation: Read the "but" as a contrast between the performance and the sound
solution.result: The performance is positive ("elegant and polished"), so Blank (ii) must be negative
solution.description: Use the contrast conjunction to set the required charge of the second blank: since the first half of the contrast is praise, the description of the sound has to run the other way.

solution.operation: Add the second condition from "given the energy the players seemed to be putting into it"
solution.result: The sound must also contrast with the apparent energy of the performers
solution.description: Layer on the closing clause, which demands not just any negative word but one that clashes with visible energy, tightening what Blank (ii) can accept.

solution.operation: Screen the Blank (ii) choices against both conditions
solution.result: Only "tepid" meets them, so it is correct
solution.description: Apply the two conditions together to the second column and keep the single word that satisfies both.

solution.operation: Read the sentence as a whole to fix Blank (i)
solution.result: The setting had a negative effect on the performance, so "exacted a toll" fits best
solution.description: Now that the sound is established as disappointing, ask what the setting did to the performance overall and choose the phrase carrying that negative effect.

solution.operation: Test the rival Blank (i) choice "encouraged nervousness"
solution.result: Rejected: the sentence never discusses the psychological state of the musicians or audience
solution.description: Check the other negative-sounding option and discard it, because being negative is not enough when the sentence gives no support for a claim about anyone's nerves.

examples.answer: Choice A: exacted a toll; AND Choice E: tepid

key_reminders: A "but" between two descriptions fixes the polarity of the second one.
Every condition the sentence supplies must be satisfied, not just the polarity.
A choice with the right charge is still wrong if the sentence provides no support for its specific content.
common_mistakes: Choosing "clangorous" because it is negative, though a clangorous sound would not contrast with the players' energy.
Choosing "encouraged nervousness" for Blank (i) on negativity alone, when the sentence says nothing about psychological state.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal reasoning across two blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The government has no choice but to (i) ______ the incessant demands for land reform, and yet any governmental action that initiated land reform without requisite attention to agrarian reform would (ii) ______ the overall goal of economic modernization. Blank (i): A anticipate, B heed, C silence. Blank (ii): D delineate, E condone, F compromise.

solution.operation: Read "and yet" as signalling a negative consequence for the stated "overall goal"
solution.result: Blank (ii) needs a word meaning to damage that goal, and only "compromise" fits
solution.description: Use the contrast marker to see that acting without attention to agrarian reform harms the modernization goal, then take the only choice in the second column that expresses such harm.

solution.operation: Use the same "and yet" to constrain Blank (i)
solution.result: The government's response must be in line with initiating land reform, so "silence" is incorrect
solution.description: Note that the contrast only makes sense if the government is moving toward reform, which eliminates a word meaning to suppress the demands.

solution.operation: Weigh the description of the demands as "incessant"
solution.result: The demands already exist, so "anticipate" is incorrect
solution.description: Read the adjective attached to the demands: something already unceasing cannot be anticipated, so that choice contradicts the sentence.
With the other two options ruled out, confirm that the survivor actually names a fitting response to existing demands.

examples.answer: Choice B: heed; Choice F: compromise

key_reminders: "And yet" marks a contrast, so the second clause must cut against the first.
Adjectives attached to the blank's object (here "incessant") carry hard constraints.
Fill the blank that the sentence constrains most tightly first, then use it to settle the other.
common_mistakes: Choosing "silence" for Blank (i), which breaks the contrast the "and yet" sets up.
Choosing "anticipate" despite "incessant" telling you the demands are already ongoing.

concept.technique_name: modular remainder of a power (congruence reduction)

examples.problem_statement: The first two, 2 digit numbers that divide (21^(12346)-1) are?

solution.description: Test the smallest two-digit divisor, 10, by replacing 21 with the remainder it leaves on division by 10, namely 1, so the power becomes 1^{12346}.
Evaluate that reduced expression: 1 raised to any power is 1, and subtracting 1 leaves remainder 0, which confirms 10 is a divisor.
Test the next two-digit number, 11, by replacing 21 with -1, since 21 is one more than the multiple 22, so the power becomes (-1)^{12346}.
Evaluate that expression: the exponent 12346 is even so (-1)^{12346} = 1, and subtracting 1 leaves remainder 0, confirming 11 is also a divisor.
Collect the two smallest two-digit numbers that were shown to leave remainder 0, taking them in increasing order as the answer.

key_reminders: A power can be reduced modulo n by first replacing the base with its remainder modulo n.
21 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}, and (-1) raised to an even power equals 1.
a^k - 1 is divisible by n exactly when a^k leaves remainder 1 modulo n.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that the exponent 12346 is even, and taking (-1)^{12346} = -1 instead of 1 for the modulo-11 test.
Starting the search at 11 and overlooking 10, which is the smaller two-digit divisor.

concept.technique_name: overlapping sets formula with extreme-value bounds

examples.problem_statement: Of 320 consumers, 200 eat strawberries and 300 eat oranges. How many people could eat both fruits? Select all that apply. Choices: 140, 150, 170, 180, 190, 210.

solution.description: Set up the two-set overlap formula with the given totals; note that it contains two unknowns, Both and Neither, so a single value cannot be pinned down yet.

solution.result: at least 300 of the 320 eat some fruit
solution.description: Look for a hidden constraint: because 300 people eat oranges, at least 300 people must eat some kind of fruit, which limits how large Neither can be.
Count the people not covered by the orange group: only these 20 could possibly eat no fruit at all, so Neither runs from 0 up to 20.
Substitute the two endpoints of the Neither range back into the formula to get the minimum overlap of 180 and the maximum overlap of 200.
Scan the answer choices and keep every value lying between the two bounds, since any value in that range is achievable.

key_reminders: Total = Group 1 + Group 2 - Both + Neither for two overlapping sets.
The overlap is minimized when Neither is smallest and maximized when Neither is largest.
In a select-all question every value inside the valid range must be chosen, not just the endpoint.
common_mistakes: Reporting only the minimum 180 and missing 190, which also lies inside the achievable range.
Assuming Neither must be 0, which fixes Both at exactly 180 and hides the upper bound of 200.

concept.technique_name: fraction of a fraction, then complement from 1

examples.problem_statement: 1/5 of all the cars on a certain auto lot are red, and 2/3 of all the red cars are convertibles. What fraction of all the cars are NOT red convertibles?

solution.description: Recognize that the convertible fraction applies to the red cars only, so a fraction of a fraction is found by multiplying the two fractions.

solution.result: \frac{2}{15} \text{ of all cars are red convertibles}
solution.description: Carry out that multiplication across numerators and denominators to get the share of the whole lot that is both red and a convertible.
Because the question asks for the cars that are NOT red convertibles, subtract the part just found from the whole lot, represented by 1.

key_reminders: "A fraction of a fraction" means multiply the two fractions.
The second fraction is taken of the red cars, not of all the cars.
A NOT question is answered by subtracting the computed part from 1.
common_mistakes: Adding 1/5 and 2/3 instead of multiplying them, which treats the two groups as separate rather than nested.
Stopping at 2/15 and reporting the red convertibles instead of the complement 13/15.

concept.technique_name: least common multiple by listing multiples and by prime factorization

examples.problem_statement: On a radio tower, a red light flashes every 6 seconds and a blue light flashes every 10 seconds. If both lights flash together at a certain time, how many seconds later will both lights flash together the next time?

solution.result: the multiples of 6 measured in seconds after the shared flash
solution.description: List the times the red light flashes, counting seconds forward from the moment both lights flashed together.

solution.result: the multiples of 10 measured in seconds after the shared flash
solution.description: List the blue light's flash times on the same time axis so the two lists can be compared entry by entry.
Scan the two lists for the earliest number appearing in both, since that is the first moment the two lights flash at the same instant again.
Check the same answer the faster way by writing each interval as a product of primes and taking 2 once with the unshared factors 3 and 5 to build the least common multiple.

key_reminders: The next simultaneous flash occurs at the least common multiple of the two intervals.
For the LCM by prime factorization, a prime shared by both numbers is counted once, not twice.
common_mistakes: Multiplying 6 by 10 to get 60, which double-counts the shared factor 2 and gives the second simultaneous flash rather than the first.
Taking the greatest common factor 2 instead of the least common multiple.

concept.technique_name: HCF-LCM structure via common-factor substitution

examples.problem_statement: If 'a' is a natural number and HCF of a, a + 5 is 5. If the LCM of the two numbers is a three-digit number, then what is the difference between the maximum & minimum possible values of the smaller number? (a) 25 (b) 35 (c) 40 (d) 45

solution.result: the two numbers are 5k and 5(k+1), with k and k+1 consecutive hence co-prime
solution.description: Because the HCF is 5, write the smaller number as 5 times some integer k; then a + 5 becomes 5(k+1), and the co-factors k and k+1 share no factor.
Since the co-factors are co-prime, the LCM is the common factor 5 multiplied by both co-factors, giving the expression 5k(k+1) that must land in the three-digit range.
Find the smallest k that pushes 5k(k+1) up to three digits: k = 4 gives an LCM of exactly 100, so the smallest permissible value of a is 20.
Find the largest k that keeps 5k(k+1) at three digits: k = 13 yields 910, so the largest permissible value of a is 65.
Subtract the minimum value of the smaller number from its maximum value to get the required difference.

key_reminders: HCF h means both numbers can be written as h times co-prime co-factors.
For co-prime co-factors, LCM = HCF x (product of the co-factors).
Consecutive integers k and k+1 are always co-prime.
common_mistakes: Taking the LCM as 5k(k+1)/1 but then reporting the LCM value (100 or 910) instead of the smaller number a = 5k.
Pushing k to 14, where 5(14)(15) = 1050 is four digits and no longer allowed.

concept.technique_name: identifying a necessary assumption by locating the conclusion-evidence gap

examples.problem_statement: Inorganic pesticides remain active on the surfaces of fruits and vegetables for several days after spraying, while organic pesticides dissipate within a few hours after application, leaving the surface of the sprayed produce free of pesticide residue. Therefore, when purchasing from a farm that uses inorganic pesticides, one must be careful to wash the produce thoroughly before eating it to prevent the ingestion of toxins. But one need not worry about ingesting pesticides when purchasing from farms that use only organic pesticides. The argument above assumes that (A) Consumers are aware of the origins of the produce they purchase. (B) Produce from farms that use organic pesticides reaches the consumer within hours after it is picked or harvested. (C) No farm uses both organic and inorganic pesticides. (D) No pesticide is capable of penetrating the skin of a fruit or vegetable. (E) The use of either type of pesticide does not increase the cost of produce.

solution.operation: Isolate the conclusion: one need not worry about ingesting pesticides when buying from farms that use only organic pesticides.
solution.description: Strip the passage down to the claim it is trying to establish, which is the final sentence about organic-only farms being safe to eat from.

solution.operation: Isolate the evidence: organic pesticides leave the surface of the produce within a few hours of spraying.
solution.description: Name the single fact offered in support of that claim, namely that organic pesticide disappears from the produce surface quickly.

solution.operation: Compare evidence about the surface with a conclusion about ingestion.
solution.result: gap: the argument covers only surface residue, never pesticide that is no longer on the surface
solution.description: Set the evidence beside the conclusion and see that safety is asserted for eating the produce, while the fact given speaks only about the surface being clear.

solution.operation: State the assumption that closes the gap: the organic pesticide does not remain in the produce in any lasting way.
solution.result: the argument must assume pesticides cannot penetrate the skin of a fruit or vegetable, which is choice (D)
solution.description: Supply the unstated premise the argument needs: if a pesticide could pass through the skin, it could dissipate from the surface yet stay inside the fruit, so the author must be assuming no such penetration occurs.

solution.operation: Test the remaining choices against the conclusion's scope.
solution.result: (A) origins are already stipulated as known, (B) if anything argues against the conclusion, (C) is already covered by the phrase 'only organic pesticides', (E) cost is off-topic
solution.description: Check each other option and reject it: awareness of origin, delivery speed, mixed-pesticide farms and cost all fall outside the residue-and-ingestion link the conclusion depends on.

key_reminders: A necessary assumption must bridge the exact gap between the stated evidence and the conclusion.
Evidence about one location or aspect (the surface) does not establish a conclusion about a broader one (ingestion).
An option that merely restates a stated premise, or that weakens the argument, cannot be the required assumption.
common_mistakes: Choosing (C), which only repeats the conclusion's own restriction to farms using 'only organic pesticides'.
Choosing (B) without noticing that quick delivery would make pesticide exposure more likely, not less.

concept.technique_name: percentage-to-degree conversion on a pie chart
concept.sub_category: Pie chart comparison across two years

examples.problem_statement: The following pie charts show the number of workers of different categories A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H of a factory for two different years. Total number of workers in 1997 = 1900; in 1998 = 1800. The 1997 shares are A 10%, B 15%, C 12%, D 25%, E 8%, F 15%, G 6%, H 9% (giving A 190, B 285, C 228, D 475, E 152, F 285, G 114, H 171). The 1998 shares are A 12.5%, B 13%, C 10%, D 20%, E 8%, F 12.5%, G 9%, H 15% (giving A 225, B 234, C 180, D 360, E 144, F 225, G 162, H 270). What is the difference between the number of workers of category F for the two years, and the difference between the angular values of the same category for the two years?

solution.description: Take the category F headcounts for the two years, 285 in 1997 and 225 in 1998, and subtract to get the difference in workers.
Take the category F percentage shares for the two years and subtract them, since the sector angle depends on the share rather than on the headcount.
Convert the percentage scale to the angular scale by dividing the full 360 degrees of a pie by the 100 percent it represents.
Multiply the 2.5 percentage-point gap by the degrees-per-percent factor to get the difference in the sector angles for category F.

key_reminders: A pie chart's full circle of 360 degrees corresponds to 100 percent, so 1 percent = 3.6 degrees.
The sector angle depends only on the percentage share, not on the total on which that share is taken.
Worker counts must be taken as percentage of each year's own total, since the two totals differ.
common_mistakes: Converting the 60-worker difference into degrees, instead of converting the 2.5 percentage-point difference.
Using a single total for both years even though 1997 has 1900 workers and 1998 has 1800.

concept.technique_name: division of surds by equating fractional exponents to a common denominator

examples.problem_statement: Divide 12 \times 4^{1/3} by 3\sqrt{2}.

solution.description: Divide the rational coefficients 12 by 3 to get 4, and rewrite the square root of 2 as 2 raised to the power one half so both surds are in exponent form.

solution.result: both surds now carry the common order 6
solution.description: Rewrite the two fractional exponents over the common denominator 6, which puts the surds on the same order so they can be combined under one radical.
Pull the shared exponent one sixth outside, leaving the bases raised to their numerators inside a single sixth-order radical.
Reduce the fraction inside the radical, 16 divided by 8 giving 2, and attach the coefficient 4 kept from the first step.

key_reminders: A radical of order n is the same as an exponent of 1/n, so \sqrt{2} = 2^{1/2}.
Surds of different orders can be combined only after their fractional exponents are written over a common denominator.
With a common exponent 1/n, the quotient a^{p/n}/b^{q/n} equals (a^{p}/b^{q})^{1/n}.
common_mistakes: Dividing the bases 4 and 2 directly without first matching the orders 1/3 and 1/2.
Dividing 12 by 3 but forgetting to carry the coefficient 4 through to the final expression.

concept.technique_name: smart numbers plug-in for regular figures

examples.problem_statement: The circumference of a circle is 7/8 the perimeter of a square. Quantity A: the area of the square. Quantity B: the area of the circle. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Note that all squares are in proportion to all other squares and all circles to all other circles, and the two figures are tied by a fixed relation, so a single set of plugged-in values settles the comparison. Pick the value for the square — choosing the circle's radius first would drag \pi into every square calculation.
Turn the chosen side into the square's perimeter, since the perimeter is what the given 7/8 relationship refers to.
Square the chosen side to get the area of the square, which is Quantity A.
Apply the given relationship to the perimeter found in step 2 to get the circle's circumference.
Set the circumference formula equal to 7 and solve for the radius, the quantity the circle's area needs.

solution.result: Quantity B is smaller than 4, so Quantity A is larger
solution.description: Square the radius from step 5 in the circle-area formula and evaluate it on the calculator with 3.14 for \pi, then compare that value against the square's area of 4.

key_reminders: A square's perimeter is 4s and its area is s^2.
A circle's circumference is 2\pi r and its area is \pi r^2.
Squares are all similar to one another and circles are all similar to one another, so when the two are locked in a fixed ratio, one plug-in gives the answer for every case.
common_mistakes: Plugging in the circle first (e.g. r = 2, C = 4\pi), which forces the square's perimeter to 32\pi/7 and leaves \pi in the square's area — awkward rather than wrong.
Assuming the 7/8 ratio of circumference to perimeter carries over to a 7/8 ratio of areas.

concept.technique_name: chained ratio scaled by a known difference

examples.problem_statement: The ratio of Jim's salary for October to his salary for November was 9 : 8 and the ratio of the salary for November to that for December was 3 : 4. The worker got 40 rupees more for December than for October and received a bonus constituting 40 per cent of the salary for three months. Find the bonus. (Assume that the number of workdays is the same in every month.)

solution.description: Join the two ratios on their shared November term so all three months sit on one scale; November stays at 8, which sends December's 4 up to 10.666.

solution.result: 1.666 ratio units correspond to the 40 rupee gap
solution.description: Subtract October's share from December's on that common scale, because the problem tells you what this particular gap is worth in rupees.
Divide the 40 rupees across the 1.666 units from step 2 to get the value of a single unit, the scale factor for everything else.
Add the three monthly shares, since the bonus is a percentage of the salary for all three months together.
Convert the three-month total into rupees with the step 3 unit value and take 40 per cent of it to get the bonus.

key_reminders: Two ratios sharing a term combine into one chain by holding that shared term fixed.
A stated difference in real money fixes the value of one ratio unit.
40 per cent is applied as the multiplier 0.4.
common_mistakes: Treating the 40 rupees as the value of one ratio unit instead of the 1.666-unit gap between December and October.
Combining 9 : 8 with 3 : 4 without first making November agree, which corrupts December's share.

concept.technique_name: logarithm of a power of the base

solution.result: the argument is rewritten as a power of 10
solution.description: Rewrite the decimal as a power of the base 10 so the logarithm's argument matches its base.

solution.result: the exponent moves out in front
solution.description: Bring the exponent from step 1 down as a coefficient using the power rule for logarithms.
Replace \log_{10}10 with 1 since any log of its own base is 1, and multiply out.

key_reminders: \log_b(x^n) = n\log_b x.
common_mistakes: Reporting 4 instead of -4 by counting the four decimal places and dropping the negative sign on the exponent.

concept.technique_name: ordering constraints bounding a variable's placement

examples.problem_statement: Exactly six piano classes are given sequentially on Monday: two with more than one student and four with exactly one student. Exactly four females — Gimena, Holly, Iyanna, and Kate — and five males — Leung, Nate, Oscar, Pedro, and Saul — attend these classes. Each student attends exactly one class. The following must obtain: Iyanna and Leung together constitute one class. Pedro and exactly two others together constitute one class. Kate is the first female, but not the first student, to attend a class. Gimena's class is at some time after Iyanna's but at some time before Pedro's. Oscar's class is at some time after Gimena's. Question: Which one of the following is a complete and accurate list of classes any one of which could be the class Gimena attends? (A) the fourth, the fifth (B) the fourth, the sixth (C) the second, the fourth, the fifth (D) the third, the fifth, the sixth (E) the second, the third, the fourth

solution.result: three separate classes must sit ahead of Gimena's
solution.description: Collect the groups forced earlier than Gimena: the opening N/S slot, Kate's class, and the Iyanna-Leung class each has to come before her.

solution.result: Gimena's earliest possible class is the fourth
solution.description: Count the three classes from step 1 as occupying the first three slots, which pushes Gimena no earlier than the fourth class.

solution.result: Gimena cannot attend the last class
solution.description: Use the rule that Pedro's class follows Gimena's — something must come after her, so the sixth class is unavailable to her.

solution.result: the fourth and the fifth, which is choice (A)
solution.description: Combine the floor from step 2 with the ceiling from step 3 and match the surviving pair of classes against the answer choices.

key_reminders: Each group that must precede a variable consumes one earlier slot, setting a floor on that variable's position.
A variable that must be followed by another cannot occupy the final slot.
common_mistakes: Counting only Iyanna-Leung as preceding Gimena and letting her sit third, which is what makes choices (D) and (E) tempting.
Forgetting that Pedro comes after Gimena and admitting the sixth class, as in choice (B).

concept.technique_name: area-perimeter optimization via the square

examples.problem_statement: What is the minimum possible perimeter of a quadrilateral with an area of 1,600 square feet?

solution.operation: \text{minimize } P \text{ for fixed } A \Rightarrow \text{quadrilateral is a square}
solution.description: Start by fixing the shape: among all quadrilaterals of a given area, the square is the one with the smallest perimeter, so treat the figure as a square.
Use the square's area formula, side length squared, set it equal to 1,600 square feet, and take the square root to get the side length.
Multiply that side length by four, since a square's perimeter is four times its side, to get the minimum perimeter.

key_reminders: For a fixed area, the quadrilateral of minimum perimeter is a square.
Area of a square is s^2, so s = \sqrt{A}.
Perimeter of a square is 4s.
common_mistakes: Solving for a maximum perimeter instead: with non-integer sides there is no maximum, since 1600 \times 1, 3200 \times 0.5, and so on give ever-longer perimeters as the shape flattens toward a line.
Reporting the side length 40 instead of the perimeter 160.

concept.technique_name: percent change on a shifting base

examples.problem_statement:
From 2003 to 2004, the rent on a certain property increased by x%. From 2004 to 2005, the rent then decreased by x%. x is a positive integer.
Quantity A: The difference between 2004's rent and 2003's rent, in dollars.
Quantity B: The difference between 2004's rent and 2005's rent, in dollars.
(A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: 2004's rent is the larger of the two bases
solution.description: Notice that the actual rent is unknown, but because 2003 to 2004 was an increase, 2004's rent must be higher than 2003's - that comparison of the two bases is the whole question.

solution.result: Quantity A is x percent of 2003's price
solution.description: Express the first dollar change: the rise from 2003 to 2004 is x percent taken of 2003's price.

solution.result: Quantity B is x percent of 2004's price
solution.description: Express the second dollar change: the fall from 2004 to 2005 is the same x percent, but taken of 2004's price.
Compare the two expressions: the same percent applied to a larger whole gives a larger dollar amount, so the second change beats the first.
Confirm with numbers by picking a rent of $100 and x = 10, which gives $110 in 2004 and $99 in 2005; the $11 drop is bigger than the $10 rise.

key_reminders: A percent change is always taken of the value it starts from, so the base matters as much as the rate.
An x% increase followed by an x% decrease does not return to the original value.
Picking a base of 100 is a fast way to verify a percent comparison.
common_mistakes: Assuming the up-x% and down-x% changes cancel and choosing (C) because the rate x is identical in both years.
Choosing (D) because the actual 2003 rent is never given, when the direction of the comparison is fixed regardless of that rent.

concept.technique_name: inference from passage detail with choice elimination

examples.problem_statement:
Select one answer choice. Based on the accompanying reading passage about male nightingales' song rate: The passage implies that during the day before a night on which a male nightingale's song rate is high, that nightingale probably does which of the following?
A. Expends less of its reserves on thermoregulation than on other days
B. Stores more energy as body reserves than on other days
C. Hides to avoid predators

solution.operation: test A against the thermoregulation reference in line 24
solution.description: Check choice A by locating the passage's only mention of thermoregulation, at line 24, and note that it describes nighttime activity rather than what the bird does during the day.

solution.operation: test B against the second paragraph on fat deposits and body mass at dusk
solution.description: Check choice B against the second paragraph, which says birds store energy as fat deposits estimable from body mass and that body mass at dusk was significantly higher before high-song-rate nights - that higher dusk mass means more was stored during the day.

solution.operation: test C against the predator reference in line 3 and the foraging reference in line 20
solution.description: Check choice C: the passage says singing exposes birds to predators at line 3 but never suggests any special hiding effort, and line 20 says nightingales spend extra time foraging, which is the opposite of hiding.

solution.operation: select the only choice with passage support
solution.description: With A and C eliminated on textual grounds, select B as the one implication the passage actually supports.

examples.answer: Choice B: Stores more energy as body reserves than on other days

key_reminders: An inference must be traceable to specific lines of the passage, not to plausible outside reasoning.
Match the time frame the question asks about - here daytime behavior, not nighttime.
A detail the passage mentions is not automatically an answer unless it supports the claim in the choice.
common_mistakes: Picking A because thermoregulation is genuinely discussed, without checking that the discussion is about the night rather than the preceding day.
Picking C by extending the passage's predator remark into a hiding behavior the passage never states, while it in fact reports extra foraging.

concept.technique_name: vocabulary-in-context blank filling using signal words

examples.problem_statement: Once the candidate established herself as the clear frontrunner, it took but a brief interlude in the clamor for all her erstwhile (i) _________ to gather around her and to begin loudly proclaiming their (ii) _________. It seemed, in other words, to cause these newcomers not an iota of discomfort to behave in a manner that a casual observer might have characterized as (iii) _________ outright hypocrisy. Blank (i): factotums / detractors / zealots. Blank (ii): reputability / magnanimity / fealty. Blank (iii): tantamount to / reciprocal with / hinging on.

solution.operation: Read the signal word: erstwhile = "past" or "former"
solution.result: Blank (i) names a role these people held before, one different from their present gathering around the candidate
solution.description: Pin down the word erstwhile, since it is what tells you the people in blank (i) used to behave in a way unlike their current behavior.

solution.operation: Choose the blank (i) word meaning "those who criticized her": detractors
solution.description: Select the option that names people who were formerly criticizing, or detracting from, the candidate, matching the contrast erstwhile sets up.

solution.operation: Match "loudly proclaiming their _____" to the sense "loyalty": fealty
solution.description: Fill blank (ii) with the word for loyalty, because what these former critics now proclaim is deeply inconsistent with their past actions.

solution.operation: Apply the definition of tantamount to = "much the same as" or "equivalent to" in front of "outright hypocrisy"
solution.description: Choose the phrase that says the behavior is equivalent to outright hypocrisy, which is what an observer of this reversal would call it.

key_reminders: erstwhile means past or former, and signals a contrast between prior and present behavior
tantamount to means equivalent to or much the same as
fealty means loyalty or allegiance
common_mistakes: Reading erstwhile as a synonym for "eager" or "earnest" and picking zealots for blank (i), which erases the required before/after contrast
Picking reputability or magnanimity for blank (ii), neither of which is the thing a former critic would loudly proclaim about a frontrunner

concept.technique_name: percentage-of-total applied across two fleets

examples.problem_statement: In 2000, if an equal percentage of passenger cars and demand-response vehicles experienced mechanical problems, and the number of passenger cars that experienced such problems was 13,436, approximately how many demand-response vehicles experienced mechanical problems? (A) 1,352 (B) 2,928 (C) 4,099 (D) 7,263 (E) 9,221

solution.operation: Set the plan: rate = (cars with problems) / (total cars), then answer = rate \times (total demand-response vehicles)
solution.result: One unknown rate links the two fleets
solution.description: Lay out the plan the question invites: because the same percentage applies to both fleets, find that percentage from the passenger-car side and reuse it on the demand-response side.
Read from the second pie that passenger cars are 59.5% of private highway vehicles and from the top chart that there are about 225,000 such vehicles, then multiply to get the passenger-car total.

solution.result: About 10% of passenger cars had mechanical problems
solution.description: Divide the given number of problem cars by the passenger-car total to get the percentage that, by the question's condition, holds for demand-response vehicles too.
Get the other fleet total the same way: the bottom pie gives demand-response vehicles as 24.4% of public transit vehicles, and the top chart gives roughly 120,000 public transit vehicles.

solution.result: About 2,928 demand-response vehicles had mechanical problems
solution.description: Apply the 10% found in step 3 to the demand-response total to get the requested count.

key_reminders: The two percentages come from different pies with different bases: 59.5% of private highway vehicles, 24.4% of public transit vehicles
"An equal percentage" licenses computing the rate on one fleet and reusing it on the other
Percent of a total means multiply the total by the decimal form of the percent
common_mistakes: Applying 24.4% to the 225,000 private highway total (or 59.5% to the 120,000 public transit total) by pulling both percentages against the same chart figure
Reporting 29,280 (the whole demand-response fleet) or its 10% mis-scaled, instead of applying the rate found from 13,436 / 133,875

concept.technique_name: sentence-equivalence pairing by logical fit and shared meaning

examples.problem_statement: It seems obvious that Miles Davis' ______ the Juilliard School, which resulted in his decision to drop out, was based on the school's training of musicians for a kind of music that he did not want to play. Choices: A disaffection with, B dislocation of, C disentanglement from, D subversion of, E displacement of, F estrangement from.

solution.operation: Identify the logical relationship the sentence asserts: Davis' attitude toward the school (the blank) resulted in his decision to drop out
solution.result: The blank must name an attitude that would cause someone to leave
solution.description: Read the sentence for the causal link it states, since the blank has to be the attitude that produced the decision to drop out.

solution.operation: Test each choice against "consistent with a decision to drop out"
solution.result: Only disaffection with and estrangement from survive
solution.description: Eliminate the choices that do not name an attitude compatible with leaving the school, keeping the two that do.

solution.operation: Check that the two survivors produce sentences nearly alike in meaning
solution.result: disaffection with and estrangement from form the required pair
solution.description: Confirm the pair requirement of this question type: substituting either word yields sentences with essentially the same meaning, so these two are the answer.

examples.answer: Choice A: disaffection with AND Choice F: estrangement from

key_reminders: This format needs two words that both fit the sentence and yield sentences alike in meaning
The clause "which resulted in his decision to drop out" is the constraint the blank must satisfy
A word that merely fits grammatically is wrong if no second choice matches its meaning
common_mistakes: Choosing disentanglement from as a partner for estrangement from on surface similarity, though it does not name the attitude that caused the decision to drop out
Selecting only one word when the question requires a pair of choices

concept.technique_name: subject-verb pair test for sentence fragments

examples.problem_statement: Answer (A) repeats the original sentence; choose the version with correct sentence structure. Original: The computer science instructor assigned a new textbook focused on recent advances in artificial intelligence. (A) The computer science instructor assigned a new textbook focused on recent advances in artificial intelligence. (B) A new textbook that is focused on recent advances in artificial intelligence assigned by our instructor.

solution.operation: In choice (A), locate the subject and its verb: subject = instructor, verb = assigned
solution.description: Check the original sentence first: pick out the noun doing the action and the working verb attached to it, and confirm they pair up.

solution.operation: In choice (B), locate every verb: the only verb is is, which sits inside the dependent clause that ... intelligence
solution.result: (B) has no main verb, so it is a fragment
solution.description: Scan the alternative for verbs. Its single verb is trapped in a dependent clause, which leaves the main clause verbless and makes the sentence a fragment.

solution.operation: Note the repair for (B): insert was before assigned, giving a textbook ... was assigned
solution.result: Adding was turns the modifier into a working verb, confirming (B) as written is broken
solution.description: Confirm the diagnosis by seeing what (B) would need: supplying was makes assigned a real main verb, which shows the printed version lacks one.

solution.operation: Select the choice that already has a main verb
solution.description: Since only (A) contains a complete subject-verb pair in the main clause, it is the correct answer.

key_reminders: Every complete sentence needs a subject paired with a main verb outside any dependent clause.
A verb inside a that-clause belongs to that clause and cannot serve as the sentence's main verb.
A past participle such as assigned is a modifier, not a verb, until a helping verb like was is added.
common_mistakes: Treating is in that is focused on recent advances as the sentence's main verb in choice (B).
Reading assigned by our instructor in (B) as a working verb phrase rather than a modifier of textbook.

concept.technique_name: sentence-clue matching for text completion blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. In his initial works, the playwright made physical disease (i) ______ factor in the action; from this, his early critics inferred that he had a predilection for focusing on (ii) ______ subject matter. Blank (i): A a pivotal, B a nonexistent, C an obscure. Blank (ii): D recondite, E uncomplicated, F morbid.

solution.operation: Interpret the phrase a predilection for focusing on: a writer with such a predilection makes that thing prominent in the work
solution.result: Blank (i) must mean prominent or significant
solution.description: Read the clue in the second half of the sentence. Because the critics infer a predilection, disease must have been made prominent, which fixes the meaning Blank (i) has to carry.

solution.operation: Match prominent or significant against A a pivotal, B a nonexistent, C an obscure
solution.description: Test each Blank (i) option against the required meaning; only pivotal expresses prominence, so it is selected.

solution.operation: Determine what Blank (ii) must describe: the subject matter of physical disease
solution.result: Blank (ii) needs a word characterizing disease as subject matter
solution.description: Identify the referent for the second blank. The critics are characterizing the playwright's focus on physical disease, so the word must describe that content.

solution.operation: Match that requirement against D recondite, E uncomplicated, F morbid
solution.description: Compare the Blank (ii) options to a description of disease as subject matter; morbid is the choice that fits.

examples.answer: Choice A: a pivotal; Choice F: morbid

key_reminders: The word for a blank must be supported by an explicit clue elsewhere in the sentence.
A predilection for focusing on something implies that thing is prominent in the work.
Each blank is answered from its own column of choices.
common_mistakes: Choosing B a nonexistent for Blank (i), which contradicts the critics' inference that the playwright dwelt on disease.
Choosing D recondite for Blank (ii) by matching the tone of obscure rather than the actual subject matter, physical disease.

concept.technique_name: Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya sutra for rational-to-quadratic equations

examples.problem_statement: Using the Quadratic Equations via Vedic Mathematics technique (Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya sutra, which gives two routes to the roots based on numerator-denominator relationships), solve \frac{3x+6}{6x+3} = \frac{5x+4}{2x+7} and state both roots.

solution.result: A rational equation that reduces to a quadratic
solution.description: Label the two numerators and two denominators so the sutra's conditions can be tested; recognise the equation as a rational one that simplifies to a quadratic.
Add the numerators and add the denominators; they come out equal, so the first condition of the sutra is satisfied and its shortcut applies.
Because the sums are equal, the sutra lets you set that common sum to zero; solving the resulting linear equation delivers the first root immediately.

solution.operation: Apply the second condition: N_1 - D_1 = N_2 - D_2 = 0
solution.result: A second equation supplied by the sutra
solution.description: Move to the sutra's other route: form the numerator-minus-denominator differences and set them to zero to obtain the remaining root.
Subtract the first denominator from the first numerator and set the difference to zero, then solve the linear equation for x.
Repeat the subtraction on the second fraction as a check; it yields the same value, confirming the second root.

solution.operation: Collect the roots from both routes: x = -\frac{5}{4}, \; x = 1
solution.description: Gather the results of the two conditions and confirm they are consistent, giving both roots of the quadratic.

examples.answer: The two roots are x = -5/4 and x = 1, found using Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya sutra with conditions N1+N2 = D1+D2 and N1-D1 = N2-D2.

key_reminders: Sunyam Sam Samuchchaya: when N_1+N_2 equals D_1+D_2, that common sum may be set to zero to give a root.
The second route applies when N_1-D_1 equals N_2-D_2; setting that difference to zero gives the other root.
Both conditions must be verified on the actual expressions before the shortcut is used.
common_mistakes: Cross-multiplying and expanding the quadratic instead of noticing that N_1+N_2 and D_1+D_2 are both 8x+10.
Sign slips when forming (3x+6)-(6x+3) = -3x+3, which flips the root away from x = 1.

concept.technique_name: out-of-order blank filling using logical connectors

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. Repression of painful memories is sometimes called “willed forgetting.” Yet true forgetting is (i) ______ than the phenomenon of repressed memory. In spite of the effort that it (ii) ______, repressing unwanted memories is less (iii) ______ than truly forgetting them, for repressed memories are prone to come back. Blank (i): A less controlled, B different in its effect, C far more common. Blank (ii): D eases, E conveys, F entails. Blank (iii): G permanent, H arduous, I immediate.

solution.operation: Start with Blank (iii): the word for indicates that repressed memories are prone to come back is the basis of the comparison
solution.result: Blank (iii) must relate to the tendency of memories to come back
solution.description: Do not work left to right. The connector for marks the final clause as the evidence for the third blank, so tackle that blank first.

solution.operation: Test G permanent, H arduous, I immediate against the tendency to come back
solution.description: Compare each Blank (iii) option with the stated evidence; only permanent bears on whether memories return, so it is selected.

solution.operation: Work backward to Blank (ii): the clause opens with In spite of, so the blank must set up an expectation contrary to what follows
solution.result: Blank (ii) must express that repressing costs effort, since effort would ordinarily make something more permanent
solution.description: Use the concessive opener. In spite of demands that the blank create an expectation the sentence then overturns, and one expects effort to yield more permanence, not less.

solution.operation: Test D eases, E conveys, F entails against that requirement
solution.description: Eliminate the Blank (ii) options that set up no such expectation; neither eases nor conveys does, leaving entails.

solution.operation: With blanks (ii) and (iii) filled, evaluate Blank (i) options A less controlled, B different in its effect, C far more common against the completed text
solution.result: Choice B, different in its effect
solution.description: Return to the first blank last. Nothing in the finished text supports more common or less controlled, but the text does establish that true forgetting differs in effect by being more permanent.

examples.answer: Choice B: different in its effect; Choice F: entails; Choice G: permanent

key_reminders: Fill the blank with the strongest textual clue first, not necessarily the first blank.
The connector for introduces the reason or evidence supporting the preceding claim.
In spite of signals that the expectation set up by the clause is about to be reversed.
common_mistakes: Choosing C far more common for Blank (i), a comparison the passage never supports.
Choosing H arduous for Blank (iii), which repeats the effort idea already carried by Blank (ii) instead of matching the come-back evidence.
Choosing D eases for Blank (ii), which removes the effort that In spite of requires.

concept.technique_name: testing with suitable numerical values (AP and GP sums with common endpoints)

examples.problem_statement: A = a + A_1 + A_2 + \dots + A_N + b and B = a + G_1 + G_2 + \dots + G_N + b. A is the sum of n + 2 terms of an A.P. with first term a and last term b. B is the sum of n + 2 terms of a G.P. with first term a and last term b. What can be said about the relative values of A and B?

solution.operation: Choose a concrete G.P. with 6 terms: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32
solution.description: Instead of arguing in general, pick suitable values: fix a G.P. whose first and last terms will serve as the shared endpoints a and b.

solution.operation: Build the A.P. on the same endpoints: 1, 7.2, 13.4, 19.6, 25.8, 32
solution.description: Construct an A.P. with the same number of terms and the same first and last terms, so the two sums are compared on equal footing.
Add up the six A.P. terms to get the value of A for this instance.
Add up the six G.P. terms to get the value of B for the same endpoints.
Set the two sums side by side; the A.P. sum exceeds the G.P. sum, which settles the relative values.

key_reminders: For a 'compare in general' question with no constraint on a and b, a well-chosen concrete pair of sequences is enough to fix the relation.
The two sequences must share the same number of terms and the same first and last terms, or the comparison is not valid.
An A.P. is pinned down by its endpoints and term count via the common difference d = (b - a)/(n + 1).
common_mistakes: Picking an A.P. with a convenient whole-number difference instead of one that actually ends at 32, so the two sums no longer share endpoints.
Counting the terms wrongly: both sums here have n + 2 = 6 terms, including a and b themselves.

concept.technique_name: parity rules applied statement by statement

examples.problem_statement: If x is odd, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) x + 3 is even. (B) 2x is odd. (C) 3x + 1 is odd.

solution.result: \text{one fact to test against each of (A), (B), (C)}
solution.description: The problem supplies only the parity of x, so each statement has to be checked against that single fact.
Adding 3 to an odd value always lands on an even value, as the sample values confirm, so keep (A).
Multiplying any integer by an even number produces an even result, so 2x cannot be odd and (B) is eliminated.
Multiplying an odd integer by 3 keeps it odd, and adding 1 to an odd value makes it even, so 3x + 1 cannot be odd and (C) is eliminated.

key_reminders: odd + odd = even, so an odd x plus 3 is always even.
Any integer times an even number is even, whatever the parity of the integer.
odd times odd is odd, and odd + 1 is even.
common_mistakes: Reading 2x as odd because x is odd, forgetting that the even factor 2 decides the parity.
Stopping after 3x is odd in (C) and not carrying out the '+ 1', which flips the parity to even.

concept.technique_name: distance-rate-time applied leg by leg, then compared with a hypothetical trip

examples.problem_statement: Claudette travels the first 2/3 of a 60-mile trip at 20 miles per hour (mph) and the remainder of the trip at 30 mph. How many minutes later would she have arrived if she had completed the entire trip at 20 mph?

solution.description: Find the length of the first leg by taking two-thirds of the total 60-mile distance.
Divide the first leg's distance by its 20 mph rate to get the time spent on that leg, converted to minutes.
Subtract the first leg from the total to get the remaining distance travelled at the faster rate.
Divide the second leg's distance by its 30 mph rate to get the time spent on that leg, in minutes.
Add the two leg times to get the total duration of the trip as actually travelled.
Now price the hypothetical trip: cover the whole 60 miles at 20 mph to get its duration in minutes.
Subtract the real trip's time from the hypothetical one to see how much later she would have arrived.

key_reminders: time = distance / rate, applied separately to each leg because the rate changes partway.
Total time for a multi-rate trip is the sum of the leg times, never the distance divided by an averaged rate.
The question asks for minutes, so convert each hour figure (2 h, 2/3 h, 3 h) before comparing.
common_mistakes: Averaging 20 and 30 to 25 mph and computing 60/25, which ignores that more distance is covered at the slower rate.
Splitting the 60 miles into two 30-mile halves instead of the 2/3 and 1/3 split the problem specifies.
Reporting the hypothetical trip's 180 minutes rather than the 20-minute difference the question asks for.

concept.technique_name: geometric progression common ratio

examples.problem_statement: Preliminary screening: a first look at the series should be enough to give the next term. Find the missing term. 4, -8, 16, -32, 64, ?

solution.description: Divide each term by the one before it; every quotient is the same, so the series advances by multiplying by -2 each time.
Apply that multiplier to the last given term, 64, to produce the next term. Note the book prints this next term as -132, which is a typo for -128; the answer key is preserved as printed.

key_reminders: In this series each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by -2.
A constant ratio (not a constant difference) is what preliminary screening is looking for here.
common_mistakes: Reading the pattern as 'double and alternate signs' but forgetting to carry the sign, giving +128 instead of a negative next term.
Treating the jumps 4, -8, 16 as differences rather than as a multiplication by -2.

concept.technique_name: base method multiplication (cross-addition with surplus product)

examples.problem_statement: Base 100, both numbers above the base. Solve: 102 x 103 = ?

solution.description: Write each number against the base 100 and record how much it exceeds the base.
Cross-add: add one number to the other number's surplus. Either crossing gives the same value, which is the left-hand part of the answer.
Multiply the two surpluses to get the right-hand part, then pad it to two digits because the base 100 carries two zeros.
Write the cross-addition result beside the padded surplus product to read off the final answer.

key_reminders: Both cross-additions (102+3 and 103+2) must agree; that agreement is the built-in check.
The right-hand part carries as many digits as the base has zeros, so 6 is written as 06.
common_mistakes: Writing the surplus product as a single digit and reporting 1056 instead of 10506.
Adding the two surpluses (2+3) to 100 in some other order instead of cross-adding a full number to the other's surplus.

concept.technique_name: weighted total from a rate table

examples.problem_statement: Various food-grains are sold by farmers at the prices per kg shown in the table. Farmer A: Rice 30, Corn 22.5, Bajra 22, Paddy 24, Jowar 18. If farmer A sells 350 kg of Rice, 150 kg of Corn and 250 kg of Jowar, how much would he earn?

solution.result: farmer A's per-kg rates for the three grains asked about
solution.description: Read farmer A's row of the table and pull only the three rates the question uses, ignoring Bajra and Paddy.
Multiply the rice quantity by farmer A's rice rate to get the earnings from rice.
Multiply the corn quantity by the corn rate of 22.5 to get the earnings from corn.
Multiply the jowar quantity by the jowar rate to get the earnings from jowar.
Add the three grain-wise earnings to get farmer A's total earnings.
Match the total against the choices; 18375 is listed as option (d).

key_reminders: Earnings for each grain = quantity sold times that farmer's per-kg rate for that grain.
Use only farmer A's row; each farmer has a different price list.
Total earnings is the sum of the grain-wise products.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong row of the table (farmer B's 36 for rice) and getting a much larger total.
Mishandling the decimal rate 22.5 for corn, e.g. computing 150 x 22 = 3300 and landing on a different option.

concept.technique_name: consecutive integer algebra

examples.problem_statement: The sum of four consecutive integers is -2. Quantity A: The smallest of the four integers. Quantity B: -2. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: an equation in one variable x, where x is the smallest integer
solution.description: Let x stand for the smallest of the four consecutive integers, so the next three are x+1, x+2 and x+3, and write their sum as equal to -2.
Combine the four x terms into 4x and add the constants 1+2+3 to get 6, collapsing the left side into a single linear expression.
Subtract 6 from both sides so the x term stands alone.
Divide both sides by 4 to solve for the smallest integer.

solution.result: the smallest integer is -2, which equals Quantity B
solution.description: List the four integers from x = -2 and compare the smallest of them against Quantity B; both are -2, so the quantities are equal.

key_reminders: Four consecutive integers can be written x, x+1, x+2, x+3 with x the smallest.
The constants of consecutive terms add to a fixed offset (here 1+2+3 = 6) that must be removed before dividing.
Quantity A asks for the smallest integer, which is exactly the variable x that was solved for.
common_mistakes: Letting x be the largest or a middle integer, which makes x = -2 the wrong member of the set.
Dividing the sum -2 by 4 directly and treating -0.5 as the smallest integer, ignoring the +6 offset.
Sign slips when subtracting 6 from -2, giving 4x = 4 instead of 4x = -8.

concept.technique_name: average correction via sum adjustment

examples.problem_statement: The average of 10 integers is found to be 10. But after the calculation, it was detected that, by mistake, the integer 20 was copied as 30, while calculating the average. After the due correction is made, the new average will be:

solution.description: Recover the wrong total by multiplying the reported average of 10 by the 10 integers it was taken over.
Correct that total by removing the value 30 that was wrongly copied in and adding back the true value 20.
Divide the corrected total by the same count of 10 integers to get the new average.

key_reminders: Sum = average times count, so a reported average can always be turned back into a total.
A miscopied entry changes only the sum; the count of 10 integers stays the same.
Undo the error by subtracting the wrong value and adding the correct one to the total.
common_mistakes: Adding 30 and subtracting 20, moving the average to 11 instead of 9.
Adjusting the average directly by 10 instead of adjusting the sum by 10 and then dividing by 10.
Changing the divisor from 10 as though an entry had been removed rather than miscopied.

concept.technique_name: grouping inference from a filled group

examples.problem_statement: Six doctors - Haddad, Johnson, Kwong, Lester, Murray, and Nelson - are assigned to the following three training rotations: orthopedics, pediatrics, surgery. Each doctor is assigned to exactly one rotation, and each rotation is assigned exactly two doctors. No other doctors are assigned. The following conditions must be met: Kwong is not assigned to the same rotation as Lester. Murray is not assigned to surgery. If Lester is assigned to orthopedics, then Haddad is assigned to surgery. Johnson is assigned to surgery. Question: If Kwong is assigned to surgery, each of the following could be true EXCEPT: (A) Murray is assigned to pediatrics. (B) Haddad is assigned to orthopedics. (C) Lester is assigned to orthopedics. (D) Nelson is assigned to pediatrics. (E) Nelson is assigned to orthopedics.

solution.operation: rephrase "each of the following could be true EXCEPT" as "which one must be false?"
solution.result: the task is to find the single answer choice that is impossible
solution.description: Rewrite the EXCEPT stem so you are hunting for the one choice that cannot happen, rather than checking four choices for possibility.

solution.operation: place J and K into the surgery group
solution.result: S = \{J, K\}, a full group of two
solution.description: Combine the standing rule that Johnson is in surgery with the question's new condition that Kwong is in surgery; since each rotation takes exactly two doctors, surgery is now closed to anyone else.

solution.operation: test L in O: L \rightarrow H \text{ in } S, \text{ but } S = \{J, K\}
solution.result: contradiction - there is no room in surgery for Haddad
solution.description: Try putting Lester in orthopedics; the conditional rule then forces Haddad into surgery, but surgery is already full, so this placement breaks the setup.

solution.result: choice (C) is the statement that must be false
solution.description: Because that placement is impossible, the choice asserting Lester is assigned to orthopedics is the one that cannot be true, which is what the EXCEPT stem asks for.

key_reminders: An EXCEPT question of the form "each could be true EXCEPT" is asking which single statement must be false.
Each rotation holds exactly two doctors, so a group with two names in it is closed.
A conditional rule is violated when its trigger is satisfied but its result has nowhere to go.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that Johnson is already in surgery, so Kwong's assignment fills the group rather than leaving a seat open.
Reading the conditional backwards and testing Haddad in orthopedics (choice B) instead of Lester in orthopedics.
Answering with a choice that merely could be false, such as a Nelson placement, instead of the one that must be false.

concept.technique_name: number line scaling
concept.sub_category: number line placement and tick-mark intervals

examples.problem_statement: Place 40 on the number line printed in the book (the line's tick marks are labeled).

solution.operation: Read consecutive labeled tick marks left to right and take their difference: each step = 10
solution.result: The tick marks ascend by increments of 10
solution.description: Compare neighbouring labels on the printed line to find the constant spacing between tick marks, which fixes the scale of the line.

solution.result: 40 sits two tick marks to the right of 20
solution.description: Divide the gap between 40 and the labeled 20 by the increment found in step 1 to count how many tick marks to move right from 20.

examples.answer: Two tick marks to the right of 20

key_reminders: Tick marks on a number line are evenly spaced, so one increment is the difference between consecutive labels.
Values increase from left to right, so a larger number lies to the right of a labeled point.
common_mistakes: Assuming each tick mark is worth 1 instead of reading the printed increment of 10, which would put 40 twenty marks past 20.
Counting from 0 rather than from the labeled 20, giving four tick marks instead of two.

concept.technique_name: cylinder volume formula

examples.problem_statement: What is the height of a right circular cylinder with radius 1 and volume 16\pi?

solution.result: The relation linking volume, radius and height
solution.description: Write down the volume formula for a right circular cylinder, the single relation that connects the two given values to the unknown height.
Substitute the given volume 16\pi and radius 1 into the formula, so the only remaining unknown is h.
Divide both sides by \pi, which cancels since the radius squared is 1, leaving the height directly.

key_reminders: The volume of a right circular cylinder is V = \pi r^2 h.
Squaring the radius comes before multiplying by the height; here 1^2 = 1, so the radius contributes nothing.
\pi appears on both sides and cancels, so no decimal approximation is needed.
common_mistakes: Dropping \pi from only one side and reporting h = 16\pi.
Using the lateral surface area 2\pi r h instead of the volume formula, which would give h = 8.

concept.technique_name: pick numbers with sign analysis

examples.problem_statement: a < b < 0 < c < d. Quantity A: abc. Quantity B: c - d. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: From a < b < 0 < c < d, mark a and b negative and c and d positive
solution.result: Two negative variables and two positive variables, possibly fractions
solution.description: Read the sign of each variable off the inequality chain before picking anything, since the signs are what the comparison will turn on.

solution.operation: Pick integers a = -2, b = -1, c = 1, d = 2: (-2)(-1)(1) = 2 versus 1 - 2 = -1
solution.result: 2 > -1, so Quantity A is greater in this case; eliminate (B) and (C)
solution.description: Start with an easy integer set obeying the ordering and evaluate both quantities, using the one result to knock out the choices that claim B is greater or the two are equal.

solution.operation: Test extremes that push Quantity B up: a = -2, b = -1, c = 100, d = 101, giving (-2)(-1)(100) = 200 versus 100 - 101 = -1
solution.description: Maximize c while keeping d only just above it, so that c - d is as large as it can get, and check whether that is enough to overturn the first case.

solution.operation: Consider minimizing a and b: their product is positive, so a smaller (more negative) a or b enlarges abc
solution.result: Shrinking a or b cannot reduce abc; abc is always positive
solution.description: Rule out the remaining lever on Quantity A by noting that two negatives multiply to a positive, so pushing a and b down only makes abc bigger, never smaller.

solution.operation: Since c and d are positive with d > c, the difference c - d is negative; fractions do not change these relationships
solution.result: Quantity A is always positive and Quantity B always negative, so A is greater
solution.description: Close the argument in general: a positive quantity always beats a negative one, and swapping integers for fractions preserves the signs, so the choice holds for every legal set of values.

key_reminders: The product of two negatives and one positive is positive, so abc > 0 throughout.
If d > c and both are positive, then c - d is negative.
One counterexample eliminates a choice, but a general sign argument is what confirms (A) over (D).
common_mistakes: Stopping after the single test set -2, -1, 1, 2 and choosing (D) on the grounds that only one case was checked.
Reading Quantity B as d - c and making it positive, which would flip the comparison.
Assuming fractional values between -1 and 0 could make abc negative, when the two negative factors still multiply to a positive.

concept.technique_name: inference from a stated definition

examples.problem_statement:
For each of Questions 1 to 9, select one answer choice unless otherwise instructed. Based on the passage about grassland mammals: It can be inferred from the passage that in animals less intelligent than the mammals discussed in the passage
A past experience is less helpful in ensuring survival
B attention is more highly focused
C muscular coordination is less highly developed
D there is less need for competition among species
E environment is more important in establishing the proper ratio of prey to predator

solution.operation: Locate the author's definition of intelligence in lines 18-20
solution.result: Intelligence is defined in terms of an animal's use of past experience
solution.description: Find the place where the passage says what intelligence means, because the question asks about animals ranked by intelligence and the definition is the hinge of the inference.

solution.operation: Invert the definition for the less intelligent case: more intelligent animals use past experience better to survive, so less intelligent ones use it less well
solution.result: Choice A, past experience is less helpful in ensuring survival, follows from the passage
solution.description: Apply the definition in the direction the question asks, reading down the intelligence scale from the grassland mammals to less intelligent animals to reach the supported inference.

solution.operation: Check choice B against the second paragraph
solution.result: B is incorrect: the passage says attention is more highly focused in animals of greater intelligence, not less
solution.description: Test the one distractor the passage actually speaks to, and reject it because the passage states the opposite direction of the relationship.

solution.operation: Check choices C, D and E for textual support
solution.result: C, D and E are incorrect: muscular coordination is never discussed as an element of intelligence, no claim is made about less need for competition, and how a prey-to-predator ratio is established is never discussed
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining options by confirming the passage says nothing on their subjects, since an inference must rest on something the author actually wrote.

examples.answer: Choice A: past experience is less helpful in ensuring survival

key_reminders: An inference must follow from what the passage states, not from outside knowledge about animals.
When the passage defines a term, apply that definition rather than the everyday meaning.
A choice on a topic the passage never raises cannot be the supported inference.
common_mistakes: Picking B by remembering that the passage discusses focused attention while missing that it attributes this to more intelligent animals.
Picking C because less developed muscular coordination sounds plausible for simpler animals, though the passage never links it to intelligence.

concept.technique_name: pivot-word context analysis

examples.problem_statement: Churchill conceded that Russia, (i) _________ an ally of France and Great Britain, was in fact (ii) _________ to their security, but argued that Russian national interest would compel it to make (iii) _________ with those countries. Blank (i): steadfastly / nominally / sporadically. Blank (ii): pledged / indifferent / immune. Blank (iii): common cause / rack and ruin / vim and vigor.

solution.operation: Read the pivot phrase "in fact" joining the first two blanks
solution.result: Russia did not show the concern for French and British security that an ally would be expected to show
solution.description: Locate the phrase "in fact" and use it to set the direction of the sentence: it flags that Russia's real stance falls short of what its ally status implies.

solution.operation: For blank (i), require a word describing an ally that is not fully committed
solution.description: Choose the blank (i) word from the requirement set in step 1 - the word must qualify "ally" as incomplete, and "nominally" does exactly that by making the alliance one of name alone.

solution.operation: For blank (ii), require a word meaning "not concerned"
solution.description: Fill blank (ii) with the word matching the meaning "not concerned": "indifferent" says Russia did not really care about their security.

solution.operation: Read the "but" that introduces the final clause
solution.result: Churchill argued Russia would nevertheless act as an ally, for its own national reasons
solution.description: Use the contrast word "but" to reverse direction for the last clause: despite the indifference just established, Russia is predicted to behave as an ally.

solution.operation: For blank (iii), require an idiom meaning "to act as an ally"
solution.description: Select the blank (iii) phrase that carries the acting-as-an-ally meaning established in step 4 - to make common cause is to act as an ally.

key_reminders: "In fact" signals that the reality contradicts the label just applied.
"But" reverses the direction of the clause it introduces.
"Nominally" means in name only; "to make common cause" means to act as an ally.
common_mistakes: Choosing "steadfastly" for blank (i), which agrees with "ally" instead of setting up the contrast that "in fact" demands.
Reading the final "but" as continuing the indifference, which pushes blank (iii) toward a hostile phrase rather than an allied one.

concept.technique_name: plugging in values to test a comparison
concept.sub_category: Quantitative Comparison with a linear equation

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B, given x + y = -1. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: y. Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: x = 0, y = -1, so x is greater than y
solution.description: Plug an easy value into one variable and read off the other: setting x to 0 forces y to -1, and this pair makes Quantity A the larger one.

solution.result: y = 0, x = -1, so y is greater than x
solution.description: Repeat the plug-in with the roles swapped: setting y to 0 forces x to -1, and now Quantity B is the larger one.

solution.result: y expressed directly in terms of x
solution.description: Solve the constraint for y so that any chosen x immediately gives its matching y, which makes further testing quicker.

solution.result: y < 0, so x is greater than y for every positive x
solution.description: Read the rewritten equation for positive x: the minus sign in front of x drives y below zero, so Quantity A wins on this whole range.

solution.result: y > 0, so y is greater than x on that range
solution.description: Read the same equation for x below -1: now -x - 1 comes out positive, so Quantity B wins on this range.

solution.operation: Compare the two ranges of outcomes found in steps 4 and 5
solution.result: Both orderings occur among pairs satisfying the equation, so no fixed relationship exists
solution.description: Collect the conflicting results: because some valid pairs make x larger and others make y larger, the comparison cannot be settled from the given information.

examples.answer: Choice D: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

key_reminders: A single equation in two variables leaves infinitely many valid pairs, so one test case never settles a comparison.
Two test cases that give opposite orderings are enough to prove the relationship cannot be determined.
Solving for one variable (y = -x - 1) makes it easy to scan whole ranges of x at once.
common_mistakes: Stopping after the single pair x = 0, y = -1 and concluding Quantity A is greater.
Testing only positive values of x, which hides the x < -1 range where y becomes greater.

concept.technique_name: picking numbers in a formula

examples.problem_statement: The cost of a certain commodity is expressed by the formula tb^4, where t and b are both greater than 0. If b is doubled, by what factor will the cost of the commodity increase? (A) 2 (B) 6 (C) 8 (D) 16

solution.result: a concrete starting value for b
solution.description: Pick an easy number for the variable being doubled so the two costs can be compared numerically rather than symbolically.
Evaluate the cost formula at the picked value: with b = 1 the fourth power contributes nothing and the cost is just t.
