solution.result: A reduced number carrying the information about the remaining middle digit
solution.description: Strip out the contribution already accounted for by R, then drop the trailing zero the subtraction leaves behind.

solution.operation: Form 3R^2M and choose M so that the unit digit of 3R^2M matches the relevant digit of the subtraction result
solution.result: The middle digit M of the cube root is fixed
solution.description: Match unit digits in the expression 3R^2M, which is the term that carries M into that digit position, to pin M down.

solution.operation: Write L, M and R side by side in that order
solution.description: Assemble the digits found in steps 2, 3 and 5 into their place-value positions to state the final root.

examples.answer: Example 5: Cube root of 84604519 = 439; Example 6: Cube root of 279726264 has R=4 (incomplete solution in this chunk)

key_reminders: Group digits in threes from the right: one group yields one digit of the cube root.
The unit digit of a perfect cube determines the unit digit R of its root uniquely (Table 1).
The leading digit L comes from the largest cube below the leftmost group (Table 2).
common_mistakes: Grouping the digits in threes from the left instead of from the right, which misplaces the leading group and so gives the wrong L.
Forgetting to drop the trailing zero after subtracting R^3, which shifts the digit compared against 3R^2M and yields the wrong M.

concept.technique_name: sentence logic via clue-word direction matching

examples.problem_statement: The (i) ______ of Vladimir Nabokov as one of North America's literary giants has thrown the spotlight on his peripheral activities and has thus served to (ii) ______ his efforts as an amateur entomologist. Blank (i): A stigmatization, B lionization, C marginalization. Blank (ii): D foreground, E transcend, F obscure.

solution.operation: Reduce the sentence to its claim: something that happened to Nabokov has called attention to some of his peripheral activities.
solution.result: Both blanks must carry a 'calling attention to' direction.
solution.description: Strip the sentence to its core assertion first, so that each blank can be judged against a single directional requirement rather than against the vocabulary in isolation.

solution.operation: Test blank (i): reject 'stigmatization' and 'marginalization' because each represents a turning away from him, not a calling attention to him.
solution.result: Choice B, lionization, survives, since to lionize means to treat as important.
solution.description: Eliminate the two blank (i) options whose direction is away from attention; the remaining word is the one that matches the attention-calling direction the sentence requires.

solution.operation: Use the given fact that Nabokov is a literary giant to classify entomology as one of his peripheral activities, then fill blank (ii) with a word meaning 'call attention to'.
solution.description: Identify which activity the spotlight falls on, then pick the blank (ii) word whose meaning matches the spotlight relationship the sentence has already set up.

solution.operation: Check the rejected blank (ii) options: spotlighting something would not result in transcending it or obscuring it.
solution.result: E and F are ruled out, confirming B and D.
solution.description: Confirm the choice by testing the two discarded words against the spotlight image, so the answer rests on elimination as well as on selection.

examples.answer: Choice B: lionization; Choice D: foreground

key_reminders: Either blank may be the starting point; begin with whichever one the sentence's own logic pins down.
The connective 'and has thus served to' forces both blanks to point in the same direction.
A word is correct only if it matches the sentence's direction, not merely its topic.
common_mistakes: Reading 'peripheral activities' as a negative cue and choosing marginalization for blank (i).
Choosing 'obscure' for blank (ii) because entomology is peripheral, ignoring that the spotlight clause reverses that direction.

concept.technique_name: ordering powers by substituting small natural numbers

examples.problem_statement: If A = n^{(2n)^n}, B = n^{n^{2n}}, C = (n^{2n})^n and D = (n^n)^{n^2}, where n is a natural number and n \neq 1, arrange A, B, C and D in terms of their values.

solution.description: Substitute the smallest permitted value of n into A and B and reduce each tower to a single power of 2; the two agree, so equality is possible between them.
Do the same substitution for C and D at n = 2; these two also collapse to the same power, so equality is possible between them as well.

solution.result: B > A > D > C at n = 3
solution.description: Move to the next value of n to break the ties; with a common base of 3 the four expressions are ranked simply by comparing their exponents.

solution.operation: Verify that the same ranking holds for n = 4 and merge it with the n = 2 equalities.
solution.description: Confirm the n = 3 pattern persists at n = 4, then combine it with the equalities found at n = 2 so the equal signs appear only where the n = 2 case demands them.

key_reminders: Powers of the same base are ordered by comparing their exponents alone.
A tower must be collapsed from the top down before the exponents can be compared.
Equalities at one value of n and strict inequalities at larger n combine into a \geq relation.
common_mistakes: Testing only n = 2, where A = B and C = D, and concluding all four are pairwise equal.
Reading A as n^{2n \cdot n} instead of collapsing (2n)^n first, which changes the ranking.

concept.technique_name: part : part : whole ratio with an unknown multiplier

examples.problem_statement: Laura established a new flower garden, planting 4 tulip plants to every 1 rose plant, and no other plants. If she planted a total of 50 plants in the garden, how many of those plants were tulips?

solution.description: Extend the given part-to-part ratio into a part : part : whole ratio by adding the two parts, since the question asks about a total rather than about roses.

solution.operation: Write the ratio with an unknown integer multiplier x:\ 4x : 1x : 5x
solution.description: Attach a common multiplier to every term so the ratio becomes actual plant counts that still sit in the required proportion.
Set the whole term equal to the 50 plants actually planted and solve for the multiplier, which is the single unknown linking the ratio to the real counts.
Substitute the multiplier back into the tulip term, since the question asks for tulips and not for the multiplier itself.

key_reminders: A part : part ratio becomes a part : part : whole ratio by summing the parts.
Every term of a ratio shares one unknown integer multiplier.
Solve for the multiplier first, then substitute it into the term the question asks about.
common_mistakes: Dividing 50 by 4 instead of by 5, using the tulip part in place of the whole.
Stopping at x = 10 and reporting the multiplier rather than 4x.

concept.technique_name: profit percentage on cost price versus on selling price

examples.problem_statement: A shopkeeper calculates percentage profit on the buying price and another on the selling price. What will be their difference in profits if both claim a profit of 20% on goods sold for ₹ 3000?

solution.result: buying price of the first shopkeeper is 2500
solution.description: For the shopkeeper who reckons profit on the buying price, a 20 percent mark-up on his cost must land on 3000, so divide the selling price 3000 by 1.20 to recover that cost.
Subtract the cost of 2500 just found from the selling price of 3000 to get the rupee profit the first shopkeeper actually makes.
The second shopkeeper takes his 20 percent directly on the selling price, so apply 20 percent to 3000 itself rather than to a cost.
Subtract the two rupee profits computed above to get the gap between the two ways of claiming the same 20 percent.

key_reminders: A 20 percent profit on the buying price means selling price = 1.2 \times cost, so cost = selling price / 1.2.
A 20 percent profit on the selling price is taken on 3000 itself, not on any cost.
The same stated percentage produces different rupee profits depending on which base it is applied to.
common_mistakes: Taking 20 percent of 3000 for both shopkeepers and concluding the difference is zero.
Subtracting 20 percent from 3000 (getting 2400) instead of dividing by 1.20 to find the first shopkeeper's cost.

concept.technique_name: weaken the conclusion by attacking the unstated assumption

examples.problem_statement: An anti-litter public service advertisement that shows many people littering may lead viewers to feel that littering is normal or accepted; the author concludes that an advertisement seeking to discourage a bad behavior should not show or discuss that behavior at all. Which of the following, if true, most undermines the argument's conclusion?

solution.operation: Isolate the premise: showing many people actively littering can make littering look normal or accepted.
solution.result: premise concerns ads in which many people engage in the bad behavior
solution.description: Read off what the argument actually offers as evidence, noting that the evidence is limited to ads depicting many people doing the behavior.

solution.operation: Isolate the conclusion: the bad behavior should not be shown or discussed at all in a discouraging ad.
solution.result: conclusion bans any depiction or mention of the behavior
solution.description: Separate the recommendation from the evidence, since the recommendation is far broader than the evidence that supports it.

solution.operation: Compare premise scope (many people) with conclusion scope (any mention) to name the assumption.
solution.result: assumption: any mention of the behavior is enough to make it seem normal or accepted
solution.description: Locate the gap the author leaps across, because a weakener must strike that gap rather than the evidence itself.

solution.operation: Test (A): a highly effective anti-smoking ad showed one person smoking amid a disapproving crowd.
solution.result: (A) shows an effective ad that did depict the discouraged behavior, so the assumption fails
solution.description: Apply the choice against the assumption named in step 3; because an effective ad featured the bad behavior, the blanket ban is undermined.

solution.operation: Check the remaining choices against the conclusion's actual claim about what not to do.
solution.result: (B), (C), (D) miss the conclusion's scope and (E) strengthens it
solution.description: Eliminate the rest: (B) concerns the most effective way to influence behavior, (C) concerns awareness that actors pretend, (D) concerns teenagers and rival methods, and (E) describes a best ad that avoids the behavior, which supports rather than weakens the author.

key_reminders: A weakener must attack the gap between premise and conclusion, not merely raise a related fact.
When the premise speaks of many people doing the behavior and the conclusion bans any mention of it, the scope shift is the assumption.
A choice that supports the author's recommendation is a strengthener and is wrong on a weaken question.
common_mistakes: Choosing (E), which describes an effective ad that avoids the behavior and therefore strengthens the author's blanket ban.
Choosing (B) or (D) because they discuss advertisement effectiveness, though the conclusion is about what should not be done rather than which method works best.

concept.technique_name: chain rule with direct and inverse proportion

examples.problem_statement: When wheat is Rs 1.30 per kg, 60 men can be fed for 15 days at a certain cost. How many men can be fed for 45 days at the same cost, when wheat is Re 1 per kg?

solution.description: Begin the chain with the given quantity of the same kind as the answer, namely the number of men, since the question asks for a number of men.

solution.result: factor \frac{15}{45} applied for the change in days
solution.description: Days rise from 15 to 45, and a longer feeding period at the same cost feeds fewer men, so attach the days fraction in its less-than-one orientation.

solution.result: factor \frac{1.30}{1} applied for the change in price
solution.description: The price falls from 1.30 to 1 per kg, and cheaper wheat at the same cost feeds more men, so attach the price fraction in its greater-than-one orientation.
Multiply the starting 60 by both fractions built above to obtain the number of men that can be fed.

key_reminders: Start the chain with the given value of the quantity being asked for.
More days at the same cost means fewer men, so the days factor is written as a fraction less than 1, here 15/45.
A lower price at the same cost means more men, so the price factor is written as a fraction greater than 1, here 1.30/1.
common_mistakes: Writing the days factor as 45/15 instead of 15/45, which inflates the answer instead of reducing it.
Writing the price factor as 1/1.30 because the price dropped, when the drop in price should raise the count of men.

concept.technique_name: sum of the first n odd numbers equals n squared

examples.problem_statement: What is the total of all the odd numbers from 1 to 51?

solution.result: there are 26 odd numbers in the range
solution.description: Count how many odd numbers the range holds by adding 1 to the last odd number 51 and halving the result.
Square that count of 26, since the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared.

key_reminders: The count of odd numbers from 1 to an odd n is (n + 1)/2.
The sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2.
common_mistakes: Squaring 51 rather than the count 26, since the formula squares how many odd numbers there are, not the last term.

concept.technique_name: rounding by the next-place digit

examples.problem_statement: x is a digit in the decimal 12.15x9, which, if rounded to the nearest hundredth, would equal 12.16. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 4. Choose whether Quantity A is greater, Quantity B is greater, the two quantities are equal, or the relationship cannot be determined.

solution.result: the digit that decides the rounding is x, sitting in the thousandths place
solution.description: Locate the hundredths digit (5) and see that the digit immediately to its right, which controls whether that 5 stays or rounds up, is x.
Because the decimal rounds up from 12.15 to 12.16, the thousandths digit x must be 5 or greater, leaving only the digits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.

solution.result: every allowed value of x exceeds 4, so Quantity A is greater
solution.description: Test each surviving possibility for x against Quantity B; since all of them are greater than 4, the comparison is settled in favour of Quantity A.

key_reminders: A decimal rounds up at a given place only when the digit immediately to its right is 5 or more.
Digits further right than the deciding digit (here the final 9) do not change the rounding decision.
A quantitative comparison is determined when every value allowed by the constraints falls on the same side.
common_mistakes: Letting the trailing 9 of 12.15x9 drive the rounding instead of x, the digit directly after the hundredths place.
Reading x \ge 5 as x > 5 and dropping the case x = 5.
Choosing (D) on the grounds that x is not a single fixed value, even though all admissible values give the same comparison.

concept.technique_name: sum of triangular numbers via series decomposition

examples.problem_statement: Find the sum of 20 terms of the series 3 + 6 + 10 + 15 + \ldots

solution.result: each given term is a running sum of consecutive integers, i.e. a triangular number
solution.description: Rewrite the listed terms as sums of consecutive integers to expose that the series is made of triangular numbers, just starting one step in.

solution.result: the required sum equals the sum of 21 terms of the full triangular series, less 1
solution.description: Prepend the missing first triangular number 1 so the series begins at its natural start, which adds one term, then subtract that 1 back out to keep the value unchanged.

solution.result: a closed form for the n-th term of the completed series
solution.description: Replace each bracketed run of consecutive integers with the standard formula for the sum of the first n integers, so the series can be summed term-formula-wise.
Add the closed-form terms over the 21 terms of the completed series to get the total the book reports for that extended sum.
Remove the 1 that was inserted in step 2 to return to the sum of the 20 terms actually asked for.

key_reminders: 1 + 2 + \ldots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
Adding a missing leading term to make a series regular is legitimate only if the same amount is subtracted back.
Padding the series to its natural start shifts the term count: 20 asked-for terms become 21 terms of the completed series.
common_mistakes: Summing 20 terms of the completed series instead of 21, forgetting that inserting the leading 1 shifted the index.
Adding the 1 back at the end instead of subtracting it.
Treating 3, 6, 10, 15 as an arithmetic progression because the first two gaps look regular, when the differences 3, 4, 5 are themselves increasing.

concept.technique_name: base-shift multiplication with correction row

examples.problem_statement: Approximation during multiplication is sensitive: a small change in the multiplier or multiplicand can badly skew the result, so the common trick of increasing one factor and decreasing the other should be avoided when the answer choices are close together. Find the approximate value of 384 \times 299. Choices: 1) 1,14,000  2) 1,15,000  3) 1,16,000

solution.result: the naive rounding lands on 114000, off by 816 from the true product
solution.description: Try the widely used shortcut of nudging one factor up and the other down first, and see that its answer deviates enough to pick the wrong choice when the options are close.

solution.result: each factor is split into a round base plus a small signed change
solution.description: Shift each factor to the nearest convenient multiple of ten and record the leftover as a signed correction, writing +4 under 380 and -1 under 300.

solution.result: a base product plus a cross-correction row
solution.description: Expand the product so the easy base term 380 \times 300 sits on the first row and the cross terms formed by the two corrections make the second row.
Evaluate the correction row roughly rather than exactly, discarding the tiny product of the two corrections, since only an approximate value is wanted.
Add the correction row to the base product from the first row to obtain the sharpened estimate.
Round the sharpened estimate to the nearest listed choice, which the naive method could not distinguish from 1,14,000.

key_reminders: Shift each factor to the nearest (highest possible) power of ten and carry the leftover as a signed correction.
(a + p)(b + q) = ab + pb + qa + pq, and the correction row pb + qa carries the deviation.
The correction row is meant to be estimated roughly; the pq term is small enough to neglect.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 380 \times 300 = 1,14,000 and picking choice 1, which is exactly the trap the deviation creates.
Getting the sign of the 299 correction wrong and adding 1 \times 380 instead of subtracting it, which pushes the estimate towards 1,16,000.
Computing the correction row exactly and losing the speed advantage the method exists for.

concept.technique_name: slope-intercept form and intercept plotting

examples.problem_statement: Which quadrants, if any, do not contain any points on the line represented by x - y = 18 ?

solution.description: Rewrite the given equation in slope-intercept form by solving for y, so the line's slope and y-intercept are visible.
Set x = 0 in the rewritten equation to find the y-intercept of the line.
Set y = 0 in the same equation to find the x-intercept of the line.

solution.operation: \text{plot } (0, -18) \text{ and } (18, 0), \text{ draw the line through them}
solution.result: a line rising through the fourth, first and third quadrants
solution.description: Plot the two intercepts on the coordinate plane and draw the line joining them, so you can see which regions it sweeps through.

solution.operation: \text{read off the quadrant the drawn line never enters}
solution.description: Inspect the drawn line and identify the quadrant it does not pass through.

key_reminders: Solving a linear equation for y puts it in slope-intercept form y = mx + b.
Setting x = 0 gives the y-intercept; setting y = 0 gives the x-intercept.
Two plotted points determine the line, and the drawn line shows which quadrants it occupies.
common_mistakes: Rearranging x - y = 18 as y = 18 - x (sign error on y), which flips the slope and points at the wrong empty quadrant.
Swapping the intercepts and plotting (-18, 0) and (0, 18) instead of (0, -18) and (18, 0).

concept.technique_name: Pythagorean triple plus rectangle area equality

examples.problem_statement: Rectangles ABCD and EFGH have equal areas. In the figure, right triangle ACD has hypotenuse AC = 10 and leg AD = 8, and rectangle EFGH has side EF = 12. What is the length of side FG?

solution.description: Use the right triangle ACD, whose two known sides make it a 6-8-10 Pythagorean triple (or apply the Pythagorean Theorem), to get the missing side CD.
Multiply the length AD by the width CD to get the area of rectangle ABCD.
Transfer the area you just computed to rectangle EFGH, since the problem states the two rectangles have equal areas.
Write the area of EFGH as its known side EF times the unknown side FG, setting it equal to 48.
Divide both sides by 12 to solve the equation for FG.

key_reminders: A right triangle with a leg of 8 and hypotenuse 10 is the 6-8-10 Pythagorean triple.
Area of a rectangle = length x width.
Equal areas let you carry a computed area from one figure straight into the other.
common_mistakes: Treating 10 as a leg and computing CD from 8 and 10 as legs instead of recognizing 10 as the hypotenuse.
Dividing 48 by 6 or 8 instead of by the given side EF = 12 when solving for FG.

concept.technique_name: successive percent change by picking 100

examples.problem_statement: If your stock portfolio increased by 25% and then decreased by 20%, what percent of the original value would your new stock portfolio have?

solution.description: Since no real starting amount is given, pick $100 as the original value of the portfolio.
Apply the 25% increase to the picked value: it grows by $25 to a new value of $125.
Apply the 20% decrease by multiplying the new value by 0.8, since dropping 20% is the same as keeping 80%.
Compare the final value to the value you started with to express the result as a percent of the original.
Check the same result algebraically by multiplying the two successive percent multipliers, which come to exactly 1.

key_reminders: When no real amount is specified in a percent problem, pick 100 for the starting value.
A decrease of 20% means multiplying by 100% - 20% = 80%, i.e. 0.8.
Successive percent changes multiply: Original x 1.25 x 0.80 = New.
common_mistakes: Adding and subtracting the percents (25% - 20% = 5%) instead of applying them successively.
Taking the 20% decrease off the original 100 rather than off the new value of 125.

concept.technique_name: locating a median by cumulative percent in grouped data
concept.sub_category: circle graph - median of grouped data

examples.problem_statement:
A circle graph separates 10 million unemployed manufacturing industry workers into five groups by length of unemployment in weeks, giving the percent of workers in each group: the 1-to-4 week group holds 40% of the workers and the next group, 5 to 10 weeks, holds 20%. Which of the following could be the median length of unemployment, in weeks, for manufacturing industry workers who were unemployed for at least 1 week?
(A) 4  (B) 8  (C) 12  (D) 16  (E) 20

solution.operation: 10{,}000{,}000 \text{ lengths, one per worker, grouped into five intervals with given percents}
solution.result: an ordered list of 10 million whole-number week lengths
solution.description: Read the circle graph as one unemployment length per worker, so the five sectors describe how 10 million rounded whole-number lengths split across the intervals.

solution.operation: \text{median} = \text{value at which } 50\% \text{ of the ordered lengths have been listed}
solution.description: Restate the median as the middle of the ordered list, that is, the point where 50% of the lengths have already been listed.
Start the ordered list with the shortest group, 1 to 4 weeks, which accounts for the first 40% of the lengths.

solution.result: the 50\% mark falls inside the 5-to-10 week group
solution.description: Add the next group, 5 to 10 weeks at 20%, which carries the cumulative count past the 50% mark, so the median sits in that interval.
Test each answer choice against the 5-to-10 week interval and keep the only one that lies inside it.

key_reminders: The median is the value at which 50% of the ordered data has been listed.
With grouped data you only need cumulative percents, not the individual values, to locate which interval contains the median.
Percents in a circle graph can be accumulated in order from the smallest interval upward.
common_mistakes: Choosing 4, the top of the 40% group, by stopping at the largest interval before the 50% mark is reached.
Averaging the interval midpoints or the answer choices instead of tracking the cumulative percent to 50%.

concept.technique_name: blank-by-blank clue matching in a three-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: The fact that the average life expectancy ten thousand years ago was so much shorter than it is now is often (i) ________ as evidence supporting the notion that the world always improves with time. However, if you (ii) _________ for the fact that most children in that epoch died in childbirth, it turns out that life expectancy back then was nearly the same as it is now. On a (iii) _________ note, it also turns out that many “barbaric” hunter-gatherer tribes were taller on average than the average person now living.

solution.operation: Blank (i): read the clause "shorter life expectancy ten thousand years ago ... as evidence supporting the notion that the world always improves with time"
solution.description: Begin with blank (i), where a fact about life expectancy is being related to the claim that the world improves with time; because longer life expectancy today would genuinely support that claim, the fact is simply being put forward as evidence, so the plain reporting word cited fills the blank.

solution.operation: Blank (ii): apply the signal "However ... if you _____ for the fact that most children in that epoch died in childbirth"
solution.description: Handle blank (ii) by noticing that the sentence says the statistic is misleading once a new fact is taken into account; the blank therefore needs a verb meaning to adjust the figure for that new piece of information, which gives correct (correct for).

solution.operation: Blank (iii): compare the final sentence's topic (average height of hunter-gatherer tribes) with the preceding topic (life expectancy)
solution.description: For blank (iii), observe that the last sentence suddenly shifts from life expectancy to height, so the note is slightly off the main topic; choose tangential to mark that shift.

solution.operation: Check the blank (iii) distractor "sidereal" against its actual definition
solution.result: sidereal rejected: it means "related to the stars"
solution.description: Before committing to blank (iii), test the tempting look-alike sidereal: despite resembling "side," it has nothing to do with being off to the side and instead means related to the stars, so it cannot describe an off-topic remark.

key_reminders: Fill the blank whose clue is most explicit first; here blank (i) is anchored by the "evidence supporting" phrase.
A contrast signal such as "However" tells you the second blank must adjust or qualify the earlier statistic, not repeat it.
Match a word to its real definition, not to a familiar-looking root inside it.
common_mistakes: Choosing disregarded for blank (i), which reverses the logic — the fact is being used as evidence, not dismissed.
Picking sidereal for blank (iii) because it looks like "side," when it actually means related to the stars.
Reading the height sentence as contradicting the life-expectancy discussion rather than as a side note, and so wanting a contrast word instead of tangential.

concept.technique_name: blank-meaning prediction then synonym pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. At nearly 450 pages, the novel is ______ : the author does not often resist the temptation to finish off a chapter, section, or even paragraph with some unnecessary flourish. (A) instructive (B) complex (C) prolix (D) educational (E) long-winded (F) explicit

solution.operation: Read the clause after the colon and state what the blank must convey: the novel is not merely long, it is padded with unnecessary flourishes
solution.result: Target meaning for the blank: excessively long because of unnecessary material
solution.description: Use the colon clause as the definition of the blank. Because the author keeps adding unnecessary flourishes, the blank must combine length with superfluity, not length alone.

solution.operation: Test 'instructive' (A) and 'educational' (D) against that target meaning
solution.result: Both eliminated: they describe instructional value, not the novel's length
solution.description: Reject these two because, whatever the novel may teach, neither word properly describes the novel's length, which is what the sentence is characterizing.

solution.operation: Test 'complex' (B) and 'explicit' (F) against the target meaning and against the same-meaning requirement
solution.result: Both eliminated: they may correlate with length but do not characterize it, and they do not yield sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Reject these two because correlating with length is not the same as describing it, and pairing them would not produce two completed sentences that mean the same thing.

solution.result: Both mean needlessly wordy, so the two completed sentences are alike in meaning
solution.description: Confirm the surviving pair: each word carries the sense of length plus unnecessary wordiness demanded in step 1, and they are synonyms, satisfying the equivalence requirement.

examples.answer: Choice C: prolix; AND Choice E: long-winded

key_reminders: The blank must capture the whole idea signalled after the colon, here length plus unnecessary material, not just length.
Sentence Equivalence needs two words that both fit AND produce sentences alike in meaning.
A word that merely correlates with a quality does not characterize that quality.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'complex' because a 450-page novel sounds complex, though complexity is not what the colon clause describes.
Pairing the near-synonyms 'instructive' and 'educational' on synonymy alone, ignoring that they do not fit the sentence's meaning.

concept.technique_name: 4-step Critical Reasoning process for a Strengthen fill-in-the-blank

examples.problem_statement: Which of the following best completes the passage below? A nonprofit organization in Motor City has proposed that local college students be given the option to buy half-price monthly passes for the city's public transportation system. The nonprofit claims that this plan will reduce air pollution in Motor City while increasing profits for the city's public transportation system. However, this plan is unlikely to meet its goals, since ___________. (A) most college students in Motor City view public transportation as unsafe (B) most college students in Motor City view public transportation as prohibitively expensive (C) college students typically do not have the 9-to-5 schedules of most workers, and can thus be expected to ride public transportation at times when there are plenty of empty seats (D) a bus produces more air pollution per mile than does a car (E) a large proportion of the college students in Motor City live off campus

solution.operation: Identify the question: the blank at the end signals Fill in the Blank, and the word 'since' just before the blank signals a Strengthen question
solution.description: Classify the question first. 'Since' introduces a reason for the statement just made, so the right answer must support the author's claim rather than attack it.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument sentence by sentence: proposal (nonprofit offers half-price passes to college students) = fact; nonprofit's claim (less air pollution, more transit profit); final sentence 'this plan is unlikely to meet its goals' = the conclusion
solution.result: Conclusion: the plan will not work; the nonprofit's claim is a premise being attacked, not the conclusion
solution.description: Map the argument on paper and locate the conclusion, which in fill-in-the-blank questions sits in the final sentence. The nonprofit's claim is not labelled the conclusion for that reason.

solution.operation: State the goal: find the answer choice that gives a reason the half-price-pass plan will fail to cut pollution or raise profits
solution.result: Goal: support the author's belief that the plan will not work
solution.description: Fix the target before reading answers, so any choice that makes the plan more likely to succeed can be dismissed immediately as Reverse Logic.

solution.operation: Evaluate (A): most college students view public transportation as unsafe
solution.result: Keep: students would avoid transit even at a discount, so the plan is unlikely to succeed
solution.description: Test this choice against the goal. If students refuse to ride on safety grounds, cutting the price does not get them onto buses, which is exactly the support the author needs.

solution.operation: Evaluate (B): students view public transportation as prohibitively expensive
solution.result: Eliminate as Reverse Logic: a discount would then make them ride more, helping the plan
solution.description: Reject this choice because it identifies price as the barrier, and the plan removes half the price, so it strengthens the plan instead of undermining it.

solution.operation: Evaluate (C): students ride at off-peak times when there are plenty of empty seats
solution.result: Eliminate as Reverse Logic: filling currently empty seats is good news for transit profits
solution.description: Reject this choice because riders who fill otherwise-empty off-peak seats add revenue, supporting the profit goal rather than casting doubt on it.

solution.operation: Evaluate (D): a bus produces more air pollution per mile than a car
solution.result: Eliminate: the plan adds riders to already-running buses, and one bus can replace ten or more cars
solution.description: Reject this tempting choice by checking what the plan actually changes. No new buses are added, and per-mile comparison of one bus to one car ignores that a bus carries many car-loads of people.

solution.operation: Evaluate (E): a large proportion of students live off campus
solution.result: Eliminate as Reverse Logic: those students need transportation and might switch from cars to buses
solution.description: Reject this choice because off-campus students are precisely the ones who could shift out of cars, which would help both goals rather than hurt them.

key_reminders: 'Since' before the blank marks a Strengthen question: the answer supplies a reason for the preceding statement.
In fill-in-the-blank Critical Reasoning the conclusion is in the final sentence, not in a claim attributed to someone else.
Every problem in this set contains at least one Reverse Logic trap, an answer that helps the plan rather than hurting it.
common_mistakes: Treating the nonprofit's claim about pollution and profits as the conclusion instead of the author's 'unlikely to meet its goals'.
Falling for (D) by comparing one bus to one car, when the plan adds riders to buses already running.
Picking (B), (C), or (E), each of which supports the plan and so reverses the required direction.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal analysis with cross-blank synonym linkage

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. While many outside the company attributed the company's success to its president's (i) ______ , insiders realized that this success owed more to the president's inflexibility than to any (ii) ______ that the president might be supposed to have displayed. Blank (i): A perseverance, B popularity, C prescience. Blank (ii): D obduracy, E caprice, F foresight.

solution.operation: Read the second half of the sentence for its contrast: the actual cause of success is the negative quality 'inflexibility', set against the quality named by Blank (ii) that outsiders supposed to be the cause
solution.result: Blank (ii) must name a positive quality, contrasted with 'inflexibility'
solution.description: Extract the contrast the sentence sets up. 'Owed more to X than to any (ii)' pits the real, negative cause against a supposed one, so Blank (ii) has to be positive.

solution.operation: Scan the Blank (ii) choices for the only positive quality among obduracy, caprice, and foresight
solution.result: 'Foresight' (Choice F) is the sole positive quality
solution.description: Apply the positive-quality requirement to the second column. Obduracy and caprice both name unfavorable traits, leaving foresight as the only fit.

solution.operation: Use the sentence's structure, in which outsiders attributed success to Blank (i) and Blank (ii) names that same supposed quality, to find the Blank (i) choice synonymous with 'foresight'
solution.result: 'Prescience' (Choice C) is the synonym of foresight, unlike perseverance or popularity
solution.description: Match the first blank to the second. Since both blanks name the quality outsiders credited, Blank (i) must mean roughly what foresight means, and only prescience does.

examples.answer: Choice C: prescience; Choice F: foresight

key_reminders: 'Owed more to inflexibility than to any (ii)' signals a contrast between a negative actual cause and a positive supposed one.
When both blanks describe the same supposed quality, the two answers must be close in meaning.
Filter the second blank first when it carries the clearer signal, then use it to constrain the first.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'obduracy' for Blank (ii) because it echoes 'inflexibility', when the blank needs the contrasting positive quality.
Selecting 'perseverance' for Blank (i) as a plausible-sounding cause of success, without checking that it matches 'foresight'.

concept.technique_name: testing candidate blank combinations for a coherent statement

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The activists' energetic work in the service of both woman suffrage and the temperance movement in the late nineteenth century (i) ______ the assertion that the two movements were (ii) ______ . Blank (i): A undermines, B supports, C underscores. Blank (ii): D diffuse, E inimical, F predominant.

solution.operation: State what the sentence is doing: it reports what the activists' energetic work in both movements implies for some assertion about the relationship between those two movements
solution.result: Blank (i) is the implication verb; Blank (ii) fixes the content of the assertion, which is otherwise obscured
solution.description: Frame the sentence before choosing words. The two blanks are interdependent, since the verb in Blank (i) makes sense only once the assertion described by Blank (ii) is known.

solution.operation: Enumerate the two coherent readings: work in both movements could support an assertion that they were similar, or undermine an assertion that they were opposed
solution.result: Two candidate combinations, one requiring a 'similar' word in Blank (ii), the other requiring an 'opposed' word
solution.description: Reason from the evidence itself. People working energetically for both causes is evidence of compatibility, which either backs a similarity claim or damages an opposition claim.

solution.operation: Check Blank (ii) for a word meaning 'similar' or 'compatible' among diffuse, inimical, and predominant
solution.result: No such word exists, so 'supports' and the similar 'underscores' both fail
solution.description: Test the first candidate reading against the actual choices. Since nothing in the second column means similar or compatible, the supporting-verb route cannot be completed.

solution.operation: Take the remaining reading: pair 'undermines' (Choice A) with 'inimical' (Choice E), which means hostile or opposed
solution.result: 'Undermines' and 'inimical' make the only meaningful statement
solution.description: Complete the surviving combination. Evidence of activists serving both causes weakens an assertion that the movements were hostile to each other, which reads coherently, unlike the other pairings.

examples.answer: Choice A: undermines; Choice E: inimical

key_reminders: When one blank obscures the claim, generate the possible readings and test each against the available choices.
Evidence of shared participation in two movements bears on whether those movements were compatible or opposed.
If a first-blank choice has no partner in the second column, that whole reading is dead.
common_mistakes: Picking 'supports' or 'underscores' on the intuition that shared activism confirms a link, without checking that no Blank (ii) choice means 'similar'.
Treating 'underscores' and 'supports' as distinguishable here, when both fail for the same missing-partner reason.

concept.technique_name: lateral surface area of a cone via slant height

examples.problem_statement: Your friend’s cap is in the shape of a right circular cone of base radius 14 cm and height 26.5 cm. The approximate area of the sheet required to make 7 such caps is

solution.result: Sheet area for one cap = lateral surface area of the cone
solution.description: Identify that the sheet forms only the curved side of the cap, so the area needed for one cap is the cone's lateral surface area \pi r l, not the total surface area.
Combine the base radius 14 and the vertical height 26.5 with the Pythagorean relation to get the slant height l, which the area formula needs.
Round the slant height to 30, the approximation the book uses since the question asks only for an approximate area.
Multiply the one-cap lateral area by 7 to cover all seven caps, substituting r = 14 and the rounded l = 30.

key_reminders: Lateral (curved) surface area of a right circular cone is \pi r l.
The slant height l comes from r^2 + h^2 = l^2; it is not the given vertical height.
Scale the single-object area by the count only after the per-object area is fixed.
common_mistakes: Using the vertical height 26.5 directly in \pi r l instead of first computing the slant height 29.97.
Computing the area of one cap and forgetting the factor of 7.
Adding the base circle area \pi r^2, which a cap does not require.

concept.technique_name: unit conversion by multiplying conversion ratios so units cancel

examples.problem_statement: Joe’s car can travel 36 miles per gallon of fuel. Approximately how many kilometers can the car travel on 10 liters of fuel? (5 miles = approximately 8 kilometers; 1 gallon = approximately 4 liters)

solution.result: miles and gallons cancel, leaving kilometers per liter
solution.description: Write the given fuel economy against the two conversion ratios, orienting each ratio so that the miles unit and the gallons unit cancel and only km per L survives.
Carry out the arithmetic of that chain of ratios to get the car's fuel economy expressed in kilometers per liter.
Apply the converted rate to the 10 liters actually in the tank, since the question asks for distance rather than a rate.

key_reminders: Orient each conversion ratio so the unwanted unit appears once on top and once on the bottom and cancels.
Convert the rate fully before multiplying by the given quantity of fuel.
common_mistakes: Inverting a ratio, e.g. multiplying by 5/8 instead of 8/5, or by 4 liters per gallon instead of 1 gallon per 4 liters.
Stopping at 14.4 and reporting the rate instead of multiplying by the 10 liters.

concept.technique_name: successive percentage change via multiplying factors

examples.problem_statement: Abhimanyu Banerjee has 72% vision in his left eye and 68% vision in his right eye. On corrective therapy, he starts wearing contact lenses, which augment his vision by 15% in the left eye and 11% in the right eye. Find out the percentage of normal vision that he possesses after corrective therapy. (Assume that a person’s eyesight is a multiplicative construct of the eyesight’s of his left and right eyes)

solution.result: the single product that represents post-therapy vision
solution.description: Set up one product: each eye contributes its current vision as a decimal and each augmentation contributes a multiplier of 1 plus the percentage increase, because the problem states eyesight is a multiplicative construct.
Evaluate the left-eye pair, applying the 15% augmentation to the 72% base vision of the left eye.
Evaluate the right-eye pair, applying the 11% augmentation to the 68% base vision of the right eye.
Multiply the two corrected eye values together to combine them into overall vision, then read the decimal as a percentage of normal vision.

key_reminders: An increase of x% is applied as a multiplier of 1 + x/100, never by adding x to a percentage base.
Successive multiplicative effects compose by multiplying their factors in any order.
common_mistakes: Adding the augmentations to the base vision (72 + 15 and 68 + 11) instead of multiplying by 1.15 and 1.11.
Averaging the two eyes instead of multiplying them, despite the stated multiplicative construct.

concept.technique_name: causal assumption (negation test on correlation-to-causation)

examples.problem_statement:
Smoking is a known cause of certain serious health problems, including emphysema and lung cancer. Now, an additional concern can be added to the list of maladies caused by smoking. A recent study surveyed both smokers and nonsmokers, and found that smokers are significantly more anxious and nervous than nonsmokers. Which of the following is an assumption on which the argument rests?
(A) Anxiety and nervousness can lead to serious health problems.
(B) Anxiety and nervousness do not make individuals more likely to start smoking.
(C) Equivalent numbers of smokers and nonsmokers were surveyed for the study.
(D) Smokers are aware of the various health problems attributed to smoking, including lung cancer and emphysema.
(E) Smokers who had smoked a cigarette immediately before responding to the survey were more anxious and nervous than smokers who had not smoked for several hours.

solution.operation: Split the argument: premise = the survey shows smokers are more anxious than nonsmokers; conclusion = smoking causes anxiety and nervousness
solution.result: A premise that establishes only a correlation supporting a causal conclusion, A causes B
solution.description: Write the premise and the conclusion separately so the gap between them is visible: the study reports an association, while the conclusion asserts causation.

solution.operation: Apply the rule that an assumption behind a causal conclusion must protect the causal direction A \to B
solution.result: The needed assumption either rules out an alternate cause (C causes B) or rules out reversed causation (B causes A)
solution.description: Narrow the search to the two shapes an assumption can take in a causal argument, so the answer choices can be screened against them.

solution.operation: Test choice (B) by denying it: suppose anxiety and nervousness do make people more likely to start smoking
solution.result: Then B caused A, the anxiety preceded the smoking, and the conclusion that smoking causes the anxiety fails
solution.description: Negate the candidate and check whether the argument survives; here it collapses, which is exactly what marks (B) as a required assumption.

solution.operation: Check (A) and (D) against the conclusion's scope, which is only that smoking causes anxiety and nervousness
solution.result: Both are irrelevant: (A) concerns downstream effects of anxiety, (D) concerns smokers' awareness of health risks
solution.description: Discard choices that talk about consequences or beliefs the conclusion never claims anything about.

solution.operation: Check (C) and (E) against the same conclusion
solution.result: (C) is about the number of respondents, which the conclusion does not depend on; (E) compares some smokers to other smokers, a comparison the argument never makes
solution.description: Eliminate the remaining two by noting the mismatch between what each describes and what the argument actually rests on.

key_reminders: A survey showing that two things go together establishes correlation, not causation.
An assumption in a causal argument must preserve the direction of causation: it blocks either an alternate cause or the reverse direction.
A choice that lies outside the conclusion's scope cannot be a required assumption, however true it sounds.
common_mistakes: Choosing (A) by chaining anxiety onward to serious health problems, which strengthens the opening sentence rather than the argument's own conclusion.
Choosing (C) on the belief that a survey comparison needs equal group sizes, when the conclusion does not depend on the sample counts.
Missing the reverse-causation trap: anxious people may already be the ones who take up smoking.

concept.technique_name: ratio proportion with relative speed
concept.sub_category: Trains - two trains crossing each other

examples.problem_statement: The speeds of two trains are in the ratio 3 : 4. They are going in opposite directions along parallel tracks. If each takes 3 seconds to cross a telegraph post, find the time taken by the trains to cross each other completely?

solution.operation: Since each train crosses a telegraph post in the same 3 seconds, length = speed \times 3, so lengths are in the same ratio as speeds, 3 : 4
solution.result: Lengths can be written as 3x and 4x metres
solution.description: Convert the equal post-crossing times into a statement about lengths: with time fixed, length is proportional to speed, so the length ratio copies the speed ratio.

solution.operation: Recover the speeds from those lengths: \frac{3x}{3} and \frac{4x}{3}
solution.result: Speeds are x m/s and \frac{4x}{3} m/s
solution.description: Divide each assigned length by the 3-second post-crossing time to express both speeds in terms of the same x.

solution.operation: Because the trains move in opposite directions, add the speeds: x + \frac{4x}{3}
solution.description: Use the opposite-direction rule, where the speeds add, to get the single rate at which the gap between the trains closes.

solution.operation: Add the two lengths, since crossing completely means covering both: 3x + 4x
solution.description: Set the distance for a complete crossing equal to the sum of the two train lengths.
Apply time = distance / speed; the x cancels, so the unknown scale factor never has to be found.

solution.operation: Generalise with speed ratio a : b and lengths ax, bx: \frac{x(a+b)}{\frac{x(a+b)}{3}}
solution.result: 3 seconds for any ratio a : b
solution.description: Repeat the same division with a general ratio to see that the ratio cancels entirely, giving the quicker rule: when both trains take the same time to pass a post, they take that same time to cross each other.

key_reminders: Crossing a telegraph post means covering exactly the train's own length.
For a fixed crossing time, length is proportional to speed, so the length ratio equals the speed ratio.
Trains moving in opposite directions have relative speed equal to the sum of their speeds, and crossing each other means covering the sum of their lengths.
common_mistakes: Treating the 3 : 4 speed ratio as though the answer must depend on it, and hunting for a time other than 3 seconds.
Subtracting the speeds (the same-direction rule) instead of adding them for opposite directions.
Using only one train's length as the crossing distance rather than 3x + 4x.

concept.technique_name: term-by-term inequality comparison of products

examples.problem_statement:
The number line shows four positive variables ordered as 0 < a < b < c < d (the spacing shown is not stated to be even).
Quantity A: a \times c
Quantity B: b \times d
(A) Quantity A is greater.
(B) Quantity B is greater.
(C) The two quantities are equal.
(D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: Record what the figure actually gives: 0 < a < b < c < d
solution.result: All four variables are positive and strictly increasing in that order
solution.description: Extract the only usable information, the ordering and positivity of the four variables.

solution.operation: Note what is not given: the exact values, and whether the variables are evenly spaced
solution.result: No numeric values may be assumed, and even spacing may not be inferred from the figure's appearance
solution.description: Guard against reading extra structure out of the picture, since a figure that looks evenly spaced is not stated to be.

solution.operation: Pair the factors and compare term by term: a < b and c < d, with all terms positive, so a \times c < b \times d
solution.description: Multiply the two smaller numbers against the two larger ones; positivity is what licenses multiplying the inequalities in the same direction.

solution.operation: Sanity-check with real numbers: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, then a = 0.5, b = 7, c = 11, d = 45
solution.result: 1 \times 3 < 2 \times 4 and 0.5 \times 11 < 7 \times 45, in both the evenly and unevenly spaced cases
solution.description: Plug in one evenly spaced set and one deliberately uneven set to confirm the ordering holds regardless of spacing.

solution.operation: Conclude from the general argument, which covers every scenario meeting 0 < a < b < c < d
solution.description: Since the comparison was proved for all admissible values rather than just the test cases, the relationship is determined and (D) is ruled out.

key_reminders: Inequalities between positive numbers may be multiplied term by term in the same direction.
Never assume a number line's tick marks are evenly spaced unless the problem says so.
'Cannot be determined' applies only when some admissible set of values flips the comparison.
common_mistakes: Choosing (D) because a, b, c, d have no numeric values, even though the ordering alone settles the comparison.
Assuming even spacing from the figure and reasoning about differences such as c - a versus d - b instead of the products.
Forgetting the positivity condition, which is what makes the term-by-term multiplication valid.

concept.technique_name: counting terms of an arithmetic progression

examples.problem_statement: At Goli-Vadapav, an automatic machine makes vadapavs at 1 vadapav per half a minute, adding fillings as follows: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, ... vadapavs get a chicken patty; the 1st, 5th, 9th, ... get a vegetable patty; the 1st, 8th, 17th, ... get a mushroom patty; and the rest get plain cheese and tomato fillings. The machine makes exactly 500 vadapavs per day. How many vadapavs per day are made with cheese and tomato as fillings?

solution.description: Start from the daily output stated in the data: the machine makes exactly 500 vadapavs per day, which is the pool every filling is carved out of.
Count the terms of the odd-numbered chicken-patty series up to 499; that count, 250, is how many vadapavs are chicken-filled and therefore not plain.
Count the terms of the series 8, 22, 36, ... to get the 36 vadapavs that take a mushroom patty without already being counted among the chicken ones.
Subtract both filled groups from the daily total, leaving the vadapavs that received no patty at all and so got cheese and tomato.

key_reminders: The number of terms in an arithmetic series a, a+d, ..., L is (L-a)/d + 1.
Vadapavs that receive no patty from any of the listed series are exactly the ones with cheese and tomato.
Groups must be counted without double counting: only the mushroom vadapavs not already counted as chicken are subtracted.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the full mushroom series count instead of only the mushroom-only count, double counting positions that are already odd-numbered.
Treating the vegetable-patty series (1, 5, 9, ...) as a separate subtraction, though every one of its terms is odd and already inside the chicken count.

concept.technique_name: row scan for monotonic trend

examples.problem_statement: Study the following table of loans disbursed by 5 banks (Rupees in Crores) and answer the question below. Bank A: 1982 = 18, 1983 = 23, 1984 = 45, 1985 = 30, 1986 = 70. Bank B: 27, 33, 18, 41, 37. Bank C: 29, 29, 22, 17, 11. Bank D: 31, 16, 28, 32, 43. Bank E: 13, 19, 27, 34, 42. Total: 118, 120, 140, 154, 203. In which of the following banks did the disbursement of loans continuously increase over the years?

solution.description: Pull out the five yearly figures for bank E from the table so the year-on-year movement can be read off in one line.

solution.result: every year is higher than the one before it
solution.description: Compare each figure with the one to its left; each comparison holds, so the row rises without a single dip.

solution.operation: \text{match the continuously rising row to its option}
solution.description: Since E is the row whose values rise at every step, pick the answer choice naming bank E.

key_reminders: "Continuously increase" requires every consecutive year to be higher, not just the last year above the first.
A single dip anywhere in a row disqualifies that bank.
common_mistakes: Choosing bank A because it ends far higher (18 to 70) while ignoring the drop from 45 in 1984 to 30 in 1985.
Choosing bank D on its overall rise while ignoring the fall from 31 to 16 between 1982 and 1983.

concept.technique_name: vertical angles and angles on a straight line

examples.problem_statement: In the figure, angles b, c, and d lie along a straight line, and angles c and f are vertical angles. If c + f = 70, and d = 80, what is b?

solution.result: c and f have equal measure
solution.description: Recognise that c and f are vertical angles, which lets you treat their two measures as one unknown.
Replace f by c in the given sum and halve it, giving the individual measure of each of the two equal angles.
Write the straight-line relation for b, c, and d, then substitute the value of c just found and the given d.
Solve the straight-line equation for b by subtracting the two known angle measures from 180.

key_reminders: Vertical angles are equal in measure.
Angles that together form a straight line sum to 180 degrees.
common_mistakes: Using 70 directly as c instead of splitting the given sum of the two equal vertical angles into 35 each.
Setting b + c + d equal to 90 or 360 rather than the 180 degrees of a straight line.

concept.technique_name: testing answer choices for full determination in a hybrid ordering-grouping game

examples.problem_statement: A photographer will take three photographs of a high school math team. The seven members of the team - P, R, S, T, V, W, and X - will each appear in exactly one of the photographs. There will be exactly one member in the first photograph, three members in the second photograph, and three members in the third photograph. The following conditions apply: P does not appear in a later photo than does T or X. R and S will appear in the same photograph together. V and X will not be photographed together. Which of the following pairs of assignments would determine the team members for each photograph?

solution.operation: \text{list what the correct answer must settle: place the RS chunk, arrange P, T, X, and keep V apart from X}
solution.result: three jobs the winning pair of assignments has to finish
solution.description: Before testing choices, note everything that must be pinned down, so a choice that leaves any of these open can be dropped fast.

solution.operation: \text{(A) V in Photo 1, R in Photo 2}
solution.description: This fixes V and the chunk, and forces T and X into group 3 since neither may precede P; but groups 2 and 3 each keep one open slot that W or P could fill either way.

solution.operation: \text{(B) V in Photo 1, R in Photo 3}
solution.description: This forces P into group 2, yet group 3's remaining place could still go to T, X, or W, leaving the arrangement even less settled than (A).

solution.operation: \text{(C) P in Photo 1, R in Photo 2}
solution.description: This locks in P and the chunk and, by requiring V and X to be split between groups 2 and 3, forces T and W into group 3; but V and X remain interchangeable.

solution.operation: \text{(D) P in Photo 1, V in Photo 3}
solution.description: This places P, X, and V in groups 1, 2, and 3, but nothing here says where the RS chunk goes, so the photographs are not settled.

solution.operation: \text{(E) W in Photo 1, R in Photo 2} \Rightarrow X \text{ barred from group 2}
solution.result: V in group 2; P, T, X form group 3 - fully determined
solution.description: This locks the chunk into group 2 with W alone in group 1; since X cannot come before P it cannot take group 2's last slot, so V goes there and P, T, and X fill group 3, settling every photograph.

key_reminders: R and S must occupy the same photograph, so they move as a single two-person chunk.
P may not appear later than T or X, which bars X from any group ahead of P.
V and X can never share a photograph, so they must be split across the two three-member groups.
common_mistakes: Accepting a choice like (A) or (C) that fixes most placements while two members stay interchangeable, since "determine" demands a single complete arrangement.
Forgetting to apply the P-before-X restriction when filling the last open slot in group 2, which is exactly what settles choice (E).

concept.technique_name: cube surface area to side to volume

examples.problem_statement: A perfect cube has surface area 96. What is its volume?

solution.description: Write the cube's surface area as 6 times the area of one face, since all six faces of a cube are identical squares.
Set the surface-area formula equal to the given 96 and divide both sides by 6 to isolate the squared side.
Take the square root of 16 to get the edge length of the cube.
Cube the edge length just found, because the volume of a cube is the side raised to the third power.

key_reminders: Surface area of a cube = 6(side)^2, since all faces are congruent squares.
Volume of a cube = (side)^3.
Solve for the side first; it is the bridge between surface area and volume.
common_mistakes: Dividing 96 by 6 and stopping at 16, reporting the face area instead of taking its square root to get the side 4.
Cubing the surface area or the face area rather than the edge length of 4.

concept.technique_name: percent change

examples.problem_statement: Tae Yang has a stack of $20 bills totaling $1,600 and a stack of $10 bills totaling $1,050. (Assume that all bills have the same thickness.) Quantity A: The percent by which the height of the stack of $10 bills is greater than that of the stack of $20 bills. Quantity B: 33.5%. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: comparing heights reduces to comparing bill counts
solution.description: Note that all bills have the same thickness, so the percent difference in stack height equals the percent difference in the number of bills.
Divide the $1,600 total by the $20 denomination to count the bills in the taller-denomination stack.
Divide the $1,050 total by the $10 denomination to count the bills in the other stack.
Plug the two counts into the percent change formula, using the $20 stack as the base since Quantity A asks how much greater the $10 stack is than it.

solution.result: Quantity A is less than Quantity B
solution.description: Convert the decimal to a percent and compare it with Quantity B, which is the larger of the two.

key_reminders: Equal-thickness bills mean stack height is proportional to bill count, not to dollar value.
Percent change = (new - original) / original, with the quantity being compared against as the base.
Convert the decimal result to a percent before comparing it with a percent quantity.
common_mistakes: Comparing the dollar totals 1,600 and 1,050 directly, since the larger dollar total belongs to the shorter stack.
Dividing by 105 instead of 80, which uses the $10 stack as the base rather than the $20 stack named in Quantity A.
Reading 0.3125 as 3.125% or 0.3125% instead of 31.25%, which flips the comparison against 33.5%.

concept.technique_name: in-sentence definition and contrast clues

examples.problem_statement: Freud's structural model of the psyche should be understood as (i) _________ device, useful for inciting and guiding discovery, rather than as an attempt to (ii) _________ physical relationships among parts of the human brain. Blank (i): a heuristic / a hermeneutic / an allegorical. Blank (ii): dictate / ameliorate / represent.

solution.operation: isolate the appositive defining blank (i): "device, useful for inciting and guiding discovery"
solution.result: blank (i) needs a word meaning "aiding discovery"
solution.description: Notice that the sentence itself defines the first blank, so read the phrase that follows it as the definition the answer must match.

solution.operation: match "useful for inciting and guiding discovery" to the blank (i) choices
solution.description: Select the choice whose meaning is precisely that definition; heuristic means exactly a device that aids discovery.

solution.operation: read "rather than as an attempt to (ii) ___ physical relationships"
solution.result: blank (ii) needs a word meaning "show" or "depict"
solution.description: Use the contrast: the model is not to be taken as a guide to the brain's physical structure, so the second blank must be a verb about depicting those relationships.

solution.operation: match "show" or "depict" to the blank (ii) choices
solution.description: Pick the choice closest to that meaning; represent is the nearest of dictate, ameliorate, and represent.

key_reminders: When a sentence supplies its own definition of a blank, the answer is the word that definition names.
"Rather than" signals a contrast, so build the second blank from what the model is being denied.
Predict a plain-English word before looking at the choices, then take the closest match.
common_mistakes: Choosing hermeneutic for blank (i) because it also sounds scholarly, though it concerns interpretation rather than aiding discovery.
Choosing dictate for blank (ii), which asserts control over the brain's structure rather than depicting it.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal inference

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for the blank from the column of choices, filling it in the way that best completes the text. Early studies often concluded that the public was ______ the propagandistic influence of mass communications, but one recent study indicates that, on the contrary, mass communications seldom produce marked changes in social attitudes or actions.

solution.operation: Locate the contrast signals "but" and "on the contrary" joining the two clauses
solution.result: The recent study's finding is opposed to what the early studies concluded
solution.description: Read the connectives that link the two halves of the sentence; they tell you the early studies and the recent study point in opposite directions, so the blank must oppose the recent finding.

solution.operation: State what the recent study found: mass communications "seldom produce marked changes in social attitudes or actions"
solution.result: The recent study found the effect of mass communications on the public to be negligible
solution.description: Paraphrase the second clause on its own terms, so you have a fixed meaning to reverse in the next step.

solution.operation: Reverse the recent finding to recover what the early studies must have concluded
solution.result: The early studies found the influence of mass communications significant, so the blank must say the public is swayed by such communications
solution.description: Because the contrast makes the earlier conclusion the opposite of the recent one, flip "negligible effect" to "significant influence" and let that fix the meaning required in the blank.

solution.operation: Test each choice against the required meaning "swayed by"
solution.result: "unaware of" and "unimpressed by" state the opposite; "scornful of" and "coping with" both indicate resistance to mass communications
solution.description: Eliminate every option that fails the required meaning: two choices assert the opposite outcome and two more assert resistance rather than susceptibility.

solution.operation: Keep the only choice that expresses being swayed: "susceptible to"
solution.description: Of the five options, only this one makes the early studies say the public was influenced, matching the meaning the contrast demands.

key_reminders: "but" and "on the contrary" force the blank to oppose the clause that follows.
A word indicating resistance or indifference cannot fill a blank that requires being influenced.
common_mistakes: Filling the blank with "unaware of" or "unimpressed by", which echo the recent study instead of contradicting it.
Reading "scornful of" as merely negative and missing that scorn implies resistance to the influence, not susceptibility to it.

concept.technique_name: arithmetic sequence jump counting

examples.problem_statement: If each number of a sequence is 4 more than the previous number, and the 3rd number in the sequence is 13, what is the 114th number in the sequence?

solution.description: Count the jumps that separate the known 3rd term from the 114th term; subtracting the term positions gives the number of steps taken, not the number of terms.
Multiply the jump count by the size of each jump, since every step adds 4, to get the total increase from the 3rd term to the 114th.
Add that total increase to the value of the 3rd term to land on the value of the 114th term.

key_reminders: The number of jumps between two terms is the difference of their positions, not the count of terms.
Total change equals number of jumps times the common difference.
common_mistakes: Using 114 jumps instead of 111, which treats the 1st term rather than the 3rd as the starting point.
Multiplying 114 by 4 and ignoring that the given value 13 already sits at position 3.

concept.technique_name: similarity-signal inference

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Ever a demanding reader of the fiction of others, the novelist Chase was likewise often the object of ______ analyses by his contemporaries.

solution.operation: Register the word "likewise" linking the two halves of the sentence
solution.result: The analyses his contemporaries made of Chase were like the readings Chase gave the fiction of others
solution.description: Identify the similarity signal; it tells you the blank must echo, not oppose, how Chase himself read.

solution.operation: Take the description of Chase as a "demanding reader" as the meaning the blank must match
solution.result: The blank calls for a word similar in meaning to "demanding"
solution.description: Carry the phrase describing Chase across the "likewise" link to set the target meaning for the blank.

solution.operation: Check which choices are close in meaning to "demanding"
solution.result: "exacting" (Choice A) and "meticulous" (Choice F) meet the requirement and produce sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Scan the options for words that carry the sense of demanding rigor, and confirm the pair yields two completed sentences that mean the same thing.

solution.result: They mean close to the same thing as each other, but both differ sharply from "demanding", so neither fits the blank
solution.description: Reject a pair that satisfies the alike-in-meaning requirement alone; a pair must also fit the sentence's own meaning, and harshness is not rigor.
Commit to the two words that both match "demanding" and produce equivalent sentences.

examples.answer: Choice A: exacting; AND Choice F: meticulous

key_reminders: "likewise" makes the blank parallel the earlier description rather than contrast with it.
A correct pair must both fit the sentence and produce completed sentences alike in meaning.
common_mistakes: Choosing "acerbic" and "scathing" because they are synonyms of each other, ignoring that they do not match "demanding".
Reading "demanding reader" as harsh criticism rather than rigorous attention.

concept.technique_name: elimination by sentence logic plus alike-in-meaning pairing

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Parkin's characterization of the movement as neoscholastic is too ______ to be accepted without further investigation.

solution.operation: Read what the sentence asks of the blank: the characterization is too ______ to be accepted without further investigation
solution.result: The blank must name a quality that makes further investigation necessary
solution.description: Fix the logical requirement first, so each option can be tested against a single criterion.

solution.result: Both are rejected: if the characterization is too complete or too self-evident, there is nothing further to investigate
solution.description: Discard the two words that would remove the need for investigation instead of creating it, contradicting the sentence.

solution.result: Rejected: a characterization that is detailed but not flawed gives no reason to investigate further
solution.description: Eliminate the word that describes thoroughness without any defect, since thoroughness alone does not prompt further scrutiny.

solution.result: Rejected: it does suggest further investigation is necessary, but no other choice produces a sentence alike in meaning to pair with it
solution.description: Reject a word that passes the meaning test but fails the pairing requirement, because this question type needs two words yielding equivalent sentences.
Select the two surviving words, which are alike in meaning and make the characterization too superficial to accept unexamined.

examples.answer: Choice A: cursory; AND Choice C: perfunctory

key_reminders: "too ______ to be accepted without further investigation" requires a quality that creates doubt, not one that settles the matter.
A word that fits the sentence still fails if no second choice produces a sentence alike in meaning.
common_mistakes: Selecting "biased" because it plausibly justifies further investigation, despite it having no alike-in-meaning partner among the choices.
Choosing "detailed" or "complete", which would make further investigation unnecessary rather than necessary.

concept.technique_name: fragment detection via missing main verb
concept.sub_category: Sentence Structure - subject/verb and participial modifiers

examples.problem_statement: Multiple choice with one correct answer; answer (A) repeats the original sentence, and only two choices are offered. Watch for sentence-structure issues. Sentence: "Some of the earliest computer games designed to involve many players at once and first developed before the widespread availability of high-speed internet connections." (A) Some of the earliest computer games designed to involve many players at once and first developed before the widespread availability of high-speed internet connections. (B) First developed before the widespread availability of high-speed internet connections, some of the earliest computer games were designed to involve many players at once.

solution.operation: Search choice (A) for a conjugated main verb
solution.result: the only verb-like words found are designed and developed
solution.description: Read the original sentence hunting for a working verb attached to the subject; the book points to designed and developed as the only candidates.

solution.operation: Classify designed and developed as participles, not verbs
solution.result: both are modifiers that only masquerade as verbs
solution.description: Test the two candidates: the book identifies them as participles, so they modify the subject rather than serve as its verb.

solution.operation: Conclude (A) has no main verb at all
solution.description: With every verb candidate ruled out as a modifier, the book declares the sentence verbless and therefore a fragment, so (A) is wrong.

solution.operation: Check choice (B) for the missing main verb
solution.result: (B) supplies the main verb were designed
solution.description: Look at the alternative: the book notes (B) fixes the mistake by turning the participle into the main verb were designed, giving the sentence a complete core.

key_reminders: A participle such as designed or developed is a modifier, not a main verb.
A sentence with no main verb is a fragment, no matter how long it is.
The fix for a verbless sentence is to convert one participle into a working verb (were designed).
common_mistakes: Reading designed and developed as the sentence's verbs because they follow the subject directly.
Being reassured by the sentence's length and the and joining the two participles, and so missing that nothing predicates the subject.

concept.technique_name: logical-clue text completion across linked blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. "The reason minimum temperatures are going up more rapidly than maximums may involve cloud cover and evaporative cooling. Clouds tend to keep the days cooler by reflecting sunlight, and the nights warmer by (i) ______ loss of heat from Earth's surface. Greater amounts of moisture in the soil from additional precipitation and cloudiness (ii) ______ the daytime temperature increases because part of the solar energy is (iii) ______ the evaporation of that moisture." Blank (i): A inhibiting, B exacerbating, C replicating. Blank (ii): D augment, E mask, F restrain. Blank (iii): G intensified by, H unrelated to, I used up in.

solution.operation: Read the second sentence: clouds make nights warmer by acting on heat loss
solution.result: Blank (i) needs a word meaning preventing or slowing heat loss, so inhibiting
solution.description: Follow the book's logic that less heat lost means more warmth, so the blank must slow heat loss; exacerbating means the opposite and replicating makes no sense here.

solution.operation: Use the first sentence: daytime highs rise less rapidly than nighttime lows
solution.result: Blank (ii) needs a verb of moderation, so restrain
